**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 12, verses 1–2:**

(Surat Yusuf: one hundred and eleven verses, Meccan)

(In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful)

﴿Alif-Lam-Ra. These are the verses of the Clear Book.﴾ ﴿Indeed, We have sent it down as an Arabic Qur'an, that you may understand.﴾ ﴿We relate to you the best of stories, by what We have revealed to you of this Qur'an, though before it you were certainly among the unaware.﴾ [Yusuf: 3] ﴿When Joseph said to his father, "O my father, indeed I saw eleven stars and the sun and the moon; I saw them prostrating to me."﴾ [Yusuf: 4] ﴿He said, "O my son, do not relate your vision to your brothers, lest they plot against you a scheme. Indeed, Satan is to man a clear enemy."﴾ [Yusuf: 5] ﴿And thus your Lord will choose you and teach you the interpretation of events, and complete His favor upon you and upon the family of Jacob, just as He completed it upon your two forefathers before, Abraham and Isaac. Indeed, your Lord is Knowing and Wise.﴾ [Yusuf: 6] ﴿Certainly there were in Joseph and his brothers signs for those who ask.﴾ [Yusuf: 7] ﴿When they said, "Joseph and his brother are more beloved to our father than we, while we are a group. Indeed, our father is in manifest error."﴾ [Yusuf: 8] ﴿"Kill Joseph or throw him out to some land, so that your father's face will be clear for you, and you will be a righteous people after him."﴾ [Yusuf: 9] ﴿A speaker among them said, "Do not kill Joseph, but throw him into the bottom of the well; some travelers will pick him up, if you are going to act."﴾ [Yusuf: 10] ﴿They said, "O our father, what is wrong with you that you do not entrust us with Joseph, though we are indeed his sincere advisers?"﴾ [Yusuf: 11] ﴿"Send him with us tomorrow to enjoy himself and play, and indeed we will be his guardians."﴾ [Yusuf: 12] ﴿He said, "Indeed, it grieves me that you take him away, and I fear that the wolf will devour him while you are heedless of him."﴾ [Yusuf: 13] ﴿They said, "If the wolf devours him while we are a group, then indeed we would be losers."﴾ [Yusuf: 14] ﴿So when they took him away and agreed to put him at the bottom of the well, and We revealed to him, "You will certainly inform them of this affair of theirs while they do not perceive."﴾ [Yusuf: 15] ﴿And they came to their father in the evening, weeping.﴾ [Yusuf: 16] ﴿They said, "O our father, indeed we went racing and left Joseph with our belongings, and the wolf devoured him. But you will not believe us, even if we are truthful."﴾ [Yusuf: 17] ﴿And they brought his shirt stained with false blood. He said, "Rather, your souls have made a matter seem fine to you. So patience is beautiful, and Allah is the One sought for help against what you describe."﴾ [Yusuf: 18] ﴿And a caravan came, and they sent their water-drawer, and he let down his bucket. He said, "Good news! This is a boy!" And they concealed him as merchandise, while Allah was Knowing of what they did.﴾ [Yusuf: 19] ﴿And they sold him for a low price, a few counted dirhams, and they were of those who had no desire for him.﴾ [Yusuf: 20] ﴿And the one who bought him from Egypt said to his wife, "Make his residence honorable; perhaps he will benefit us, or we may adopt him as a son." And thus We established Joseph in the land, and that We might teach him the interpretation of events. And Allah is dominant over His affair, but most of the people do not know.﴾ [Yusuf: 21] ﴿And when he reached his maturity, We gave him judgment and knowledge. And thus We reward the doers of good.﴾ [Yusuf: 22] ﴿And she in whose house he was sought to seduce him from himself, and she closed the doors and said, "Come, you." He said, "I seek refuge in Allah. Indeed, he is my lord who has made my residence good. Indeed, the wrongdoers will not succeed."﴾ [Yusuf: 23] ﴿And she certainly desired him, and he would have desired her had he not seen the proof of his Lord. Thus [it was], that We might turn away from him evil and immorality. Indeed, he was of Our chosen servants.﴾ [Yusuf: 24] ﴿And they raced to the door, and she tore his shirt from behind, and they found her husband at the door. She said, "What is the penalty for one who intended harm to your wife, except that he be imprisoned or suffer a painful punishment?"﴾ [Yusuf: 25]

(p-276) Al-Tarh (الطَّرْح) for a thing is throwing it and casting it away. One says "taraha ʿalayhi al-thawb" (he cast the garment upon him), and "taraḥtu al-shay'" (I removed the thing far away). From this is the saying of ʿUrwah ibn al-Ward:

"Whoever is like me, with dependents and in want of wealth, will cast himself into every place (matrah)."

And al-Naww (النَّوى) means distant, far places (al-ṭurūḥ al-baʿīdah). Al-Jubb (الجُبّ) is the uncovered well (al-rakiyyah allatī lam tuṭw), and when it is lined with stone, it becomes a bi'r (well). Al-Aʿsha said:

"Even if you were in a well eighty cubits deep, and you were raised by the ladder of the heavens' paths."

It is plural as jubab, jibab, and ajbab. It was called jubb because it was cut into the earth, from jabbabtu, meaning I cut. Al-Iltiqat (الِالتِقاط) is taking up a thing from the road. One says laqatahu and iltaqatahu. Someone said: "A watering place (manhal) I picked up by pickings (iltiqatan)." From this come al-luqatah (lost property) and al-laqīt (foundling).

Irtaʿā (ارْتَعى) is from the root "ra'y" (افْتَعَلَ مِنَ الرَّعْيِ) in the sense of protection (al-murāʿāh), which is safeguarding a thing; or from ra'y, which is the eating of grass and plants. One says: "the livestock grazed the pasture (raʿat al-māshiyatu al-kalaʾ), grazing it (tarʿāhu ruʿyan), eating it." Al-Ruʿy with a kasrah is pasture, and irtaʿā is similar. Al-Aʿsha said:

"They graze the slope, then the sand dune, then the dhāt qār, then the meadow of the sand-grouse, then the dhāt al-rimāl."

Rataʿa (رَتَعَ): he stayed in abundance and luxury. From this is the saying of al-Ghadban ibn al-Qabʿthara: "the fetter, the enjoyment, and the scarcity of luxury." And the words of the poet:

"Do you disbelieve after the death was turned away from me, and after your gift of the hundred rita'an (luxurious camels)?"

Al-Dhiʾb (الذِّئْب) is a well-known predator, and it is not found in our Andalusian region. Its plurals are adhʾub, dhiʾab, and dhuʾbān. He said:

"A man with a sharp gaze who stretches through distant lands, whose wolves and foxes howl around him."

And ardun madhʾabah means a land with many wolves. Tadhāʾabat al-rīḥ means the wind came from here and from there, like the action of a wolf. From the same root is al-dhuʾābah (the forelock of hair), because it sways here and there. Al-Kadb (الكَدْب) with a dal (ḍ/d) of the unpointed letter (الدّالِ المُهْمَلَة) means turbidity, and it was said to mean freshness. Sawwala (سَوَّلَ) is from al-sawal, and its meaning is to make easy, and it was said to mean to adorn.

Adlā al-dalw (أدْلى الدَّلْوَ) means he sent the bucket to fill it. Dallāhā yadlūhā means he drew it up and brought it out of the well. He said: "Do not tie them, and draw them as a bucket (dalwan)." Al-Dahr (the time/age) is well known, and it is feminine, so its diminutive is duleyyah. It is plural as adlun, dilāʾ, and duliyy.

Al-Biḍāʿah (البِضاعَة) is a portion of wealth set aside for trade, from baḍaʿtuhu, when you cut it. From this is al-mibḍaʿ (the scalpel). Al-Murāwadah (المُراوَدَة) is seeking gently with softness of speech. Al-Rawd (الرَّوْد) is patience. One says "arwidnī" (give me time). Al-Riyādah is seeking marriage. "Mashā ruwaydan" means walking gently.

He closed the door and locked it and bolted it, with the same meaning. Al-Farazdaq said:

"I kept closing doors and opening them, until I came to Abu ʿAmr ibn ʿAmmar."

Hayta (هَيْتَ) is an imperative verb (ism fiʿl) meaning "hasten." Qadda al-thawb means he tore the garment. Al-Sayyid (السَّيِّد) is on the pattern fayʿil from sāda yasūdu. It is applied to the owner and to the chief of a people. Fayʿil is a pattern specific to the defective root (المُعْتَلّ). Irregular forms are baytis and sayqal, which is the name of a woman. Al-Sijn (السِّجْن) is confinement.

﴿Alif-Lam-Ra. These are the verses of the Clear Book.﴾ ﴿Indeed, We have sent it down as an Arabic Qur'an, that you may understand.﴾ This surah is entirely Meccan. Ibn ʿAbbas and Qatadah said: except the first three verses of it. The cause of its revelation was that the disbelievers of Mecca were instructed by the Jews to ask the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about the cause that brought the Children of Israel down to Egypt, and then it was revealed. It was also said: its cause was to console the Messenger (ﷺ) regarding what his people did to him, by what Joseph's brothers did to him. It was also said: the Jews asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to narrate to them the affair of Jacob and his sons and the matter of Joseph. Saʿd ibn Abi Waqqas said: the Qur'an was sent down, and he recited it to them for a time, and they said: "O Messenger of Allah, if only you would relate to us," and then this was revealed.

The aspect of its connection with what came before it and its linkage is that at the end of the preceding surah is: ﴿And We relate to you from the news of the messengers that by it We strengthen your heart﴾ [Hud: 120]. Among those related accounts were what the prophets encountered from their peoples. So He followed this with the story of Joseph and what he encountered from his brothers, and what his condition ended with of good outcome, so that there might be for the Messenger (ﷺ) a comprehensive consolation for what he encounters of harm from the distant and the near. This story came in a lengthy and complete form, so for that reason it is not repeated in the Qur'an except what the believer of the family of Pharaoh reported in Surat Ghafir.

The reference of "Those are the verses" (تِلْكَ آياتُ) is to "Alif-Lam-Ra" and the rest of the letters of the alphabet from which the verses of the Qur'an are composed. Or it refers to the Torah and the Gospel, or to the verses mentioned in Surat Hud, or to the verses of this surah. And "the Clear Book" (الكِتابِ المُبِينِ) — these are sayings: that is, those verses that were sent down to you in this surah. The apparent meaning is that the Book is the Qur'an, and "the Clear" (المُبِينُ) is either clear in itself, its matter manifest in the inimitability (إعْجاز) of the Arabs and in rebuking them; or it makes clear the lawful and unlawful, the limits and rulings, and what is needed of the matter of religion, as Ibn ʿAbbas and Mujahid said; or it is the Clear in guidance, right direction, and blessing, as Qatadah said; or it is the Clear in what the Jews asked about, or what they were told to ask about regarding the migration of Jacob from Syria to Egypt and about the story of Joseph; or it is the Clear in terms of the clarity and excellence of the Arabic tongue, for in it there are six letters not gathered in one language. This was narrated from Muʿadh ibn Jabal. The commentators said: they are the ṭāʾ, ẓāʾ, ḍād, ṣād, ʿayn, and khāʾ, and the discussion ends.

The pronoun in "Indeed We have sent it down" (إنّا أنْزَلْناهُ) refers to the Book in which the story of Joseph is found. It was said to refer to the Qur'an, and it was said to refer to the news of Joseph, as al-Zajjaj and Ibn al-Anbari said. It was also said it is the pronoun of the sending down, and "Qur'anan" is what is conjoined with it. These two are weak. "Qur'anan" is in the accusative; it was said as a substitute (badal) for the pronoun, and it was said as a preparatory circumstantial state (ḥāl al-muwaṭṭi'ah). The Qur'an was called "Qur'an" because it is a generic noun (ism jins) applied to the few and the many. "ʿArabiyyan" is attributed to the Arabs, and "al-ʿArab" is the plural of ʿArabī, like Rūm and Rūmī. ʿArabah is the area of the house of Ismaʿil ibn Ibrahim, peace be upon them both. The poet said:

"And the land of ʿArabah, whose sacred things none may make lawful among people except the clever and shrewd."

He means the Prophet (ﷺ), for Mecca was made lawful for him. The poet made the "rāʾ" of "ʿArabah" quiescent out of necessity. It was said: if you wish, you may attribute the Qur'an to it from the beginning, that is, according to the dialect of the people of this region. "Perhaps you will understand" (لَعَلَّكم تَعْقِلُونَ) means: what it contains of meanings, and what it includes of eloquence and inimitability, so that you may believe. For if it were in other than Arabic, it would have been said: "Why were its verses not detailed?" [Fussilat: 44].

For if it were in other than Arabic, it would have been said: "Why were its verses not detailed?" [Fussilat: 44].

We narrate to you the best of narratives, by Our revealing to you this Qur'an, though before it you were indeed among the unaware. (12:3)

When Joseph said to his father, "O my father, I have seen eleven stars, and the sun and the moon; I saw them prostrating to me." (12:4)

He said, "O my son, do not relate your vision to your brothers, lest they plot against you a scheme. Indeed, Satan is to man a clear enemy." (12:5)

"And thus your Lord will choose you and teach you the interpretation of events, and complete His favor upon you and upon the family of Jacob, as He completed it upon your two fathers before, Abraham and Isaac. Indeed, your Lord is Knowing and Wise." (12:6)

(al-Qasas): It is a verbal noun of qassa (to narrate), and it may be an ism maf'ul (passive participle), either because it is named by the verbal noun, or because the verb is used in the sense of the object, like al-qabd (the seizing) and al-naqs (the diminishing). Here, al-qasas may carry all three meanings. If it is the verbal noun, then the meaning of its being "the best" is that it was narrated in the most excellent manner and the finest style. Do you not see that this story is narrated in the books of the earlier peoples and in the books of histories, yet you will not find its narration in any of those books close to its narration in the Qur'an? If it is the object (maf'ul), then it is the best because of what it contains of lessons, wisdoms, subtle points and marvels that are not found elsewhere. The apparent meaning is that it is the best of what is narrated within its genre, just as one says of a man, "He is the most knowledgeable of people and the most virtuous," meaning in his field.

It has been said: this surah was "the best of narratives" because it is unique among the others in what it contains of the mention of prophets, the righteous, angels, devils, jinn, humans, livestock, birds, the biographies of kings and kingdoms, merchants, scholars, men and women, and their cunning and deceit; together with what it contains of the mention of monotheism, jurisprudence, conduct, politics, good governance, forgiveness when able, good companionship, stratagems, the management of livelihood, the Hereafter, the good outcome of chastity, struggle, deliverance from what is feared to what is desired, the mention of the beloved and the beloved's companion, the sight of years, the interpretation of dreams, and marvels that are suitable for both religion and worldly life. It has also been said: it was the best of narratives because everyone mentioned in it had a destiny of happiness. Consider Joseph, his father, his brothers, the wife of the al-Aziz, the king who embraced Islam through Joseph and whose Islam was good, the interpreter of the dream (the cupbearer), and the witness (as is said).

It has also been said: (ahsana, "the best") here is not the elative form (af'al al-tafdil), but has the sense of hasan (good). It is as if it were said: "the good narrative," by way of the attribution of an adjective to its noun, that is, al-qasas al-hasan. The "ma" in bi-ma awhayna ("by what We revealed") is a verbal (masdariyya) particle, meaning "by Our revelation." If al-qasas is a verbal noun, then the object of naqussu (We narrate) in meaning is hadha al-Qur'an ("this Qur'an"), but this is an instance of "alignment" (al-i'mal), since it is governed by both naqussu and awhayna, and the second was made to govern on the basis of the more common practice. The pronoun in min qablihi ("before it") refers to the revelation. The views of the grammarians have been mentioned regarding the light (mukhaffafa) "an" and the coming of the lam in the second of the two parts. The meaning of "among the unaware" (al-ghafilin) (Al-A'raf: 205) is: you had no awareness of this story, nor had you any prior knowledge of it, nor had a fragment of it reached your hearing. As for the governing element of idh ("when"), al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya said it is "remember" (udhkur). Al-Zamakhshari also permitted that it be a substitute (badal) for "the best of narratives," and said: it is a badal al-ishtimal (substitution of inclusion), because the time includes the narratives, and the narrated thing is what is narrated; so when he narrated the time, he narrated. Ibn 'Atiyya said: it is permissible for naqussu to govern it, so that the meaning would be: "We narrate to you the situation, when..." These estimations cannot stand unless idh is stripped of its indication of past time and made into an absolute time suitable for all times, by way of substitution.

Makki reported that the governing element of idh is "al-ghafilin," but what appears is that its governing element is "qala ya bunayya" ("he said, O my son"), as you say: "When Zayd stood up, 'Amr stood up." Idh remains in its original function as an adverb of past time.

Yusuf (Joseph) is a Hebrew name, and six dialects have been mentioned for it. Its being non-diptote (not taking tanwin, i.e., prevented from nunation) is evidence against the view of those who claim it is an Arabic word derived from al-asaf (grief); although in some of its dialects the dominant pattern (wazn) may be present in it, because it is impossible for it to be a non-Arabic word and yet not non-Arabic. Talha ibn Musarrif read with a hamza and a fatha on the sin. Ibn 'Amir, Abu Ja'far and al-A'raj read "ya abata" with a fatha on the ta'; the rest of the seven and the majority read it with a kasra. The two sons (Ibn Kathir and...) stopped on it with a ha' (ya abatah). This ta' is a substitute ('iwad) for the ya' of possession, so the two cannot be combined. The alif that is a substitute for the ta' is combined with it, as the poet said:

"O father, perhaps you or your like..." (ya abata 'allaka aw 'asaka)

The reason for limiting it to a fathah on the ta' is that the speaker suffices with the fathah in place of the alif; or the ta' was apocopated (rukhkhima) by deleting the ta' then reinserted, as Abu 'Ali said. Or the alif in "abata" is for the vocative of lamentation (nudba), and it was deleted, as al-Farra', Abu 'Ubayd, Abu Hatim and Qutrub said; this was refuted on the grounds that it is not a place of lamentation. Or the original is "ya abatan" with tanwin, which was deleted, and the verb of calling ("nadi") was deleted, as Qutrub said; this was refuted on the grounds that tanwin is not deleted from the nasb (accusative) vocative, as in "ya darriban rajulan." Abu Ja'far pronounced the ya' of "inni" with a fatha.

Al-Hasan, Abu Ja'far and Talha ibn Sulayman read "ahada 'ashara" with a sukun on the 'ayn, to avoid a succession of vowels and to make clear that the two words are made into one word. "Ra'aytu" here is a dream-seeing (hulmiyya), because its complement indicates that it was a dream. The apparent meaning is that he saw in his dream the stars, the sun and the moon. It has been said: he saw his brothers and his parents, and he expressed them by those; he expressed the sun as his mother, and it has been said: as his maternal aunt Rachel, since his mother had died. From the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah: that a Jew came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said: "O Muhammad, tell me the names of the stars which Joseph saw." He remained silent, and Gabriel descended and informed him of their names. So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ summoned the Jew and said: "Will you believe if I inform you of that?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Jarayan, al-Tariq, al-Dhayyal, Dhu al-Kiftayn, Qabis, Wuthab, 'Amudan, al-Faliq, al-Musbih, al-Daruh, al-Furugh, al-Diya', and al-Nur." The Jew said: "Indeed, by Allah, these are their names." Al-Suhayli mentioned, with an isnad to al-Harith ibn Abi Usama, the hadith, and in it there is some variation, and he mentioned "al-Nath'h" (the butting) instead of "al-Musbih." From Wahb: Joseph saw, when he was seven years old, that eleven long staffs were fixed in the ground in the shape of a circle, and suddenly a small staff leapt upon them until it uprooted and overpowered them. He described that to his father, and he said: "Beware of mentioning this to your brothers." Then, when he was twelve years old, he saw the sun, the moon and the stars prostrating to him, and he related it to his father, who said to him: "Do not relate it to them, lest they plot against you." Between Joseph's vision and his brothers' journey to him there were forty years, and it has been said eighty. It was narrated that Joseph's vision was on the Night of Power, a Friday night.

The apparent meaning is that the sun and the moon are not included among the eleven stars; that is why, when the Messenger ﷺ counted them for the Jew, he mentioned eleven stars other than the sun and the moon. But it appears from al-Zamakhshari's speech that they are included among the eleven.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: why did he delay mention of the sun and the moon?" I answer: he delayed them in order to conjoin them with the stars in a manner of distinction, affirming their excellence and their singular superiority over other risers, just as Gabriel and Michael were delayed after the angels and then conjoined to them for that reason. It is also permissible that the waw be in the sense of "with"; that is, "I saw the stars with the sun and the moon." End of quote. What appears is that the delay is only by way of ascending from the lower to the higher, and the ascent did not occur in the sun and the moon in accordance with what is established in the Qur'an: that when they are combined, the sun is mentioned first. Allah the Exalted says: "The sun and the moon by reckoning" (55:5); and "the sun and the moon are brought together" (75:9); and "He it is who made the sun a radiance and the moon a light" (10:5). The sun was put first because of the brightness of its light, the greatness of its body, the strangeness of its course, its drawing of the moon's light from it, and its high place. The apparent meaning is that "I saw them" was repeated for emphasis because of the length created by the objects; just as "indeed you" was repeated in His saying "that you will be brought forth" (23:35), due to the long separation by the adverbial phrase and what is connected to it.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: what is the meaning of the repetition of 'I saw them'?" I answer: it is not a repetition; it is a resumed statement on the presumption of a question which came as an answer to it. Jacob, peace be upon him, said to him, when he said "Indeed I saw eleven stars and the sun and the moon," "How did you see them?", asking about the state of his seeing; so he said: "I saw them prostrating to me." End of quote. He treated them with the plural for rational beings, because the prostration proceeded from them to him, and that is a description of rational beings. This is permissible in the speech of the Arabs: to give a thing the ruling of another thing due to sharing in some attribute, even if that attribute is originally specific to one of them. The prostration here is the prostration of honor, just as the angels prostrated to Adam. It has also been said: at that time prostration was a greeting of some to others.

When Joseph addressed his father with "O my father," in which there is a display of obedience and piety and an alert to the place of compassion by the nature of fatherhood, his father addressed him with "O my son," a diminutive of affection, nearness and compassion. Hafs read here and in Luqman and al-Saffat "ya bunayya" with a fatha on the ya'; Ibn Kathir in Luqman read "ya bunayya la tushrik" (31:13); Qunbul read "ya bunayya aqim" with a sukun on it; the rest of the seven read with a kasra. Zayd ibn 'Ali read "la taqussu" with assimilation, which is the dialect of Tamim, while the majority read it with separation, which is the dialect of the Hijaz. "Ru'ya" is a verbal noun like "buqya." Al-Zamakhshari said: "Ru'ya" has the meaning of "ru'ya" (seeing), except that it is specific to what occurs in sleep and not waking; they were distinguished by the two feminine letters, as is said "qurba" and "qurba" (nearness). The majority read "ru'yaka" (your vision), and "ru'ya" wherever it occurs is with a hamza without imala (inclination). Al-Kisa'i read with imala and without the hamza, which is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz.

The brothers of Joseph are: Kad, Benjamin, Yahudha, Naftali, Zabulun, Shim'un, Ruben; it is said with a lam, like Jibril and Jibrin; and Yusakha, Lawi, Dhan, and Yashir. "Fa-yakidu laka" ("so that they plot against you") is in the subjunctive by the implicit "an" as an answer to the prohibition. "Fa-yakidu" was transitive with the lam, and in "fa-kidun" it was transitive by itself. It may be from the pattern of "shakartu Zaydan" and "shakartu li-Zayd" (I thanked Zayd), and it may be an instance of tadmin (implicit meaning): "fa-yakidu" implies the meaning of what is transitive with the lam, so it is as if he said "fa-yahtalu laka bil-kayd" (they will scheme against you with deceit). Tadmin is more eloquent, because it indicates the meaning of both verbs, and for emphasis it was reinforced with the verbal noun.

Ya'qub drew attention to the cause of the plotting, namely what Satan adorns for man and embellishes for him, due to the enmity between them. He always strives to bring him into sins, to make him enter them and to urge him toward them. Joseph's dream had shown Jacob, peace be upon them both, that Allah the Exalted would bring him to a high level of wisdom, choose him for prophethood, and bless him with the honor of both abodes, as He had done with his forefathers; so he feared for him the envy of his brothers, and forbade him from relating his dream to them. In Jacob's address to Joseph there is a prohibition against relating it to his brothers out of fear of their plot, an indication of warning a Muslim brother against one whom he fears for him, and a drawing of attention to something which is not fitting; and that is not included in the category of backbiting. "And thus will your Lord choose you": that is, like that choosing, namely what He showed him in that dream, which indicated the greatness of his rank and the nobility of his station, and that his end would be prophethood, messengership and kingship. "Yajtabika" means: your Lord chooses you for prophethood and kingship. Al-Hasan said: for prophethood. Muqatil said: for prostration to you. Al-Zamakhshari said: for great matters.

﴿And He will teach you the interpretation of events (ta'wil al-ahadith)﴾ is a new, independent sentence and is not part of the simile. It is as if he said: "And He teaches you." Mujahid and al-Suddi said: "ta'wil al-ahadith" means the interpretation of dreams. Al-Hasan said: the outcomes of matters. It was also said that it is general, covering this and other unseen matters. Muqatil said: the strange features of dreams. Ibn Zayd said: knowledge and wisdom.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "al-ahadith" means dreams, because dreams are either an expression of the self, or of an angel, or of a devil. Their ta'wil is their interpretation (ibarah) and explanation (tafsir). Yusuf, peace be upon him, was the most skilled of people at interpreting dreams and the most accurate in their interpretation. It is also permissible that ta'wil al-ahadith means the meanings of the books of Allah and the biographies of the prophets, and what is obscure and confusing to people regarding their purposes and aims: he explains and clarifies it for them, and guides them to the hidden wisdoms within them. They are called "ahadith" because they are related (tuhaddath) from Allah and His messengers, so one says: "Allah said," and "the Messenger said such-and-such." Do you not see His saying: ﴿So in what statement after it will they believe?﴾ [al-A'raf: 185] and ﴿Allah has sent down the best statement, a Book﴾ [al-Zumar: 23]. And it (ahadith) is an ism jam' (a collective noun) of hadith, and not a plural of uhdutha. End of quotation.

Abu Hayyan says: It is not an ism jam' as was mentioned; rather it is a jam' taksir (broken plural) of hadith, irregular in form, as they say abatil and abatil (from batil). No ism jam' has come on this pattern. And if they say of 'abadid and yanadir that they are jam' taksir and no singular has been pronounced for them, then why would ahadith and abatil not be jam' taksir?

﴿And He will complete His favour upon you﴾: its completion is that He, exalted is He, joined to them the blessing of this world, by making them prophets and kings, with the blessing of the Hereafter, by raising them to the highest ranks in Paradise. Muqatil said: by elevating your word and fulfilling your dream. Al-Hasan said: this is something Allah made known to Ya'qub, that He would give Yusuf prophethood. It was also said: by making your brothers need you, so that you would repay wrongdoing with forgiveness and evil with goodness. It was also said: by saving you from every hardship.

"Family of Ya'qub" (ali Ya'qub): the apparent meaning is that it refers to his sons and their offspring, meaning We will place prophethood among them. Al-Zamakhshari said: they are his offspring and others. It was also said: the people of his religion and his followers, as in the hadith: "Who are your family?" He said: "Every pious person." It was also said: his wife and his eleven sons. It was also said: the intended meaning is Ya'qub himself alone.

The completion of the favour upon Ibrahim was through intimate friendship (khullah), being saved from the fire, and the destruction of his enemy Nimrod. Upon Ishaq it was through bringing forth Ya'qub and the tribes (al-asbat) from his loins. The grandfather and the great-grandfather are called "fathers" (abawayn), because they are in the direct line of descent, as He said: ﴿and the God of your fathers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 133]. For this reason they say "the son of so-and-so," even if there are many generations between them in the direct line.

﴿Indeed your Lord is All-Knowing﴾ of who deserves selection (al-ijtiba'), (Wise) who places things in their right places. These two attributes are fitting for this promise which He made to Ya'qub and Yusuf, peace be upon them both, in His saying: ﴿And thus your Lord will choose you﴾.

It was said: Ya'qub, peace be upon him, knew this from the supplication of Ishaq, peace be upon him, when he was mistaken for Esau (Ay'su) by him.

We narrate to you the best of narratives, by Our revealing to you this Qur'an, though before it you were indeed among the unaware. (12:3)

When Joseph said to his father, "O my father, I have seen eleven stars, and the sun and the moon; I saw them prostrating to me." (12:4)

He said, "O my son, do not relate your vision to your brothers, lest they plot against you a scheme. Indeed, Satan is to man a clear enemy." (12:5)

Jacob, peace be upon him, said to him, when he said "Indeed I saw eleven stars and the sun and the moon," "How did you see them?", asking about the state of his seeing; so he said: "I saw them prostrating to me." End of quote. He treated them with the plural for rational beings, because the prostration proceeded from them to him, and that is a description of rational beings. This is permissible in the speech of the Arabs: to give a thing the ruling of another thing due to sharing in some attribute, even if that attribute is originally specific to one of them. The prostration here is the prostration of honor, just as the angels prostrated to Adam. It has also been said: at that time prostration was a greeting of some to others.

When Joseph addressed his father with "O my father," in which there is a display of obedience and piety and an alert to the place of compassion by the nature of fatherhood, his father addressed him with "O my son," a diminutive of affection, nearness and compassion. Hafs read here and in Luqman and al-Saffat "ya bunayya" with a fatha on the ya'; Ibn Kathir in Luqman read "ya bunayya la tushrik" (31:13); Qunbul read "ya bunayya aqim" with a sukun on it; the rest of the seven read with a kasra. Zayd ibn 'Ali read "la taqussu" with assimilation, which is the dialect of Tamim, while the majority read it with separation, which is the dialect of the Hijaz. "Ru'ya" is a verbal noun like "buqya." Al-Zamakhshari said: "Ru'ya" has the meaning of "ru'ya" (seeing), except that it is specific to what occurs in sleep and not waking; they were distinguished by the two feminine letters, as is said "qurba" and "qurba" (nearness). The majority read "ru'yaka" (your vision), and "ru'ya" wherever it occurs is with a hamza without imala (inclination). Al-Kisa'i read with imala and without the hamza, which is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz.

The brothers of Joseph are: Kad, Benjamin, Yahudha, Naftali, Zabulun, Shim'un, Ruben; it is said with a lam, like Jibril and Jibrin; and Yusakha, Lawi, Dhan, and Yashir. "Fa-yakidu laka" ("so that they plot against you") is in the subjunctive by the implicit "an" as an answer to the prohibition. "Fa-yakidu" was transitive with the lam, and in "fa-kidun" it was transitive by itself. It may be from the pattern of "shakartu Zaydan" and "shakartu li-Zayd" (I thanked Zayd), and it may be an instance of tadmin (implicit meaning): "fa-yakidu" implies the meaning of what is transitive with the lam, so it is as if he said "fa-yahtalu laka bil-kayd" (they will scheme against you with deceit). Tadmin is more eloquent, because it indicates the meaning of both verbs, and for emphasis it was reinforced with the verbal noun.

Ya'qub drew attention to the cause of the plotting, namely what Satan adorns for man and embellishes for him, due to the enmity between them. He always strives to bring him into sins, to make him enter them and to urge him toward them. Joseph's dream had shown Jacob, peace be upon them both, that Allah the Exalted would bring him to a high level of wisdom, choose him for prophethood, and bless him with the honor of both abodes, as He had done with his forefathers; so he feared for him the envy of his brothers, and forbade him from relating his dream to them. In Jacob's address to Joseph there is a prohibition against relating it to his brothers out of fear of their plot, an indication of warning a Muslim brother against one whom he fears for him, and a drawing of attention to something which is not fitting; and that is not included in the category of backbiting. "And thus will your Lord choose you": that is, like that choosing, namely what He showed him in that dream, which indicated the greatness of his rank and the nobility of his station, and that his end would be prophethood, messengership and kingship. "Yajtabika" means: your Lord chooses you for prophethood and kingship. Al-Hasan said: for prophethood. Muqatil said: for prostration to you. Al-Zamakhshari said: for great matters.

﴿And He will teach you the interpretation of events (ta'wil al-ahadith)﴾ is a new, independent sentence and is not part of the simile. It is as if he said: "And He teaches you." Mujahid and al-Suddi said: "ta'wil al-ahadith" means the interpretation of dreams. Al-Hasan said: the outcomes of matters. It was also said that it is general, covering this and other unseen matters. Muqatil said: the strange features of dreams. Ibn Zayd said: knowledge and wisdom.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "al-ahadith" means dreams, because dreams are either an expression of the self, or of an angel, or of a devil. Their ta'wil is their interpretation (ibarah) and explanation (tafsir). Yusuf, peace be upon him, was the most skilled of people at interpreting dreams and the most accurate in their interpretation. It is also permissible that ta'wil al-ahadith means the meanings of the books of Allah and the biographies of the prophets, and what is obscure and confusing to people regarding their purposes and aims: he explains and clarifies it for them, and guides them to the hidden wisdoms within them. They are called "ahadith" because they are related (tuhaddath) from Allah and His messengers, so one says: "Allah said," and "the Messenger said such-and-such." Do you not see His saying: ﴿So in what statement after it will they believe?﴾ [al-A'raf: 185] and ﴿Allah has sent down the best statement, a Book﴾ [al-Zumar: 23]. And it (ahadith) is an ism jam' (a collective noun) of hadith, and not a plural of uhdutha. End of quotation.

Abu Hayyan says: It is not an ism jam' as was mentioned; rather it is a jam' taksir (broken plural) of hadith, irregular in form, as they say abatil and abatil (from batil). No ism jam' has come on this pattern. And if they say of 'abadid and yanadir that they are jam' taksir and no singular has been pronounced for them, then why would ahadith and abatil not be jam' taksir?

﴿And He will complete His favour upon you﴾: its completion is that He, exalted is He, joined to them the blessing of this world, by making them prophets and kings, with the blessing of the Hereafter, by raising them to the highest ranks in Paradise. Muqatil said: by elevating your word and fulfilling your dream. Al-Hasan said: this is something Allah made known to Ya'qub, that He would give Yusuf prophethood. It was also said: by making your brothers need you, so that you would repay wrongdoing with forgiveness and evil with goodness. It was also said: by saving you from every hardship.

"Family of Ya'qub" (ali Ya'qub): the apparent meaning is that it refers to his sons and their offspring, meaning We will place prophethood among them. Al-Zamakhshari said: they are his offspring and others. It was also said: the people of his religion and his followers, as in the hadith: "Who are your family?" He said: "Every pious person." It was also said: his wife and his eleven sons. It was also said: the intended meaning is Ya'qub himself alone.

The completion of the favour upon Ibrahim was through intimate friendship (khullah), being saved from the fire, and the destruction of his enemy Nimrod. Upon Ishaq it was through bringing forth Ya'qub and the tribes (al-asbat) from his loins. The grandfather and the great-grandfather are called "fathers" (abawayn), because they are in the direct line of descent, as He said: ﴿and the God of your fathers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 133]. For this reason they say "the son of so-and-so," even if there are many generations between them in the direct line.

﴿Indeed your Lord is All-Knowing﴾ of who deserves selection (al-ijtiba'), (Wise) who places things in their right places. These two attributes are fitting for this promise which He made to Ya'qub and Yusuf, peace be upon them both, in His saying: ﴿And thus your Lord will choose you﴾.

It was said: Ya'qub, peace be upon him, knew this from the supplication of Ishaq, peace be upon him, when he was mistaken for Esau (Ay'su) by him.

We narrate to you the best of narratives, by Our revealing to you this Qur'an, though before it you were indeed among the unaware. (12:3)

When Joseph said to his father, "O my father, I have seen eleven stars, and the sun and the moon; I saw them prostrating to me." (12:4)

He said, "O my son, do not relate your vision to your brothers, lest they plot against you a scheme. Indeed, Satan is to man a clear enemy." (12:5)

"And thus your Lord will choose you and teach you the interpretation of events, and complete His favor upon you and upon the family of Jacob, as He completed it upon your two fathers before, Abraham and Isaac. Indeed, your Lord is Knowing and Wise." (12:6)

(al-Qasas): It is a verbal noun of qassa (to narrate), and it may be an ism maf'ul (passive participle), either because it is named by the verbal noun, or because the verb is used in the sense of the object, like al-qabd (the seizing) and al-naqs (the diminishing). Here, al-qasas may carry all three meanings. If it is the verbal noun, then the meaning of its being "the best" is that it was narrated in the most excellent manner and the finest style. Do you not see that this story is narrated in the books of the earlier peoples and in the books of histories, yet you will not find its narration in any of those books close to its narration in the Qur'an? If it is the object (maf'ul), then it is the best because of what it contains of lessons, wisdoms, subtle points and marvels that are not found elsewhere. The apparent meaning is that it is the best of what is narrated within its genre, just as one says of a man, "He is the most knowledgeable of people and the most virtuous," meaning in his field.

It has been said: this surah was "the best of narratives" because it is unique among the others in what it contains of the mention of prophets, the righteous, angels, devils, jinn, humans, livestock, birds, the biographies of kings and kingdoms, merchants, scholars, men and women, and their cunning and deceit; together with what it contains of the mention of monotheism, jurisprudence, conduct, politics, good governance, forgiveness when able, good companionship, stratagems, the management of livelihood, the Hereafter, the good outcome of chastity, struggle, deliverance from what is feared to what is desired, the mention of the beloved and the beloved's companion, the sight of years, the interpretation of dreams, and marvels that are suitable for both religion and worldly life. It has also been said: it was the best of narratives because everyone mentioned in it had a destiny of happiness. Consider Joseph, his father, his brothers, the wife of the al-Aziz, the king who embraced Islam through Joseph and whose Islam was good, the interpreter of the dream (the cupbearer), and the witness (as is said).

It has also been said: (ahsana, "the best") here is not the elative form (af'al al-tafdil), but has the sense of hasan (good). It is as if it were said: "the good narrative," by way of the attribution of an adjective to its noun, that is, al-qasas al-hasan. The "ma" in bi-ma awhayna ("by what We revealed") is a verbal (masdariyya) particle, meaning "by Our revelation." If al-qasas is a verbal noun, then the object of naqussu (We narrate) in meaning is hadha al-Qur'an ("this Qur'an"), but this is an instance of "alignment" (al-i'mal), since it is governed by both naqussu and awhayna, and the second was made to govern on the basis of the more common practice. The pronoun in min qablihi ("before it") refers to the revelation. The views of the grammarians have been mentioned regarding the light (mukhaffafa) "an" and the coming of the lam in the second of the two parts. The meaning of "among the unaware" (al-ghafilin) (Al-A'raf: 205) is: you had no awareness of this story, nor had you any prior knowledge of it, nor had a fragment of it reached your hearing. As for the governing element of idh ("when"), al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya said it is "remember" (udhkur). Al-Zamakhshari also permitted that it be a substitute (badal) for "the best of narratives," and said: it is a badal al-ishtimal (substitution of inclusion), because the time includes the narratives, and the narrated thing is what is narrated; so when he narrated the time, he narrated. Ibn 'Atiyya said: it is permissible for naqussu to govern it, so that the meaning would be: "We narrate to you the situation, when..." These estimations cannot stand unless idh is stripped of its indication of past time and made into an absolute time suitable for all times, by way of substitution.

Makki reported that the governing element of idh is "al-ghafilin," but what appears is that its governing element is "qala ya bunayya" ("he said, O my son"), as you say: "When Zayd stood up, 'Amr stood up." Idh remains in its original function as an adverb of past time.

Yusuf (Joseph) is a Hebrew name, and six dialects have been mentioned for it. Its being non-diptote (not taking tanwin, i.e., prevented from nunation) is evidence against the view of those who claim it is an Arabic word derived from al-asaf (grief); although in some of its dialects the dominant pattern (wazn) may be present in it, because it is impossible for it to be a non-Arabic word and yet not non-Arabic. Talha ibn Musarrif read with a hamza and a fatha on the sin. Ibn 'Amir, Abu Ja'far and al-A'raj read "ya abata" with a fatha on the ta'; the rest of the seven and the majority read it with a kasra. The two sons (Ibn Kathir and...) stopped on it with a ha' (ya abatah). This ta' is a substitute ('iwad) for the ya' of possession, so the two cannot be combined. The alif that is a substitute for the ta' is combined with it, as the poet said:

"O father, perhaps you or your like..." (ya abata 'allaka aw 'asaka)

The reason for limiting it to a fathah on the ta' is that the speaker suffices with the fathah in place of the alif; or the ta' was apocopated (rukhkhima) by deleting the ta' then reinserted, as Abu 'Ali said. Or the alif in "abata" is for the vocative of lamentation (nudba), and it was deleted, as al-Farra', Abu 'Ubayd, Abu Hatim and Qutrub said; this was refuted on the grounds that it is not a place of lamentation. Or the original is "ya abatan" with tanwin, which was deleted, and the verb of calling ("nadi") was deleted, as Qutrub said; this was refuted on the grounds that tanwin is not deleted from the nasb (accusative) vocative, as in "ya darriban rajulan." Abu Ja'far pronounced the ya' of "inni" with a fatha.

Al-Hasan, Abu Ja'far and Talha ibn Sulayman read "ahada 'ashara" with a sukun on the 'ayn, to avoid a succession of vowels and to make clear that the two words are made into one word. "Ra'aytu" here is a dream-seeing (hulmiyya), because its complement indicates that it was a dream. The apparent meaning is that he saw in his dream the stars, the sun and the moon. It has been said: he saw his brothers and his parents, and he expressed them by those; he expressed the sun as his mother, and it has been said: as his maternal aunt Rachel, since his mother had died. From the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah: that a Jew came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said: "O Muhammad, tell me the names of the stars which Joseph saw." He remained silent, and Gabriel descended and informed him of their names. So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ summoned the Jew and said: "Will you believe if I inform you of that?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Jarayan, al-Tariq, al-Dhayyal, Dhu al-Kiftayn, Qabis, Wuthab, 'Amudan, al-Faliq, al-Musbih, al-Daruh, al-Furugh, al-Diya', and al-Nur." The Jew said: "Indeed, by Allah, these are their names." Al-Suhayli mentioned, with an isnad to al-Harith ibn Abi Usama, the hadith, and in it there is some variation, and he mentioned "al-Nath'h" (the butting) instead of "al-Musbih." From Wahb: Joseph saw, when he was seven years old, that eleven long staffs were fixed in the ground in the shape of a circle, and suddenly a small staff leapt upon them until it uprooted and overpowered them. He described that to his father, and he said: "Beware of mentioning this to your brothers." Then, when he was twelve years old, he saw the sun, the moon and the stars prostrating to him, and he related it to his father, who said to him: "Do not relate it to them, lest they plot against you." Between Joseph's vision and his brothers' journey to him there were forty years, and it has been said eighty. It was narrated that Joseph's vision was on the Night of Power, a Friday night.

The apparent meaning is that the sun and the moon are not included among the eleven stars; that is why, when the Messenger ﷺ counted them for the Jew, he mentioned eleven stars other than the sun and the moon. But it appears from al-Zamakhshari's speech that they are included among the eleven.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: why did he delay mention of the sun and the moon?" I answer: he delayed them in order to conjoin them with the stars in a manner of distinction, affirming their excellence and their singular superiority over other risers, just as Gabriel and Michael were delayed after the angels and then conjoined to them for that reason. It is also permissible that the waw be in the sense of "with"; that is, "I saw the stars with the sun and the moon." End of quote. What appears is that the delay is only by way of ascending from the lower to the higher, and the ascent did not occur in the sun and the moon in accordance with what is established in the Qur'an: that when they are combined, the sun is mentioned first. Allah the Exalted says: "The sun and the moon by reckoning" (55:5); and "the sun and the moon are brought together" (75:9); and "He it is who made the sun a radiance and the moon a light" (10:5). The sun was put first because of the brightness of its light, the greatness of its body, the strangeness of its course, its drawing of the moon's light from it, and its high place. The apparent meaning is that "I saw them" was repeated for emphasis because of the length created by the objects; just as "indeed you" was repeated in His saying "that you will be brought forth" (23:35), due to the long separation by the adverbial phrase and what is connected to it.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: what is the meaning of the repetition of 'I saw them'?" I answer: it is not a repetition; it is a resumed statement on the presumption of a question which came as an answer to it. Jacob, peace be upon him, said to him, when he said "Indeed I saw eleven stars and the sun and the moon," "How did you see them?", asking about the state of his seeing; so he said: "I saw them prostrating to me." End of quote. He treated them with the plural for rational beings, because the prostration proceeded from them to him, and that is a description of rational beings. This is permissible in the speech of the Arabs: to give a thing the ruling of another thing due to sharing in some attribute, even if that attribute is originally specific to one of them. The prostration here is the prostration of honor, just as the angels prostrated to Adam. It has also been said: at that time prostration was a greeting of some to others.

It is as if it were said: "the good narrative," by way of the attribution of an adjective to its noun, that is, al-qasas al-hasan. The "ma" in bi-ma awhayna ("by what We revealed") is a verbal (masdariyya) particle, meaning "by Our revelation." If al-qasas is a verbal noun, then the object of naqussu (We narrate) in meaning is hadha al-Qur'an ("this Qur'an"), but this is an instance of "alignment" (al-i'mal), since it is governed by both naqussu and awhayna, and the second was made to govern on the basis of the more common practice. The pronoun in min qablihi ("before it") refers to the revelation. The views of the grammarians have been mentioned regarding the light (mukhaffafa) "an" and the coming of the lam in the second of the two parts. The meaning of "among the unaware" (al-ghafilin) (Al-A'raf: 205) is: you had no awareness of this story, nor had you any prior knowledge of it, nor had a fragment of it reached your hearing. As for the governing element of idh ("when"), al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya said it is "remember" (udhkur). Al-Zamakhshari also permitted that it be a substitute (badal) for "the best of narratives," and said: it is a badal al-ishtimal (substitution of inclusion), because the time includes the narratives, and the narrated thing is what is narrated; so when he narrated the time, he narrated. Ibn 'Atiyya said: it is permissible for naqussu to govern it, so that the meaning would be: "We narrate to you the situation, when..." These estimations cannot stand unless idh is stripped of its indication of past time and made into an absolute time suitable for all times, by way of substitution.

Makki reported that the governing element of idh is "al-ghafilin," but what appears is that its governing element is "qala ya bunayya" ("he said, O my son"), as you say: "When Zayd stood up, 'Amr stood up." Idh remains in its original function as an adverb of past time.

Yusuf (Joseph) is a Hebrew name, and six dialects have been mentioned for it. Its being non-diptote (not taking tanwin, i.e., prevented from nunation) is evidence against the view of those who claim it is an Arabic word derived from al-asaf (grief); although in some of its dialects the dominant pattern (wazn) may be present in it, because it is impossible for it to be a non-Arabic word and yet not non-Arabic. Talha ibn Musarrif read with a hamza and a fatha on the sin. Ibn 'Amir, Abu Ja'far and al-A'raj read "ya abata" with a fatha on the ta'; the rest of the seven and the majority read it with a kasra. The two sons (Ibn Kathir and...) stopped on it with a ha' (ya abatah). This ta' is a substitute ('iwad) for the ya' of possession, so the two cannot be combined. The alif that is a substitute for the ta' is combined with it, as the poet said:

"O father, perhaps you or your like..." (ya abata 'allaka aw 'asaka)

The reason for limiting it to a fathah on the ta' is that the speaker suffices with the fathah in place of the alif; or the ta' was apocopated (rukhkhima) by deleting the ta' then reinserted, as Abu 'Ali said. Or the alif in "abata" is for the vocative of lamentation (nudba), and it was deleted, as al-Farra', Abu 'Ubayd, Abu Hatim and Qutrub said; this was refuted on the grounds that it is not a place of lamentation. Or the original is "ya abatan" with tanwin, which was deleted, and the verb of calling ("nadi") was deleted, as Qutrub said; this was refuted on the grounds that tanwin is not deleted from the nasb (accusative) vocative, as in "ya darriban rajulan." Abu Ja'far pronounced the ya' of "inni" with a fatha.

Al-Hasan, Abu Ja'far and Talha ibn Sulayman read "ahada 'ashara" with a sukun on the 'ayn, to avoid a succession of vowels and to make clear that the two words are made into one word. "Ra'aytu" here is a dream-seeing (hulmiyya), because its complement indicates that it was a dream. The apparent meaning is that he saw in his dream the stars, the sun and the moon. It has been said: he saw his brothers and his parents, and he expressed them by those; he expressed the sun as his mother, and it has been said: as his maternal aunt Rachel, since his mother had died. From the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah: that a Jew came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said: "O Muhammad, tell me the names of the stars which Joseph saw." He remained silent, and Gabriel descended and informed him of their names. So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ summoned the Jew and said: "Will you believe if I inform you of that?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Jarayan, al-Tariq, al-Dhayyal, Dhu al-Kiftayn, Qabis, Wuthab, 'Amudan, al-Faliq, al-Musbih, al-Daruh, al-Furugh, al-Diya', and al-Nur." The Jew said: "Indeed, by Allah, these are their names." Al-Suhayli mentioned, with an isnad to al-Harith ibn Abi Usama, the hadith, and in it there is some variation, and he mentioned "al-Nath'h" (the butting) instead of "al-Musbih." From Wahb: Joseph saw, when he was seven years old, that eleven long staffs were fixed in the ground in the shape of a circle, and suddenly a small staff leapt upon them until it uprooted and overpowered them. He described that to his father, and he said: "Beware of mentioning this to your brothers." Then, when he was twelve years old, he saw the sun, the moon and the stars prostrating to him, and he related it to his father, who said to him: "Do not relate it to them, lest they plot against you." Between Joseph's vision and his brothers' journey to him there were forty years, and it has been said eighty. It was narrated that Joseph's vision was on the Night of Power, a Friday night.

The apparent meaning is that the sun and the moon are not included among the eleven stars; that is why, when the Messenger ﷺ counted them for the Jew, he mentioned eleven stars other than the sun and the moon. But it appears from al-Zamakhshari's speech that they are included among the eleven.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: why did he delay mention of the sun and the moon?" I answer: he delayed them in order to conjoin them with the stars in a manner of distinction, affirming their excellence and their singular superiority over other risers, just as Gabriel and Michael were delayed after the angels and then conjoined to them for that reason. It is also permissible that the waw be in the sense of "with"; that is, "I saw the stars with the sun and the moon." End of quote. What appears is that the delay is only by way of ascending from the lower to the higher, and the ascent did not occur in the sun and the moon in accordance with what is established in the Qur'an: that when they are combined, the sun is mentioned first. Allah the Exalted says: "The sun and the moon by reckoning" (55:5); and "the sun and the moon are brought together" (75:9); and "He it is who made the sun a radiance and the moon a light" (10:5). The sun was put first because of the brightness of its light, the greatness of its body, the strangeness of its course, its drawing of the moon's light from it, and its high place. The apparent meaning is that "I saw them" was repeated for emphasis because of the length created by the objects; just as "indeed you" was repeated in His saying "that you will be brought forth" (23:35), due to the long separation by the adverbial phrase and what is connected to it.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: what is the meaning of the repetition of 'I saw them'?" I answer: it is not a repetition; it is a resumed statement on the presumption of a question which came as an answer to it. Jacob, peace be upon him, said to him, when he said "Indeed I saw eleven stars and the sun and the moon," "How did you see them?", asking about the state of his seeing; so he said: "I saw them prostrating to me." End of quote. He treated them with the plural for rational beings, because the prostration proceeded from them to him, and that is a description of rational beings. This is permissible in the speech of the Arabs: to give a thing the ruling of another thing due to sharing in some attribute, even if that attribute is originally specific to one of them. The prostration here is the prostration of honor, just as the angels prostrated to Adam. It has also been said: at that time prostration was a greeting of some to others.

When Joseph addressed his father with "O my father," in which there is a display of obedience and piety and an alert to the place of compassion by the nature of fatherhood, his father addressed him with "O my son," a diminutive of affection, nearness and compassion. Hafs read here and in Luqman and al-Saffat "ya bunayya" with a fatha on the ya'; Ibn Kathir in Luqman read "ya bunayya la tushrik" (31:13); Qunbul read "ya bunayya aqim" with a sukun on it; the rest of the seven read with a kasra. Zayd ibn 'Ali read "la taqussu" with assimilation, which is the dialect of Tamim, while the majority read it with separation, which is the dialect of the Hijaz. "Ru'ya" is a verbal noun like "buqya." Al-Zamakhshari said: "Ru'ya" has the meaning of "ru'ya" (seeing), except that it is specific to what occurs in sleep and not waking; they were distinguished by the two feminine letters, as is said "qurba" and "qurba" (nearness). The majority read "ru'yaka" (your vision), and "ru'ya" wherever it occurs is with a hamza without imala (inclination). Al-Kisa'i read with imala and without the hamza, which is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz.

The brothers of Joseph are: Kad, Benjamin, Yahudha, Naftali, Zabulun, Shim'un, Ruben; it is said with a lam, like Jibril and Jibrin; and Yusakha, Lawi, Dhan, and Yashir. "Fa-yakidu laka" ("so that they plot against you") is in the subjunctive by the implicit "an" as an answer to the prohibition. "Fa-yakidu" was transitive with the lam, and in "fa-kidun" it was transitive by itself. It may be from the pattern of "shakartu Zaydan" and "shakartu li-Zayd" (I thanked Zayd), and it may be an instance of tadmin (implicit meaning): "fa-yakidu" implies the meaning of what is transitive with the lam, so it is as if he said "fa-yahtalu laka bil-kayd" (they will scheme against you with deceit). Tadmin is more eloquent, because it indicates the meaning of both verbs, and for emphasis it was reinforced with the verbal noun.

Ya'qub drew attention to the cause of the plotting, namely what Satan adorns for man and embellishes for him, due to the enmity between them. He always strives to bring him into sins, to make him enter them and to urge him toward them. Joseph's dream had shown Jacob, peace be upon them both, that Allah the Exalted would bring him to a high level of wisdom, choose him for prophethood, and bless him with the honor of both abodes, as He had done with his forefathers; so he feared for him the envy of his brothers, and forbade him from relating his dream to them. In Jacob's address to Joseph there is a prohibition against relating it to his brothers out of fear of their plot, an indication of warning a Muslim brother against one whom he fears for him, and a drawing of attention to something which is not fitting; and that is not included in the category of backbiting. "And thus will your Lord choose you": that is, like that choosing, namely what He showed him in that dream, which indicated the greatness of his rank and the nobility of his station, and that his end would be prophethood, messengership and kingship. "Yajtabika" means: your Lord chooses you for prophethood and kingship. Al-Hasan said: for prophethood. Muqatil said: for prostration to you. Al-Zamakhshari said: for great matters.

﴿And He will teach you the interpretation of events (ta'wil al-ahadith)﴾ is a new, independent sentence and is not part of the simile. It is as if he said: "And He teaches you." Mujahid and al-Suddi said: "ta'wil al-ahadith" means the interpretation of dreams. Al-Hasan said: the outcomes of matters. It was also said that it is general, covering this and other unseen matters. Muqatil said: the strange features of dreams. Ibn Zayd said: knowledge and wisdom.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "al-ahadith" means dreams, because dreams are either an expression of the self, or of an angel, or of a devil. Their ta'wil is their interpretation (ibarah) and explanation (tafsir). Yusuf, peace be upon him, was the most skilled of people at interpreting dreams and the most accurate in their interpretation. It is also permissible that ta'wil al-ahadith means the meanings of the books of Allah and the biographies of the prophets, and what is obscure and confusing to people regarding their purposes and aims: he explains and clarifies it for them, and guides them to the hidden wisdoms within them. They are called "ahadith" because they are related (tuhaddath) from Allah and His messengers, so one says: "Allah said," and "the Messenger said such-and-such." Do you not see His saying: ﴿So in what statement after it will they believe?﴾ [al-A'raf: 185] and ﴿Allah has sent down the best statement, a Book﴾ [al-Zumar: 23]. And it (ahadith) is an ism jam' (a collective noun) of hadith, and not a plural of uhdutha. End of quotation.

Abu Hayyan says: It is not an ism jam' as was mentioned; rather it is a jam' taksir (broken plural) of hadith, irregular in form, as they say abatil and abatil (from batil). No ism jam' has come on this pattern. And if they say of 'abadid and yanadir that they are jam' taksir and no singular has been pronounced for them, then why would ahadith and abatil not be jam' taksir?

﴿And He will complete His favour upon you﴾: its completion is that He, exalted is He, joined to them the blessing of this world, by making them prophets and kings, with the blessing of the Hereafter, by raising them to the highest ranks in Paradise. Muqatil said: by elevating your word and fulfilling your dream. Al-Hasan said: this is something Allah made known to Ya'qub, that He would give Yusuf prophethood. It was also said: by making your brothers need you, so that you would repay wrongdoing with forgiveness and evil with goodness. It was also said: by saving you from every hardship.

"Family of Ya'qub" (ali Ya'qub): the apparent meaning is that it refers to his sons and their offspring, meaning We will place prophethood among them. Al-Zamakhshari said: they are his offspring and others. It was also said: the people of his religion and his followers, as in the hadith: "Who are your family?" He said: "Every pious person." It was also said: his wife and his eleven sons. It was also said: the intended meaning is Ya'qub himself alone.

The completion of the favour upon Ibrahim was through intimate friendship (khullah), being saved from the fire, and the destruction of his enemy Nimrod. Upon Ishaq it was through bringing forth Ya'qub and the tribes (al-asbat) from his loins. The grandfather and the great-grandfather are called "fathers" (abawayn), because they are in the direct line of descent, as He said: ﴿and the God of your fathers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 133]. For this reason they say "the son of so-and-so," even if there are many generations between them in the direct line.

﴿Indeed your Lord is All-Knowing﴾ of who deserves selection (al-ijtiba'), (Wise) who places things in their right places. These two attributes are fitting for this promise which He made to Ya'qub and Yusuf, peace be upon them both, in His saying: ﴿And thus your Lord will choose you﴾.

It was said: Ya'qub, peace be upon him, knew this from the supplication of Ishaq, peace be upon him, when he was mistaken for Esau (Ay'su) by him.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 12, verses 7–10:

[p. 282] ﴿Indeed, in Joseph and his brothers are signs for those who ask.﴾ ﴿When they said, "Joseph and his brother are dearer to our father than we are, though we are a group. Indeed, our father is in manifest error."﴾ ﴿"Kill Joseph or cast him into some land, so that your father's face will be devoted to you, and after him you will be a righteous people."﴾

"Signs" (āyāt) means indications and proofs of God's power and wisdom in everything, "for those who ask," meaning for whoever asks about them and learns their story. It has also been said: they are signs of the prophethood of the Prophet (ﷺ) for those Jews who asked him about them, and he informed them of the truth without having heard it from anyone and without reading a book. What appears to be the case is that the signs are the evidences of the truthfulness of the Messenger, and of what God showed in the story of Joseph regarding the consequences of transgression against him, the truth of his dream, the correctness of its interpretation, his control over himself and his restraint of it until he fulfilled the trust, and the arrival of joy after despair. It has also been said: the meaning is "for those who ask and for those who do not ask," based on His saying, ﴿alike for those who ask﴾ [Fussilat: 10], meaning alike for those who ask and those who do not ask. The omission is acceptable because the context of the speech indicates it, as in His saying, ﴿garments that protect you from the heat﴾ [al-Nahl: 81], meaning "and the cold."

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: His saying "for those who ask" implies an exhortation to people to learn these reports, because the intended meaning is "signs for people," so He described them as askers, since everyone should ask about stories of this kind, for they are the seat of lessons and admonition. The names of Joseph's brothers have been mentioned earlier, transcribed from the handwriting of al-Husayn ibn Aḥmad ibn al-Qāḍī al-Fāḍil ʿAbd al-Raḥīm al-Bīsānī, and he copied them from the handwriting of the noble naqīb and genealogist Abu al-Barakat Muḥammad ibn Asʿad al-Ḥusaynī al-Jawwānī, written with diacritical dots. They appear in the books of tafsir distorted and varied. Reuben was the eldest of them, and he is Ruwbil. Then Judah (Yahudha), Simeon (Shamʿun), Levi (Lawi), Zebulun (Zabulun), and Issachar (Yasakhar), full brothers through their mother Leah, daughter of Layan ibn Nahir ibn Azar, who was the daughter of Jacob's maternal uncle. Then Dan, Naphtali, Gad, and Asher, four from the two concubines whom Leah and her sister Rachel had, and they gave them to Jacob. He combined them (in marriage) with him, and combining two sisters was not permitted for anyone after him. The names of the two concubines, it is said, were Layya and Talta. The mother of the seven died, and after her Jacob married her sister Rachel, who bore him Joseph and Benjamin, and she died in childbirth with him.

Mujāhid, Shibl, the people of Mecca, and Ibn Kathīr read ʾāyatun in the singular. The majority read āyātun. In the codex of Ubayy, "a lesson (ʿibra) for those who ask" stands in place of "sign" (āya). The pronoun in "they said" refers to Joseph's brothers. "And his brother" is Benjamin. Since the two were full brothers, they attributed him to Joseph. The lām in "Joseph" (la-Yūsufu) is the lām of initiation (lām al-ibtidāʾ), and in it there is emphasis and affirmation of the content of the sentence, meaning that the abundance of his love for the two of them is firmly established without any doubt. "Dearer" (aḥabb) is an elative (afʿal al-tafḍīl), and it is derived from the passive participle, irregularly (shudhūdh), and for this reason it is followed by "to" (ilā). For when what it is connected to is semantically the agent, it takes "ilā"; and when it is semantically the object, it takes "fī." You say, "Zayd is dearer to ʿAmr than Khālid," so the pronoun in "dearer" is semantically the object, and ʿAmr is the one who loves. And when you say, "Zayd is dearer to ʿAmr than Khālid," the pronoun is the agent and ʿAmr is the one loved, and "than Khālid" in the first example is the one loved, and in the second is the agent.

[aḥabb] was not declined in the masculine form because it is followed by "min" (than). Benjamin was younger than Joseph, so Jacob loved them both because of their youth and the death of their mother. The love of the young and compassion for them is innate in human nature. It was said to the daughter of al-Ḥasan: "Which of your sons do you love most?" She said: "The young one until he grows up, the absent one until he returns, and the sick one until he recovers." Poets have composed verses about love for a young child, both in ancient and modern times. Among them is what the vizier Abū Marwān ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Idrīs al-Jazīrī said in his qaṣīda that he sent to his sons while he was in prison:

"Your youngest, ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, for I conceal over his separation a longing that has not grown less.
He is the one foremost in the heart, even though he has grown to be an equal to you in lineage and origin.
Indeed, the five daughters are equals together, and the ornament, apart from all of them, is for the little finger.
And when the youth, after his youth, is elevated, the love of sons is his, but not like the love of the youngest."

"And we are a group" (naḥnu ʿuṣba) is a circumstantial clause (jumla ḥāliyya), meaning: you prefer them over us in love, while they are two small boys with no sufficiency or benefit in them, and we are a group of ten capable men who carry out the work, so we are more deserving of increased love than they are. Al-Naẓẓāl ibn Sabra narrated from ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, may God be pleased with him, the reading "naḥnu ʿuṣbatan." It was said: the meaning is "and we gather as a group," so the predicate is omitted, and it is the governing element of "ʿuṣba," which is in the accusative as a circumstantial accusative. This is like the saying of the Arabs: "Your judgment is well-arranged" (ḥukmuka musammaṭan), where the predicate is omitted. Al-Mubarrad said: al-Farazdaq said:

"O Lahdham, your judgment is well-arranged."

He meant "your judgment is well-arranged for you." This became common usage, and so it was omitted for brevity, since the listener knows what the speaker intends, like your saying: "The crescent, by God!" meaning "This is the crescent." Al-musammaṭ means the one sent forth, not rejected. Ibn al-Anbārī said: This is like the Arabs' saying: "Indeed the Amirite is his turban," meaning he wraps his turban. He concluded. But it is not like this, because "ʿuṣba" is neither a verbal noun nor a state, so the better view is that it is of the type "your judgment is well-arranged." Some have construed it as: "Your judgment has been established well-arranged."

From Ibn ʿAbbās: "ʿuṣba" is more than ten. From him also: between ten and forty. From Qatāda: above ten up to forty. From Mujāhid: from ten up to fifteen. From Muqātil: ten. From Ibn Jubayr: six or seven. It was said: from one to ten. It was said: up to fifteen. From al-Farrāʾ: ten or more. From Ibn Zayd, al-Zajjāj, and Ibn Qutayba: "ʿuṣba" is three men; when they exceed that, they are a "rahṭ" up to nine; when they exceed that, they are a "ʿuṣba." And "ʿuṣba" is not said of fewer than ten.

"Error" (ḍalāl) here is desire, as said by Ibn ʿAbbās; or mistaken opinion, as said by Ibn Zayd; or injustice in action, as said by Ibn Kāmil; or error in worldly affairs. It is related that after he informed his father of the dream, he would embrace him at every moment against his chest, as though his heart had become certain of the separation and could hardly bear to be apart from him. The apparent reading is that "kill Joseph" is part of their speech. It has been said that it is the words of a group whom Joseph's brothers consulted about what should be done to him, and they said this. The apparent reading is that "cast him" is in their speech, that they should do one of two things to him. It is permissible that "or" (aw) is for distribution, meaning: some said "kill Joseph," and some said "cast him."

"Some land" (arḍan) is in the accusative by the omission of the preposition, as said by al-Ḥawfī and Ibn ʿAṭiyya, meaning: in a land far from the land in which he is, near the land of Jacob. It was said: it is a second object, by implying the meaning "put him down" (anzilūhu), as you say, "I made Zayd descend the house." A group said: it is an adverbial of place (ẓarf), and al-Zamakhsharī chose it, and Abū al-Baqāʾ followed him. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "Land" (arḍan) is indefinite and unknown, far from inhabited areas, and this is the meaning of its indefiniteness and its being empty of people. Because it is vague in this respect, it is put in the accusative like vague adverbs of place. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: That is an error if it is taken as an accusative of place. He said: because an adverb of place should be vague, and this is not like that; rather it is a land restricted by being far or remote and the like, so its vagueness is removed by that. It is known that Joseph was not without being in some land, so it becomes clear that they meant a far-off land other than the one in which he was near his father. He concluded. This objection is correct: if you say, "I sat a distant house," or "I sat a distant place," it is not valid except through the mediation of "fī" (in), and it is not permissible to omit it except in poetic necessity, or with "dakhaltu" (I entered), according to the disagreement over whether "dakhala" is intransitive or transitive. The face here is said to be the person itself, meaning: your father will be devoted to you. It has also been said that it is a metaphor for his being occupied with them and turning his affection toward them, because whoever turns toward you directs his face toward you. This is like the saying of the ostrich when its mother loved it after it had killed its brothers, and previously she did not love it. It said: "Bereavement has turned her (arāmahā)," meaning it inclined her. The pronoun in "after him" refers to Joseph, or to his killing, or to casting him away. Their righteousness is either the righteousness of their condition before their father, which is the view of Muqātil, or their righteousness through repentance and disavowal of this deed, and this is more apparent, and it is the view of the majority, including al-Kalbī. "You will be" (takūnū) could be jussive, coordinated with a jussive, or in the subjunctive by implicit "an."

The speaker of ﴿Do not kill Joseph﴾ was Reuben, as said by Qatāda and Ibn Isḥāq; or Simeon, as said by Mujāhid; or Judah, who was the wisest and best of them in opinion, and he is the one who said ﴿so I will not leave this land﴾ [Yusuf: 80]. He said to them, "Killing is a great matter," as said by al-Suddī. Or Dan. These are four opinions. This was a kindness from them toward their brother, when God willed the execution of His decree and the preservation of his life, and a cause of their deliverance from falling into this great sin, which is destroying a soul by killing. Al-Harawī said: "al-ghayāba" in the well is like a niche or an opening in the well above the water, in which what is inside is hidden from the eyes. Al-Kalbī said: "al-ghayāba" is a hiding in the bottom of the well, because its lower part is wide and its top is narrow, so the observer can hardly see what is in its sides. Al-Zamakhsharī said: its depth, which is what is hidden from the sight of the observer, and its lower part is dark. He concluded. From this it is said of the grave: "ghayāba." Al-Munkhal al-Saʿdī said:

"If one day my hiding place conceals me, then travel in my manner among the clan and the family."

The majority read "ghayābati" in the singular. Nāfiʿ read "ghayābāt" in the plural, making each part of what he is hidden in a "ghayāba." Ibn Hurmuz read "ghayyābāt" with doubling and plural. What appears is that it was named by the active participle of intensification, so it is originally an attribute. Abū ʿAlī attached it to the name of the form "fiʿāl" like what Sībawayh mentioned, "al-ghayād." Abū al-Fatḥ said: I have found of this kind "al-mabār" (the greatly destroyed) and "al-fakhār" (the pottery). Ṣāḥib al-Lawāmiḥ said: it may be "faʿʿālāt" like "ḥammāmāt," and it may be "fayʿālāt" like "shayṭānāt" in the plural of "shayṭāna." Both are for intensification. al-Ḥasan read "fī ghaybatin" (in a hidden place). It may be originally a verbal noun like "al-ghalaba," and it may be the plural of "ghāʾib" like "ṣāniʿ" and "ṣanʿa." In the codex of Ubayy, "ghaybatin" is with a sukūn on the yāʾ, and it is the darkness of the well. Qatāda, with a group, said: "al-jubb" is the well of Jerusalem. Wahb said: in the land of Jordan.
