What appears is that it was named by the active participle of intensification, so it is originally an attribute. Abū ʿAlī attached it to the name of the form "fiʿāl" like what Sībawayh mentioned, "al-ghayād." Abū al-Fatḥ said: I have found of this kind "al-mabār" (the greatly destroyed) and "al-fakhār" (the pottery). Ṣāḥib al-Lawāmiḥ said: it may be "faʿʿālāt" like "ḥammāmāt," and it may be "fayʿālāt" like "shayṭānāt" in the plural of "shayṭāna." Both are for intensification. al-Ḥasan read "fī ghaybatin" (in a hidden place). It may be originally a verbal noun like "al-ghalaba," and it may be the plural of "ghāʾib" like "ṣāniʿ" and "ṣanʿa." In the codex of Ubayy, "ghaybatin" is with a sukūn on the yāʾ, and it is the darkness of the well. Qatāda, with a group, said: "al-jubb" is the well of Jerusalem. Wahb said: in the land of Jordan. Muqātil said: three farsakhs from the dwelling of Jacob. It was said: between Madyan and Egypt.

Al-Ḥasan, Mujāhid, Qatāda, and Abū Rajāʾ read "taltaqitu" with a feminine ta, feminizing it according to the meaning, as the poet said:

"When some years have made us acquainted, they have sufficed the orphans for the loss of the orphan's father."

"al-sayyāra" is the plural of "sayyār," which is one who travels much on the earth. The apparent reading is that the well had water in it, and for this reason they said, ﴿some of the caravan will pick him up﴾. It was said: there was much water in it which would drown Joseph, so a stone rose from the bottom of the well until Joseph stood upon it. It was said: there was no water, and God brought it forth in it until people came to it. It is related that they lowered a rope into the well for him, and he held on with his hands until they tied his hands, took off his shirt, and threw him. Then they intended to crush him with stones, but their brother who advised casting him prevented them from that. The object of "doers" (fāʿilīna) is omitted; meaning: doing what would achieve your aim of separating him from his father.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 12, verses 7–10:

[p. 282] ﴿Indeed, in Joseph and his brothers are signs for those who ask.﴾ ﴿When they said, "Joseph and his brother are dearer to our father than we are, though we are a group. Indeed, our father is in manifest error."﴾ ﴿"Kill Joseph or cast him into some land, so that your father's face will be devoted to you, and after him you will be a righteous people."﴾

"Signs" (āyāt) means indications and proofs of God's power and wisdom in everything, "for those who ask," meaning for whoever asks about them and learns their story. It has also been said: they are signs of the prophethood of the Prophet (ﷺ) for those Jews who asked him about them, and he informed them of the truth without having heard it from anyone and without reading a book. What appears to be the case is that the signs are the evidences of the truthfulness of the Messenger, and of what God showed in the story of Joseph regarding the consequences of transgression against him, the truth of his dream, the correctness of its interpretation, his control over himself and his restraint of it until he fulfilled the trust, and the arrival of joy after despair. It has also been said: the meaning is "for those who ask and for those who do not ask," based on His saying, ﴿alike for those who ask﴾ [Fussilat: 10], meaning alike for those who ask and those who do not ask. The omission is acceptable because the context of the speech indicates it, as in His saying, ﴿garments that protect you from the heat﴾ [al-Nahl: 81], meaning "and the cold."

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: His saying "for those who ask" implies an exhortation to people to learn these reports, because the intended meaning is "signs for people," so He described them as askers, since everyone should ask about stories of this kind, for they are the seat of lessons and admonition. The names of Joseph's brothers have been mentioned earlier, transcribed from the handwriting of al-Husayn ibn Aḥmad ibn al-Qāḍī al-Fāḍil ʿAbd al-Raḥīm al-Bīsānī, and he copied them from the handwriting of the noble naqīb and genealogist Abu al-Barakat Muḥammad ibn Asʿad al-Ḥusaynī al-Jawwānī, written with diacritical dots. They appear in the books of tafsir distorted and varied. Reuben was the eldest of them, and he is Ruwbil. Then Judah (Yahudha), Simeon (Shamʿun), Levi (Lawi), Zebulun (Zabulun), and Issachar (Yasakhar), full brothers through their mother Leah, daughter of Layan ibn Nahir ibn Azar, who was the daughter of Jacob's maternal uncle. Then Dan, Naphtali, Gad, and Asher, four from the two concubines whom Leah and her sister Rachel had, and they gave them to Jacob. He combined them (in marriage) with him, and combining two sisters was not permitted for anyone after him. The names of the two concubines, it is said, were Layya and Talta. The mother of the seven died, and after her Jacob married her sister Rachel, who bore him Joseph and Benjamin, and she died in childbirth with him.

Mujāhid, Shibl, the people of Mecca, and Ibn Kathīr read ʾāyatun in the singular. The majority read āyātun. In the codex of Ubayy, "a lesson (ʿibra) for those who ask" stands in place of "sign" (āya). The pronoun in "they said" refers to Joseph's brothers. "And his brother" is Benjamin. Since the two were full brothers, they attributed him to Joseph. The lām in "Joseph" (la-Yūsufu) is the lām of initiation (lām al-ibtidāʾ), and in it there is emphasis and affirmation of the content of the sentence, meaning that the abundance of his love for the two of them is firmly established without any doubt. "Dearer" (aḥabb) is an elative (afʿal al-tafḍīl), and it is derived from the passive participle, irregularly (shudhūdh), and for this reason it is followed by "to" (ilā). For when what it is connected to is semantically the agent, it takes "ilā"; and when it is semantically the object, it takes "fī." You say, "Zayd is dearer to ʿAmr than Khālid," so the pronoun in "dearer" is semantically the object, and ʿAmr is the one who loves. And when you say, "Zayd is dearer to ʿAmr than Khālid," the pronoun is the agent and ʿAmr is the one loved, and "than Khālid" in the first example is the one loved, and in the second is the agent.

[aḥabb] was not declined in the masculine form because it is followed by "min" (than). Benjamin was younger than Joseph, so Jacob loved them both because of their youth and the death of their mother. The love of the young and compassion for them is innate in human nature. It was said to the daughter of al-Ḥasan: "Which of your sons do you love most?" She said: "The young one until he grows up, the absent one until he returns, and the sick one until he recovers." Poets have composed verses about love for a young child, both in ancient and modern times. Among them is what the vizier Abū Marwān ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Idrīs al-Jazīrī said in his qaṣīda that he sent to his sons while he was in prison:

"Your youngest, ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, for I conceal over his separation a longing that has not grown less.
He is the one foremost in the heart, even though he has grown to be an equal to you in lineage and origin.
Indeed, the five daughters are equals together, and the ornament, apart from all of them, is for the little finger.
And when the youth, after his youth, is elevated, the love of sons is his, but not like the love of the youngest."

"And we are a group" (naḥnu ʿuṣba) is a circumstantial clause (jumla ḥāliyya), meaning: you prefer them over us in love, while they are two small boys with no sufficiency or benefit in them, and we are a group of ten capable men who carry out the work, so we are more deserving of increased love than they are. Al-Naẓẓāl ibn Sabra narrated from ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, may God be pleased with him, the reading "naḥnu ʿuṣbatan." It was said: the meaning is "and we gather as a group," so the predicate is omitted, and it is the governing element of "ʿuṣba," which is in the accusative as a circumstantial accusative. This is like the saying of the Arabs: "Your judgment is well-arranged" (ḥukmuka musammaṭan), where the predicate is omitted. Al-Mubarrad said: al-Farazdaq said:

"O Lahdham, your judgment is well-arranged."

He meant "your judgment is well-arranged for you." This became common usage, and so it was omitted for brevity, since the listener knows what the speaker intends, like your saying: "The crescent, by God!" meaning "This is the crescent." Al-musammaṭ means the one sent forth, not rejected. Ibn al-Anbārī said: This is like the Arabs' saying: "Indeed the Amirite is his turban," meaning he wraps his turban. He concluded. But it is not like this, because "ʿuṣba" is neither a verbal noun nor a state, so the better view is that it is of the type "your judgment is well-arranged." Some have construed it as: "Your judgment has been established well-arranged."

From Ibn ʿAbbās: "ʿuṣba" is more than ten. From him also: between ten and forty. From Qatāda: above ten up to forty. From Mujāhid: from ten up to fifteen. From Muqātil: ten. From Ibn Jubayr: six or seven. It was said: from one to ten. It was said: up to fifteen. From al-Farrāʾ: ten or more. From Ibn Zayd, al-Zajjāj, and Ibn Qutayba: "ʿuṣba" is three men; when they exceed that, they are a "rahṭ" up to nine; when they exceed that, they are a "ʿuṣba." And "ʿuṣba" is not said of fewer than ten.

"Error" (ḍalāl) here is desire, as said by Ibn ʿAbbās; or mistaken opinion, as said by Ibn Zayd; or injustice in action, as said by Ibn Kāmil; or error in worldly affairs. It is related that after he informed his father of the dream, he would embrace him at every moment against his chest, as though his heart had become certain of the separation and could hardly bear to be apart from him. The apparent reading is that "kill Joseph" is part of their speech. It has been said that it is the words of a group whom Joseph's brothers consulted about what should be done to him, and they said this. The apparent reading is that "cast him" is in their speech, that they should do one of two things to him. It is permissible that "or" (aw) is for distribution, meaning: some said "kill Joseph," and some said "cast him."

"Some land" (arḍan) is in the accusative by the omission of the preposition, as said by al-Ḥawfī and Ibn ʿAṭiyya, meaning: in a land far from the land in which he is, near the land of Jacob. It was said: it is a second object, by implying the meaning "put him down" (anzilūhu), as you say, "I made Zayd descend the house." A group said: it is an adverbial of place (ẓarf), and al-Zamakhsharī chose it, and Abū al-Baqāʾ followed him. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "Land" (arḍan) is indefinite and unknown, far from inhabited areas, and this is the meaning of its indefiniteness and its being empty of people. Because it is vague in this respect, it is put in the accusative like vague adverbs of place. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: That is an error if it is taken as an accusative of place. He said: because an adverb of place should be vague, and this is not like that; rather it is a land restricted by being far or remote and the like, so its vagueness is removed by that. It is known that Joseph was not without being in some land, so it becomes clear that they meant a far-off land other than the one in which he was near his father. He concluded. This objection is correct: if you say, "I sat a distant house," or "I sat a distant place," it is not valid except through the mediation of "fī" (in), and it is not permissible to omit it except in poetic necessity, or with "dakhaltu" (I entered), according to the disagreement over whether "dakhala" is intransitive or transitive. The face here is said to be the person itself, meaning: your father will be devoted to you. It has also been said that it is a metaphor for his being occupied with them and turning his affection toward them, because whoever turns toward you directs his face toward you. This is like the saying of the ostrich when its mother loved it after it had killed its brothers, and previously she did not love it. It said: "Bereavement has turned her (arāmahā)," meaning it inclined her. The pronoun in "after him" refers to Joseph, or to his killing, or to casting him away. Their righteousness is either the righteousness of their condition before their father, which is the view of Muqātil, or their righteousness through repentance and disavowal of this deed, and this is more apparent, and it is the view of the majority, including al-Kalbī. "You will be" (takūnū) could be jussive, coordinated with a jussive, or in the subjunctive by implicit "an."

The speaker of ﴿Do not kill Joseph﴾ was Reuben, as said by Qatāda and Ibn Isḥāq; or Simeon, as said by Mujāhid; or Judah, who was the wisest and best of them in opinion, and he is the one who said ﴿so I will not leave this land﴾ [Yusuf: 80]. He said to them, "Killing is a great matter," as said by al-Suddī. Or Dan. These are four opinions. This was a kindness from them toward their brother, when God willed the execution of His decree and the preservation of his life, and a cause of their deliverance from falling into this great sin, which is destroying a soul by killing. Al-Harawī said: "al-ghayāba" in the well is like a niche or an opening in the well above the water, in which what is inside is hidden from the eyes. Al-Kalbī said: "al-ghayāba" is a hiding in the bottom of the well, because its lower part is wide and its top is narrow, so the observer can hardly see what is in its sides. Al-Zamakhsharī said: its depth, which is what is hidden from the sight of the observer, and its lower part is dark. He concluded. From this it is said of the grave: "ghayāba." Al-Munkhal al-Saʿdī said:

"If one day my hiding place conceals me, then travel in my manner among the clan and the family."

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 12, verses 11–14:**

﴿They said, "O our father, why do you not trust us with Joseph, when we are indeed his sincere well-wishers?"﴾ ﴿Send him with us tomorrow so he may enjoy himself and play, and we will indeed guard him.﴾ ﴿He said, "It grieves me that you take him away, and I fear that the wolf may devour him while you are heedless of him."﴾ ﴿They said, "If the wolf devours him while we are a group, then indeed we would be losers."﴾

When the separation between Joseph and his father had been settled in their minds, they devised a scheme against Jacob and treated him gently in order to take Joseph out with them. They mentioned their counsel to him and that sending him with them would bring relief to his heart through grazing and play, since that is what delights children. They also mentioned their protection of him from anything that might trouble him. In their words, ﴿why do you not trust us﴾, there is evidence that they had earlier made a request that Joseph go out with them. They mentioned the cause of trust, which is sincere counsel; that is, "Why do you not trust us with him when our condition is this?" Sincere counsel is evidence of trustworthiness, and for this reason the two are joined in His words, ﴿a trustworthy counselor﴾ [al-A'raf: 68]. Jacob had already sensed from them something that required him not to trust them with Joseph. The clause ﴿why do you not trust us﴾ is a circumstantial clause (jumla haliyya), and this interrogative was accompanied by surprise (ta'ajjub).

Zayd ibn Ali, Abu Ja'far, al-Zuhri and Amr ibn Ubayd read the nun of ﴿ta'manna﴾ as assimilated (idgham) into the nun of the pronoun, without ishmam (partial vowel-indication). The phrase "after Malik" is part of the chain of the reading. The meaning indicates that it is a negation, not a prohibition. It is not like the expression "how good we are!" in exclamation, because if it were assimilated it would be confused with the negation. The majority read with assimilation and ishmam (indicating the vowel of damm, "u"). Some transmitted the suppression of the vowel (ikhfa' al-haraka), so it is not a pure assimilation. Ibn Hurmuz read with a damma on the mim, so that the damma is transferred to the mim from the first nun, after the mim was stripped of its own vowel, and the nun was assimilated into the nun. Ubayy, al-Hasan, Talha ibn Musarrif and al-A'mash read ﴿la ta'mununa﴾ with clear pronunciation (idhhar) and a damma on the nun, according to the original form, while the Mushaf is written with a single nun. Ibn Wuththab and Abu Razin read ﴿la yatmanna﴾ according to the dialect of Tamim. Ibn Wuththab eased the hamza after a kasra.

In the word ﴿send him﴾ there is evidence that he used to hold him and keep him close at all times. ﴿Tomorrow﴾ (ghadan) is in the accusative as an adverb of time (zarf). It is a future time-adverb which applies to the day that follows your day, and to an indefinite future time not restricted to the day following your day. Its original form is ghudu, and its final radical was deleted, although it has come in full form (ghaduwwun). The majority read ﴿yarta' wa-yal'ab﴾ with ya' and jazm (the jussive). The two sons (Ibn Kathir and Abu Amr) read with nun and jazm, and the two Makkans (Ibn Kathir and Ibn Amir) read with nun, jazm and kasra on the 'ayn, while Qunbul differed in affirming or deleting the ya'. It is narrated from Ibn Kathir that ﴿wa-yal'ab﴾ is read with ya', and this is the reading of Ja'far ibn Muhammad. Al-Ala' ibn Sayaba read ﴿yarta'i﴾ with ya' and kasra on the 'ayn, in the jussive, with the final radical deleted, and ﴿wa-yal'abu﴾ with ya' and damma on the ba', as the predicate of a deleted subject; that is, "and he plays." Mujahid, Qatada and Ibn Muhaysin read with a damma-marked nun from irta'na ("we graze"), and ﴿nal'ab﴾ with nun. Abu Raja' did likewise, except that he used ya' in both. The two readings are based on the deletion of the object; that is, "he grazes the livestock or other things." Al-Nakha'i read ﴿narta'﴾ with nun and ﴿yal'ab﴾ with ya', attributing the playing to Joseph alone because of his youth. This also came from Abu Ishaq and Ya'qub. In all these readings the two verbs are active. Zayd ibn Ali read ﴿yurta'﴾ and ﴿yul'ab﴾ with damma on both ya's, in the passive, and he explained it as the implied object that was not named as subject being a pronoun referring to "tomorrow." The original was "yarta' fihi wa-yal'ab fihi" ("graze in it and play in it"); then the preposition was deleted and the verb was extended, so that the verb reached the pronoun directly, giving the estimate "yarta'uhu wa-yal'abuhu." Then he made it passive, and the pronoun that had been in the accusative became hidden because it stood in place of the subject. Here "play" (al-la'ib) means racing and archery-contest, through which they would train for fighting the enemy. They named it "play" because it had the form of play. It was not for mere amusement, as evidenced by their saying, "We went out to race" (inna dhahabna nastabiq). Had it been frivolous play, Jacob would not have allowed them to do it.

Whoever read ﴿yarta'i﴾ with kasra on the 'ayn is using the form yaftaʿil (the reflexive form). Mujahid said it is from mura'ah, that is, "one of us watches over the other and guards him." Ibn Zayd said it is from ra'y al-ibil (herding camels), that is, "he trains himself in herding and guarding property," or from the grazing of plants and pasture, meaning "he grazes," with an elided noun, that is, "our livestock." As for whoever affirmed the ya' in ﴿yal'ab﴾: Ibn 'Atiyya said, "This is a weak reading that is permissible only in poetry, like the saying of the poet:"

Did it not reach you, while news spreads,
of what the she-camel of the sons of Ziyad suffered?

He finished. It was said that the deletion of the vowel on the ya' is a dialect, and on this view it is not a necessity (darura). Whoever read with a sukun on the 'ayn, the meaning is "let us remain in abundance and ease," and they mean in eating and drinking. ﴿And we will indeed guard him﴾ is a circumstantial clause, and the element governing it is the imperative or the response. This is not a case of "action of the governing word" (i'mal), because the circumstantial element cannot be elided, and because the i'mal requires an elided pronoun when the first is the governing one.

Then Jacob pleaded with them on two grounds. The first is immediate, at the present moment: the grief that he would suffer by being separated from him, for he could not endure being without him. The second is his fear for him from the wolf, if they became heedless of him through their grazing and playing, or through their lack of concern and care for guarding him, so that it would devour him and he would grieve over him with everlasting grief. He singled out the wolf because it was the predominant beast of prey in his region, or because Joseph was young, so he feared for him this lowly beast, and this was a warning that he feared for him something even more ravenous. Because of the wolf's lowliness, al-Rabi' ibn Dhaba' al-Fazari singled it out as what he feared when he reached old age, in his saying:

The wolf is what I fear if I pass by it,
alone, while I fear the winds and the rain.

Jacob, by his saying ﴿and I fear that the wolf may devour him﴾, taught them the excuse they should give when they came back without Joseph. So they were taught this and made it a ready answer. The disagreement of the readers over ﴿yahzun﴾ has been mentioned earlier. Zayd ibn Ali, Ibn Hurmuz and Ibn Muhaysin read ﴿la-yahzunni﴾ with a shadda on the nun, while the majority read it without assimilation. ﴿Layahzununi﴾ is an imperfect verb referring to the future, not to the present, because when the imperfect is attached to something anticipated, it becomes restricted to the future, since that anticipated thing is future and is the cause of its effect. It is impossible for the effect to precede it. So the going away has not occurred, and the grief has not occurred, as he said:

It frightens you that you should die while you are
one who has not attained what would save you from punishment.

Zayd ibn Ali read ﴿tadhhabu bihi﴾ from adhhaba (the causative form, four-radical). This can be explained by the extra ba' in "bihi," as some have explained ﴿tanbutu bil-duhn﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 20] in the reading of the one who read with damma on the ta' and kasra on the ba': that is, "it causes the oil to grow and you cause it to go away."

The majority read ﴿al-dhi'b﴾ (the wolf) with hamza, which is the dialect of the Hijaz. Al-Kisa'i, Warsh and Hamza, when pausing, read without hamza. Nasr said: "I heard Abu Amr, and he did not pronounce the hamza." Joseph's brothers avoided one of the two things, namely his grief over their taking him away, because the grief would be brief, and they gave the impression that they would bring him back to him soon. They turned instead to the matter of the wolf, which was the strongest cause for preventing him from letting them take him. So they swore to him that if what he feared, the wolf snatching his brother from among them, were to happen, and their condition was that they were ten men with the likes of them, through whom affairs are managed and calamities are averted, then ﴿indeed we would be a people who are losers﴾; that is, they would be destroyed by weakness, feebleness and incapacity, or they would deserve to be destroyed, because for them there would be no sufficiency nor benefit in their lives, or they would deserve to be cursed with ruin and destruction, and it would be said, "God has brought them to loss and destruction when the wolf devoured some of them while they were present." It was also said: if we are unable to protect some of us, then our livestock has been destroyed and we have lost.

It was narrated that Jacob saw in a dream as if he were on the top of a mountain, while Joseph was in the bottom of a valley. Then ten wolves surrounded him, wanting to eat him, but one of them drove them off from him. Then the earth split open, and Joseph disappeared into it for three days.

So they swore to him that if what he feared, the wolf snatching his brother from among them, were to happen, and their condition was that they were ten men with the likes of them, through whom affairs are managed and calamities are averted, then ﴿indeed we would be a people who are losers﴾; that is, they would be destroyed by weakness, feebleness and incapacity, or they would deserve to be destroyed, because for them there would be no sufficiency nor benefit in their lives, or they would deserve to be cursed with ruin and destruction, and it would be said, "God has brought them to loss and destruction when the wolf devoured some of them while they were present." It was also said: if we are unable to protect some of us, then our livestock has been destroyed and we have lost.

It was narrated that Jacob saw in a dream as if he were on the top of a mountain, while Joseph was in the bottom of a valley. Then ten wolves surrounded him, wanting to eat him, but one of them drove them off from him. Then the earth split open, and Joseph disappeared into it for three days.

[Part 1 of the Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah Yusuf, verses 15–19]

﴿So when they took him away and agreed to put him into the depths of the well. And We revealed to him: "You will surely inform them of this matter of theirs, while they do not perceive."﴾ ﴿And they came to their father at nightfall, weeping.﴾ ﴿They said: "O our father, we went racing one another and left Yusuf with our belongings, and the wolf devoured him. But you will not believe us, even though we are truthful."﴾ ﴿And they brought his shirt stained with false blood. He said: "Rather, your own souls have made a matter seem good to you. So patience is beautiful, and Allah is the One whose help is sought against what you describe."﴾ ﴿And a caravan came, and they sent their water-drawer, and he let down his bucket. He said: "O good news! This is a boy!" And they hid him as merchandise, and Allah knows what they were doing.﴾

[p. 287] It is related that they said to Yusuf: "Ask your father to send you with us." So he turned to Yusuf and said: "Do you want that?" He said: "Yes." Ya'qub said: "If it is tomorrow, I will give you permission." When morning came, Yusuf put on his clothes and tied his belt around himself, and went out with his brothers. Ya'qub bade them farewell and said: "O my sons, I charge you with fear of Allah, and with (caring for) my beloved Yusuf." Then he turned to Yusuf, embraced him to his chest, kissed him between his eyes, and said: "I entrust you to Allah, Lord of the worlds." Then he turned back. They carried Yusuf on their shoulders for as long as Ya'qub could see them. Then, when they were out of his sight, they threw him down so that he would run with them, in order to harm him. The commentators have mentioned many things that describe how he was put into the depths of the well and how they treated him, things that would soften a rock, yet they only grew harder. Neither the Qur'an nor an authentic hadith addressed any of these things, so that they could be relied upon from the books of tafsir. Between this sentence and the sentences before it there is an omitted element, which the meaning indicates, and its estimated wording is: "So he granted them what they asked and sent Yusuf with them."

﴿So when they took him away and agreed﴾: that is, they resolved and agreed to cast him into the well. The phrase ﴿an yaj'aluhu﴾ ("that they should put him") is the object of (ajma'u) ("they agreed"). It is said: ajma'a al-amr and azma'ahu, meaning "he resolved upon it." It is possible that al-ja'l (putting) here means "casting" and also "making" (i.e., transforming). The grammarians differed regarding the answer of (lamma) ("when"): is it expressed or omitted? Whoever says it is expressed says that it is their statement ﴿They said: "O our father, we went racing one another"﴾, meaning: when such and such happened, they said. This is a good interpretation. It has also been said that the answer is (awhayna) ("We revealed"), and the waw is extra. According to this view, the Kufan school holds that (idha) and (hatta) may take an extra element after (lamma). On this basis they explained His saying: ﴿So when they both submitted and he laid him down upon his forehead﴾ [al-Saffat: 103], meaning "and We called him," and His saying: ﴿until, when they came to it and its gates were opened﴾ [al-Zumar: 73], meaning "its gates were opened." And the line of Imru' al-Qays:

*So when we crossed the courtyard of the tribe and he inclined,*

meaning: "he inclined." Whoever says it is omitted, which is the view of the Basran school, al-Zamakhshari estimated it as: "they did to him what they did of harm," and he related the long account of what they did to him and what they said to him and he to them. Some estimated it as: "So when they took him away and agreed to put him into the depths of the well, their trial became great." Others estimated it as: "They put him into it," and this is better, since His saying ﴿and agreed that they should put him﴾ indicates it. The apparent reading is that the pronoun in ﴿And We revealed to him﴾ refers to Yusuf, and it was an inspiration of inner conviction (ilham), as Mujahid said. It has also been related from Ibn 'Abbas that it was a dream. Al-Dahhak and Qatadah said: Jibril descended to him in the well. Al-Hasan said: Allah gave him prophethood in the well while he was young, just as He revealed to Yahya and 'Isa, peace be upon them both. This is the apparent meaning of (awhayna). That the pronoun refers to Yusuf is supported by His saying, when he said to them: ﴿Do you know what you did to Yusuf and his brother when you were ignorant?﴾ [Yusuf: 89]. It has also been said that the pronoun in (ilayhi) refers to Ya'qub, and the revelation was sent to him [p. 288] so that he would find comfort in the darkness of loneliness, and so that he would be given good news of what his affair would lead to. Its meaning is: for deliverance from what you are in. "And you will tell your brothers of what they did to you." The phrase ﴿while they do not perceive﴾ is a circumstantial clause (jumla haliyya) following His saying ﴿You will surely inform them of this matter of theirs﴾, meaning: they will not know, at the time of the informing, that you are Yusuf. This was said by Ibn Jurayj. That is because of your high rank and the greatness of your authority, the distance of your condition from their minds, and the long passage of time which changes appearances and forms. It is mentioned that when they entered upon him seeking provisions, he recognized them while they did not recognize him. He called for the drinking cup, placed it on his hand, struck it, and it hummed. He said: "This cup informs me that you had a brother from your father, called Yusuf, whom he preferred over you. You took him away, threw him into the depths of the well, and you told your father: 'The wolf devoured him,' and he was sold for a paltry price."

It is also permissible that ﴿while they do not perceive﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) from (awhayna) ("We revealed"), meaning: while they do not perceive. This was said by Qatadah, that is: by Our revelation to you and what We informed you of your deliverance and your long life, until you inform them of what they did to you. The reading of the majority is ﴿latunabbi'annahum﴾ with the second-person address (ta' al-khitab), while Ibn 'Umar read it with the third-person (ya' al-ghayba), and so it is in some Basran codices. And (salamun) was read with a nun.

What appears from the context of the reports and stories is that Yusuf was young. It has been said his age at that time was seven years, and it has been said six, as al-Dahhak said. Those who said he was twelve, eighteen, both from al-Hasan, or seventeen, as Ibn al-Sa'ib said, are far removed from the truth. What indicates that he was young, to the point that he could not defend himself, is His saying: ﴿And I fear that the wolf will devour him﴾ [Yusuf: 13], (and that he would frolic and play), ﴿and indeed We are its guardians﴾ [Yusuf: 12], the caravan's taking him, the statement of the water-drawer: ﴿This is a boy!﴾, the statement of the chief of Egypt: ﴿perhaps he will benefit us, or we may adopt him as a son﴾ [Yusuf: 21], and the reports of their carrying him one after another, and his words to his brother Yahudha: "Have mercy on my weakness, my helplessness, and my youth, and have mercy on the heart of your father Ya'qub." Whoever is eighteen years old is not feared to be taken by the wolf, especially if he is in company, and it would not be said of him: ﴿and indeed We are its guardians﴾ [Yusuf: 63], because at that age he is able to devise means to save himself. Also, he would not be called "boy" except metaphorically, and it would not be said of him: ﴿or we may adopt him as a son﴾ [Yusuf: 21].

(ʿishaan) ("at nightfall") is in the accusative as an adverb of time (zarf), or it derives from (al-ashwa) ("darkness"), and (al-ʿashwa) is darkness. It is plural on the pattern (fiʿal), like (ra'in) and (ri'a') ("shepherd" and "shepherds"). Its accusative may be as a circumstantial element (hal), like the reading of al-Hasan ('ushan), on the pattern of (duja) ("darkness"), the plural of (ʿashin), from which the ta' is dropped, as it is dropped in (malik), whose original form is (malika). From al-Hasan also (ʿushayyan) with the diminutive. It has been said: they came at nightfall so that they would be better able to make excuses in the darkness. Therefore it is said: "Do not seek your need at night, for shame is in the eyes; and do not make excuses for a sin during the day, or you will stammer in your excuse." In the speech there is an omission, whose estimated form is: "And they came to their father, without Yusuf, at nightfall, weeping." Then he said: "Where is Yusuf?" They said: "We went..." It is related that when Ya'qub heard their weeping, he said: "What is wrong with you? Has something happened to the sheep?" They said: "No." He said: "Then where is Yusuf?" They said: "We went racing one another and the wolf devoured him." So he wept, cried out, and fell unconscious. They poured water over him, but he did not move. They called to him, but he did not answer. Yahudha placed his hand over the openings of his breath, but he sensed no breath and no vein moved for him. Then he said: "Woe to us from the Judge of the Day of Judgment! We lost our brother and we killed our father!" He did not recover until the cool of dawn. Al-A'mash said: "No weeping person is believed after the brothers of Yusuf."

(nastabiq) ("we race"): that is, we shoot arrows at targets, or we race on foot to see which of us runs faster, or we compete in tasks we divide among ourselves, such as watering, pasturing, and gathering firewood, or we hunt. These are four opinions.

﴿at our belongings﴾: that is, at our clothing and what we had stripped off during the racing. This also indicates that Yusuf was young, for if he were eighteen or seventeen he would have been racing with them. ﴿So the wolf devoured him﴾: We have already mentioned that they took this answer from their father's words: ﴿And I fear that the wolf will devour him﴾ [Yusuf: 13], because the wolf devouring him was the thing he most feared for him.

﴿But you will not believe us﴾: that is, you will not accept us as truthful now, ﴿even though we are truthful.﴾ Or: are you not one who accepts us as truthful in every case, even in the case of truth, because of the suspicion and dislike of Yusuf that had overcome you? We are constantly plotting against him and devising schemes against him. By their saying ﴿even though we are truthful﴾ they gave the impression that they were truthful about the wolf devouring Yusuf, so their truthfulness would be restricted to this incident. Or it means they were people of truthfulness and trust in Ya'qub's eyes before this incident, because of your great love for Yusuf. How much more so, since you now think ill of us in this incident and do not trust our words about him!

It is related that they took a young goat or a kid and slaughtered it, smeared Yusuf's shirt with its blood, and said to Ya'qub: "This is Yusuf's shirt." He took it, smeared his face with it, and wept. Then he examined it and saw no tear and no mark, so he doubted. He inferred from this the opposite of what they claimed, and said to them: "When was the wolf so gentle that it would devour Yusuf and not tear his shirt?" It was said: there were three signs in Yusuf's shirt. It was evidence for Ya'qub that Yusuf had not been eaten by the wolf, and when it was thrown over his face, he regained his sight. It was also evidence of Yusuf's innocence, when it was torn from behind.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, "What is the position of ﴿upon his shirt﴾?" I say: its position is the accusative as an adverbial of place (zarf), as if it were said: "They came with blood above his shirt," just as you say: "He came upon his camels with loads." If you ask: "Could it be a preceding circumstantial element?" I say: No, because the circumstantial element of a prepositional phrase does not precede it. End of quotation.

The meaning does not support taking (ʿala) ("upon") as an adverb of place meaning "above," because the governing verb in that case would be (jaa'u) ("they came"), and "above" cannot be an adverb of place for them. Al-Hawfi said that (ʿala) is connected to (jaa'u) but this is also not valid. As for the example al-Zamakhshari mentioned, "He came upon his camels with loads," it is possible that it is an adverb of place for the one who came, because the adverbial sense is established in it through the change from one camel to another camel, and "with loads" is in the position of a circumstantial element, meaning: accompanied by loads. Abu al-Baqa' said: ﴿upon his shirt﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial element of the blood, because the estimate is: "they came with false blood upon his shirt." Placing a circumstantial element before a preposition that is not extra is a matter of disagreement regarding its permissibility. Whoever permitted it cited as evidence that it exists in the language of the Arabs and recited examples for this, which are mentioned in the science of grammar. The meaning points to what Abu al-Baqa' said.

The majority read (kadhibin) ("false") as an adjective of (dam) ("blood") by way of emphasis, or by omitting a modified noun, meaning "blood of falsehood," since the word indicates falsehood, it is described by it, even though the falsehood came from someone else. Zayd ibn 'Ali read (kadhiban) ("falsely") in the accusative, which may be a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial element, or an object of purpose. 'A'isha and al-Hasan read (kadibin) with the letter dal without a dot, and it was explained as "turbid," and it was said "fresh," and it was said "dry." The author of al-Lawami' said: its meaning is "with a mark," that is, a trace, because (al-kadhib) is a whiteness that appears on the nails of young men and affects them, so it is like a design. That whiteness is called al-Fawf, so this is a metaphor for its effect on the shirt, like the effect of that on the nails.

He said: ﴿Rather, your own souls have made [a matter] seem good to you﴾: here an element is omitted, its estimate being: "The wolf did not devour him, rather your souls made it seem good." Ibn 'Abbas said: "You commanded yourselves to do a matter." Qatadah said: "Adorned it for you." It was said: "They were pleased with a matter," that is, an ugly deed. It was also said: "They made it easy." ﴿So patience is beautiful﴾: that is, my affair is beautiful patience, or: beautiful patience is better. Ubayy, al-Ashhab, and 'Isa ibn 'Umar read (sabran jamilan) ("patience, beautiful") with both in the accusative, and so it is in the codex of Ubayy and the codex of Anas ibn Malik, and it is related likewise from al-Kisa'i. They put it in the accusative as a declarative verbal noun, meaning: "So be patient with beautiful patience." It has been said this is a weak reading according to Sibawayh, and that the accusative in such a case is appropriate only with a command. Likewise the accusative is appropriate in the line:

*My camel complained to me of the length of the journey: "Patience, beautiful patience, for both of us are tested."*

﴿And Allah is the One whose help is sought against what you describe.﴾

﴿A caravan came and they sent their water-drawer, and he let down his bucket.﴾ He said: "O good news!"

[End of part 1]

Abu Hayyan's commentary (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 12, verses 15–19 (part 2 of 2):

It is also narrated in the line of poetry as "ṣabrun jamīlun" (nominative). The reading in the accusative (naṣb), *ṣabran jamīlan*, is sound only if we assume that Ya'qub turned to addressing himself, as though he said: "Be patient, O self, with beautiful patience." In a hadith: "Beautiful patience is that which contains no complaint," meaning complaint to creation. Do you not see His saying: ﴿I only complain of my anguish and my grief to God﴾ [Yusuf: 86]? It was also said: "I will display patience before you, so I will not keep company with you in gloom of face and frowning brow, but rather as I was with you." Al-Thawri said: "Part of patience is that you do not speak of what pains you, nor of your calamity, and that you do not weep for yourself."

﴿And God is the One whose help is sought﴾, meaning: the One from whom aid is requested to bear what you describe of Yusuf's destruction, and to endure the calamity.

﴿A caravan came﴾. It was said: they were from Madyan, heading for Egypt. It was also said: there is an omission (ḥadhf) in the speech, its sense being: Yusuf remained in the well for three days, and his brother Yahudha (p. 290) used to bring him food secretly from his brothers. It was also said: the caravan came on the second day after he was cast into the well. It was also said: glorification (of God) was his nourishment in the well. It was said: the caravan was lost, traveling from land to land. It was also said: it was a caravan on the road that missed its way, so they alighted near the well. It was in a desolate wasteland far from settlements, frequented only by herdsmen. Among them was Malik ibn Du'r al-Khuza'i, and they sent him to seek water for them. The *wārid* is the one who comes to the water to draw it for the people. The annexation (iḍāfa) of *wārid* to the pronoun is like its annexation in the phrase "I destroyed their earner (kāsibahum)": it is not an annexation to the object, but rather the meaning is "the one who comes to them" and "the one who earns for them." The apparent meaning is that the *wārid* is one person. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "The *wārid* here may apply to one person and to a group," end of quote. The verb is construed according to the sense of the caravan (*sayyāra*) in His saying ﴿So they sent﴾. Had it been construed according to the wording, the sequence would have been "so she sent her *wārid*."

﴿So he lowered his bucket﴾, meaning: he sent it down to draw water. He said: ﴿O my good news!﴾. There is an omission in the speech, its sense being: Yusuf clung to the rope of the bucket, and when the one lowering it saw him, he said: "O my good news!" His clinging to the rope indicates his youth, for had he been eighteen or seventeen, the rope would generally not have borne him. The word *ghulām* (youth) supports this, since it is applied literally to one between the age of two and puberty, and it may also be applied to a grown man, as in the words of Layla al-Akhyaliyya about al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf:

*A youth who, when he shakes the spear, gives it drink.*

His saying "O my good news!" expresses joy and delight at Yusuf, for he saw the most beautiful of God's creation. Al-Suddi went too far in claiming that *Bushrā* is the name of a man. The speaker attributed the good news to himself, as though God Most High said: "This is from your times." The Kufans read ﴿O good news!﴾ without the annexation. Warsh narrated from Nafi': "*Yā bushrāy*," with the ya' of annexation pronounced with sukun. This is a juxtaposition of two sakins not in the manner of emphasis, and the explanation of the like of this was preceded in "*wa-maḥyāy*" (my life). Abu al-Tufayl, al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Ishaq and al-Jahdari read ﴿O good news!﴾ with the alif changed into a ya' and merged into the ya' of annexation. This is a dialect of Hudhayl and others, and its discussion was preceded in al-Baqarah at ﴿whoever follows My guidance (hudāya)﴾ [al-Baqarah: 38].

It was said: the *wārid* took him away, and when he drew near his companions he cried out with that, and they gave him good news of him and concealed him. The apparent meaning is that the pronoun refers to the caravan, of which the *wārid* was one, that is: they concealed him from the company. Or they concealed the matter of him from their finding him in the well, and they said: "The people of the water handed him over to us so that we might sell him for them in Egypt." Ibn ʿAbbas said: the pronoun in ﴿they concealed him﴾ and ﴿they sold him﴾ [Yusuf: 20] refers to Yusuf's brothers, and that they said to the company: "This is a runaway slave of ours, so buy him from us." Yusuf kept silent for fear that they would kill him. This is because it is narrated that some of them returned to the well to ascertain the matter of Yusuf and to be certain of his disappearance. When they learned that the *wārid* had taken him, they came to them and said that statement. The word *biḍāʿatan* is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl), meaning: a merchandise and a source of gain for them.

﴿And God is All-Knowing of what they do﴾, meaning: their secrets were not hidden from Him. It is a warning to them, since they sold what was not theirs. Or: God is All-Knowing of the deed of Yusuf's brothers toward their father and their brother, of evil conduct. In this is the greatest reminder of what they did to Yusuf. It was said: God revealed to him in the well that he should not inform his father or anyone else of his condition, for a wisdom He willed to carry out. What happened afterward became apparent: his appointment over the treasuries of the earth, his brothers' need of him, the raising of his parents upon the throne, and whatever followed this course of things that had been hidden in the decree.

[Part 1 of the Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah Yusuf, verses 15–19]

What appears from the context of the reports and stories is that Yusuf was young. It has been said his age at that time was seven years, and it has been said six, as al-Dahhak said. Those who said he was twelve, eighteen, both from al-Hasan, or seventeen, as Ibn al-Sa'ib said, are far removed from the truth. What indicates that he was young, to the point that he could not defend himself, is His saying: ﴿And I fear that the wolf will devour him﴾ [Yusuf: 13], (and that he would frolic and play), ﴿and indeed We are its guardians﴾ [Yusuf: 12], the caravan's taking him, the statement of the water-drawer: ﴿This is a boy!﴾, the statement of the chief of Egypt: ﴿perhaps he will benefit us, or we may adopt him as a son﴾ [Yusuf: 21], and the reports of their carrying him one after another, and his words to his brother Yahudha: "Have mercy on my weakness, my helplessness, and my youth, and have mercy on the heart of your father Ya'qub." Whoever is eighteen years old is not feared to be taken by the wolf, especially if he is in company, and it would not be said of him: ﴿and indeed We are its guardians﴾ [Yusuf: 63], because at that age he is able to devise means to save himself. Also, he would not be called "boy" except metaphorically, and it would not be said of him: ﴿or we may adopt him as a son﴾ [Yusuf: 21].

(ʿishaan) ("at nightfall") is in the accusative as an adverb of time (zarf), or it derives from (al-ashwa) ("darkness"), and (al-ʿashwa) is darkness. It is plural on the pattern (fiʿal), like (ra'in) and (ri'a') ("shepherd" and "shepherds"). Its accusative may be as a circumstantial element (hal), like the reading of al-Hasan ('ushan), on the pattern of (duja) ("darkness"), the plural of (ʿashin), from which the ta' is dropped, as it is dropped in (malik), whose original form is (malika). From al-Hasan also (ʿushayyan) with the diminutive. It has been said: they came at nightfall so that they would be better able to make excuses in the darkness. Therefore it is said: "Do not seek your need at night, for shame is in the eyes; and do not make excuses for a sin during the day, or you will stammer in your excuse." In the speech there is an omission, whose estimated form is: "And they came to their father, without Yusuf, at nightfall, weeping." Then he said: "Where is Yusuf?" They said: "We went..." It is related that when Ya'qub heard their weeping, he said: "What is wrong with you? Has something happened to the sheep?" They said: "No." He said: "Then where is Yusuf?" They said: "We went racing one another and the wolf devoured him." So he wept, cried out, and fell unconscious. They poured water over him, but he did not move. They called to him, but he did not answer. Yahudha placed his hand over the openings of his breath, but he sensed no breath and no vein moved for him. Then he said: "Woe to us from the Judge of the Day of Judgment! We lost our brother and we killed our father!" He did not recover until the cool of dawn. Al-A'mash said: "No weeping person is believed after the brothers of Yusuf."

(nastabiq) ("we race"): that is, we shoot arrows at targets, or we race on foot to see which of us runs faster, or we compete in tasks we divide among ourselves, such as watering, pasturing, and gathering firewood, or we hunt. These are four opinions.

﴿at our belongings﴾: that is, at our clothing and what we had stripped off during the racing. This also indicates that Yusuf was young, for if he were eighteen or seventeen he would have been racing with them. ﴿So the wolf devoured him﴾: We have already mentioned that they took this answer from their father's words: ﴿And I fear that the wolf will devour him﴾ [Yusuf: 13], because the wolf devouring him was the thing he most feared for him.

﴿But you will not believe us﴾: that is, you will not accept us as truthful now, ﴿even though we are truthful.﴾ Or: are you not one who accepts us as truthful in every case, even in the case of truth, because of the suspicion and dislike of Yusuf that had overcome you? We are constantly plotting against him and devising schemes against him. By their saying ﴿even though we are truthful﴾ they gave the impression that they were truthful about the wolf devouring Yusuf, so their truthfulness would be restricted to this incident. Or it means they were people of truthfulness and trust in Ya'qub's eyes before this incident, because of your great love for Yusuf. How much more so, since you now think ill of us in this incident and do not trust our words about him!

It is related that they took a young goat or a kid and slaughtered it, smeared Yusuf's shirt with its blood, and said to Ya'qub: "This is Yusuf's shirt." He took it, smeared his face with it, and wept. Then he examined it and saw no tear and no mark, so he doubted. He inferred from this the opposite of what they claimed, and said to them: "When was the wolf so gentle that it would devour Yusuf and not tear his shirt?" It was said: there were three signs in Yusuf's shirt. It was evidence for Ya'qub that Yusuf had not been eaten by the wolf, and when it was thrown over his face, he regained his sight. It was also evidence of Yusuf's innocence, when it was torn from behind.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, "What is the position of ﴿upon his shirt﴾?" I say: its position is the accusative as an adverbial of place (zarf), as if it were said: "They came with blood above his shirt," just as you say: "He came upon his camels with loads." If you ask: "Could it be a preceding circumstantial element?" I say: No, because the circumstantial element of a prepositional phrase does not precede it. End of quotation.

The meaning does not support taking (ʿala) ("upon") as an adverb of place meaning "above," because the governing verb in that case would be (jaa'u) ("they came"), and "above" cannot be an adverb of place for them. Al-Hawfi said that (ʿala) is connected to (jaa'u) but this is also not valid. As for the example al-Zamakhshari mentioned, "He came upon his camels with loads," it is possible that it is an adverb of place for the one who came, because the adverbial sense is established in it through the change from one camel to another camel, and "with loads" is in the position of a circumstantial element, meaning: accompanied by loads. Abu al-Baqa' said: ﴿upon his shirt﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial element of the blood, because the estimate is: "they came with false blood upon his shirt." Placing a circumstantial element before a preposition that is not extra is a matter of disagreement regarding its permissibility. Whoever permitted it cited as evidence that it exists in the language of the Arabs and recited examples for this, which are mentioned in the science of grammar. The meaning points to what Abu al-Baqa' said.

The majority read (kadhibin) ("false") as an adjective of (dam) ("blood") by way of emphasis, or by omitting a modified noun, meaning "blood of falsehood," since the word indicates falsehood, it is described by it, even though the falsehood came from someone else. Zayd ibn 'Ali read (kadhiban) ("falsely") in the accusative, which may be a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial element, or an object of purpose. 'A'isha and al-Hasan read (kadibin) with the letter dal without a dot, and it was explained as "turbid," and it was said "fresh," and it was said "dry." The author of al-Lawami' said: its meaning is "with a mark," that is, a trace, because (al-kadhib) is a whiteness that appears on the nails of young men and affects them, so it is like a design. That whiteness is called al-Fawf, so this is a metaphor for its effect on the shirt, like the effect of that on the nails.

He said: ﴿Rather, your own souls have made [a matter] seem good to you﴾: here an element is omitted, its estimate being: "The wolf did not devour him, rather your souls made it seem good." Ibn 'Abbas said: "You commanded yourselves to do a matter." Qatadah said: "Adorned it for you." It was said: "They were pleased with a matter," that is, an ugly deed. It was also said: "They made it easy." ﴿So patience is beautiful﴾: that is, my affair is beautiful patience, or: beautiful patience is better. Ubayy, al-Ashhab, and 'Isa ibn 'Umar read (sabran jamilan) ("patience, beautiful") with both in the accusative, and so it is in the codex of Ubayy and the codex of Anas ibn Malik, and it is related likewise from al-Kisa'i. They put it in the accusative as a declarative verbal noun, meaning: "So be patient with beautiful patience." It has been said this is a weak reading according to Sibawayh, and that the accusative in such a case is appropriate only with a command. Likewise the accusative is appropriate in the line:

*My camel complained to me of the length of the journey: "Patience, beautiful patience, for both of us are tested."*

﴿And Allah is the One whose help is sought against what you describe.﴾

﴿A caravan came and they sent their water-drawer, and he let down his bucket.﴾ He said: "O good news!"

[End of part 1]

Abu Hayyan's commentary (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 12, verses 15–19 (part 2 of 2):

It is also narrated in the line of poetry as "ṣabrun jamīlun" (nominative). The reading in the accusative (naṣb), *ṣabran jamīlan*, is sound only if we assume that Ya'qub turned to addressing himself, as though he said: "Be patient, O self, with beautiful patience." In a hadith: "Beautiful patience is that which contains no complaint," meaning complaint to creation. Do you not see His saying: ﴿I only complain of my anguish and my grief to God﴾ [Yusuf: 86]? It was also said: "I will display patience before you, so I will not keep company with you in gloom of face and frowning brow, but rather as I was with you." Al-Thawri said: "Part of patience is that you do not speak of what pains you, nor of your calamity, and that you do not weep for yourself."

﴿And God is the One whose help is sought﴾, meaning: the One from whom aid is requested to bear what you describe of Yusuf's destruction, and to endure the calamity.

﴿A caravan came﴾. It was said: they were from Madyan, heading for Egypt. It was also said: there is an omission (ḥadhf) in the speech, its sense being: Yusuf remained in the well for three days, and his brother Yahudha (p. 290) used to bring him food secretly from his brothers. It was also said: the caravan came on the second day after he was cast into the well. It was also said: glorification (of God) was his nourishment in the well. It was said: the caravan was lost, traveling from land to land. It was also said: it was a caravan on the road that missed its way, so they alighted near the well. It was in a desolate wasteland far from settlements, frequented only by herdsmen. Among them was Malik ibn Du'r al-Khuza'i, and they sent him to seek water for them. The *wārid* is the one who comes to the water to draw it for the people. The annexation (iḍāfa) of *wārid* to the pronoun is like its annexation in the phrase "I destroyed their earner (kāsibahum)": it is not an annexation to the object, but rather the meaning is "the one who comes to them" and "the one who earns for them." The apparent meaning is that the *wārid* is one person. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "The *wārid* here may apply to one person and to a group," end of quote. The verb is construed according to the sense of the caravan (*sayyāra*) in His saying ﴿So they sent﴾. Had it been construed according to the wording, the sequence would have been "so she sent her *wārid*."

﴿So he lowered his bucket﴾, meaning: he sent it down to draw water. He said: ﴿O my good news!﴾. There is an omission in the speech, its sense being: Yusuf clung to the rope of the bucket, and when the one lowering it saw him, he said: "O my good news!" His clinging to the rope indicates his youth, for had he been eighteen or seventeen, the rope would generally not have borne him. The word *ghulām* (youth) supports this, since it is applied literally to one between the age of two and puberty, and it may also be applied to a grown man, as in the words of Layla al-Akhyaliyya about al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf:

*A youth who, when he shakes the spear, gives it drink.*

His saying "O my good news!" expresses joy and delight at Yusuf, for he saw the most beautiful of God's creation. Al-Suddi went too far in claiming that *Bushrā* is the name of a man. The speaker attributed the good news to himself, as though God Most High said: "This is from your times." The Kufans read ﴿O good news!﴾ without the annexation. Warsh narrated from Nafi': "*Yā bushrāy*," with the ya' of annexation pronounced with sukun. This is a juxtaposition of two sakins not in the manner of emphasis, and the explanation of the like of this was preceded in "*wa-maḥyāy*" (my life). Abu al-Tufayl, al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Ishaq and al-Jahdari read ﴿O good news!﴾ with the alif changed into a ya' and merged into the ya' of annexation. This is a dialect of Hudhayl and others, and its discussion was preceded in al-Baqarah at ﴿whoever follows My guidance (hudāya)﴾ [al-Baqarah: 38].

It was said: the *wārid* took him away, and when he drew near his companions he cried out with that, and they gave him good news of him and concealed him. The apparent meaning is that the pronoun refers to the caravan, of which the *wārid* was one, that is: they concealed him from the company. Or they concealed the matter of him from their finding him in the well, and they said: "The people of the water handed him over to us so that we might sell him for them in Egypt." Ibn ʿAbbas said: the pronoun in ﴿they concealed him﴾ and ﴿they sold him﴾ [Yusuf: 20] refers to Yusuf's brothers, and that they said to the company: "This is a runaway slave of ours, so buy him from us." Yusuf kept silent for fear that they would kill him. This is because it is narrated that some of them returned to the well to ascertain the matter of Yusuf and to be certain of his disappearance. When they learned that the *wārid* had taken him, they came to them and said that statement. The word *biḍāʿatan* is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl), meaning: a merchandise and a source of gain for them.

﴿And God is All-Knowing of what they do﴾, meaning: their secrets were not hidden from Him. It is a warning to them, since they sold what was not theirs. Or: God is All-Knowing of the deed of Yusuf's brothers toward their father and their brother, of evil conduct. In this is the greatest reminder of what they did to Yusuf. It was said: God revealed to him in the well that he should not inform his father or anyone else of his condition, for a wisdom He willed to carry out. What happened afterward became apparent: his appointment over the treasuries of the earth, his brothers' need of him, the raising of his parents upon the throne, and whatever followed this course of things that had been hidden in the decree.

[Part 1 of the Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah Yusuf, verses 15–19]

﴿So when they took him away and agreed to put him into the depths of the well. And We revealed to him: "You will surely inform them of this matter of theirs, while they do not perceive."﴾ ﴿And they came to their father at nightfall, weeping.﴾ ﴿They said: "O our father, we went racing one another and left Yusuf with our belongings, and the wolf devoured him. But you will not believe us, even though we are truthful."﴾ ﴿And they brought his shirt stained with false blood. He said: "Rather, your own souls have made a matter seem good to you. So patience is beautiful, and Allah is the One whose help is sought against what you describe."﴾ ﴿And a caravan came, and they sent their water-drawer, and he let down his bucket. He said: "O good news! This is a boy!" And they hid him as merchandise, and Allah knows what they were doing.﴾

[p. 287] It is related that they said to Yusuf: "Ask your father to send you with us." So he turned to Yusuf and said: "Do you want that?" He said: "Yes." Ya'qub said: "If it is tomorrow, I will give you permission." When morning came, Yusuf put on his clothes and tied his belt around himself, and went out with his brothers. Ya'qub bade them farewell and said: "O my sons, I charge you with fear of Allah, and with (caring for) my beloved Yusuf." Then he turned to Yusuf, embraced him to his chest, kissed him between his eyes, and said: "I entrust you to Allah, Lord of the worlds." Then he turned back. They carried Yusuf on their shoulders for as long as Ya'qub could see them. Then, when they were out of his sight, they threw him down so that he would run with them, in order to harm him. The commentators have mentioned many things that describe how he was put into the depths of the well and how they treated him, things that would soften a rock, yet they only grew harder. Neither the Qur'an nor an authentic hadith addressed any of these things, so that they could be relied upon from the books of tafsir. Between this sentence and the sentences before it there is an omitted element, which the meaning indicates, and its estimated wording is: "So he granted them what they asked and sent Yusuf with them."

﴿So when they took him away and agreed﴾: that is, they resolved and agreed to cast him into the well. The phrase ﴿an yaj'aluhu﴾ ("that they should put him") is the object of (ajma'u) ("they agreed"). It is said: ajma'a al-amr and azma'ahu, meaning "he resolved upon it." It is possible that al-ja'l (putting) here means "casting" and also "making" (i.e., transforming). The grammarians differed regarding the answer of (lamma) ("when"): is it expressed or omitted? Whoever says it is expressed says that it is their statement ﴿They said: "O our father, we went racing one another"﴾, meaning: when such and such happened, they said. This is a good interpretation. It has also been said that the answer is (awhayna) ("We revealed"), and the waw is extra. According to this view, the Kufan school holds that (idha) and (hatta) may take an extra element after (lamma). On this basis they explained His saying: ﴿So when they both submitted and he laid him down upon his forehead﴾ [al-Saffat: 103], meaning "and We called him," and His saying: ﴿until, when they came to it and its gates were opened﴾ [al-Zumar: 73], meaning "its gates were opened." And the line of Imru' al-Qays:

*So when we crossed the courtyard of the tribe and he inclined,*

meaning: "he inclined." Whoever says it is omitted, which is the view of the Basran school, al-Zamakhshari estimated it as: "they did to him what they did of harm," and he related the long account of what they did to him and what they said to him and he to them. Some estimated it as: "So when they took him away and agreed to put him into the depths of the well, their trial became great." Others estimated it as: "They put him into it," and this is better, since His saying ﴿and agreed that they should put him﴾ indicates it. The apparent reading is that the pronoun in ﴿And We revealed to him﴾ refers to Yusuf, and it was an inspiration of inner conviction (ilham), as Mujahid said. It has also been related from Ibn 'Abbas that it was a dream. Al-Dahhak and Qatadah said: Jibril descended to him in the well. Al-Hasan said: Allah gave him prophethood in the well while he was young, just as He revealed to Yahya and 'Isa, peace be upon them both. This is the apparent meaning of (awhayna). That the pronoun refers to Yusuf is supported by His saying, when he said to them: ﴿Do you know what you did to Yusuf and his brother when you were ignorant?﴾ [Yusuf: 89]. It has also been said that the pronoun in (ilayhi) refers to Ya'qub, and the revelation was sent to him [p. 288] so that he would find comfort in the darkness of loneliness, and so that he would be given good news of what his affair would lead to. Its meaning is: for deliverance from what you are in. "And you will tell your brothers of what they did to you." The phrase ﴿while they do not perceive﴾ is a circumstantial clause (jumla haliyya) following His saying ﴿You will surely inform them of this matter of theirs﴾, meaning: they will not know, at the time of the informing, that you are Yusuf. This was said by Ibn Jurayj. That is because of your high rank and the greatness of your authority, the distance of your condition from their minds, and the long passage of time which changes appearances and forms. It is mentioned that when they entered upon him seeking provisions, he recognized them while they did not recognize him. He called for the drinking cup, placed it on his hand, struck it, and it hummed. He said: "This cup informs me that you had a brother from your father, called Yusuf, whom he preferred over you. You took him away, threw him into the depths of the well, and you told your father: 'The wolf devoured him,' and he was sold for a paltry price."

It is also permissible that ﴿while they do not perceive﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) from (awhayna) ("We revealed"), meaning: while they do not perceive. This was said by Qatadah, that is: by Our revelation to you and what We informed you of your deliverance and your long life, until you inform them of what they did to you.
