The author of al-Lawami' said: its meaning is "with a mark," that is, a trace, because (al-kadhib) is a whiteness that appears on the nails of young men and affects them, so it is like a design. That whiteness is called al-Fawf, so this is a metaphor for its effect on the shirt, like the effect of that on the nails.

He said: ﴿Rather, your own souls have made [a matter] seem good to you﴾: here an element is omitted, its estimate being: "The wolf did not devour him, rather your souls made it seem good." Ibn 'Abbas said: "You commanded yourselves to do a matter." Qatadah said: "Adorned it for you." It was said: "They were pleased with a matter," that is, an ugly deed. It was also said: "They made it easy." ﴿So patience is beautiful﴾: that is, my affair is beautiful patience, or: beautiful patience is better. Ubayy, al-Ashhab, and 'Isa ibn 'Umar read (sabran jamilan) ("patience, beautiful") with both in the accusative, and so it is in the codex of Ubayy and the codex of Anas ibn Malik, and it is related likewise from al-Kisa'i. They put it in the accusative as a declarative verbal noun, meaning: "So be patient with beautiful patience." It has been said this is a weak reading according to Sibawayh, and that the accusative in such a case is appropriate only with a command. Likewise the accusative is appropriate in the line:

*My camel complained to me of the length of the journey: "Patience, beautiful patience, for both of us are tested."*

﴿And Allah is the One whose help is sought against what you describe.﴾

﴿A caravan came and they sent their water-drawer, and he let down his bucket.﴾ He said: "O good news!"

[End of part 1]

Abu Hayyan's commentary (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 12, verses 15–19 (part 2 of 2):

It is also narrated in the line of poetry as "ṣabrun jamīlun" (nominative). The reading in the accusative (naṣb), *ṣabran jamīlan*, is sound only if we assume that Ya'qub turned to addressing himself, as though he said: "Be patient, O self, with beautiful patience." In a hadith: "Beautiful patience is that which contains no complaint," meaning complaint to creation. Do you not see His saying: ﴿I only complain of my anguish and my grief to God﴾ [Yusuf: 86]? It was also said: "I will display patience before you, so I will not keep company with you in gloom of face and frowning brow, but rather as I was with you." Al-Thawri said: "Part of patience is that you do not speak of what pains you, nor of your calamity, and that you do not weep for yourself."

﴿And God is the One whose help is sought﴾, meaning: the One from whom aid is requested to bear what you describe of Yusuf's destruction, and to endure the calamity.

﴿A caravan came﴾. It was said: they were from Madyan, heading for Egypt. It was also said: there is an omission (ḥadhf) in the speech, its sense being: Yusuf remained in the well for three days, and his brother Yahudha (p. 290) used to bring him food secretly from his brothers. It was also said: the caravan came on the second day after he was cast into the well. It was also said: glorification (of God) was his nourishment in the well. It was said: the caravan was lost, traveling from land to land. It was also said: it was a caravan on the road that missed its way, so they alighted near the well. It was in a desolate wasteland far from settlements, frequented only by herdsmen. Among them was Malik ibn Du'r al-Khuza'i, and they sent him to seek water for them. The *wārid* is the one who comes to the water to draw it for the people. The annexation (iḍāfa) of *wārid* to the pronoun is like its annexation in the phrase "I destroyed their earner (kāsibahum)": it is not an annexation to the object, but rather the meaning is "the one who comes to them" and "the one who earns for them." The apparent meaning is that the *wārid* is one person. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "The *wārid* here may apply to one person and to a group," end of quote. The verb is construed according to the sense of the caravan (*sayyāra*) in His saying ﴿So they sent﴾. Had it been construed according to the wording, the sequence would have been "so she sent her *wārid*."

﴿So he lowered his bucket﴾, meaning: he sent it down to draw water. He said: ﴿O my good news!﴾. There is an omission in the speech, its sense being: Yusuf clung to the rope of the bucket, and when the one lowering it saw him, he said: "O my good news!" His clinging to the rope indicates his youth, for had he been eighteen or seventeen, the rope would generally not have borne him. The word *ghulām* (youth) supports this, since it is applied literally to one between the age of two and puberty, and it may also be applied to a grown man, as in the words of Layla al-Akhyaliyya about al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf:

*A youth who, when he shakes the spear, gives it drink.*

His saying "O my good news!" expresses joy and delight at Yusuf, for he saw the most beautiful of God's creation. Al-Suddi went too far in claiming that *Bushrā* is the name of a man. The speaker attributed the good news to himself, as though God Most High said: "This is from your times." The Kufans read ﴿O good news!﴾ without the annexation. Warsh narrated from Nafi': "*Yā bushrāy*," with the ya' of annexation pronounced with sukun. This is a juxtaposition of two sakins not in the manner of emphasis, and the explanation of the like of this was preceded in "*wa-maḥyāy*" (my life). Abu al-Tufayl, al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Ishaq and al-Jahdari read ﴿O good news!﴾ with the alif changed into a ya' and merged into the ya' of annexation. This is a dialect of Hudhayl and others, and its discussion was preceded in al-Baqarah at ﴿whoever follows My guidance (hudāya)﴾ [al-Baqarah: 38].

It was said: the *wārid* took him away, and when he drew near his companions he cried out with that, and they gave him good news of him and concealed him. The apparent meaning is that the pronoun refers to the caravan, of which the *wārid* was one, that is: they concealed him from the company. Or they concealed the matter of him from their finding him in the well, and they said: "The people of the water handed him over to us so that we might sell him for them in Egypt." Ibn ʿAbbas said: the pronoun in ﴿they concealed him﴾ and ﴿they sold him﴾ [Yusuf: 20] refers to Yusuf's brothers, and that they said to the company: "This is a runaway slave of ours, so buy him from us." Yusuf kept silent for fear that they would kill him. This is because it is narrated that some of them returned to the well to ascertain the matter of Yusuf and to be certain of his disappearance. When they learned that the *wārid* had taken him, they came to them and said that statement. The word *biḍāʿatan* is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl), meaning: a merchandise and a source of gain for them.

﴿And God is All-Knowing of what they do﴾, meaning: their secrets were not hidden from Him. It is a warning to them, since they sold what was not theirs. Or: God is All-Knowing of the deed of Yusuf's brothers toward their father and their brother, of evil conduct. In this is the greatest reminder of what they did to Yusuf. It was said: God revealed to him in the well that he should not inform his father or anyone else of his condition, for a wisdom He willed to carry out. What happened afterward became apparent: his appointment over the treasuries of the earth, his brothers' need of him, the raising of his parents upon the throne, and whatever followed this course of things that had been hidden in the decree.

[Part 1 of the Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah Yusuf, verses 15–19]

﴿So when they took him away and agreed to put him into the depths of the well. And We revealed to him: "You will surely inform them of this matter of theirs, while they do not perceive."﴾ ﴿And they came to their father at nightfall, weeping.﴾ ﴿They said: "O our father, we went racing one another and left Yusuf with our belongings, and the wolf devoured him. But you will not believe us, even though we are truthful."﴾ ﴿And they brought his shirt stained with false blood. He said: "Rather, your own souls have made a matter seem good to you. So patience is beautiful, and Allah is the One whose help is sought against what you describe."﴾ ﴿And a caravan came, and they sent their water-drawer, and he let down his bucket. He said: "O good news! This is a boy!" And they hid him as merchandise, and Allah knows what they were doing.﴾

[p. 287] It is related that they said to Yusuf: "Ask your father to send you with us." So he turned to Yusuf and said: "Do you want that?" He said: "Yes." Ya'qub said: "If it is tomorrow, I will give you permission." When morning came, Yusuf put on his clothes and tied his belt around himself, and went out with his brothers. Ya'qub bade them farewell and said: "O my sons, I charge you with fear of Allah, and with (caring for) my beloved Yusuf." Then he turned to Yusuf, embraced him to his chest, kissed him between his eyes, and said: "I entrust you to Allah, Lord of the worlds." Then he turned back. They carried Yusuf on their shoulders for as long as Ya'qub could see them. Then, when they were out of his sight, they threw him down so that he would run with them, in order to harm him. The commentators have mentioned many things that describe how he was put into the depths of the well and how they treated him, things that would soften a rock, yet they only grew harder. Neither the Qur'an nor an authentic hadith addressed any of these things, so that they could be relied upon from the books of tafsir. Between this sentence and the sentences before it there is an omitted element, which the meaning indicates, and its estimated wording is: "So he granted them what they asked and sent Yusuf with them."

﴿So when they took him away and agreed﴾: that is, they resolved and agreed to cast him into the well. The phrase ﴿an yaj'aluhu﴾ ("that they should put him") is the object of (ajma'u) ("they agreed"). It is said: ajma'a al-amr and azma'ahu, meaning "he resolved upon it." It is possible that al-ja'l (putting) here means "casting" and also "making" (i.e., transforming). The grammarians differed regarding the answer of (lamma) ("when"): is it expressed or omitted? Whoever says it is expressed says that it is their statement ﴿They said: "O our father, we went racing one another"﴾, meaning: when such and such happened, they said. This is a good interpretation. It has also been said that the answer is (awhayna) ("We revealed"), and the waw is extra. According to this view, the Kufan school holds that (idha) and (hatta) may take an extra element after (lamma). On this basis they explained His saying: ﴿So when they both submitted and he laid him down upon his forehead﴾ [al-Saffat: 103], meaning "and We called him," and His saying: ﴿until, when they came to it and its gates were opened﴾ [al-Zumar: 73], meaning "its gates were opened." And the line of Imru' al-Qays:

*So when we crossed the courtyard of the tribe and he inclined,*

meaning: "he inclined." Whoever says it is omitted, which is the view of the Basran school, al-Zamakhshari estimated it as: "they did to him what they did of harm," and he related the long account of what they did to him and what they said to him and he to them. Some estimated it as: "So when they took him away and agreed to put him into the depths of the well, their trial became great." Others estimated it as: "They put him into it," and this is better, since His saying ﴿and agreed that they should put him﴾ indicates it. The apparent reading is that the pronoun in ﴿And We revealed to him﴾ refers to Yusuf, and it was an inspiration of inner conviction (ilham), as Mujahid said. It has also been related from Ibn 'Abbas that it was a dream. Al-Dahhak and Qatadah said: Jibril descended to him in the well. Al-Hasan said: Allah gave him prophethood in the well while he was young, just as He revealed to Yahya and 'Isa, peace be upon them both. This is the apparent meaning of (awhayna). That the pronoun refers to Yusuf is supported by His saying, when he said to them: ﴿Do you know what you did to Yusuf and his brother when you were ignorant?﴾ [Yusuf: 89]. It has also been said that the pronoun in (ilayhi) refers to Ya'qub, and the revelation was sent to him [p. 288] so that he would find comfort in the darkness of loneliness, and so that he would be given good news of what his affair would lead to. Its meaning is: for deliverance from what you are in. "And you will tell your brothers of what they did to you." The phrase ﴿while they do not perceive﴾ is a circumstantial clause (jumla haliyya) following His saying ﴿You will surely inform them of this matter of theirs﴾, meaning: they will not know, at the time of the informing, that you are Yusuf. This was said by Ibn Jurayj. That is because of your high rank and the greatness of your authority, the distance of your condition from their minds, and the long passage of time which changes appearances and forms. It is mentioned that when they entered upon him seeking provisions, he recognized them while they did not recognize him. He called for the drinking cup, placed it on his hand, struck it, and it hummed. He said: "This cup informs me that you had a brother from your father, called Yusuf, whom he preferred over you. You took him away, threw him into the depths of the well, and you told your father: 'The wolf devoured him,' and he was sold for a paltry price."

It is also permissible that ﴿while they do not perceive﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) from (awhayna) ("We revealed"), meaning: while they do not perceive. This was said by Qatadah, that is: by Our revelation to you and what We informed you of your deliverance and your long life, until you inform them of what they did to you. The reading of the majority is ﴿latunabbi'annahum﴾ with the second-person address (ta' al-khitab), while Ibn 'Umar read it with the third-person (ya' al-ghayba), and so it is in some Basran codices. And (salamun) was read with a nun.

What appears from the context of the reports and stories is that Yusuf was young. It has been said his age at that time was seven years, and it has been said six, as al-Dahhak said. Those who said he was twelve, eighteen, both from al-Hasan, or seventeen, as Ibn al-Sa'ib said, are far removed from the truth. What indicates that he was young, to the point that he could not defend himself, is His saying: ﴿And I fear that the wolf will devour him﴾ [Yusuf: 13], (and that he would frolic and play), ﴿and indeed We are its guardians﴾ [Yusuf: 12], the caravan's taking him, the statement of the water-drawer: ﴿This is a boy!﴾, the statement of the chief of Egypt: ﴿perhaps he will benefit us, or we may adopt him as a son﴾ [Yusuf: 21], and the reports of their carrying him one after another, and his words to his brother Yahudha: "Have mercy on my weakness, my helplessness, and my youth, and have mercy on the heart of your father Ya'qub." Whoever is eighteen years old is not feared to be taken by the wolf, especially if he is in company, and it would not be said of him: ﴿and indeed We are its guardians﴾ [Yusuf: 63], because at that age he is able to devise means to save himself. Also, he would not be called "boy" except metaphorically, and it would not be said of him: ﴿or we may adopt him as a son﴾ [Yusuf: 21].

(ʿishaan) ("at nightfall") is in the accusative as an adverb of time (zarf), or it derives from (al-ashwa) ("darkness"), and (al-ʿashwa) is darkness. It is plural on the pattern (fiʿal), like (ra'in) and (ri'a') ("shepherd" and "shepherds"). Its accusative may be as a circumstantial element (hal), like the reading of al-Hasan ('ushan), on the pattern of (duja) ("darkness"), the plural of (ʿashin), from which the ta' is dropped, as it is dropped in (malik), whose original form is (malika). From al-Hasan also (ʿushayyan) with the diminutive. It has been said: they came at nightfall so that they would be better able to make excuses in the darkness. Therefore it is said: "Do not seek your need at night, for shame is in the eyes; and do not make excuses for a sin during the day, or you will stammer in your excuse." In the speech there is an omission, whose estimated form is: "And they came to their father, without Yusuf, at nightfall, weeping." Then he said: "Where is Yusuf?" They said: "We went..." It is related that when Ya'qub heard their weeping, he said: "What is wrong with you? Has something happened to the sheep?" They said: "No." He said: "Then where is Yusuf?" They said: "We went racing one another and the wolf devoured him." So he wept, cried out, and fell unconscious. They poured water over him, but he did not move. They called to him, but he did not answer. Yahudha placed his hand over the openings of his breath, but he sensed no breath and no vein moved for him. Then he said: "Woe to us from the Judge of the Day of Judgment! We lost our brother and we killed our father!" He did not recover until the cool of dawn. Al-A'mash said: "No weeping person is believed after the brothers of Yusuf."

(nastabiq) ("we race"): that is, we shoot arrows at targets, or we race on foot to see which of us runs faster, or we compete in tasks we divide among ourselves, such as watering, pasturing, and gathering firewood, or we hunt. These are four opinions.

﴿at our belongings﴾: that is, at our clothing and what we had stripped off during the racing. This also indicates that Yusuf was young, for if he were eighteen or seventeen he would have been racing with them. ﴿So the wolf devoured him﴾: We have already mentioned that they took this answer from their father's words: ﴿And I fear that the wolf will devour him﴾ [Yusuf: 13], because the wolf devouring him was the thing he most feared for him.

﴿But you will not believe us﴾: that is, you will not accept us as truthful now, ﴿even though we are truthful.﴾ Or: are you not one who accepts us as truthful in every case, even in the case of truth, because of the suspicion and dislike of Yusuf that had overcome you? We are constantly plotting against him and devising schemes against him. By their saying ﴿even though we are truthful﴾ they gave the impression that they were truthful about the wolf devouring Yusuf, so their truthfulness would be restricted to this incident. Or it means they were people of truthfulness and trust in Ya'qub's eyes before this incident, because of your great love for Yusuf. How much more so, since you now think ill of us in this incident and do not trust our words about him!

It is related that they took a young goat or a kid and slaughtered it, smeared Yusuf's shirt with its blood, and said to Ya'qub: "This is Yusuf's shirt." He took it, smeared his face with it, and wept. Then he examined it and saw no tear and no mark, so he doubted. He inferred from this the opposite of what they claimed, and said to them: "When was the wolf so gentle that it would devour Yusuf and not tear his shirt?" It was said: there were three signs in Yusuf's shirt. It was evidence for Ya'qub that Yusuf had not been eaten by the wolf, and when it was thrown over his face, he regained his sight. It was also evidence of Yusuf's innocence, when it was torn from behind.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, "What is the position of ﴿upon his shirt﴾?" I say: its position is the accusative as an adverbial of place (zarf), as if it were said: "They came with blood above his shirt," just as you say: "He came upon his camels with loads." If you ask: "Could it be a preceding circumstantial element?" I say: No, because the circumstantial element of a prepositional phrase does not precede it. End of quotation.

The meaning does not support taking (ʿala) ("upon") as an adverb of place meaning "above," because the governing verb in that case would be (jaa'u) ("they came"), and "above" cannot be an adverb of place for them. Al-Hawfi said that (ʿala) is connected to (jaa'u) but this is also not valid. As for the example al-Zamakhshari mentioned, "He came upon his camels with loads," it is possible that it is an adverb of place for the one who came, because the adverbial sense is established in it through the change from one camel to another camel, and "with loads" is in the position of a circumstantial element, meaning: accompanied by loads. Abu al-Baqa' said: ﴿upon his shirt﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial element of the blood, because the estimate is: "they came with false blood upon his shirt." Placing a circumstantial element before a preposition that is not extra is a matter of disagreement regarding its permissibility. Whoever permitted it cited as evidence that it exists in the language of the Arabs and recited examples for this, which are mentioned in the science of grammar. The meaning points to what Abu al-Baqa' said.

The majority read (kadhibin) ("false") as an adjective of (dam) ("blood") by way of emphasis, or by omitting a modified noun, meaning "blood of falsehood," since the word indicates falsehood, it is described by it, even though the falsehood came from someone else. Zayd ibn 'Ali read (kadhiban) ("falsely") in the accusative, which may be a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial element, or an object of purpose. 'A'isha and al-Hasan read (kadibin) with the letter dal without a dot, and it was explained as "turbid," and it was said "fresh," and it was said "dry." That whiteness is called al-Fawf, so this is a metaphor for its effect on the shirt, like the effect of that on the nails.

He said: ﴿Rather, your own souls have made [a matter] seem good to you﴾: here an element is omitted, its estimate being: "The wolf did not devour him, rather your souls made it seem good." Ibn 'Abbas said: "You commanded yourselves to do a matter." Qatadah said: "Adorned it for you." It was said: "They were pleased with a matter," that is, an ugly deed. It was also said: "They made it easy." ﴿So patience is beautiful﴾: that is, my affair is beautiful patience, or: beautiful patience is better. ﴿And Allah is the One whose help is sought against what you describe.﴾

﴿A caravan came and they sent their water-drawer, and he let down his bucket.﴾ He said: "O good news!"

[End of part 1]

The word *biḍāʿatan* is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl), meaning: a merchandise and a source of gain for them.

﴿And God is All-Knowing of what they do﴾, meaning: their secrets were not hidden from Him. It is a warning to them, since they sold what was not theirs. Or: God is All-Knowing of the deed of Yusuf's brothers toward their father and their brother, of evil conduct. In this is the greatest reminder of what they did to Yusuf. It was said: God revealed to him in the well that he should not inform his father or anyone else of his condition, for a wisdom He willed to carry out. What happened afterward became apparent: his appointment over the treasuries of the earth, his brothers' need of him, the raising of his parents upon the throne, and whatever followed this course of things that had been hidden in the decree.

[Part 1 of the Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah Yusuf, verses 15–19]

﴿So when they took him away and agreed to put him into the depths of the well. And We revealed to him: "You will surely inform them of this matter of theirs, while they do not perceive."﴾ ﴿And they came to their father at nightfall, weeping.﴾ ﴿They said: "O our father, we went racing one another and left Yusuf with our belongings, and the wolf devoured him. But you will not believe us, even though we are truthful."﴾ ﴿And they brought his shirt stained with false blood. He said: "Rather, your own souls have made a matter seem good to you. So patience is beautiful, and Allah is the One whose help is sought against what you describe."﴾ ﴿And a caravan came, and they sent their water-drawer, and he let down his bucket. He said: "O good news! This is a boy!" And they hid him as merchandise, and Allah knows what they were doing.﴾

[p. 287] It is related that they said to Yusuf: "Ask your father to send you with us." So he turned to Yusuf and said: "Do you want that?" He said: "Yes." Ya'qub said: "If it is tomorrow, I will give you permission." When morning came, Yusuf put on his clothes and tied his belt around himself, and went out with his brothers. Ya'qub bade them farewell and said: "O my sons, I charge you with fear of Allah, and with (caring for) my beloved Yusuf." Then he turned to Yusuf, embraced him to his chest, kissed him between his eyes, and said: "I entrust you to Allah, Lord of the worlds." Then he turned back. They carried Yusuf on their shoulders for as long as Ya'qub could see them. Then, when they were out of his sight, they threw him down so that he would run with them, in order to harm him. The commentators have mentioned many things that describe how he was put into the depths of the well and how they treated him, things that would soften a rock, yet they only grew harder. Neither the Qur'an nor an authentic hadith addressed any of these things, so that they could be relied upon from the books of tafsir. Between this sentence and the sentences before it there is an omitted element, which the meaning indicates, and its estimated wording is: "So he granted them what they asked and sent Yusuf with them."

﴿So when they took him away and agreed﴾: that is, they resolved and agreed to cast him into the well. The phrase ﴿an yaj'aluhu﴾ ("that they should put him") is the object of (ajma'u) ("they agreed"). It is said: ajma'a al-amr and azma'ahu, meaning "he resolved upon it." It is possible that al-ja'l (putting) here means "casting" and also "making" (i.e., transforming). The grammarians differed regarding the answer of (lamma) ("when"): is it expressed or omitted? Whoever says it is expressed says that it is their statement ﴿They said: "O our father, we went racing one another"﴾, meaning: when such and such happened, they said. This is a good interpretation. It has also been said that the answer is (awhayna) ("We revealed"), and the waw is extra. According to this view, the Kufan school holds that (idha) and (hatta) may take an extra element after (lamma). On this basis they explained His saying: ﴿So when they both submitted and he laid him down upon his forehead﴾ [al-Saffat: 103], meaning "and We called him," and His saying: ﴿until, when they came to it and its gates were opened﴾ [al-Zumar: 73], meaning "its gates were opened." And the line of Imru' al-Qays:

*So when we crossed the courtyard of the tribe and he inclined,*

meaning: "he inclined." Whoever says it is omitted, which is the view of the Basran school, al-Zamakhshari estimated it as: "they did to him what they did of harm," and he related the long account of what they did to him and what they said to him and he to them. Some estimated it as: "So when they took him away and agreed to put him into the depths of the well, their trial became great." Others estimated it as: "They put him into it," and this is better, since His saying ﴿and agreed that they should put him﴾ indicates it. The apparent reading is that the pronoun in ﴿And We revealed to him﴾ refers to Yusuf, and it was an inspiration of inner conviction (ilham), as Mujahid said. It has also been related from Ibn 'Abbas that it was a dream. Al-Dahhak and Qatadah said: Jibril descended to him in the well. Al-Hasan said: Allah gave him prophethood in the well while he was young, just as He revealed to Yahya and 'Isa, peace be upon them both. This is the apparent meaning of (awhayna). That the pronoun refers to Yusuf is supported by His saying, when he said to them: ﴿Do you know what you did to Yusuf and his brother when you were ignorant?﴾ [Yusuf: 89]. It has also been said that the pronoun in (ilayhi) refers to Ya'qub, and the revelation was sent to him [p. 288] so that he would find comfort in the darkness of loneliness, and so that he would be given good news of what his affair would lead to. Its meaning is: for deliverance from what you are in. "And you will tell your brothers of what they did to you." The phrase ﴿while they do not perceive﴾ is a circumstantial clause (jumla haliyya) following His saying ﴿You will surely inform them of this matter of theirs﴾, meaning: they will not know, at the time of the informing, that you are Yusuf. This was said by Ibn Jurayj. That is because of your high rank and the greatness of your authority, the distance of your condition from their minds, and the long passage of time which changes appearances and forms. It is mentioned that when they entered upon him seeking provisions, he recognized them while they did not recognize him. He called for the drinking cup, placed it on his hand, struck it, and it hummed. He said: "This cup informs me that you had a brother from your father, called Yusuf, whom he preferred over you. You took him away, threw him into the depths of the well, and you told your father: 'The wolf devoured him,' and he was sold for a paltry price."

It is also permissible that ﴿while they do not perceive﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) from (awhayna) ("We revealed"), meaning: while they do not perceive. This was said by Qatadah, that is: by Our revelation to you and what We informed you of your deliverance and your long life, until you inform them of what they did to you. The reading of the majority is ﴿latunabbi'annahum﴾ with the second-person address (ta' al-khitab), while Ibn 'Umar read it with the third-person (ya' al-ghayba), and so it is in some Basran codices. And (salamun) was read with a nun.

What appears from the context of the reports and stories is that Yusuf was young. It has been said his age at that time was seven years, and it has been said six, as al-Dahhak said. Those who said he was twelve, eighteen, both from al-Hasan, or seventeen, as Ibn al-Sa'ib said, are far removed from the truth. What indicates that he was young, to the point that he could not defend himself, is His saying: ﴿And I fear that the wolf will devour him﴾ [Yusuf: 13], (and that he would frolic and play), ﴿and indeed We are its guardians﴾ [Yusuf: 12], the caravan's taking him, the statement of the water-drawer: ﴿This is a boy!﴾, the statement of the chief of Egypt: ﴿perhaps he will benefit us, or we may adopt him as a son﴾ [Yusuf: 21], and the reports of their carrying him one after another, and his words to his brother Yahudha: "Have mercy on my weakness, my helplessness, and my youth, and have mercy on the heart of your father Ya'qub." Whoever is eighteen years old is not feared to be taken by the wolf, especially if he is in company, and it would not be said of him: ﴿and indeed We are its guardians﴾ [Yusuf: 63], because at that age he is able to devise means to save himself. Also, he would not be called "boy" except metaphorically, and it would not be said of him: ﴿or we may adopt him as a son﴾ [Yusuf: 21].

(ʿishaan) ("at nightfall") is in the accusative as an adverb of time (zarf), or it derives from (al-ashwa) ("darkness"), and (al-ʿashwa) is darkness. It is plural on the pattern (fiʿal), like (ra'in) and (ri'a') ("shepherd" and "shepherds"). Its accusative may be as a circumstantial element (hal), like the reading of al-Hasan ('ushan), on the pattern of (duja) ("darkness"), the plural of (ʿashin), from which the ta' is dropped, as it is dropped in (malik), whose original form is (malika). From al-Hasan also (ʿushayyan) with the diminutive. It has been said: they came at nightfall so that they would be better able to make excuses in the darkness. Therefore it is said: "Do not seek your need at night, for shame is in the eyes; and do not make excuses for a sin during the day, or you will stammer in your excuse." In the speech there is an omission, whose estimated form is: "And they came to their father, without Yusuf, at nightfall, weeping." Then he said: "Where is Yusuf?" They said: "We went..." It is related that when Ya'qub heard their weeping, he said: "What is wrong with you? Has something happened to the sheep?" They said: "No." He said: "Then where is Yusuf?" They said: "We went racing one another and the wolf devoured him." So he wept, cried out, and fell unconscious. They poured water over him, but he did not move. They called to him, but he did not answer. Yahudha placed his hand over the openings of his breath, but he sensed no breath and no vein moved for him. Then he said: "Woe to us from the Judge of the Day of Judgment! We lost our brother and we killed our father!" He did not recover until the cool of dawn. Al-A'mash said: "No weeping person is believed after the brothers of Yusuf."

(nastabiq) ("we race"): that is, we shoot arrows at targets, or we race on foot to see which of us runs faster, or we compete in tasks we divide among ourselves, such as watering, pasturing, and gathering firewood, or we hunt. These are four opinions.

﴿at our belongings﴾: that is, at our clothing and what we had stripped off during the racing. This also indicates that Yusuf was young, for if he were eighteen or seventeen he would have been racing with them. ﴿So the wolf devoured him﴾: We have already mentioned that they took this answer from their father's words: ﴿And I fear that the wolf will devour him﴾ [Yusuf: 13], because the wolf devouring him was the thing he most feared for him.

﴿But you will not believe us﴾: that is, you will not accept us as truthful now, ﴿even though we are truthful.﴾ Or: are you not one who accepts us as truthful in every case, even in the case of truth, because of the suspicion and dislike of Yusuf that had overcome you? We are constantly plotting against him and devising schemes against him. By their saying ﴿even though we are truthful﴾ they gave the impression that they were truthful about the wolf devouring Yusuf, so their truthfulness would be restricted to this incident. Or it means they were people of truthfulness and trust in Ya'qub's eyes before this incident, because of your great love for Yusuf. How much more so, since you now think ill of us in this incident and do not trust our words about him!

It is related that they took a young goat or a kid and slaughtered it, smeared Yusuf's shirt with its blood, and said to Ya'qub: "This is Yusuf's shirt." He took it, smeared his face with it, and wept. Then he examined it and saw no tear and no mark, so he doubted. He inferred from this the opposite of what they claimed, and said to them: "When was the wolf so gentle that it would devour Yusuf and not tear his shirt?" It was said: there were three signs in Yusuf's shirt. It was evidence for Ya'qub that Yusuf had not been eaten by the wolf, and when it was thrown over his face, he regained his sight. It was also evidence of Yusuf's innocence, when it was torn from behind.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, "What is the position of ﴿upon his shirt﴾?" I say: its position is the accusative as an adverbial of place (zarf), as if it were said: "They came with blood above his shirt," just as you say: "He came upon his camels with loads." If you ask: "Could it be a preceding circumstantial element?" I say: No, because the circumstantial element of a prepositional phrase does not precede it. End of quotation.

The meaning does not support taking (ʿala) ("upon") as an adverb of place meaning "above," because the governing verb in that case would be (jaa'u) ("they came"), and "above" cannot be an adverb of place for them. Al-Hawfi said that (ʿala) is connected to (jaa'u) but this is also not valid. As for the example al-Zamakhshari mentioned, "He came upon his camels with loads," it is possible that it is an adverb of place for the one who came, because the adverbial sense is established in it through the change from one camel to another camel, and "with loads" is in the position of a circumstantial element, meaning: accompanied by loads. Abu al-Baqa' said: ﴿upon his shirt﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial element of the blood, because the estimate is: "they came with false blood upon his shirt." Placing a circumstantial element before a preposition that is not extra is a matter of disagreement regarding its permissibility. Whoever permitted it cited as evidence that it exists in the language of the Arabs and recited examples for this, which are mentioned in the science of grammar. The meaning points to what Abu al-Baqa' said.

The majority read (kadhibin) ("false") as an adjective of (dam) ("blood") by way of emphasis, or by omitting a modified noun, meaning "blood of falsehood," since the word indicates falsehood, it is described by it, even though the falsehood came from someone else. Zayd ibn 'Ali read (kadhiban) ("falsely") in the accusative, which may be a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial element, or an object of purpose. 'A'isha and al-Hasan read (kadibin) with the letter dal without a dot, and it was explained as "turbid," and it was said "fresh," and it was said "dry." The author of al-Lawami' said: its meaning is "with a mark," that is, a trace, because (al-kadhib) is a whiteness that appears on the nails of young men and affects them, so it is like a design. That whiteness is called al-Fawf, so this is a metaphor for its effect on the shirt, like the effect of that on the nails.

He said: ﴿Rather, your own souls have made [a matter] seem good to you﴾: here an element is omitted, its estimate being: "The wolf did not devour him, rather your souls made it seem good." Ibn 'Abbas said: "You commanded yourselves to do a matter." Qatadah said: "Adorned it for you." It was said: "They were pleased with a matter," that is, an ugly deed. It was also said: "They made it easy." ﴿So patience is beautiful﴾: that is, my affair is beautiful patience, or: beautiful patience is better. Ubayy, al-Ashhab, and 'Isa ibn 'Umar read (sabran jamilan) ("patience, beautiful") with both in the accusative, and so it is in the codex of Ubayy and the codex of Anas ibn Malik, and it is related likewise from al-Kisa'i. They put it in the accusative as a declarative verbal noun, meaning: "So be patient with beautiful patience." It has been said this is a weak reading according to Sibawayh, and that the accusative in such a case is appropriate only with a command. Likewise the accusative is appropriate in the line:

*My camel complained to me of the length of the journey: "Patience, beautiful patience, for both of us are tested."*

﴿And Allah is the One whose help is sought against what you describe.﴾

﴿A caravan came and they sent their water-drawer, and he let down his bucket.﴾ He said: "O good news!"

[End of part 1]

Abu Hayyan's commentary (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 12, verses 15–19 (part 2 of 2):

It is also narrated in the line of poetry as "ṣabrun jamīlun" (nominative). The reading in the accusative (naṣb), *ṣabran jamīlan*, is sound only if we assume that Ya'qub turned to addressing himself, as though he said: "Be patient, O self, with beautiful patience." In a hadith: "Beautiful patience is that which contains no complaint," meaning complaint to creation. Do you not see His saying: ﴿I only complain of my anguish and my grief to God﴾ [Yusuf: 86]? It was also said: "I will display patience before you, so I will not keep company with you in gloom of face and frowning brow, but rather as I was with you." Al-Thawri said: "Part of patience is that you do not speak of what pains you, nor of your calamity, and that you do not weep for yourself."

﴿And God is the One whose help is sought﴾, meaning: the One from whom aid is requested to bear what you describe of Yusuf's destruction, and to endure the calamity.

﴿A caravan came﴾. It was said: they were from Madyan, heading for Egypt. It was also said: there is an omission (ḥadhf) in the speech, its sense being: Yusuf remained in the well for three days, and his brother Yahudha (p. 290) used to bring him food secretly from his brothers. It was also said: the caravan came on the second day after he was cast into the well. It was also said: glorification (of God) was his nourishment in the well. It was said: the caravan was lost, traveling from land to land. It was also said: it was a caravan on the road that missed its way, so they alighted near the well. It was in a desolate wasteland far from settlements, frequented only by herdsmen. Among them was Malik ibn Du'r al-Khuza'i, and they sent him to seek water for them. The *wārid* is the one who comes to the water to draw it for the people. The annexation (iḍāfa) of *wārid* to the pronoun is like its annexation in the phrase "I destroyed their earner (kāsibahum)": it is not an annexation to the object, but rather the meaning is "the one who comes to them" and "the one who earns for them." The apparent meaning is that the *wārid* is one person. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "The *wārid* here may apply to one person and to a group," end of quote. The verb is construed according to the sense of the caravan (*sayyāra*) in His saying ﴿So they sent﴾. Had it been construed according to the wording, the sequence would have been "so she sent her *wārid*."

﴿So he lowered his bucket﴾, meaning: he sent it down to draw water. He said: ﴿O my good news!﴾. There is an omission in the speech, its sense being: Yusuf clung to the rope of the bucket, and when the one lowering it saw him, he said: "O my good news!" His clinging to the rope indicates his youth, for had he been eighteen or seventeen, the rope would generally not have borne him. The word *ghulām* (youth) supports this, since it is applied literally to one between the age of two and puberty, and it may also be applied to a grown man, as in the words of Layla al-Akhyaliyya about al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf:

*A youth who, when he shakes the spear, gives it drink.*

His saying "O my good news!" expresses joy and delight at Yusuf, for he saw the most beautiful of God's creation. Al-Suddi went too far in claiming that *Bushrā* is the name of a man. The speaker attributed the good news to himself, as though God Most High said: "This is from your times." The Kufans read ﴿O good news!﴾ without the annexation. Warsh narrated from Nafi': "*Yā bushrāy*," with the ya' of annexation pronounced with sukun. This is a juxtaposition of two sakins not in the manner of emphasis, and the explanation of the like of this was preceded in "*wa-maḥyāy*" (my life). Abu al-Tufayl, al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Ishaq and al-Jahdari read ﴿O good news!﴾ with the alif changed into a ya' and merged into the ya' of annexation. This is a dialect of Hudhayl and others, and its discussion was preceded in al-Baqarah at ﴿whoever follows My guidance (hudāya)﴾ [al-Baqarah: 38].

It was said: the *wārid* took him away, and when he drew near his companions he cried out with that, and they gave him good news of him and concealed him. The apparent meaning is that the pronoun refers to the caravan, of which the *wārid* was one, that is: they concealed him from the company. Or they concealed the matter of him from their finding him in the well, and they said: "The people of the water handed him over to us so that we might sell him for them in Egypt." Ibn ʿAbbas said: the pronoun in ﴿they concealed him﴾ and ﴿they sold him﴾ [Yusuf: 20] refers to Yusuf's brothers, and that they said to the company: "This is a runaway slave of ours, so buy him from us." Yusuf kept silent for fear that they would kill him. This is because it is narrated that some of them returned to the well to ascertain the matter of Yusuf and to be certain of his disappearance. When they learned that the *wārid* had taken him, they came to them and said that statement. The word *biḍāʿatan* is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl), meaning: a merchandise and a source of gain for them.

﴿And God is All-Knowing of what they do﴾, meaning: their secrets were not hidden from Him. It is a warning to them, since they sold what was not theirs. Or: God is All-Knowing of the deed of Yusuf's brothers toward their father and their brother, of evil conduct. In this is the greatest reminder of what they did to Yusuf. It was said: God revealed to him in the well that he should not inform his father or anyone else of his condition, for a wisdom He willed to carry out. What happened afterward became apparent: his appointment over the treasuries of the earth, his brothers' need of him, the raising of his parents upon the throne, and whatever followed this course of things that had been hidden in the decree.

(p. 291) *Shara* can mean "sold" and can also mean "bought." Yazid ibn Mufarragh al-Himyari said:

*"I bought a cloak, would that I had been, after the cloak, a cloak (i.e., a hapless one)..."*

That is, "I sold a cloak, and the cloak of his servant." Another poet said:

*"Had this death accepted a ransom, I would have bought Abu Zayd with all that my hand possesses."*

That is, "I bought Abu Zayd." The apparent reading is that the pronoun in ﴿وشَرَوْهُ﴾ refers to ﴿السَّيّارَةِ﴾ (the caravan) [Yusuf 12:10]: "they sold Yusuf." Whoever holds that the pronoun in ﴿وأسَرُّوهُ﴾ [Yusuf 12:19] refers to Yusuf's brothers makes it refer to them here as well, meaning: they sold their brother Yusuf for a paltry price. *Bakhs* is a verbal noun used as an adjective in the sense of *mabkhus* (diminished). Muqatil said: "a counterfeit, of deficient weight." Ikrimah and al-Sha'bi said: "a small amount." This is also the meaning of al-Zamakhshari: "lacking in value by an evident deficiency." Ibn Qutaybah said: "*al-bakhs* is the base (trifling) price at which the seller cheated." Qatadah said: "*bakhs* is injustice, because they wronged him in the sale." Ibn Abbas and Qatadah, and others, also said: "*bakhs* is unlawful (haram)." Ibn 'Ata' said: "He called it *bakhs* only because it was the exchange for a noble soul, which cannot be matched by any exchange, however great." End of quotation.

That is because, if the sellers were the caravan, they were not given any price for him, so whatever they took from him was pure profit. If they were his brothers, the aim was to clear their father's face of him, not to gain his price. ﴿دراهم﴾ (*darahim*, "dirhams") is an apposition to (*thaman*, "price"), so they did not sell him for dinars. (*Ma'dudah*, "counted") indicates a small amount. It was their custom not to weigh anything unless it reached an *uqiyyah*, which is forty dirhams, because a large quantity is hard to count, unlike a small one. Ikrimah, in a report from Ibn Abbas and Ibn Ishaq, said: forty dirhams. It was also said: thirty dirhams, and a pair of sandals and a garment. Al-Suddi said: they were twenty-two dirhams, as al-Zamakhshari transmitted from him. Ibn 'Atiyyah transmitted from Mujahid that his brothers took them two dirhams each, and the author of *al-Tahrir* transmitted it from him and from Ibn Abbas. Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Abbas in one report, Ikrimah in one report, Nawf al-Shami, Wahb, al-Sha'bi, 'Atiyyah, al-Suddi, Muqatil and others said: twenty dirhams. Also from Ibn Abbas: twenty, and a garment and a pair of sandals. It was also said: eighteen dirhams, with which they bought shoes and sandals. It was said: ten dirhams.

The apparent reading is that the pronoun in (*fihi*, "in him") refers to Yusuf, meaning: they did not know his station with Allah, the Exalted. This was said by al-Dahhak and Ibn Juraij. It was also said that it refers to the price, and their disinterest in it was due to the poor quality of the price, or because they intended to remove Yusuf (far away), not because of the price. This applies when the pronoun in ﴿وشَرَوْهُ﴾ and (*wa kanu*, "and they were") refers to Yusuf's brothers. But if it refers to the caravan, then their disinterest in him was because they doubted him, or because his brothers had described him as treacherous and a runaway, or because they knew he was free.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿من الزاهدين﴾ means among those who are indifferent to what is in their hand, so they sell it for whatever small price it fetches, because they had picked him up, and one who picks up an item is careless about it and does not mind what he sells it for. Also, he fears that a rightful claimant may appear and take it from his hand, so he sells it to the first bidder at the lowest price. It is also possible that the meaning of ﴿وشَرَوْهُ﴾ is "they bought him," meaning the company, from among his brothers.

﴿وكانوا فيه من الزاهدين﴾: because they believed of him that he was a runaway slave, and they feared that they would risk what they had in him. It is related that his brothers followed them, saying: "Secure him so he does not run away." End of quotation. A similar case has been discussed earlier in ﴿إني لكما لمن الناصحين﴾ [al-A'raf 7:21]. It was noted that the attachment of the prepositional phrase is either to a suppressed verb (*ba'ani*, "sold me"), or to an omitted element indicated by ﴿من الزاهدين﴾, meaning: "they were indifferent to him, among the indifferent," or to ﴿الزاهدين﴾ itself, since latitude is permitted with prepositional phrases and adverbial expressions, so things are allowed with them that are not allowed with other constructions.

﴿وقال الذي اشتراه من مصر﴾: they mentioned contradictory statements about the one who bought him and the price for which he was bought. The interpretation of Allah's Book does not depend on those contradictory statements. It was said: a man from the Amalekites bought him, who had believed in Yusuf and died during Yusuf's lifetime. It was said: at that time the king in Egypt was al-Rayyan ibn al-Walid ibn Barwan ibn Arashah ibn Faran ibn 'Amr ibn 'Imlaq ibn Lawadh ibn Sam ibn Nuh. After him, Qabus ibn Mus'ab ibn Tamr ibn al-Salwas ibn Faran ibn 'Amr, who is mentioned in al-Rayyan's lineage, reigned. Yusuf invited him to faith, but he refused. The *'Aziz* bought him when he was seventeen years old, and he remained in his house for thirteen years. Al-Rayyan ibn al-Walid made him his vizier when he was thirty years old. Allah gave him wisdom and knowledge when he was thirty-three, and he died at the age of one hundred and twenty. It was also said: the king in his days was Pharaoh of Moses, who lived four hundred years, based on the saying of Allah: ﴿ولقد جاءكم يوسف من قبل بالبينات﴾ [Ghafir 40:34]. It was also said: Pharaoh of Moses was among the descendants of Pharaoh of Yusuf. It was also said: he was put up for sale in the market, and he was the most beautiful of people. Bidding for him reached a great price, until it was said that his weight in gold, silver and silk was (the price), and the *'Aziz* bought him. He was the king's companion and treasurer. **Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 12, verse 23:**

﴿The woman in whose house he was sought to seduce him from himself. She locked the doors and said, "Come, you." He said, "God forbid! Indeed, he is my lord; he has made my residence good. Indeed, the wrongdoers do not succeed."﴾ ﴿Indeed, she desired him, and he would have desired her had he not seen the proof of his Lord. Thus [it was], that We might avert from him evil and immorality. Indeed, he was among Our chosen, sincere servants.﴾ [Yusuf: 24]

*al-Muraawadah* (seeking to seduce, from the verbal pattern *mufaa'alah*, Form III): asking gently and persistently. It derives from *raada yaroodu*, meaning to go and come back. It is a *mufaa'alah* from one party, like *daawaytu al-mareedh* (I treated the patient). It is used metaphorically for seeking intercourse and deceiving someone in order to obtain it. The meaning is "she deceived him away from himself," which is why it takes *'an* (from). God says ﴿the one in whose house he was﴾ and does not name her, nor name her as the wife of al-'Aziz, as a veil over what is sacred. The Arabs attribute houses to women and say *rabbat al-bayt* (mistress of the house) and *saahibat al-bayt* (owner of the house). The poet said:

*"O mistress of the house, rise without being humbled."*

﴿And she locked the doors﴾: the doubling of the letter in *ghallaqat* indicates intensity, relative to the act being performed on each and every door. It was said that there were seven doors.

﴿Haytа laka﴾: *haytа* is an *ism fi'l* (verb-noun, a word functioning as an imperative verb) meaning "hasten." *Laka* (to you) indicates the one addressed. The meaning is: "To you I say, hasten toward me." She commanded him to come to her quickly.

Al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' claimed that it is a Huwarani dialect that reached the people of the Hijaz, and they spoke it. Its meaning is "come here." Ikrimah said the same. Abu Zayd said it is Hebrew: *hayta lakh*, meaning "come here," and the Qur'an arabicized it. Ibn Abbas and al-Hasan said it is Syriac. Al-Suddi said it is Coptic: *halumma laka*. Mujahid and others said it is Arabic, and she used it to invite him to herself. It is a word of urging and welcome. (End of the quoted statement.) It is not unlikely that languages coincide in a word, since this has been found in Arabic speech alongside the languages of others. Al-Jawhari said: *hawta* and *hayta bihi* mean he cried out to him and called him.

It is not unlikely that it is derived from the *ism fi'l*, just as they derived verbs from phrases, such as *sabbaha* (he said *subhan Allah*) and *hamadaka* (he said *hamdan laka*). Since it is an *ism fi'l*, the pronoun does not appear in it. Rather, it indicates the grammatical person of the pronoun through what attaches to the *laam* of address, as in: *hayta laka* (to a man), *hayta laki* (to a woman), *hayta lakuma* (to two), *hayta lakum* (to men), and *hayta lakunna* (to women).

**Recitation variants of *haytа*:** Nafi', Ibn Dhakwan, al-A'raj, Shaybah and Abu Ja'far recited *Haytа* with a *kasrah* on the *ha'* followed by a silent *yaa'*, and a *fatha* on the *taa'*. Al-Hulwani, from Hisham, recited it the same way, except that he used a *hamzah*. Ali, Abu Wa'il, Abu Raja', Yahya, Ikrimah, Mujahid, Qatadah, Talhah, al-Muqri, Ibn Abbas, Abu 'Amr in one narration, and Hisham in one narration, recited it the same way, except that they put a *dammah* on the *taa'*. Zayd ibn Ali and Ibn Abi Ishaq recited it the same way, except that they eased the *hamzah*. Al-Nahhas mentioned that it was recited with a *kasrah* on the *ha'*, a silent *yaa'*, and a *kasrah* on the *taa'*. Ibn Kathir and the people of Makkah recited it with a *fatha* on the *ha'*, a silent *yaa'*, and a *dammah* on the *taa'*. The rest of the seven readers (Abu 'Amr, the Kufans, the Basrans) recited it as Ibn Mas'ud and al-Hasan did, except that they put a *fatha* on the *taa'*. Ibn Abbas, Abu al-Aswad, Ibn Abi Ishaq, Ibn Muhaysin and Isa of Basra recited it the same way. It is also reported from Ibn Abbas: *hayiyat*, like *hayiyat*.

These are nine recitations in which it is an *ism fi'l*, except the last recitation of Ibn Abbas, which is a passive verb (*fi'l mabni lil-maf'ul*) with an eased *hamzah*, from *hayya'tu al-shay'* (I prepared the thing). Apart from those who put a *dammah* on the *taa'* and a *kasrah* on the *ha'*, whether they used a *hamzah* or not, it is possible that it is an *ism fi'l*, like its state when the *taa'* has a *fatha* or a *kasrah*. It is also possible that it is a verb, with the speaker's pronoun from *ha' al-rajul yuhayyi'u*, meaning when a man improves his appearance, on the pattern of *jaa'a yajii'u* (came, comes). Or it may mean *tahayya'tu* (I prepared myself). It is said: *hayta* and *tahayya'tu* have one meaning. If it is a verb, the *laam* is attached to it. There are other dialects of this word.

﴿Ma'aadha Allah﴾ (God forbid) is in the accusative as a verbal noun (*masdar*): meaning "seeking refuge in God from the act of evil."

As for the pronoun in ﴿innahu﴾ (indeed he), the most correct view is that it refers to God, Exalted is He. That is, indeed God is my Lord, who has made my residence good when He rescued me from the well and placed me in the best station. Alternatively, it may be the pronoun of the matter (*dhamir al-sha'n*), and by "his Lord" he meant his master, al-'Aziz. Then it is not proper for me to betray him, since he honored my residence and entrusted me. This was said by Mujahid, al-Suddi and Ibn Ishaq. But this is very unlikely, since a noble prophet does not describe a created being as his Lord, nor does "Lord" mean "master," because in reality he was not owned by him.

﴿Indeed, the wrongdoers do not succeed﴾: that is, those who repay good with evil. It was said: they are adulterers. It was said: they are traitors.

Abu al-Tufayl and al-Jahdari recited *mathwayya* (my residence) as they recited *ya bushrayya* (O my good news). How excellent is this disavowal of falling into evil!

He first sought refuge in God, in whose hand is protection and the dominion of everything. Then he alerted her that the kindness of God, or the kindness of al-'Aziz that preceded from him, does not warrant being repaid with wrongdoing. Then he negated success from the wrongdoers. Success is attainment and gaining one's desire. So it is not fitting that I should be a wrongdoer, placing a thing in other than its place and transgressing what God, Exalted is He, has set as limits for me.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 12, verse 24:

﴿And she certainly desired him, and he would have desired her, had he not seen the proof of his Lord.﴾ (p. 295) The exegetes (mufassirun) have gone to great lengths in explaining these two desires. Some of them have attributed to Yusuf (peace be upon him) what it is not permissible to attribute even to ordinary sinners. The view I choose is that Yusuf (peace be upon him) never experienced any desire for her whatsoever. Rather, it is negated because the seeing of the proof existed, just as you say: "You would have committed the sin, had Allah not protected you." You do not say that the answer to *law la* (if not, had it not been) precedes it, although no proof establishes that this is impermissible. Rather, the clear position is that the answers of conditional particles that govern (*al-adawat al-shart al-'amila*) differ over whether their answers may precede them. The Kufans held this view, and among the leading Basran grammarians were Abu Zayd al-Ansari and Abu al-'Abbas al-Mubarrad.

Rather, we say that the answer to *law la* is omitted, because what precedes it indicates it, just as the majority of the Basran grammarians say regarding the Arab saying: "You are a wrongdoer if you do it." They estimate it as: "If you do it, then you are a wrongdoer." The statement "you are a wrongdoer" does not indicate that wrongdoing has been established; rather, it is affirmed on the assumption that the act exists. Likewise here, the estimate is: "Had it not been that he saw the proof of his Lord, he would have desired her." So he would have been inclined to her on the assumption that the seeing of the proof was absent, but he did see the proof, and so the desire was negated. There is no regard for the statement of al-Zajjaj. Had the phrase been *wa-lahum bi-ha* (and they desired her), it would be far-fetched, so how much more so with the omission of the *lam*? Because it gives the impression that the statement "and he desired her" is the answer to *law la*, and we have not said that. Rather, it is evidence of the answer. And even if it were the answer itself, the *lam* is not obligatory, since what comes as the answer to *law la* in the past tense may come with the *lam* or without it. You say: "Had it not been for Zayd, I would have honored you" and "Had it not been for Zayd, I honored you." So whoever holds that the statement "and he desired her" is itself the answer is not far from the truth.

There is also no regard for the statement of Ibn 'Atiyya that the view of those who say the speech is complete at "she certainly desired him," and that the answer to *law la* is in "and he desired her," meaning: had he not seen the proof, he would have desired her, but Yusuf (peace be upon him) did not desire her. He said: "This is a view that the Arabic language and the statements of the early generations (al-salaf) reject." End of quotation.

As for his saying that the Arabic language rejects it, this is not as he claimed. Those who hold that this is permissible have cited its occurrence in the language of the Arabs. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, she was about to disclose it, had We not steadied her heart so that she would be among the believers.﴾ [al-Qasas: 10]. So His statement ﴿she was about to disclose it﴾ [al-Qasas: 10] either can be understood as the answer, according to the view of that speaker, or it can be understood according to what we have adopted, that it is the evidence of the answer, and the estimate is: "Had We not steadied her heart, she would have disclosed it."

As for the statements of the early generations, we believe that nothing of that kind is authentically transmitted from any of them, because they are contradictory statements, some of which negate others, and because they are damaging even to some of the immoral among the Muslims, let alone those who are definitively attested to be protected from sin (al-ma'sumun). What is transmitted from the early generations is not supported by the language of the Arabs, because they estimated the answer of *law la* as omitted, and no evidence indicates it, since they did not estimate *wa-lahum bi-ha* (and they desired her). The language of the Arabs only indicates that the omitted element should be of the meaning of what precedes the conditional, because what precedes the conditional is evidence for it, and nothing is omitted without evidence for it. We have purified this book of ours from transmitting what is found in the books of tafsir that is not fitting to mention, and we have limited ourselves to what the Arabic language indicates and to the context of the verses in this surah, which indicate the protection from sin and the innocence of Yusuf (peace be upon him) from everything that would disgrace him. Whoever wishes to know what has been transmitted from the exegetes concerning this verse should consult the tafsir of al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya, and others.

The proof that Yusuf saw was what Allah had given him of knowledge indicating the prohibition of what Allah has forbidden, and Allah does not allow the desire for it to take hold of him, let alone that he should fall into it. ﴿Thus, that We may avert from him evil and immorality.﴾ Al-Zamakhshari said: The *kaf* (in *kadhalika*, "thus") is in the accusative position, meaning: "Like that firm establishment, We established him," or it is in the nominative position, meaning: "The matter is like that." Ibn 'Atiyya said: The *kaf* in His statement *kadhalika* is connected to an implied element whose estimate is: "Our actions and decrees proceeded thus, that We may avert." It is also permissible that the *kaf* be in the nominative position, with the estimate of "His protection, thus, that We may avert." It was also said: there is an inversion in the speech, its estimate being: "She desired him and he desired her, thus," then He said: "Had he not seen the proof of his Lord, that We may avert from him what he desired." End of quotation. Al-Hawfi said: The *kaf* of *kadhalika* is for comparison, in the accusative position, meaning: "We showed him the proofs thus." It was also said that it is in the nominative position, meaning: "The matter of the proofs is thus." The accusative is better because prepositions require verbs or their meanings. Abu al-Baqa' said: *kadhalika* is in the nominative position, meaning: "The matter is thus." It was also said that it is in the accusative position, meaning: "We observe it thus." End of quotation.

I say: the estimate is "like that sight" or "like that opinion." We show Our proofs so that We may avert from him. The *kaf* is governed by what is indicated by His statement ﴿had he not seen the proof of his Lord﴾. And ﴿that We may avert﴾ is connected to that verb which governs the *kaf*. The verbal noun of *ra'a* (to see) is *ru'yah* and *ra'y*. The poet said:

*And the opinion of my eyes about the youth, your father, gives abundantly; so upon you is that.*

Al-A'mash recited *li-yasrifa* with the third-person masculine *ya* (that He may avert), referring to "His Lord." The two Arab readers (al-'Arabiyyan) and Ibn Kathir recited *al-mukhlisin* (the sincere ones) wherever it occurs in this surah with a *kasra* on the *lam*, while the rest of the seven readers recited it with a *fatha*. The averting of evil and immorality from him, and his being among the sincere ones, is evidence of his protection from sin.

25: 29

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 12, verses 25–29:

﴿And they both raced to the door, and she tore his shirt from behind, and they found her husband at the door. She said: "What is the penalty for one who intended evil against your family, except that he be imprisoned or suffer a painful punishment?"﴾ ﴿He said: "It was she who sought to seduce me from myself." And a witness from her family testified: "If his shirt is torn from the front, then she has told the truth and he is among the liars."﴾ ﴿"But if his shirt is torn from behind, then she has lied and he is among the truthful."﴾ ﴿So when he saw his shirt torn from behind, he said: "Indeed, it is of your guile, women. Indeed, your guile is great."﴾ ﴿"Joseph, turn away from this. And you, ask forgiveness for your sin; indeed, you were among the sinners."﴾

That is: Joseph and the wife of the ʿAzīz (the chief minister) raced toward the door. He was racing to the door to leave and flee from her, and she was racing to stop him and to solicit him. The original construction of istabaqa is that it takes ilā ("to") after it, but here it is omitted for brevity (ittisāʿan, "by extension"). It has been mentioned that the doors were seven. So the doors would open for him one by one without a key, according to what is reported from Kaʿb, that the bolts of the locks would scatter and fall until he passed through the doors. It is also possible that the closed doors were not in sequence, one after another, but in different directions, all of them being exits from the place where they were. So they raced to a door from which he could leave, and it was not necessarily the seventh in sequence, but one of them.

﴿And she tore﴾ may be coordinated with ﴿they raced﴾, or it may be a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: "while she had torn," i.e., she pulled him from behind by the upper part of the shirt at the collar, so it split down to the bottom. Qadd means cutting and splitting, and it is mostly used for what is lengthwise. The poet said:

*"Cutting the Salūqī (a fine hunting dog) with its tightly woven fabric, and kindling with the flint the fire of al-Ḥubāḥib."*

Qaṭṭ is used for what is across (widthwise). Al-Mufaḍḍal ibn Ḥarb said: "I saw in a Qur'an copy qaṭṭ min dubur," meaning a split. Yaʿqūb said: "Shaqq (splitting) is in healthy leather and healthy cloth." Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "A group recited (qaṭṭa)."

﴿And they found her husband﴾, meaning they found or encountered her husband, who was Qiṭfīr. The wife calls her husband "my master" (sayyidī), and it is not attached to them both, because Qiṭfīr was not truly the master of Joseph. It is said: alfāhu, wāraṭahu, ṣādafahu, wālaṭahu, and lāẓahu, all with one meaning. It is said they found him coming in, wanting to enter. It is also said he was with the cousin of the woman. There is an omission in the speech, its implied meaning being: their situation alarmed him, and he said: "What is the matter with you two?" When he asked, and she feared his blame, or because Joseph had spoken first, she hurried to devise a stratagem in which she combined clearing her reputation of suspicion, her anger at Joseph, and frightening him, hoping to make him yield to her, out of fear of her scheming, having despaired that he would comply willingly. Do you not see her saying: ﴿And if he does not do what I command him, he will surely be imprisoned﴾ [Yusuf: 32]? She did not name Joseph explicitly, but used a general expression, her saying: ﴿What is the penalty for one who intended﴾, which is more forceful in frightening. As for "mā" (what), the apparent reading is that it is negative, but it may also be interrogative, meaning: "What is his penalty except imprisonment?" She began with imprisonment out of concern for her beloved, then escalated to a painful punishment. It is said this is flogging with the whip. Her saying ﴿What is the penalty﴾ implies that the offense is established and settled against him. She used the phrase "with evil" (bisūʾ), meaning with what causes harm, and it is not explicit about a grave sin, since it may refer to his speaking to her in a way that hurt her, or his striking her. Her saying ﴿except that he be imprisoned or [suffer] a painful punishment﴾ shows the great standing of imprisonment among people of rank, since she joined it with painful punishment.

Zayd ibn ʿAlī recited (ʿadhāban alīman, "a painful punishment," in the accusative). Al-Kisāʾī took it as: "or he be tormented with a painful punishment." When she aroused suspicion against Joseph and displayed the accusation, he needed to remove the accusation from himself, so he said: ﴿It was she who sought to seduce me from myself﴾. He did not speak first, out of concealing her. When he feared for himself and his pure honor, he said "she" (hiya) and used the third-person pronoun, since shame overcame him from pointing at her and specifying her with a gesture, saying "this one sought to seduce me" or "that one." This was so that he would not face her directly with what is ugly, which is less harsh in the third person. When their two statements conflicted before the ʿAzīz, and he was a man of forbearance and fairness, he demanded a witness from each of them.

﴿So a witness from her family testified﴾. Abū Hurayra, Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan, Ibn Jubayr, Hilāl ibn Yasāf, and al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: he was her nephew (son of her maternal aunt), an infant in the cradle, whom God Most High caused to speak so that he would be a clearer proof. It is reported in a ḥadīth: "He is among the infants who spoke in the cradle," and al-Ṭabarī traced it back. In Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī and Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim: "Only three spoke in the cradle: ʿĪsā ibn Maryam (Jesus son of Mary), the companion of Jurayj, and the son of the black woman." It is also said he was her cousin who was with her husband at the door. This does not contradict the saying of Qatāda: he was a forbearing man from her family, of sound judgment, whom the king consulted and took counsel from. It is also said he was an arbiter whom her husband appointed, and he judged between them. The witness being from her family was to make the proof stronger against her, and more reliable for Joseph's innocence, and more effective in removing suspicion. It is possible that he was with them in the house, in a place where he was not noticed, so he saw what passed between them, and God angered him for Joseph's sake, and he testified to the truth. The view of Mujāhid and Ibn Ḥabīb, that the witness was the torn shirt, is weak, because of the phrase ﴿a witness from her family﴾, and a shirt is not described as a witness from the family of the woman. The man was called a witness insofar as he indicated the testimony, which is the tearing of the shirt. Al-Zamakhsharī said: he called his statement a testimony because it performed the function of testimony in establishing Joseph's word and refuting hers.

﴿If his shirt﴾ is reported speech, either with an implied "he said" according to the Basran school, or with "he testified," since testimony is a kind of speech according to the Kufan school. Here "kāna" (was) has been preceded by the conditional particle, and the disagreement of al-Mubarrad and the majority was mentioned earlier regarding it: does it remain in its past sense without being changed by the conditional particle, or does the meaning become "that it becomes clear that it is so"? In reality, the conditional particle entered upon this implied clause. The answer of the conditional is ﴿then she has told the truth﴾ and ﴿then she has lied﴾, and it is with an implied "qad" (indeed), meaning "then indeed she has told the truth" and "then indeed she has lied." If it were a rigid verb or a supplication, it would not need the estimation of qad.

Al-Jumhūr recited min qubulin and min dubur with a damma on the bāʾ in both, with tanwīn. Al-Ḥasan and Abū ʿAmr, and in one narration, read them with a sukūn on the bāʾ and tanwīn, and this is the dialect of the Ḥijāz and Asad. Ibn Yaʿmar, Ibn Abī Isḥāq, al-ʿUṭāridī, Abū al-Zinād, Nūḥ al-Qāriʾ, and al-Jārūd ibn Abī Sabra, in one report from him, read them with three vowelless consonants (qubul, dubur without tanwīn). Ibn Yaʿmar, Ibn Abī Isḥāq, and al-Jārūd, in one of their reports, read them with a sukūn on the bāʾ with both built on a damma, treating them as ghāyah (a class of nouns that are adverbial and end-points), like min qablu. The meaning of ghāyah is that the noun becomes the end-point of itself after the noun governed by it had been its end-point. The original is that both are inflected, since they are fully declinable nouns and are not adverbs. Abū Ḥātim said: this is poor in Arabic, since this form occurs only in adverbs. Al-Zamakhsharī said: the meaning is "from the front of the shirt and from its back." As for the indefinite form, its meaning is "from a direction called front, and from a direction called back." It is reported from Ibn Abī Isḥāq that he read (min qubula wa min dubura) with a fatḥa, as if he made them proper names for the two directions, so they were not declined due to definiteness (ʿalamiyya) and feminine form. He also said: if you say: if "his shirt was torn from behind" shows that she is lying and that she was the one who pursued him and pulled his garment toward herself and tore it, then from where does the tearing from the front show that she is truthful and that he was her pursuer? I answer: from two aspects. One: if he was pursuing her while she was pushing him away, then she tore his shirt from in front by pushing. Two: he hastened behind her to catch her, and stumbled in front, so his shirt tore in front. End of quotation. His saying ﴿and he is among the liars﴾, ﴿and he is among the truthful﴾ are two emphatic clauses, because from her saying ﴿then she has told the truth﴾ his lying is known, and from her saying "then she has lied" his truthfulness is known. In building qudda for the passive, there is concealment of the one who tore it. Since the witness was from her family, he took the woman's side, and began by making her truthfulness depend on the clarity that the shirt was torn from the front. Since each clause is independent in itself, the noun kāna was expressed with an explicit noun rather than a pronoun, to indicate independence, and because stating it explicitly is clearer. This is similar to his saying: "Whoever obeys God and His Messenger has been guided, and whoever disobeys God and His Messenger has gone astray."

﴿So when he saw his shirt torn from behind﴾, the ʿAzīz said, or it is said the witness was the shirt torn from behind: "Indeed, it" (innahu), meaning: "indeed, your saying ﴿What is the penalty﴾ to the end," as al-Zajjāj said; or that this matter, namely her desire for Joseph, as al-Māwardī and al-Zamakhsharī mentioned; or that it refers to the tearing of the shirt, as Muqātil said. The address in ﴿of your guile﴾ is to her and her maids, or to her and to women in general. He described the guile of women as great, although it may be found in men, because they are subtler in guile by their nature and by what they are free to devote themselves to, and some of them learn from others, and they are more effective in strategy. God Most High said: ﴿And from the evil of the blowers in knots﴾ [al-Falaq: 4]. As for those in palaces, they have from this what is not found in others, because they are more free than others and more at ease with their peers.

﴿Joseph, turn away from this﴾, meaning: from this matter, and conceal it, and do not speak of it. In calling him by name there is closeness to him and gentleness. Then he turned to her and said: ﴿and ask forgiveness for your sin﴾. The apparent reading is that the speaker of this is the ʿAzīz. Ibn ʿAbbās said: the witness, who was the man who was with the ʿAzīz, called out to him and said: "Ask forgiveness for your sin," meaning for your husband and master. He then mentioned the reason for seeking forgiveness, which is his saying "for your sin," then confirmed it with his saying ﴿indeed you were among the sinners﴾. He did not say "among the sinful women" (khāṭiʾāt), because khāṭiʾīn is more general, since it applies to males and females by way of masculine prevalence. It is said: khuṭṭiʾa, when he sins deliberately. Al-Zamakhsharī said: the ʿAzīz was only forbearing. It is reported that he had little jealousy. The soil and climate of Qiṭfīr's region required this. Where is this compared with what happened to one of our kings, who was with his intimate companions in a gathering of entertainment, and a slave girl was singing to them from behind a curtain. One of his close companions asked her to repeat two verses she had sung, and soon the head of the slave girl was brought, severed, in a basin, and the king said to him: "Repeat the two verses from this head." The one asked to repeat was struck with dismay, and he fell ill for the rest of that king's life.
