As for "mā" (what), the apparent reading is that it is negative, but it may also be interrogative, meaning: "What is his penalty except imprisonment?" She began with imprisonment out of concern for her beloved, then escalated to a painful punishment. It is said this is flogging with the whip. Her saying ﴿What is the penalty﴾ implies that the offense is established and settled against him. She used the phrase "with evil" (bisūʾ), meaning with what causes harm, and it is not explicit about a grave sin, since it may refer to his speaking to her in a way that hurt her, or his striking her. Her saying ﴿except that he be imprisoned or [suffer] a painful punishment﴾ shows the great standing of imprisonment among people of rank, since she joined it with painful punishment.

Zayd ibn ʿAlī recited (ʿadhāban alīman, "a painful punishment," in the accusative). Al-Kisāʾī took it as: "or he be tormented with a painful punishment." When she aroused suspicion against Joseph and displayed the accusation, he needed to remove the accusation from himself, so he said: ﴿It was she who sought to seduce me from myself﴾. He did not speak first, out of concealing her. When he feared for himself and his pure honor, he said "she" (hiya) and used the third-person pronoun, since shame overcame him from pointing at her and specifying her with a gesture, saying "this one sought to seduce me" or "that one." This was so that he would not face her directly with what is ugly, which is less harsh in the third person. When their two statements conflicted before the ʿAzīz, and he was a man of forbearance and fairness, he demanded a witness from each of them.

﴿So a witness from her family testified﴾. Abū Hurayra, Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan, Ibn Jubayr, Hilāl ibn Yasāf, and al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: he was her nephew (son of her maternal aunt), an infant in the cradle, whom God Most High caused to speak so that he would be a clearer proof. It is reported in a ḥadīth: "He is among the infants who spoke in the cradle," and al-Ṭabarī traced it back. In Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī and Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim: "Only three spoke in the cradle: ʿĪsā ibn Maryam (Jesus son of Mary), the companion of Jurayj, and the son of the black woman." It is also said he was her cousin who was with her husband at the door. This does not contradict the saying of Qatāda: he was a forbearing man from her family, of sound judgment, whom the king consulted and took counsel from. It is also said he was an arbiter whom her husband appointed, and he judged between them. The witness being from her family was to make the proof stronger against her, and more reliable for Joseph's innocence, and more effective in removing suspicion. It is possible that he was with them in the house, in a place where he was not noticed, so he saw what passed between them, and God angered him for Joseph's sake, and he testified to the truth. The view of Mujāhid and Ibn Ḥabīb, that the witness was the torn shirt, is weak, because of the phrase ﴿a witness from her family﴾, and a shirt is not described as a witness from the family of the woman. The man was called a witness insofar as he indicated the testimony, which is the tearing of the shirt. Al-Zamakhsharī said: he called his statement a testimony because it performed the function of testimony in establishing Joseph's word and refuting hers.

﴿If his shirt﴾ is reported speech, either with an implied "he said" according to the Basran school, or with "he testified," since testimony is a kind of speech according to the Kufan school. Here "kāna" (was) has been preceded by the conditional particle, and the disagreement of al-Mubarrad and the majority was mentioned earlier regarding it: does it remain in its past sense without being changed by the conditional particle, or does the meaning become "that it becomes clear that it is so"? In reality, the conditional particle entered upon this implied clause. The answer of the conditional is ﴿then she has told the truth﴾ and ﴿then she has lied﴾, and it is with an implied "qad" (indeed), meaning "then indeed she has told the truth" and "then indeed she has lied." If it were a rigid verb or a supplication, it would not need the estimation of qad.

Al-Jumhūr recited min qubulin and min dubur with a damma on the bāʾ in both, with tanwīn. Al-Ḥasan and Abū ʿAmr, and in one narration, read them with a sukūn on the bāʾ and tanwīn, and this is the dialect of the Ḥijāz and Asad. Ibn Yaʿmar, Ibn Abī Isḥāq, al-ʿUṭāridī, Abū al-Zinād, Nūḥ al-Qāriʾ, and al-Jārūd ibn Abī Sabra, in one report from him, read them with three vowelless consonants (qubul, dubur without tanwīn). Ibn Yaʿmar, Ibn Abī Isḥāq, and al-Jārūd, in one of their reports, read them with a sukūn on the bāʾ with both built on a damma, treating them as ghāyah (a class of nouns that are adverbial and end-points), like min qablu. The meaning of ghāyah is that the noun becomes the end-point of itself after the noun governed by it had been its end-point. The original is that both are inflected, since they are fully declinable nouns and are not adverbs. Abū Ḥātim said: this is poor in Arabic, since this form occurs only in adverbs. Al-Zamakhsharī said: the meaning is "from the front of the shirt and from its back." As for the indefinite form, its meaning is "from a direction called front, and from a direction called back." It is reported from Ibn Abī Isḥāq that he read (min qubula wa min dubura) with a fatḥa, as if he made them proper names for the two directions, so they were not declined due to definiteness (ʿalamiyya) and feminine form. He also said: if you say: if "his shirt was torn from behind" shows that she is lying and that she was the one who pursued him and pulled his garment toward herself and tore it, then from where does the tearing from the front show that she is truthful and that he was her pursuer? I answer: from two aspects. One: if he was pursuing her while she was pushing him away, then she tore his shirt from in front by pushing. Two: he hastened behind her to catch her, and stumbled in front, so his shirt tore in front. End of quotation. His saying ﴿and he is among the liars﴾, ﴿and he is among the truthful﴾ are two emphatic clauses, because from her saying ﴿then she has told the truth﴾ his lying is known, and from her saying "then she has lied" his truthfulness is known. In building qudda for the passive, there is concealment of the one who tore it. Since the witness was from her family, he took the woman's side, and began by making her truthfulness depend on the clarity that the shirt was torn from the front. Since each clause is independent in itself, the noun kāna was expressed with an explicit noun rather than a pronoun, to indicate independence, and because stating it explicitly is clearer. This is similar to his saying: "Whoever obeys God and His Messenger has been guided, and whoever disobeys God and His Messenger has gone astray."

﴿So when he saw his shirt torn from behind﴾, the ʿAzīz said, or it is said the witness was the shirt torn from behind: "Indeed, it" (innahu), meaning: "indeed, your saying ﴿What is the penalty﴾ to the end," as al-Zajjāj said; or that this matter, namely her desire for Joseph, as al-Māwardī and al-Zamakhsharī mentioned; or that it refers to the tearing of the shirt, as Muqātil said. The address in ﴿of your guile﴾ is to her and her maids, or to her and to women in general. He described the guile of women as great, although it may be found in men, because they are subtler in guile by their nature and by what they are free to devote themselves to, and some of them learn from others, and they are more effective in strategy. God Most High said: ﴿And from the evil of the blowers in knots﴾ [al-Falaq: 4]. As for those in palaces, they have from this what is not found in others, because they are more free than others and more at ease with their peers.

﴿Joseph, turn away from this﴾, meaning: from this matter, and conceal it, and do not speak of it. In calling him by name there is closeness to him and gentleness. Then he turned to her and said: ﴿and ask forgiveness for your sin﴾. The apparent reading is that the speaker of this is the ʿAzīz. Ibn ʿAbbās said: the witness, who was the man who was with the ʿAzīz, called out to him and said: "Ask forgiveness for your sin," meaning for your husband and master. He then mentioned the reason for seeking forgiveness, which is his saying "for your sin," then confirmed it with his saying ﴿indeed you were among the sinners﴾. He did not say "among the sinful women" (khāṭiʾāt), because khāṭiʾīn is more general, since it applies to males and females by way of masculine prevalence. It is said: khuṭṭiʾa, when he sins deliberately. Al-Zamakhsharī said: the ʿAzīz was only forbearing. It is reported that he had little jealousy. The soil and climate of Qiṭfīr's region required this. Where is this compared with what happened to one of our kings, who was with his intimate companions in a gathering of entertainment, and a slave girl was singing to them from behind a curtain. One of his close companions asked her to repeat two verses she had sung, and soon the head of the slave girl was brought, severed, in a basin, and the king said to him: "Repeat the two verses from this head." The one asked to repeat was struck with dismay, and he fell ill for the rest of that king's life.

﴿And they both raced to the door, and she tore his shirt from behind, and they found her husband at the door. She said: "What is the penalty for one who intended evil against your family, except that he be imprisoned or suffer a painful punishment?"﴾ ﴿He said: "It was she who sought to seduce me from myself." And a witness from her family testified: "If his shirt is torn from the front, then she has told the truth and he is among the liars."﴾ ﴿"But if his shirt is torn from behind, then she has lied and he is among the truthful."﴾ ﴿So when he saw his shirt torn from behind, he said: "Indeed, it is of your guile, women. Indeed, your guile is great."﴾ ﴿"Joseph, turn away from this. And you, ask forgiveness for your sin; indeed, you were among the sinners."﴾

The original construction of istabaqa is that it takes ilā ("to") after it, but here it is omitted for brevity (ittisāʿan, "by extension"). It has been mentioned that the doors were seven. So the doors would open for him one by one without a key, according to what is reported from Kaʿb, that the bolts of the locks would scatter and fall until he passed through the doors. It is also possible that the closed doors were not in sequence, one after another, but in different directions, all of them being exits from the place where they were. So they raced to a door from which he could leave, and it was not necessarily the seventh in sequence, but one of them.

﴿And she tore﴾ may be coordinated with ﴿they raced﴾, or it may be a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: "while she had torn," i.e., she pulled him from behind by the upper part of the shirt at the collar, so it split down to the bottom. Qadd means cutting and splitting, and it is mostly used for what is lengthwise. The poet said:

*"Cutting the Salūqī (a fine hunting dog) with its tightly woven fabric, and kindling with the flint the fire of al-Ḥubāḥib."*

Qaṭṭ is used for what is across (widthwise). Al-Mufaḍḍal ibn Ḥarb said: "I saw in a Qur'an copy qaṭṭ min dubur," meaning a split. Yaʿqūb said: "Shaqq (splitting) is in healthy leather and healthy cloth." Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "A group recited (qaṭṭa)."

And when they saw him, they were struck with awe of him and cut their hands and said, "Perfect is Allah! This is not a human. This is none but a noble angel."﴾ [Yusuf: 31] ﴿She said, "That is the one about whom you blamed me. And I did seek to seduce him, but he refused. And if he does not do what I order him, he will surely be imprisoned and will be among the debased."﴾ [Yusuf: 32] ﴿He said, "My Lord, prison is more beloved to me than what they invite me to. And unless You turn their plot away from me, I might incline toward them and be among the ignorant."﴾ [Yusuf: 33] ﴿So his Lord responded to him and turned away from him their plot. Indeed, He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.﴾ [Yusuf: 34] ﴿Then it occurred to them, after they had seen the signs, to imprison him for a time.﴾ [Yusuf: 35] ﴿And there entered with him into prison two young men. Judgment belongs only to Allah. He has commanded that you worship none but Him. That is the upright religion, but most of the people do not know.﴾ [Yusuf: 40] ﴿O two companions of the prison, as for one of you, he will give his lord wine to drink; and as for the other, he will be crucified, and birds will eat from his head. The matter has been decided about which you both inquire.﴾ [Yusuf: 41] ﴿And he said to the one he thought would be saved of the two, "Mention me to your lord." O eminent ones, explain to me my vision, if you are able to interpret visions."﴾ [Yusuf: 43] ﴿They said, "Confused dreams. And we are not learned in the interpretation of dreams."﴾ [Yusuf: 44]

**An-Niswah** (women): it is with a kasra on the nun, of the pattern *fi'lah*, and it is a broken plural (*jam' taksir*) of paucity (*li-l-qillah*) that has no singular from its own form. Ibn al-Sarraj claimed that it is a collective noun (*ism jam'*). Al-Zamakhshari said: *an-niswah* is a singular noun for the plural of *al-mar'ah*, and its femininity is not real (*ghayr haqiqi*), which is why the feminine ta' is not attached to its verb, and he ended. And on the basis that it is a broken plural, the ta' is not attached, because it is permissible to say: *qamati al-hunud* and *qama al-hunud*. Its nun may also be vowelled with a damma, and then it is a collective noun. Its broken plural for multitude is *niswan*, and *al-nisa'* is also a broken plural for multitude and has no singular from its own form.

**Shaghafa**: he pierced the *shaghaf*, which is the membrane (*hijab*) of the heart. It was said: its white matter (*suwaydauh*). It was said: it is a disease that reaches the heart and penetrates to the heart. The kasra on the ghayn is the dialect of Tamim. It was said: the *shaghaf* is a thin skin called "the tongue of the heart." *Shaghafa*: the intensity reached the heart, so it burned, from the *shaghf* of the camel when one smears it with tar and burns it. *Al-mashghuf* is the one whom love has burned in his heart. From this is the saying of al-A'sha:

*He disobeys the slanderers, and love at times makes what the one smitten has done appear fine to him.*

The ghayn may also be pronounced with a kasra. **Al-muttaka'**: the cushion and the couch. **Al-matk**: the citron, and its singular is *matkah*. The poet said:

*So she sent a citron, the one that is her father's.*

It was said: it is a term that covers everything cut with a knife, the citron and other fruits. He said:

*He drinks sin openly from the cup, and we see the matk lent among us.*

It is from *matk* in the sense of *batt al-shay'*, i.e., he cut it. The author of *al-Lawami'* said: *al-mutk* with a damma, according to al-Khalil, is honey, and according to al-Asma'i, is the citron. Abu 'Umar said: and pure drink. Abu 'Umar also said: in it there are three dialects, *al-mutk* with the three vowels. It was said: with a kasra it is *al-khilal* (a toothpick), and it was said: rather, musk. Al-Kisa'i also said: in it are the three dialects, and it may be with a fatha, meaning the one perfumed with incense (*al-mujammar*), according to Qudā'ah. He also said: it may be, in the three dialects, *al-faludh al-mu'aqqad* (a kind of sweet). (p-300) Al-Fadl said: in the three dialects it is *al-bazmaward*, and every thing wrapped in meat and thin dough. He also said: *al-mutk* with a damma is the table (*al-ma'idah*), or wine in the dialect of Kindah.

**Al-sikkin** (knife): it is masculine and feminine, as said by al-Farra' and al-Kisa'i, while al-Asma'i knew of it only the masculine form.

**Hasha** (far be): al-Farra' said: among the Arabs there are those who complete it (as *hasha*), and in the dialect of the Hijaz: *hasha laka*, and some Arabs say: *hasha Zayd*, as if he intended *hasha li-Zayd*, and this is among the people of the Hijaz, and he ended. Al-Zamakhshari said: *hasha* is a word that conveys the meaning of exoneration in exception. You say: "The people wronged, *hasha Zayd*." He said:

*Far be Abu Thawban from it, that we are stingy in reviling and insult.*

It is one of the prepositions (*huruf al-jarr*), so it is placed in the position of exoneration and innocence, and the meaning of *hasha Allah* is the innocence of Allah and the glorification of Allah, and he ended. What was mentioned, that it conveys the meaning of exoneration in the chapter of exception, is not known among the grammarians. There is no difference between your saying "the people stood except Zayd" and "the people stood *hasha Zayd*." When he illustrated with his saying "the people wronged, *hasha Zayd*," and it was understood from this illustration that Zayd is innocent of wrongdoing, he made this understood from it in every place. As for what he cited, *hasha Abi Thawban*, Ibn 'Atiyyah and most grammarians recite it thus, and it is a line where they combined the first half of one verse with the second half of another, and they are from two verses, which are: "Far be Abu Thawban from it, that Abu Thawban is not a mute or a pale one.
'Amr ibn 'Abd Allah, indeed in him is a stinginess against reviling and insult."

**'Asr al-'inab** (pressing grapes): squeezing out what is in it of liquid with force.

**Al-khubz** (bread): known, its plural is *akhbaz*, and its agent noun is *khabbaz* (baker).

**Al-bid'** (a few): what lies between three and nine, said by Qatadah. Mujahid said: from three to seven. Abu 'Ubaydah said: *al-bid'* does not reach a decade nor half a decade, but it is from one to ten. Al-Farra' said: *al-bid'* is mentioned only with tens, and it is not mentioned with a hundred or a thousand.

**Al-simann** (fatness): known, and it is the verbal noun of *samina yasman*, and the agent noun is *samin*, and the verbal noun and the agent noun are irregular (*'ala ghayr qiyas*).

**Al-'ajfa'** (lean): extremely emaciated. He said:

*And the men of Mecca are lean, pacing.*

**Al-dighth** (bundle): less than a bundle (*huzmah*) and more than a handful of plants and herbage, of one kind or of mixed plants and herbage. Of one kind is what is narrated regarding His saying: ﴿And take in your hand a bundle and strike with it﴾ [Sad: 44], that he took a palm-frond cluster. It is also narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did something similar in carrying out a legal punishment on a man. Ibn Muqbil said:

*A young woman whose bed seems strewn with bundles of basil on a northern-wind morning.*

From mixtures is the Arab saying in their proverbs: *dagha 'ala imalah* (he mixed with inclination).

﴿And women in the city said...﴾

The feminine ta' was not attached, because it is a broken plural of the feminine, and both forms are permissible for it. *Niswah*, as we mentioned, is a plural of paucity. They were, as transmitted, five: a female baker, a female cupbearer, a female doorkeeper, a female jailer, and the wife of the keeper of her animals. ﴿In the city﴾ is Egypt. The meaning of ﴿in the city﴾ is that they spread this matter of the love of the wife of the chief for Yusuf, and they explicitly attributed her to the chief for the sake of exaggeration in reproach, because souls are more receptive to hearing about the great and what happens to them. She expressed it with ﴿tur'idu﴾ (is seeking to seduce), which is the present tense indicating that this became her habit: she deceives him constantly about himself, as you say: "Zayd gives and withholds." They did not say "she sought to seduce her servant boy." Then they pointed out the reason for the continuity of the seduction, which is that he had captivated her with love; that is, his love reached the core of her heart. ("Hubban") is in the accusative as a *tamyiz* (specification) transferred from the subject, like his saying: "I filled the vessel with water," its original being "the water filled the vessel," and the original of this is "his love captivated her." **Al-fata** (the youth) is the boy, and its usage is for a slave, and in a hadith: "Let none of you say 'my slave' or 'my female slave'; let him say 'my youth' (*fataya*) and 'my girl' (*fataati*)." It has been said regarding one who is not a slave. The original meaning of *al-fata* in language is the young man, but since most of the servants were young men, the name *fata* was borrowed for them.

Thabit al-Bunani recited ﴿shaghafaha﴾ with a kasra on the ghayn with a dot, while the majority recite it with a fatha. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, 'Ali ibn al-Husayn and his son Muhammad ibn 'Ali and his son Ja'far ibn Muhammad, al-Sha'bi, and 'Awf al-A'rabi recited it with a fatha on the unpointed ghayn (i.e., the 'ayn); likewise Qatadah, Ibn Hurmuz, Mujahid, Humayd, and al-Zuhri, according to a variant from them. It is narrated from Thabit al-Bunani and Ibn Raja' a kasra on the unpointed 'ayn. Ibn Zayd said: *al-shaghaf* is in love, and *al-sha'af* is in hatred. Al-Sha'bi said: *al-shaghaf* and *al-mashghuf* with the dotted ghayn are in love, and *al-shaghaf* is madness, and *al-mash'uf* is the madman. The two grammarians (Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i), Hamzah, Hisham, and Ibn Muhaysin assimilated the dal of *qad* into the shin of ﴿shaghafaha﴾.

Then they resented her for that, and said: ﴿Indeed, we see her in clear error﴾, that is: in evident bewilderment before people.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 12, verse 31 (part 1 of 2):

﴿So when she heard of their scheming, she sent for them and prepared for them a reclining-cushion, and gave each one of them a knife, and said, "Come out before them." So when they saw him, they magnified him, and cut their hands, and said, "Exalted is Allah! This is not a human being; this is none other than a noble angel."﴾

It is narrated that the statement that came out of the women was intended by them only as a scheme against the wife of the Aziz, so that they would anger her (p-302) until she would present Joseph to them, so that her excuse would be made clear, or her blame would be justified. And "their scheming" (makrihinna) is their backbiting of her, and the bad nature of their statement about her was that she had fallen in love with Joseph. Backbiting was called "scheming" because it is done in secret and in the absence of the person, just as the schemer conceals his scheme. It was also said: she had asked them to keep her secret, but they disclosed it against her. She sent for them so that they would attend. It was said: she invited forty women, among them the five mentioned. The apparent reading is that the pronoun refers to those women who spoke what they said about her.

﴿And prepared for them a reclining-cushion﴾, that is: she made ready and arranged for them what they would recline upon, of cushions, pillows and mattresses, and other things that are found in a gathering prepared for honor. It is known that this kind of honoring is not without food and drink. Here something is omitted, its estimate being: so they came and reclined. As for "reclining-cushion" (muttaka'an), it may be that the intended meaning is the genus, or the meaning may be: she prepared for each one of them a reclining-cushion, just as it came: "and gave each one of them a knife." Ibn 'Abbas said: "muttaka'an" means a gathering (majlis), mentioned by al-Zahrawi, and "muttaka'an" would then be a noun of place, i.e., a place upon which they recline; and according to what preceded, the implements upon which one reclines are meant. Mujahid said: the muttaka' is food that is cut into pieces. Al-Qutabi said: it is said "we reclined at so-and-so's" meaning "we ate," and this is a figure of speech, expressing by the posture in which the luxurious diner eats, reclining, which is the custom of the luxurious. Do you not see the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "As for me, I do not eat reclining," or as he said. Since "reclining" is not used to express what is eaten, it is known that such a gathering must have food and drink, so among the food there would be something that is cut with knives. It was said: it was meat, and they did not tear the meat with their teeth; rather they ate it by slicing it with knives. It was said: it was citron (utrunj). It was said: it was bazmaward, which resembles citron and is found in those lands. It was said: it is made of sugar, almonds and mixtures, and its substance is that it needs to be cut with a knife; and whoever cuts something usually leans upon it, so he is reclining upon it. It was said: their intention in coming out in these postures, reclining, with knives in their hands with which they would cut two things, was: first, their astonishment at seeing him and their preoccupation with themselves, so their hands would fall upon their own hands and they would cut them, and this would be a scheme against them, as they were distracted from what had befallen them of cutting their hands, and did not perceive it with the severe pain, because of the extent to which admiration for Joseph had overwhelmed them and taken away their minds. The second: to frighten Joseph with her scheme when he came out before women gathered with daggers in their hands, making him imagine that they would leap upon him, so that he would be constantly wary of a scheme, and perhaps he would consent to her desire according to her supposition; but Joseph, Allah had protected him from all the evil she desired for him.

Al-Zuhri, Abu Ja'far and Shayba read: "muttaki" with a doubled ta' without hamza, on the pattern of "muttaqi," so this admits two possibilities: first, that it is from reclining (ittika'), and in it is the easing of the hamza, as they said of "tawadda'tu": "tawdi'ah." The second: it is a muftaʻal from "awkaytu al-siqa'" when I tied it tight; i.e., they tighten upon it, either by reclining or by cutting with knives. Al-A'raj read: "muttaki'an," a mufa''al from "taki'a yattaki'u" when he reclined. Al-Hasan and Ibn Hurmuz read: "muttaka'an" with a long vowel and hamza, and it is a muftaʻal from reclining, except that he prolonged the fatha so that an alif was produced from it, as they said: "wa man dhamma al-rijala bi-muntazah," and they said:
"I seek refuge in Allah from the scorpions, the raised ones, the knotted of tails."

Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn 'Umar, Mujahid, Qatada, al-Dahhak, al-Jahdari, al-Kalbi and Iban ibn Taghlib read: "mutkan" with a damma on the mim, a sukun on the ta', and tanwin on the kaf. It was also transmitted thus from Ibn Hurmuz. 'Abdullah and Mu'adh read likewise, except that they gave the mim a fatha. The explanation of "mutkin" and "matkin" was given in al-Mufradat.

And she said, "Come out before them." This address is to Joseph, peace be upon him, and his coming out indicates his obedience to her in what does not involve disobeying Allah. In the speech there is an omission, its estimate being: so he came out before them. The meaning of "akbarnahu" is: they magnified him, and they were astonished at seeing that surpassing, splendid beauty. It was said: Joseph's superiority over people in beauty was like the superiority of the moon on the night of the full moon over the stars of the sky. And in the hadith of the Night Journey: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was informed of his meeting with Joseph, it was said: 'O Messenger of Allah, how did you see him?' He said: 'Like the moon on the night of the full moon.'" It was also said: when he walked through the alleys of Egypt, the radiance of his face would be seen on the walls, as the light of the sun is seen. It was said: he resembled Adam on the day his Lord created him. It was said: he inherited beauty from his grandmother Sarah. 'Abd al-Samad ibn 'Ali al-Hashimi, from his father, from his grandfather, said: its meaning is "they menstruated," and some women recited as proof for this interpretation:
"They come to women in their states of purity, and they do not come to women when they reach maturity (akbarna ikbaran)."

Ibn 'Atiyya said: this is a weak view, and the verse is fabricated and invented; so said al-Tabari and other verifiers, and 'Abd al-Samad is not among the transmitters of knowledge, may Allah have mercy on him. Al-Zamakhshari said: it was also said "akbarna" means "hadan" (menstruated), and the ha' is for pause; it is said: "akbarat al-mar'ah" when she menstruated, and its real meaning is from greatness (kibar), because by menstruation she leaves the limit of childhood for the limit of maturity. It seems that Abu al-Tayyib took from this interpretation his saying:
"Fear Allah and conceal this beauty with a veil, for if you appear, the young women in their chambers will menstruate." End. The consensus of the readers on dhamm the ha' in connection is evidence that it is not the ha' of pause, for if it were the ha' of pause, and whoever treats connection as pause, he would not vowel the ha'. The apparent reading is that the pronoun in "akbarnahu" refers to Joseph, if it is established that "akbara" means "menstruated," so the ha' would refer to the verbal noun, i.e., "they magnified the magnifying." "And they cut their hands," i.e., they wounded them, as you say: "I was cutting the meat, so I cut my hand." The doubling is for intensity, either with respect to the number of those cutting, or with respect to the intensity of the cutting in the hand of each one of them. So the wound seems to have occurred repeatedly in one hand, and its owner did not feel it, because of what had captivated her of Joseph's beauty; it is as though they had been absent from their senses. The apparent reading is that "aydi" are the limbs known by this name.

ʻIkrima said: "aydi" here means the sleeves. When they did this difficult act of wounding their hands, and what they saw of Joseph and his beauty overcame them, they said: "Allah forbid!" The majority read: "Hasha lillah" without an alif after the shin and with "lillah" with the genitive lam. Abu 'Amr read: "Hasha lillah" without alif and with the genitive lam. A group, including al-A'mash, read: "Hashā" on the pattern of "rama," "lillah" with the genitive lam. al-Hasan read: "Hash" with a sukun on the shin in connection and in pause, with the genitive lam. Ubayy and 'Abdullah read: "Hasha Allah" with idafa, and from them as the reading of Abu 'Amr, as said by the author of al-Lawami. al-Hasan read: "Hash al-Ilah." Ibn 'Atiyya said: "with the omission of the alif from hasha." The author of al-Lawami said: "with the deletion of the alif, and this indicates that it is a particle of the genitive governing what follows it; as for al-Ilah, he released it from assimilation, and it is a verbal noun placed in the position of the object, its meaning being 'the one worshipped.'" He said: "The alif was deleted from 'hasha' for lightness." End. What Ibn 'Atiyya and the author of al-Lawami said, that the alif in "hasha" in the reading of al-Hasan is deleted, is not determined, unless it is reported from him that he pauses in this reading with the shin sukun; if nothing is reported from him in that, it is possible that the alif was deleted due to the meeting of two sakins, since the original is "hasha al-Ilah," then it was transferred, deleting the hamza and vowelling the lam with its vowel, and this vowelling was not counted because it is incidental, as it is deleted in "yakhsha al-Ilah"; and if the vowel were counted, the alif would not be deleted. Abu al-Sammal read: "Hashan lillah" with tanwin, as in "ra'yan lillah." As for the readings "lillah" with the genitive lam in other than the reading of Abu al-Sammal, it is not permissible that what precedes it, of "hasha," "hasha," "hashā," or "hash," be a genitive particle, because a genitive particle does not enter upon a genitive particle, and because it has been inflected by deletion in both, and the original of inflection by deletion is that it not be in particles. Al-Mubarrad and others, like Ibn 'Atiyya, claimed that its verbhood is determined, and the subject is a pronoun of Joseph; i.e., "Hasha Yusuf an yuqarifa ma ramathu bihi" (Joseph is far removed from committing what she accused him of). The meaning of "lillah": for the obedience of Allah, or for a position from Allah, or for the elevation of Allah that he should be accused of what she accused him of, or that he should submit to its like, because those are the acts of humans, and he is not one of them; he is only an angel. On this view the lam in "lillah" is causal, i.e., Joseph avoided disobedience for the sake of the obedience of Allah, or on account of what had happened before. Other than al-Mubarrad went to the view that it is a noun, and its accusative is that of the verbal noun in place of the verb's utterance, as if he had said: "exaltation of Allah." What indicates its nounhood is the reading of Abu al-Sammal, "hashan," with tanwin, and on this view "lillah" is attached to an omitted element by way of explanation, like "laka" after "suqyan." In the well-known readings it was not made tanwin, observing its original from which it was transferred, which is the particle; do you not see that they said "min 'an yamīnihi," making "'an" a noun and not inflecting it, and they said "min 'alayhi," and did not keep its alif with the pronoun, but kept "'an" on its build, and turned the alif of "'alā" with the pronoun, observing its origin. As for the reading of al-Hasan and the reading of Ubayy with idafa, it is a verbal noun attached to its alif, as they said: "subhan Allah." This is the choice of al-Zamakhshari. Ibn 'Atiyya said: As for the reading of Ubayy ibn Ka'b and Ibn Mas'ud, Abu 'Ali said: "hasha" is a particle of exception, as the poet said: "Hasha Abi Thawban." End. As for the reading of al-Hasan "hash" with sukun, there is a joining of two sakins, and they have weakened this. Al-Zamakhshari said: The meaning is the exaltation of Allah from attributes of incapacity, and the wonder at His power to create a beauty like this one, a chaste one. As for His saying: "Hasha lillah, we know no evil in him" (Yusuf 51), the wonder is at His power to create a chaste one like him. "This is not a human" — since he was strange in beauty, surpassing in comeliness, beyond what the beauty of human forms is, they negated humanity from him and affirmed for him angelhood, because the beauty of an angel was fixed in natures, even though it is not seen; and Arab poets and later writers have expressed this. One of the Arabs said:
"You are not of human kind, but of an angel who descended from the air of heaven, pouring rain."
And one of the later writers said:
"A people who, when confronted, were angels in beauty, and when fought, were demons."

The accusative (*nasb*) of (*basharan*) follows the dialect of the Hijaz (*lughat al-Hijaz*), and for this reason the Qur'an has ﴿ma hunna ummahatihim, in ummahatuhum﴾ [al-Mujadila: 2] and ﴿fa-ma minkum min ahadin 'anhu hajizin﴾ [al-Haqqa: 47]. The dialect of Tamim uses the nominative (*raf'*). Ibn 'Atiyya said: "He did not read it that way." al-Zamakhshari said: "Whoever reads according to his natural speech (*saliqah*) from the Banu Tamim reads (*basharun*) with the nominative, and this is the reading of Ibn Mas'ud." End of quote.

al-Hasan and Abu al-Huwayrith al-Hanafi read: (*ma hadha bushra*). Sahib al-Lawami' said: "It is possible that its meaning is 'with something sold or bought,' i.e., this is not among the things that are bought and sold. It is also possible that it means 'not a price,' as if he said: 'He is too exalted for any of these things to apply to him.' So *al-shira'* (purchase) is a verbal noun (*masdar*) placed in the position of the object." 'Abd al-Warith, on the authority of Abu 'Amr, followed them in this, and added to them: (*illa malikun*) with a kasra on the lam, the singular of *al-muluk* (kings). By this they negated from him the humiliation of slaves and placed him in the category of kings. And Allah knows best." End of quote.

Ibn 'Atiyya attributed the kasra on the lam to al-Hasan and Abu al-Huwayrith, who read (*bushra*), and said: "When they magnified the beauty of his appearance, they said: 'This is not one who could be a slave, (*bushra*), rather this is only one who could be a noble king.'" al-Zamakhshari said: "It is also read (*ma hadha bushra*), meaning: not a base, enslaved servant. (*In hadha illa malikun karim*). You say: 'This is *bushra*,' i.e., a source of good news (*husul bushra*), in the sense of 'this is a buyer.' And you say: 'This is *lak bushra*,' i.e., a virgin (*bikran*)." He also said: "Using (*ma*) to operate like (*laysa*) is not the ancient Hijazi dialect, and the Qur'an came in it." End of quote.

He said "ancient" (*al-qudma*) because the common usage in the Hijazi dialect is to put the predicate in the genitive with the particle *bi*, so you say: *ma Zaydun bi-qa'im* ("Zayd is not standing"). Most of what came in the Qur'an is according to this. As for the accusative of the predicate, it belongs to the ancient Hijazi dialect, to the extent that the grammarians found no witness for the accusative of the predicate in the poetry of the Hijaz apart from the words of the poet:

*Wa-ana al-nadhiru bi-hurratin musawwadatin ∗∗∗ tasilu al-juyusha ilaykum aqwaduha*

"I am the warner, with a dark-clad noble host whose leaders reach you."

*Abna'uha mutakannifuna abahum ∗∗∗ hanaqu al-sudura wa-ma hum awladuha*

"Its sons surround their father; they enrage the breasts, and they are not its sons."

al-Farra', who was a reliable and trustworthy authority on dialects, said: "The people of the Hijaz almost never speak except with *bi*." When the pronunciation with *bi* predominated among the people of the Hijaz, al-Zamakhshari said: "The ancient Hijazi dialect... so the Qur'an came in both dialects, the ancient and others."

(p-305) She said, "That is the one you blamed me for. I did indeed seek to seduce him, but he remained chaste. If he does not do what I command him, he will certainly be imprisoned and will be among the humiliated." He said, "My Lord, prison is dearer to me than what they invite me to. Unless You turn their scheming away from me, I shall incline towards them and be among the ignorant." So his Lord responded to him and turned away from him their scheming; indeed He is the All-Hearing, All-Knowing. Then it occurred to them, after they had seen the signs, that they should imprison him for a time.

(Dhā) is the demonstrative noun, and the lām is for the distance of the one pointed to. (Kunna) is addressed to those women. It is possible that when she saw their bewilderment, the cutting of their hands with knives, and their saying, "This is not a human being" (Q. 12:31), she moved away from them out of consideration for them, so that their temptation would not increase and so that they might return to their beauty. Therefore she pointed to him with the demonstrative for the distant. It is also possible that she pointed to him, though he was near, with the word for the distant, in order to raise his station in beauty, to emphasise how far he was from the place of such a thing, and because, given his rarity, it is far-fetched that such a thing could come from him. The demonstrative includes the attributes mentioned earlier (p-306) concerning him, as if it were said: "He for whose sake you cut your hands, whom you exalted, and about whom you said what you said, denying him humanity and affirming for him angelic nature, is the one you blamed me for," that is, for my love of him and my infatuation with him. Al-Zamakhshari (d. 538 AH) said: "It may also be a reference to the matter expressed by their saying, 'She is infatuated with her Canaanite slave.' She says: 'This is that Canaanite slave about whom you blamed me, though you had already formed an image of him in your own minds. If you had depicted him as he truly is, and had depicted him as you have seen him, you would have excused me for being captivated by him.'" End of quotation. The pronoun in (fīhi) refers to Yusuf. Ibn 'Atiyya (d. 541 AH) said: "It may also be that the reference is to Yusuf's love, and the pronoun refers to the love, so that it is a reference to an absent thing in its usual manner." End of quotation.

Then the wife of the 'Aziz confessed before the women to having sought seduction, and she felt at ease with them in this, since she knew they had excused her.

(Fa-staʿṣama): Ibn 'Atiyya said: "Its meaning is that he sought protection (ʿiṣma), held fast to it, and refused me." Al-Zamakhshari said: "The form istiʿṣām is an intensive form indicating firm refusal and intense self-restraint, as if he were in protection while striving to increase it. It is like istamsaka (he held fast), istawsaʿa (he expanded), and istajmaʿa al-raʾy (he gathered his opinion), and istafḥala al-khaṭb (the matter became grave). This is a clarification of what Yusuf (peace be upon him) did, beyond which nothing more can be added, and a proof, brighter than any other, that he was innocent of what the people of hashw (the padders, i.e., those who insert unreliable material into reports) attributed to him, the interpretations they gave to 'the concern' and 'the proof'." End of quotation. What the morphologists (al-tasrīfiyyūn, specialists in verb-forms) mention about (istaʿṣama) is that it is equivalent in meaning to (iʿtaṣama), so that the form istafʿala here is equivalent to iftaʿala. This is better than taking istafʿala here to indicate seeking, because iʿtaṣama indicates the existence of his protection, whereas seeking protection does not indicate its attainment. As for its being an intensive form indicating striving to increase the protection, the morphologists did not mention this meaning for istafʿala. As for istamsaka, istawsaʿa, and istajmaʿa al-raʾy, the form istafʿala here is equivalent to iftaʿala, and the meaning is imtasaka (he held fast), ittasaʿa (he expanded), and ijtamaʿa al-raʾy (his opinion gathered). As for istafḥala al-khaṭb, the form istafʿala here is equivalent to tafaʿʿala, meaning tafaḥḥala al-khaṭb (the matter became grave), like istakbara and takabbara.

Then she began threatening him, swearing to that, while he heard her words, with her saying: "If he does not do what I command him" (Q. 12:32). The pronoun in (āmuruhu) refers to the relative pronoun, meaning "what I command him to do," so the preposition is omitted, as in amartuka al-khayr (I commanded you to do good). The first object of (āmuru) is omitted, and the original would be "what I command him with." If you take (mā) as a verbal noun (maṣdariyya), it is permissible, and the pronoun then refers to Yusuf, meaning "my commanding him," that is, "what I impose on him by my command."

A group recited (wa-la-yakūnanna) with the doubled nūn, and its writing in the codex with an alif follows the recitation of the majority, which uses the light nūn. It is stopped upon with an alif, as in the verse of al-A'shā:

"Do not worship Satan, but worship Allah."

(Min al-ṣāghirīn): from among the humble, the abased. Here the painful punishment is not mentioned, which she mentioned in "What is the recompense for one who intended evil to your wife?" (Q. 12:25), because at that time her anger was fresh and she was disclaiming that she was the one who sought seduction, so the severe punishment was fitting there. The pronoun in (lahum) refers to the 'Aziz and his household. The "signs" (al-āyāt) are the indications that show Yusuf's innocence. Mujāhid and others said: the tearing of the shirt. If the witness was a child, it is a great sign; if he was a man, it is an argument based on custom. What appears is that the word "sign" is used only for what is clear and manifest, and its plural indicates the appearance of several clear matters which showed his innocence. It is possible that the signs they saw were not all specified in the Qur'an, but that they saw the witness's statement, the tearing of the shirt, and other things not mentioned. As for what 'Ikrima mentioned, that among the signs was the scratching of her face, and al-Suddī that it was the cutting of their hands, there is no indication of innocence in that, so it is not a sign.

"They should imprison him" (la-yasjunnanahu) is the answer to a omitted oath, and the oath and its answer are governed by an omitted saying whose implied form is "saying." The Ḥasan recited (la-tasjunnanahu) with the tā', addressing the 'Aziz and those around him, or the 'Aziz alone in a respectful manner. Ibn Mas'ūd recited "'attā" by changing the ḥā' of ḥattā into an 'ayn, and this is the dialect of Hudhayl. He recited it so, and wrote to him instructing him to recite in the dialect of Quraysh, "ḥattā," not in the dialect of Hudhayl. The meaning is "until a time," and ḥīn indicates an unrestricted period of time. Whoever specified a time here did so with reference to the duration of Yusuf's imprisonment; it is not that the word is so defined in the language. It seems that they proposed a period so that they could see what would happen to him.

In their imprisoning Yusuf there is evidence of the cunning of women, of the seducing of a husband by a wife, of his submission to her and his infatuation with her, and of his placing the reins of his affair in her hand, even though her treachery was manifest and Yusuf was innocent. It is related that when Yusuf refused the sin and the wife of the 'Aziz despaired of him, she said to her husband: "This Hebrew youth has disgraced me among the people, and he makes excuses to them and describes the matter according to his own choice, while I am confined and kept in seclusion. Either you permit me to go out to the people and make my excuse and call him a liar, or you imprison him as I am imprisoned." Then the decision to imprison him occurred to them. Ibn 'Abbās said: "So he ordered that he be carried on a donkey, and a drum was beaten, and it was proclaimed in the markets of Egypt that Yusuf the Hebrew had sought to seduce his mistress, so this is his recompense: that he be imprisoned." Abū Ṣāliḥ said: "Ibn 'Abbās did not relate this report except that he wept."

(p-305) She said, "That is the one you blamed me for. I did indeed seek to seduce him, but he remained chaste. If he does not do what I command him, he will certainly be imprisoned and will be among the humiliated." He said, "My Lord, prison is dearer to me than what they invite me to. Unless You turn their scheming away from me, I shall incline towards them and be among the ignorant." So his Lord responded to him and turned away from him their scheming; indeed He is the All-Hearing, All-Knowing. Then it occurred to them, after they had seen the signs, that they should imprison him for a time.

(Dhā) is the demonstrative noun, and the lām is for the distance of the one pointed to. (Kunna) is addressed to those women. It is possible that when she saw their bewilderment, the cutting of their hands with knives, and their saying, "This is not a human being" (Q. 12:31), she moved away from them out of consideration for them, so that their temptation would not increase and so that they might return to their beauty. Therefore she pointed to him with the demonstrative for the distant. It is also possible that she pointed to him, though he was near, with the word for the distant, in order to raise his station in beauty, to emphasise how far he was from the place of such a thing, and because, given his rarity, it is far-fetched that such a thing could come from him. The demonstrative includes the attributes mentioned earlier (p-306) concerning him, as if it were said: "He for whose sake you cut your hands, whom you exalted, and about whom you said what you said, denying him humanity and affirming for him angelic nature, is the one you blamed me for," that is, for my love of him and my infatuation with him. Al-Zamakhshari (d. 538 AH) said: "It may also be a reference to the matter expressed by their saying, 'She is infatuated with her Canaanite slave.' She says: 'This is that Canaanite slave about whom you blamed me, though you had already formed an image of him in your own minds. If you had depicted him as he truly is, and had depicted him as you have seen him, you would have excused me for being captivated by him.'" End of quotation. The pronoun in (fīhi) refers to Yusuf. Ibn 'Atiyya (d. 541 AH) said: "It may also be that the reference is to Yusuf's love, and the pronoun refers to the love, so that it is a reference to an absent thing in its usual manner." End of quotation.

Then the wife of the 'Aziz confessed before the women to having sought seduction, and she felt at ease with them in this, since she knew they had excused her.

(Fa-staʿṣama): Ibn 'Atiyya said: "Its meaning is that he sought protection (ʿiṣma), held fast to it, and refused me." Al-Zamakhshari said: "The form istiʿṣām is an intensive form indicating firm refusal and intense self-restraint, as if he were in protection while striving to increase it. It is like istamsaka (he held fast), istawsaʿa (he expanded), and istajmaʿa al-raʾy (he gathered his opinion), and istafḥala al-khaṭb (the matter became grave). This is a clarification of what Yusuf (peace be upon him) did, beyond which nothing more can be added, and a proof, brighter than any other, that he was innocent of what the people of hashw (the padders, i.e., those who insert unreliable material into reports) attributed to him, the interpretations they gave to 'the concern' and 'the proof'." End of quotation. What the morphologists (al-tasrīfiyyūn, specialists in verb-forms) mention about (istaʿṣama) is that it is equivalent in meaning to (iʿtaṣama), so that the form istafʿala here is equivalent to iftaʿala. This is better than taking istafʿala here to indicate seeking, because iʿtaṣama indicates the existence of his protection, whereas seeking protection does not indicate its attainment. As for its being an intensive form indicating striving to increase the protection, the morphologists did not mention this meaning for istafʿala. As for istamsaka, istawsaʿa, and istajmaʿa al-raʾy, the form istafʿala here is equivalent to iftaʿala, and the meaning is imtasaka (he held fast), ittasaʿa (he expanded), and ijtamaʿa al-raʾy (his opinion gathered). As for istafḥala al-khaṭb, the form istafʿala here is equivalent to tafaʿʿala, meaning tafaḥḥala al-khaṭb (the matter became grave), like istakbara and takabbara.

Then she began threatening him, swearing to that, while he heard her words, with her saying: "If he does not do what I command him" (Q. 12:32). The pronoun in (āmuruhu) refers to the relative pronoun, meaning "what I command him to do," so the preposition is omitted, as in amartuka al-khayr (I commanded you to do good). The first object of (āmuru) is omitted, and the original would be "what I command him with." If you take (mā) as a verbal noun (maṣdariyya), it is permissible, and the pronoun then refers to Yusuf, meaning "my commanding him," that is, "what I impose on him by my command."

A group recited (wa-la-yakūnanna) with the doubled nūn, and its writing in the codex with an alif follows the recitation of the majority, which uses the light nūn. It is stopped upon with an alif, as in the verse of al-A'shā:

"Do not worship Satan, but worship Allah."

(Min al-ṣāghirīn): from among the humble, the abased. Here the painful punishment is not mentioned, which she mentioned in "What is the recompense for one who intended evil to your wife?" (Q. 12:25), because at that time her anger was fresh and she was disclaiming that she was the one who sought seduction, so the severe punishment was fitting there. Here, however, she was in a state of hope and expectation, and she had established her excuse before the women. She was softened towards him, so she threatened him with prison. The women said to him: "Obey, and do what she commands you." He said: "My Lord, prison is dearer to me than what they invite me to" (Q. 12:33). He attributed the action to them because they were advising him and beautifying for him the submission to her, and they forbade him from throwing himself into prison and humiliation, so he sought refuge in Allah the Exalted. The implied meaning is "entering prison."

'Uthmān and his freedman Ṭāriq, Zayd ibn 'Alī, al-Zuhrī, Ibn Abī Isḥāq, Ibn Hurmuz, and Ya'qub recited (al-sijnu) with a fatḥa on the sīn, which is the verbal noun of sajana, meaning: their imprisoning me is dearer to me. The word (aḥabb) here is not on its usual pattern of comparison, because he never loved what they invited him to; rather, these are two evils, and he preferred one of the two over the other, even though one of them involves hardship and the other pleasure. But because of the consequences that follow that pleasure, namely disobedience to Allah and a bad end, it never occurred to him. And because of what the other entails of enduring hardship for the sake of Allah, patience through calamities, awaiting relief, and being constantly in the presence of Allah the Exalted, supplicating Him for his deliverance, he preferred it. Then he attached his protection to Allah and submitted to Allah, as is the custom of the prophets and the righteous, and [recognised] that He the Exalted averts evil only by Himself. So he said: "Unless You turn their scheming away from me, I shall incline towards them" (Q. 12:33), that is, I shall incline to what they invite me to. He made the answer to the condition his saying "I shall incline" (aṣbu), a word which indicates only inclination, not the actual commission of sin. It was also recited as (aṣubbu ilayhinna) from ṣababtu ṣabāt, meaning I am ṣabb (infatuated); al-ṣabāba is excessive longing, as if one pours oneself into what one desires. The reading of the majority is (aṣbu) from ṣabā ila al-lahw (he inclined to amusement), yaṣbū ṣaban wa-ṣabwan. It is said also: ṣabā yaṣbā ṣaban. Al-ṣibā with a kasra is amusement and play. "And be among the ignorant" (Q. 12:33), that is, among those who do not know, because one whose knowledge is of no benefit is like one who does not know. Or it means among the foolish, because falling into agreement with women and inclining to them is foolishness. The poet said:

"Ahda bi-Layli, and the heart was not infatuated with her, / except out of folly, and a dream-like remembrance."

Allah's answering of him is mentioned without a preceding word of supplication, because his saying "Unless You turn away from me" contains the meaning of asking for the turning away and supplicating. It is as if he had said: "My Lord, turn away from me their scheming." So He turned away from him their scheming (Q. 12:34), that is, He placed between him and the sin a barrier. "Indeed He is the All-Hearing" of the supplication of those who seek refuge in Him, "the All-Knowing" of their states and what their intentions conceal.

Then it occurred to them (thumma badā lahum), that is, it appeared to them. The subject of (badā) is a pronoun explained by what the meaning indicates, meaning: it appeared to them, that is, they saw or it became apparent, as the poet said:

"A change has appeared to you concerning that she-camel, a change of mind."

This is what the grammarians (al-nuḥāh, specialists in Arabic grammar) and the exegetes have said, except for one who permitted that the clause be the subject. He claimed that his saying "they should imprison him" is in the position of the subject of (badā), meaning: they imprisoned him for a time. The refutation of this view is mentioned in the science of grammar. What I hold is that the subject is a pronoun referring to the prison implied by His saying "he will certainly be imprisoned" (Q. 12:32), or by the word "prison" (al-sijnu) in the reading of the majority, or by "prison" (al-sajnu) in the reading of those who recite the sīn with a fatḥa. Abū Ṣāliḥ said: "Ibn 'Abbās did not relate this report except that he wept."

(p-308) ﴿And there entered with him into the prison two young men. One of them said, "Indeed, I see myself pressing wine." And the other said, "Indeed, I see myself carrying on my head bread, of which the birds eat. Inform us of its interpretation. Indeed, we see you as one of the doers of good."﴾

There is an omission in the speech, and its implied meaning is: "So they imprisoned him, and there entered with him into the prison two youths." It is narrated that they belonged to the greatest king, al-Walid ibn al-Rayyan, one of them being his baker and the other his cupbearer. It is narrated that the king accused them, claiming that the baker among them intended to poison him and that the cupbearer agreed with him on this, so he imprisoned them. This was said by al-Suddi.

"Ma'a" (with) indicates companionship and its beginning, so it shows that they imprisoned the three of them at one time. When Yusuf entered the prison, he won people over through his good speech, his excellence, and his nobility. He would console their sorrowful, visit their sick, ask on behalf of their poor, and urge them toward good. So the two youths loved him and kept close to him. The keeper of the prison and the one in charge of him also loved him, and he said to him: "Stay in whichever houses you wish." Yusuf said to him: "Do not love me, may Allah have mercy on you, for love has brought upon me harms. My aunt loved me, and I was tested by her love. My father loved me, and I was tested by his love. The wife of al-Aziz loved me, and I was tested by her love, as you see."

Yusuf had said to the people of the prison: "Indeed, I interpret dreams and do it well." It is narrated that the two youths said to him: "Indeed, we love you from the time we saw you." He said: "I implore you by Allah not to love me," and he mentioned what had preceded.

From Qatada: There were people in the prison whose hope had been cut off and whose sorrow had lengthened, so he began saying: "Be patient and be of good cheer, you will be rewarded. Indeed, for this there is a reward." They said: "May Allah bless you! How good your face is, and how good your character is! We have been blessed by your neighborhood. Who are you, young man?" Yusuf said: "The son of the chosen one of Allah, Ya'qub, son of the sacrificed one of Allah, Ishaq, son of the friend of Allah, Ibrahim." The keeper of the prison said to him: "If I could, I would release your path."

As for this dream of the two youths: Mujahid said: "They saw it as a real occurrence, and they wanted to ask him about it." Ibn Mas'ud and al-Sha'bi said: "They used it in order to test him." The one who saw himself pressing wine, his name was Bunu... He said: "I saw a vine with three fine branches, upon which were fine clusters of grapes, so I was pressing them and giving the king to drink." The one who saw the bread, his name was Mulhab. He said: "I was seeing myself coming out of the king's kitchen with three baskets of bread on my head, and birds were eating from its top."

"Ra'a" here is the dream-verb (hulmiyya), which took the course of the verbs of the heart in permitting its agent and its object to be two pronouns with one referent. So in "arani" there is the implied subject pronoun, and the verb has reached the attached pronoun, which is the subject marker, and both refer to a single meaning. It is not permissible to say "idribni" or "akrimni."

Grapes were called khamr (wine) on account of what they become. It was said: khamr in the dialect of Ghassan is the name for grapes. It was also said: this is the language of the Azd of Oman. Al-Mu'tamir said: "I met a Bedouin carrying grapes in a container, and I said: 'What are you carrying?' He said: 'Khamr,' meaning grapes."

Ubayy and Abdullah recited "a'siru 'inaban" (I press grapes). This should be understood as tafsir (exegesis) rather than recitation, because it contradicts the consonantal text of the codex (mushaf), and the established recitation transmitted from them by tawatur (mass transmission) is "a'siru khamran" (I press wine).

Ibn 'Atiyya said: "It is permissible that the description of the wine is that it is 'pressed,' since pressing is for it and because of it." In the codex of Abdullah it reads: "fawqa ra'si tharidan ta'kulu al-tayru minhu" (bread-soup on my head, of which the birds eat). This too is tafsir and not a recitation.

The pronoun in "ta'wilihi" (its interpretation) refers back to what he was told about, and it is treated like a demonstrative, as if it were said: "bi-ta'wili dhalika" (the interpretation of that).

The majority said: "min al-muhsinin" (among the doers of good) means in knowledge, because they saw from him what made them know that he is a scholar. Al-Dahhak and Qatada said: it means among the doers of good in his speech with the people of the prison and in his kindness toward them. Ibn Ishaq said: they intended to inform him that they see for him a kindness toward them and a favour, if he interprets for them what they saw.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 12, verses 37–38:

﴿He said: "No food will come to you as provision but I will inform you of its interpretation (ta'wil) before it reaches you. That is part of what my Lord has taught me. I have truly abandoned the creed (millah) of a people who do not believe in God and who disbelieve in the Hereafter.﴾ ﴿I follow the creed of my fathers: Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. It was not for us to associate anything with God. That is from the bounty of God upon us and upon mankind, but most people are not grateful.﴾

[p. 309] al-Zamakhshari said: When they asked him for his help and described him as a man of goodness, he took on that obligation. Joseph described himself with what is above the knowledge of scholars, namely foretelling the unseen: that he would inform them of the food that would be brought to them in the prison before it arrived, and describe it to them, saying, "Today there will come to you food of such and such a description," and they would find it as he had told them. He made this a means of leading to his mention of monotheism, presenting faith to them, making it attractive to them, and making association with God repugnant to them. This is a method that every learned person should follow with the ignorant and the sinners: when one of them asks him for a ruling, he first presents guidance, admonition and advice, and calls him to what is more important for him and more obligatory upon him than what he asked about. Then he gives him the ruling after that. In this is the point that when a scholar's standing in knowledge is unknown, and he describes himself with what he is capable of, his aim being that people draw knowledge from him and benefit in religion, this is not a case of self-praise (tazkiyah). Its interpretation (ta'wil) is the explanation of its essence and its manner, because that resembles the explanation of the difficult (tafsir al-mushkil) and the grammatical analysis (i'rab) of something one has witnessed directly, and that is the end of his words.

What al-Zamakhshari said indicates that the arrival of the food occurs while awake. This is the view of Ibn Jurayj, who said: Joseph meant, "No food will come to you while you are awake that you are provided with, but I will inform you of it with knowledge, and of what its matter will turn out to be, before it reaches you." Accordingly, he intended to make them aware that he knows unseen matters that are not connected with dreams. This is in accordance with what is narrated, that he was given the knowledge in the prison. Al-Suddi and Ibn Ishaq said: when he knew from the interpreting of their dream that the baker's dream signified his execution, he began to speak of other matters, in order to make them forget the matter of the dream and to make them hopeful about their faith, so that the one who was to be killed would take his share of faith and his Hereafter would be secured for him. So he said to them, announcing his great knowledge of interpretation: "No food will come to you on your day, that you think you have been provided with, but I will inform you of the interpretation of that food," that is, of what its matter will turn out to be while awake, before that interpretation which I inform you of appears.

It is related that they said to him: "From where do you have this knowledge that you claim, when you are neither a soothsayer nor an astrologer?" He said to them: "That is part of what my Lord has taught me." The apparent meaning is that His words "No food will come to you" to the end refer to the waking state, and that His words "part of what my Lord has taught me" are evidence that at that time he was a prophet to whom revelation was made. The apparent meaning of His words "I have truly abandoned" is a resumed statement of information about what he was upon, since they had come to love him and were devoted to his love and his good character, so that he would make known to them what he was upon of opposition to their people, and they would follow him. In a hadith: "That God should guide one man through you is better for you than red camels." He expressed it as "abandoned" although he had never been attached to that creed at all, treating abandonment as avoidance from the very first state, and in order to attract them to abandon the creed in which they were. It is also permissible that "I have truly abandoned" be an explanation of what comes before it, meaning: "He taught me that and revealed it to me, because I rejected the creed of those people and followed the creed of the prophets, which is the upright creed (al-millah al-hanifiyyah)." Those who do not believe are the people of Egypt, and those whose religion the two youths followed. He pointed to two great foundations: belief in God, and belief in the abode of recompense. He repeated the people (hum) for emphasis and for the excellence of that separation. Al-Zamakhshari said: Their repetition as "they" indicates that they in particular are disbelievers in the Hereafter, and that others are believers in it, and to emphasize their disbelief in recompense, as a warning about what they were upon of wrongdoing and grave sins, which none commits except one who disbelieves in the abode of recompense, and that is the end of his words. The word "hum" does not indicate particularity in our view. The rest of his expressions are the expressions of the Mu'tazilites (al-Mu'tazilah).

When he mentioned that he had rejected the creed of those people, he mentioned his following the creed of his fathers, to show them that he comes from the house of prophethood, after he had made them know that he is a prophet through what he mentioned of his reports of the unseen, so that their desire to listen to him and follow his words would be strengthened. Al-Ash'hab al-'Uqayli and the Kufans read "ābā'ī" (my fathers) with the yā' sukun (silent), and this is related from Abu 'Amr. "Mā kāna lanā" means: it was not valid nor proper for us, the company of prophets, "an nushrika billāh min shay'" (that we associate anything with God). It is general in respect of the angel, the jinn and the human. How much more so is this true of an idol that neither hears nor sees! So "shay'" is used for the one who associates. It is also permissible that it refers to the verbal noun, meaning "of any kind of association," so that it covers association in general, and the generality of its objects is implied. "Min" is extra (zā'idah), because it falls within the scope of negation, since the meaning is: "We do not associate anything with God." The reference of "dhālika" is to their association and their creed. That is, that religion and that upright law in which association with God is negated. "Min fadl Allāh 'alaynā" means: upon us, the messengers, since they were singled out to be intermediaries between God and His servants. "'Alā al-nās" means: upon those to whom they were sent, since they are led by them to salvation when they are guided to it. His words "lā yashkurūn" mean: they do not give thanks for God's bounty, so they associate and do not take heed.

It has been said: "That is from the bounty of God upon us," because He set up for us the proofs which we consider and by which we reason, and He set up the same for all people without difference. But most people neither reflect nor give thanks, following their desires, so they remain disbelievers, not thankful.

﴿He said: "No food will come to you as provision but I will inform you of its interpretation (ta'wil) before it reaches you. That is part of what my Lord has taught me. Al-Suddi and Ibn Ishaq said: when he knew from the interpreting of their dream that the baker's dream signified his execution, he began to speak of other matters, in order to make them forget the matter of the dream and to make them hopeful about their faith, so that the one who was to be killed would take his share of faith and his Hereafter would be secured for him. So he said to them, announcing his great knowledge of interpretation: "No food will come to you on your day, that you think you have been provided with, but I will inform you of the interpretation of that food," that is, of what its matter will turn out to be while awake, before that interpretation which I inform you of appears.

It is related that they said to him: "From where do you have this knowledge that you claim, when you are neither a soothsayer nor an astrologer?" He said to them: "That is part of what my Lord has taught me." The apparent meaning is that His words "No food will come to you" to the end refer to the waking state, and that His words "part of what my Lord has taught me" are evidence that at that time he was a prophet to whom revelation was made. The apparent meaning of His words "I have truly abandoned" is a resumed statement of information about what he was upon, since they had come to love him and were devoted to his love and his good character, so that he would make known to them what he was upon of opposition to their people, and they would follow him. In a hadith: "That God should guide one man through you is better for you than red camels." He expressed it as "abandoned" although he had never been attached to that creed at all, treating abandonment as avoidance from the very first state, and in order to attract them to abandon the creed in which they were. It is also permissible that "I have truly abandoned" be an explanation of what comes before it, meaning: "He taught me that and revealed it to me, because I rejected the creed of those people and followed the creed of the prophets, which is the upright creed (al-millah al-hanifiyyah)." Those who do not believe are the people of Egypt, and those whose religion the two youths followed. He pointed to two great foundations: belief in God, and belief in the abode of recompense. He repeated the people (hum) for emphasis and for the excellence of that separation. Al-Zamakhshari said: Their repetition as "they" indicates that they in particular are disbelievers in the Hereafter, and that others are believers in it, and to emphasize their disbelief in recompense, as a warning about what they were upon of wrongdoing and grave sins, which none commits except one who disbelieves in the abode of recompense, and that is the end of his words. When he mentioned that he had rejected the creed of those people, he mentioned his following the creed of his fathers, to show them that he comes from the house of prophethood, after he had made them know that he is a prophet through what he mentioned of his reports of the unseen, so that their desire to listen to him and follow his words would be strengthened.
