"Mā kāna lanā" means: it was not valid nor proper for us, the company of prophets, "an nushrika billāh min shay'" (that we associate anything with God). It is general in respect of the angel, the jinn and the human. How much more so is this true of an idol that neither hears nor sees! So "shay'" is used for the one who associates. It is also permissible that it refers to the verbal noun, meaning "of any kind of association," so that it covers association in general, and the generality of its objects is implied. "Min" is extra (zā'idah), because it falls within the scope of negation, since the meaning is: "We do not associate anything with God." The reference of "dhālika" is to their association and their creed. That is, that religion and that upright law in which association with God is negated. "Min fadl Allāh 'alaynā" means: upon us, the messengers, since they were singled out to be intermediaries between God and His servants. "'Alā al-nās" means: upon those to whom they were sent, since they are led by them to salvation when they are guided to it. His words "lā yashkurūn" mean: they do not give thanks for God's bounty, so they associate and do not take heed.

It has been said: "That is from the bounty of God upon us," because He set up for us the proofs which we consider and by which we reason, and He set up the same for all people without difference. But most people neither reflect nor give thanks, following their desires, so they remain disbelievers, not thankful.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 12, verses 39–42:

﴿O my two fellow prisoners! Are scattered lords better, or God, the One, the Subduer?﴾ ﴿You worship none apart from Him except names you and your fathers have named, for which God has sent down no authority. Judgment belongs only to God. He has commanded that you worship none but Him. That is the upright religion, but most people do not know.﴾ ﴿O my two fellow prisoners!﴾

When he had mentioned the upright religion (al-din al-hanifi, the pure monotheistic faith) that he followed, he gently sought to demonstrate, with good reasoning, the corruption of what the people of the two young men were upon, namely the worship of idols. He addressed them by the title of companionship, in a difficult place where affection is made pure and sincere advice is put to the test. His words ﴿O my two fellow prisoners!﴾ could be an idafah (genitive construction) to a place, meaning: "O my two companions in the prison." It could also be an idafah to something resembling the object, as if it were said: "O inhabitants of the prison," like His words ﴿companions of the Fire﴾ [al-Baqarah: 39] and ﴿companions of the Garden﴾ [al-Hashr: 20].

Then he presented the proof of the falsehood of their people's creed with his words ﴿Are scattered lords better...﴾. He put this in the form of a question so that their natures would not recoil from being suddenly confronted with proof without a question. This is also the proper method in disputing with the ignorant: one begins with a small degree of argument that they accept. When they accept it, a further degree follows from it that is higher than it, and so on, until they submit to the truth.

He set the scattered lords against the One, and he brought the attribute "the Subduer" as a reminder that God, Exalted, possesses this attribute, whose meaning is dominance and complete power, and as an announcement that their idols are devoid of this attribute. Worship is fitting only for the one who possesses it. They knew that those idols were inanimate. The meaning is: Is the worship of many lords in number better, or the worship of one Subduer, who is God? Any rational person necessarily sees the superiority of worshipping Him.

Then, after the question, he digressed into informing them of the reality of what they worship. The address in His words ﴿what you worship﴾ is to both of them and to their people. The meaning of ﴿except names﴾ is: words you and your fathers have invented, so they are empty, with no named realities beneath them. The explanation of a similar clause has already been given in [al-A'raf]. ﴿Judgment belongs only to God﴾ means: there is no judgment for you, nor for your idols; judgment in worship and religion belongs only to God. Then he explained what He has judged, saying: He has commanded that you worship none but Him. The meaning of ﴿the upright﴾ is the established religion that the proofs point to.

﴿they do not know﴾: through their ignorance and the dominance of disbelief over them.

﴿O my two fellow prisoners! As for one of you, he will pour wine for his lord. As for the other, he will be crucified, and birds will eat from his head. The matter is decided about which you both inquire.﴾ ﴿He said to the one he thought would be saved of the two: "Mention me to your lord." But Satan made him forget to mention him to his lord, so he remained in prison for several years.﴾

When he had conveyed to them what was most important, namely the matter of religion, hoping for their faith, he addressed them a second time so that their souls would gather to hear the answer. It is related that he said to Libunu [a transmitted form, as it stands in the text]: "As for you, you will return to your position and to giving drink to your lord. The honor you have seen and its goodness is the king, and the goodness of your state with him." And he said: "As for the three branches, they are three days that pass in prison, after which you will come out and return to what you were upon." And he said to Mulahhib: "As for you, what you saw of the baskets is three days, after which you will come out and be crucified." It is related that they both said: "We saw nothing; we only dreamed to test you." It is also related that only the one who was told of the crucifixion said this, and it is related that they both saw and then denied it.

The majority read ﴿fa-yasqi rabbahu﴾ from saqa, while a group read (fa-yusqi) from asqa. The two are dialects with one meaning. In the Seven Readings, there are variants: nasqikum and nusqikum. The author of al-Lawami (Sahib al-Lawami) said: saqa and asqa have the same meaning in the language, though the known distinction is that saqahu means he handed him something to drink, while asqahu means he made water available for him. The vowelling of the fa' with a damma is attributed to 'Ikrimah and al-Jahdari. The meaning of (rabbahu) is his master. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: 'Ikrimah and al-Jahdari read (fa-yusqa rabbuhu khamran) with a damma on the ya' and a fatha on the qaf, meaning: what quenches him. Al-Zamakhshari said: 'Ikrimah read (fa-yusqa rabbuhu), meaning: he will be given what he is quenched with, in the passive voice.

Then Yusuf (peace be upon him) informed them, through knowledge of the unseen from God, that the matter has been decided and has matched the decree. It makes no difference whether this was from you both as a dream or as a feigned dream. He used the singular "the matter," though it concerned two matters, because the purpose is the outcome of their matter, for which they were imprisoned: the king's accusation against them of poisoning him. Whether they saw what they saw or dreamed it falsely, that outcome was carried out and enforced: the salvation of one of them and the death of the other.

"He said" refers to Yusuf, "to the one who thought": that is, the one who was certain, namely Yusuf, that he would be saved, and he was the cupbearer. It is possible that "thought" retains its ordinary meaning, and the pronoun refers to "the one," the cupbearer: meaning, when Yusuf told him what he told him, it became more probable to him that he would be saved. It is unlikely that the thinking is in its ordinary sense if it is attributed to Yusuf, as Qatadah and al-Zamakhshari held. Qatadah said: "Thought" here is in its ordinary sense, because interpreting a dream is a matter of conjecture. Al-Zamakhshari said: The one who thought is Yusuf, if his interpretation was by way of ijtihad (independent reasoning). That would be unlikely, because His words ﴿the matter is decided﴾ contain the certainty of what the decree has determined and its enforcement, so it appears that this was by way of revelation. Unless ﴿the matter is decided﴾ is taken to mean: "my words have been decided and I have said what I have," in which case it may refer back to Yusuf. The meaning would then be that Yusuf (peace be upon him) said to the king's cupbearer, when he knew that he would return to his former state with the king: "Mention me to the king," that is, by my knowledge and my standing and what God has given me, or: "Mention me with my injustice and the trial I was subjected to without right." This request from Yusuf was by way of seeking help and cooperation in relieving his distress, and making it, by God's permission and decree, a means of deliverance, as was related of Jesus (peace be upon him): ﴿Who are my helpers toward God?﴾ [Al 'Imran: 52], and as the Messenger used to seek someone to guard him. What I choose is that Yusuf only said to the king's cupbearer, "Mention me to your lord," so that he might reach his guidance and faith in God, just as he reached the clarification of the truth for the cupbearer and his companion.

The pronoun in ﴿made him forget﴾ refers to the cupbearer. The meaning of ﴿mention to his lord﴾ is Yusuf's mention to his lord, and the idafah (construction) may be made with the slightest connection. Satan's causing him to forget is through the whisperings that occupy him until he is distracted from what Yusuf had said to him, when God wished to grant Yusuf a greater reward through the length of his stay in prison. ﴿Several years﴾ is vague: it was said seven, and it was said twelve. The apparent meaning is that His words ﴿so he remained in prison﴾ report the duration of his stay in prison from the time he was imprisoned until he was released. It was also said that this remaining refers to the period after the two young men's release, which was seven years, and it was said two years. It was also said that the pronoun in "made him forget" refers to Yusuf. On this basis, some reports were recorded whose attribution to the prophets, peace be upon them (the prayer and peace), is not fitting.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 12, verses 39–42:

﴿O my two fellow prisoners! Are scattered lords better, or God, the One, the Subduer?﴾ ﴿You worship none apart from Him except names you and your fathers have named, for which God has sent down no authority. Judgment belongs only to God. He has commanded that you worship none but Him. That is the upright religion, but most people do not know.﴾ ﴿O my two fellow prisoners!﴾

When he had mentioned the upright religion (al-din al-hanifi, the pure monotheistic faith) that he followed, he gently sought to demonstrate, with good reasoning, the corruption of what the people of the two young men were upon, namely the worship of idols. He addressed them by the title of companionship, in a difficult place where affection is made pure and sincere advice is put to the test. His words ﴿O my two fellow prisoners!﴾ could be an idafah (genitive construction) to a place, meaning: "O my two companions in the prison." It could also be an idafah to something resembling the object, as if it were said: "O inhabitants of the prison," like His words ﴿companions of the Fire﴾ [al-Baqarah: 39] and ﴿companions of the Garden﴾ [al-Hashr: 20].

Then he presented the proof of the falsehood of their people's creed with his words ﴿Are scattered lords better...﴾. He put this in the form of a question so that their natures would not recoil from being suddenly confronted with proof without a question. This is also the proper method in disputing with the ignorant: one begins with a small degree of argument that they accept. When they accept it, a further degree follows from it that is higher than it, and so on, until they submit to the truth.

He set the scattered lords against the One, and he brought the attribute "the Subduer" as a reminder that God, Exalted, possesses this attribute, whose meaning is dominance and complete power, and as an announcement that their idols are devoid of this attribute. Worship is fitting only for the one who possesses it. They knew that those idols were inanimate. The meaning is: Is the worship of many lords in number better, or the worship of one Subduer, who is God? Any rational person necessarily sees the superiority of worshipping Him.

Then, after the question, he digressed into informing them of the reality of what they worship. The address in His words ﴿what you worship﴾ is to both of them and to their people. The meaning of ﴿except names﴾ is: words you and your fathers have invented, so they are empty, with no named realities beneath them. The explanation of a similar clause has already been given in [al-A'raf]. ﴿Judgment belongs only to God﴾ means: there is no judgment for you, nor for your idols; judgment in worship and religion belongs only to God. Then he explained what He has judged, saying: He has commanded that you worship none but Him. The meaning of ﴿the upright﴾ is the established religion that the proofs point to.

﴿they do not know﴾: through their ignorance and the dominance of disbelief over them.

﴿O my two fellow prisoners! As for one of you, he will pour wine for his lord. As for the other, he will be crucified, and birds will eat from his head. The matter is decided about which you both inquire.﴾ ﴿He said to the one he thought would be saved of the two: "Mention me to your lord." But Satan made him forget to mention him to his lord, so he remained in prison for several years.﴾

When he had conveyed to them what was most important, namely the matter of religion, hoping for their faith, he addressed them a second time so that their souls would gather to hear the answer. It is related that he said to Libunu [a transmitted form, as it stands in the text]: "As for you, you will return to your position and to giving drink to your lord. The honor you have seen and its goodness is the king, and the goodness of your state with him." And he said: "As for the three branches, they are three days that pass in prison, after which you will come out and return to what you were upon." And he said to Mulahhib: "As for you, what you saw of the baskets is three days, after which you will come out and be crucified." It is related that they both said: "We saw nothing; we only dreamed to test you." It is also related that only the one who was told of the crucifixion said this, and it is related that they both saw and then denied it.

The majority read ﴿fa-yasqi rabbahu﴾ from saqa, while a group read (fa-yusqi) from asqa. The two are dialects with one meaning. In the Seven Readings, there are variants: nasqikum and nusqikum. The author of al-Lawami (Sahib al-Lawami) said: saqa and asqa have the same meaning in the language, though the known distinction is that saqahu means he handed him something to drink, while asqahu means he made water available for him. The vowelling of the fa' with a damma is attributed to 'Ikrimah and al-Jahdari. The meaning of (rabbahu) is his master. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: 'Ikrimah and al-Jahdari read (fa-yusqa rabbuhu khamran) with a damma on the ya' and a fatha on the qaf, meaning: what quenches him. Al-Zamakhshari said: 'Ikrimah read (fa-yusqa rabbuhu), meaning: he will be given what he is quenched with, in the passive voice.

Then Yusuf (peace be upon him) informed them, through knowledge of the unseen from God, that the matter has been decided and has matched the decree. It makes no difference whether this was from you both as a dream or as a feigned dream. He used the singular "the matter," though it concerned two matters, because the purpose is the outcome of their matter, for which they were imprisoned: the king's accusation against them of poisoning him. Whether they saw what they saw or dreamed it falsely, that outcome was carried out and enforced: the salvation of one of them and the death of the other.

"He said" refers to Yusuf, "to the one who thought": that is, the one who was certain, namely Yusuf, that he would be saved, and he was the cupbearer. It is possible that "thought" retains its ordinary meaning, and the pronoun refers to "the one," the cupbearer: meaning, when Yusuf told him what he told him, it became more probable to him that he would be saved. It is unlikely that the thinking is in its ordinary sense if it is attributed to Yusuf, as Qatadah and al-Zamakhshari held. Qatadah said: "Thought" here is in its ordinary sense, because interpreting a dream is a matter of conjecture. Al-Zamakhshari said: The one who thought is Yusuf, if his interpretation was by way of ijtihad (independent reasoning). That would be unlikely, because His words ﴿the matter is decided﴾ contain the certainty of what the decree has determined and its enforcement, so it appears that this was by way of revelation. Unless ﴿the matter is decided﴾ is taken to mean: "my words have been decided and I have said what I have," in which case it may refer back to Yusuf. The meaning would then be that Yusuf (peace be upon him) said to the king's cupbearer, when he knew that he would return to his former state with the king: "Mention me to the king," that is, by my knowledge and my standing and what God has given me, or: "Mention me with my injustice and the trial I was subjected to without right." This request from Yusuf was by way of seeking help and cooperation in relieving his distress, and making it, by God's permission and decree, a means of deliverance, as was related of Jesus (peace be upon him): ﴿Who are my helpers toward God?﴾ [Al 'Imran: 52], and as the Messenger used to seek someone to guard him. What I choose is that Yusuf only said to the king's cupbearer, "Mention me to your lord," so that he might reach his guidance and faith in God, just as he reached the clarification of the truth for the cupbearer and his companion.

The pronoun in ﴿made him forget﴾ refers to the cupbearer. The meaning of ﴿mention to his lord﴾ is Yusuf's mention to his lord, and the idafah (construction) may be made with the slightest connection. Satan's causing him to forget is through the whisperings that occupy him until he is distracted from what Yusuf had said to him, when God wished to grant Yusuf a greater reward through the length of his stay in prison. ﴿Several years﴾ is vague: it was said seven, and it was said twelve. The apparent meaning is that His words ﴿so he remained in prison﴾ report the duration of his stay in prison from the time he was imprisoned until he was released. It was also said that this remaining refers to the period after the two young men's release, which was seven years, and it was said two years. It was also said that the pronoun in "made him forget" refers to Yusuf. On this basis, some reports were recorded whose attribution to the prophets, peace be upon them (the prayer and peace), is not fitting.

(p-312)﴿And the king said, "Indeed, I see seven fat cows being eaten by seven lean ones, and seven green ears [of grain] and others dry. O chiefs, explain to me my vision, if you can interpret visions."﴾ ﴿They said, "These are confused dreams, and we are not learned in the interpretation of dreams."﴾

When the relief of Yusuf (peace be upon him) drew near, the king of Egypt, al-Rayyan ibn al-Walid, saw an amazing vision that alarmed him. He saw seven fat cows coming out of a dry river, and seven lean cows, and the lean ones swallowed the fat ones. He also saw seven green ears of grain whose grain had formed, and seven others that were dry, that had been harvested and ripened. The dry ones twisted around the green ones until they overcame them. Yet there was no one among his people who could interpret it well. ("Ara," "I see") means in his sleep, and this is indicated by "explain to me my vision." And "ara" is a narration of a state (hikayat haal, a narrative of a present condition), so that is why the present tense was used instead of "ra'aytu" (I saw). As for ﴿sim\u0101n\u0130n﴾ (fat), it is an adjective of ﴿baqarat\u0130n﴾ (cows). He specified the number by a type of cows, namely the fat ones among them, and he did not use it with the lean ones. Had he made it an adjective of seven (sab'), the specification would have been by genus (jins) and not by type (naw'). The attribution of fatness to the cows entails attributing it to the seven, but attributing it to the seven does not entail attributing it to the genus, because the meaning would become "seven cows, fat." Distinguish between your saying "I have three noble men" (indi thalath rijal kiram) and "three noble men" (thalathat rijal kiram): in the first the meaning is three of the noble men, so the nobility of the three is implied, since they are part of the noble men; in the second the meaning is three men who are noble, which does not indicate that the men are described as noble.

He did not add ﴿sab'a﴾ (seven) to ﴿\u0151ij\u0101f﴾ (lean) because a number is not construed with an adjective (sifah) except in poetry; rather, the adjective follows it. Expressions such as "thalathat fursan" (three horsemen) and "khamsat ashab" (five companions) are among the adjectives that have been treated as nouns. The phrase ﴿sab'a baqarat﴾ indicates that the lean seven are cows, as if it were said: "seven lean cows," or "the cows of seven lean ones." The plural of ʿajfa\u0101' (lean, feminine) is ʿij\u0101f, whose analogical form would be ʿajaf, like khadra\u0101' or khuḍr; it was formed on the analogy of sim\u0101n (fat), since it is its opposite. The opposite may be treated analogously to its opposite, just as the counterpart may be treated analogously to its counterpart. The division mentioned for the cows requires a division for the ears of grain, so the number-noun has been omitted from ﴿wa-ukhara y\u0101bis\u0101t\u0130n﴾ (and others dry), because its two divisions and what precedes it indicate it. The construction is thus: "and seven others dry." It is not valid for ("wa-ukhar") to be in the genitive by coordination (ʿatf) with ﴿sunbul\u0101t\u0130n khuḍr\u0130n﴾ (green ears), because from the standpoint of coordination with it, it is part of the specification (tamyiz) of ("sab'a"), and from the standpoint of it being ("ukhar", other) it is distinct from ("sab'a"), so the two conflict. This differs from the construction "seven green and dry ears," which would be valid as coordination, and would mean distributing the ears into green and dry ones.

("Al-mala'") means the nobles of his state and its notables who attend the king. Abu Ja'far recited with assimilation (idgham) in ﴿al-ru'y\u0101﴾, and its pattern, after the hamza was changed into waw, then changed it into ya', because of the gathering of waw and ya', one of them having been preceded by sukun. They have stated that this is anomalous (shudhudh), because the waw is a non-obligatory substitute (badal ghayr l\u0101zim), and the lam in ﴿al-ru'y\u0101﴾ strengthens the arrival of the verb at its object (maf'ul) when it precedes it. If the object were postponed, that would not be good. This differs from the active participle, which, because of its weakness, may be strengthened by it, so you say: "Zayd is striking for ʿUmar" and "eloquent."

The apparent view is that the predicate (khabar) of ("kuntum") is ﴿ta'buron﴾ (you interpret). Al-Zamakhshari permitted several forced (mutakallifa) possibilities regarding it. One of them: that ﴿al-ru'y\u0101﴾ is for clarification (bayan), and he said: like His saying ﴿wa-k\u0101n\u016b f\u012bhi mina al-z\u0101hid\u012bn﴾ (and they were among those who were indifferent to it) [Yusuf 20]. It is then connected to an omitted element whose estimate is ("a'n\u012b f\u012bhi", I mean in it). Likewise, the estimate here is ﴿in kuntum﴾ "I mean the vision" ﴿ta'buron﴾ (you interpret). The object of ﴿ta'buron﴾ is omitted, its estimate being ﴿ta'buron-h\u0101﴾ (you interpret it).

The second: that ("al-ru'y\u0101") is the predicate (khabar) of ("kana"). He said: just as you say: "So-and-so was for this matter," if he was independent in it and empowered over it. And ﴿ta'buron﴾ is another predicate or a circumstantial state (hal).

The third: that ("ta'burun") implies the meaning of a verb that transitively takes the particle lam, as if it were said: "if you are prepared for the interpretation of the vision." The interpretation of a vision (ʿibarat al-ru'y\u0101) is derived from ʿabara al-nahr, meaning he crossed it from one bank to the other. So the interpreter of a vision reaches the end of its interpretation. ("ʿAbara al-ru'y\u0101", with the ba' lightened, in the triliteral form) is the well-known one, and some people denied the doubling of the ba'. Al-Mubarrad cited in al-K\u0101mil the verse of a poet:

I saw a vision, then I interpreted it, and I was an interpreter of dreams.

﴿Adgh\u0101th﴾ (confused) is the plural of ḍigh\u0101th, meaning mixtures of dreams, which are what arise from the self's talk, or the whisperings of Satan, or the temperament of the human being. Its origin is mixtures of plants, and it was borrowed for dreams. They made the dreams plural, while his vision was singular, either in terms of its objects, since they are things, or in terms of the permissibility of that, as you say: "So-and-so rides horses," even if he has ridden only one horse, by way of associating it with the genus. Or because he related to them, along with this vision, others. ("Al-ahl\u0101m") is the plural of ḥulm. ﴿Adgh\u0101th﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject (mubtada'), meaning: "they are confused dreams."

The apparent meaning is that they denied of themselves knowledge of the interpretation of dreams, that is, "we are not among the people of the interpretation of visions." It is also permissible that the dreams whose knowledge is negated are those they meant as characterized by confusion and falsehoods; that is: "and we are not learned in the interpretation of those dreams which are confused mixtures," that is, no knowledge of ours is connected to the interpretation of those, because they have no interpretation; interpretation belongs only to the true dream. So there is no negation in that of knowledge of the interpretation of the true dream, nor any supposition of their knowledge. The ba' in ﴿bi-ta'w\u012bl﴾ (in the interpretation) is connected to ﴿bi-'\u0101lim\u012bn﴾ (learned).

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 12, verses 45–49 (part 1 of 2):

﴿The one of the two who had been saved and remembered after a long time said, "I will inform you of its interpretation, so send me forth."﴾

﴿"Joseph, O truthful one, give us an interpretation concerning seven fat cows that are eaten by seven lean ones, and seven green ears [of grain] and others dry, that I may return to the people so that they may know."﴾

﴿He said, "You will sow for seven consecutive years. Then whatever you harvest, leave it in its ears, except a little of what you eat.﴾

﴿Then after that will come seven hard years, which will consume what you have stored up for them, except a little of what you preserve.﴾

﴿Then after that will come a year in which the people will be given rain and in which they will press [juice].﴾

[Yusuf: 50] ﴿The king said, "Bring him to me." But when the messenger came to him, he said, "Return to your lord and ask him what is the matter with the women who cut their hands. Indeed, my Lord is Knowing of their plot."﴾

[Yusuf: 51] ﴿He said, "What was your affair when you sought to seduce Joseph from himself?" They said, "Haash lillah! We know nothing evil of him." The wife of the chief said, "Now the truth has become manifest. It was I who sought to seduce him from himself, and indeed he is among the truthful."﴾

[Yusuf: 52] ﴿"That is so he may know that I did not betray him in secret, and that Allah does not guide the plot of the betrayers."﴾

[Yusuf: 53] ﴿"And I do not declare myself innocent. Indeed, the soul is ever commanding to evil, except those upon whom my Lord has mercy. Indeed, my Lord is Forgiving and Merciful."﴾

[Yusuf: 54] ﴿The king said, "Bring him to me, that I may take him exclusively for myself." So when he spoke with him, he said, "Indeed, you are today established and trusted in our presence."﴾

[Yusuf: 55] ﴿He said, "Appoint me over the treasuries of the land. Indeed, I am a knowing guardian."﴾

[Yusuf: 56] ﴿And thus We established Joseph in the land, to settle therein wherever he willed. We bestow Our mercy upon whom We will, and We do not allow the reward of the good-doers to be lost.﴾

[Yusuf: 57] ﴿And the reward of the Hereafter is better for those who believed and were fearing Allah.﴾

[Yusuf: 58] ﴿The brothers of Joseph came and entered upon him, and he recognized them, but they did not recognize him.﴾

[Yusuf: 59] ﴿And when he had furnished them with their provisions, he said, "Bring me a brother of yours from your father. Do you not see that I give full measure and that I am the best of hosts?"﴾

[Yusuf: 60] ﴿"But if you do not bring him to me, there will be no measure for you with me, and you will not approach me."﴾

[Yusuf: 61] ﴿They said, "We will seek to get him from his father, and indeed we will do it."﴾

[Yusuf: 62] ﴿And he said to his servants, "Put their merchandise back into their saddlebags, so that they may recognize it when they return to their family; perhaps they will come back."﴾

[Yusuf: 63] ﴿So when they returned to their father, they said, "O our father, measure has been withheld from us, so send our brother with us that we may get measure, and indeed we will guard him."﴾

[Yusuf: 64] ﴿He said, "Shall I entrust him to you except as I entrusted you with his brother before? But Allah is the best guardian, and He is the most merciful of the merciful."﴾

[Yusuf: 65] ﴿And when they opened their goods, they found their merchandise returned to them. They said, "O our father, what more could we desire? This is our merchandise, returned to us. We will bring provisions for our family, guard our brother, and gain an additional camel's load. That is an easy measure."﴾

Amaha yamahu amhan wa amhan: he forgot.

Yughath: it may be from al-ghawth, meaning relief (faraj). It is said: Allah granted them relief (aghathahum Allah), meaning He relieved them of their distress. It may also be from al-ghayth, meaning rain. It is said: "The lands were given rain" (ghiythat al-bilad) when they were rained upon. From this is the saying of the Bedouin woman: "We were given rain as much as we wished" (ghithna ma shi'na).

Al-khatb: the affair or matter that involves danger. Its plural is khutub. The poet said:

"A man, as long as the breath of his soul remains, will not reach the edges of misfortunes, nor the family of misfortune."

Hasḥasa: became clear after being hidden. This was said by al-Khalil. It was also said that it derives from al-hissah (share): "the truth became manifest, its share appeared apart from the share of falsehood." It was also said that it means it became firm and settled. It may be transitive, from hasḥasa al-ba'ir, when the camel sets down its knees to kneel. The poet said: "He lowered his knees upon the hard rocks."

﴿The one of the two who had been saved and remembered after a long time said, "I will inform you of its interpretation, so send me forth."﴾

﴿"Joseph, O truthful one, give us an interpretation concerning seven fat cows that are eaten by seven lean ones, and seven green ears [of grain] and others dry, that I may return to the people so that they may know."﴾

﴿He said, "You will sow for seven consecutive years. Then whatever you harvest, leave it in its ears, except a little of what you eat.﴾

﴿Then after that will come seven hard years, which will consume what you have stored up for them, except a little of what you preserve.﴾

﴿Then after that will come a year in which the people will be given rain and in which they will press [juice].﴾

[Yusuf: 50] ﴿The king said, "Bring him to me." But when the messenger came to him, he said, "Return to your lord and ask him what is the matter with the women who cut their hands. Indeed, my Lord is Knowing of their plot."﴾

[Yusuf: 51] ﴿He said, "What was your affair when you sought to seduce Joseph from himself?" They said, "Haash lillah! We know nothing evil of him." The wife of the chief said, "Now the truth has become manifest. It was I who sought to seduce him from himself, and indeed he is among the truthful."﴾

[Yusuf: 52] ﴿"That is so he may know that I did not betray him in secret, and that Allah does not guide the plot of the betrayers."﴾

[Yusuf: 53] ﴿"And I do not declare myself innocent. Indeed, the soul is ever commanding to evil, except those upon whom my Lord has mercy. Indeed, my Lord is Forgiving and Merciful."﴾

[Yusuf: 54] ﴿The king said, "Bring him to me, that I may take him exclusively for myself." So when he spoke with him, he said, "Indeed, you are today established and trusted in our presence."﴾

[Yusuf: 55] ﴿He said, "Appoint me over the treasuries of the land. Indeed, I am a knowing guardian."﴾

[Yusuf: 56] ﴿And thus We established Joseph in the land, to settle therein wherever he willed. We bestow Our mercy upon whom We will, and We do not allow the reward of the good-doers to be lost.﴾

[Yusuf: 57] ﴿And the reward of the Hereafter is better for those who believed and were fearing Allah.﴾

[Yusuf: 58] ﴿The brothers of Joseph came and entered upon him, and he recognized them, but they did not recognize him.﴾

[Yusuf: 59] ﴿And when he had furnished them with their provisions, he said, "Bring me a brother of yours from your father. Do you not see that I give full measure and that I am the best of hosts?"﴾

[Yusuf: 60] ﴿"But if you do not bring him to me, there will be no measure for you with me, and you will not approach me."﴾

[Yusuf: 61] ﴿They said, "We will seek to get him from his father, and indeed we will do it."﴾

[Yusuf: 62] ﴿And he said to his servants, "Put their merchandise back into their saddlebags, so that they may recognize it when they return to their family; perhaps they will come back."﴾

[Yusuf: 63] ﴿So when they returned to their father, they said, "O our father, measure has been withheld from us, so send our brother with us that we may get measure, and indeed we will guard him."﴾

[Yusuf: 64] ﴿He said, "Shall I entrust him to you except as I entrusted you with his brother before? But Allah is the best guardian, and He is the most merciful of the merciful."﴾

[Yusuf: 65] ﴿And when they opened their goods, they found their merchandise returned to them. They said, "O our father, what more could we desire? This is our merchandise, returned to us. We will bring provisions for our family, guard our brother, and gain an additional camel's load. That is an easy measure."﴾

Amaha yamahu amhan wa amhan: he forgot.

Yughath: it may be from al-ghawth, meaning relief (faraj). It is said: Allah granted them relief (aghathahum Allah), meaning He relieved them of their distress. It may also be from al-ghayth, meaning rain. It is said: "The lands were given rain" (ghiythat al-bilad) when they were rained upon. From this is the saying of the Bedouin woman: "We were given rain as much as we wished" (ghithna ma shi'na).

Al-khatb: the affair or matter that involves danger. Its plural is khutub. The poet said:

"A man, as long as the breath of his soul remains, will not reach the edges of misfortunes, nor the family of misfortune."

Hasḥasa: became clear after being hidden. This was said by al-Khalil. It was also said that it derives from al-hissah (share): "the truth became manifest, its share appeared apart from the share of falsehood." It was also said that it means it became firm and settled. It may be transitive, from hasḥasa al-ba'ir, when the camel sets down its knees to kneel. The poet said: "He lowered his knees upon the hard rocks."

Al-jihaz: what a traveler needs of provisions and goods, and everything that is carried. The jihaz of a bride is the furniture and bedding that accompany her. The jihaz of the dead is what is needed for his burial.

Al-rahl: what is upon the back of a mount of the rider's goods or other things. Its plural in the many sense is rihal, and in the few sense is arhul.

Mara yamiru and amara yamiru: when one brings good, which is al-mirah (provisioning). The poet said: "I sent you seeking provisions, but you remained a whole year. When will your help come to the one you aid?"

Al-ba'ir: in common usage it is the male camel, opposite the female camel (naqah), though it may be applied to the female as it is applied to the male. One says: "On this, the camel is excellent," meaning the male, because of its generality. It is not used in the most common sense for the female because of its synonymy. In one dialect its first letter is vowelled with a kasra. Its plural in the few sense is ab'irah, and in the many sense is bi'ran.

[Yusuf: 45–49 as quoted above]

When the king made an exception in his dream and the chiefs were perplexed about its interpretation, the one who had been saved from death, who was the king's cupbearer, remembered Joseph, the interpretation of his dream and the dream of his fellow prisoner. He asked to be sent to him so that he might mention it to the king.

"And remembered" means he recalled what had passed between him and Joseph. "After a long time" means after an extended period. The clause "and remembered" is in the state position (hal). Its original form was wadhtakara, the ta was changed to dal, and the dhal was assimilated into it, so it became idhdakara. This is the reading of the majority. Al-Hasan read wadhdhakara, changing the ta to dhal and assimilating the dhal. Al-Ashhab al-Uqayli read ba'da immatin with a kasra on the hamza, meaning after a favour by which he was granted deliverance from death. Ibn Atiyyah said: "after a favour which Allah bestowed upon Joseph, in an approximate sense of the term." Umma means favour. The poet said: "Oh, I do not see one who has a favour, whom the days leave, while it remains as it is."

Al-A'lam said: Umma means favour and a good condition. Ibn Abbas, Zayd ibn Ali, al-Dahhak, Qatadah, Abu Raja, Shubayl ibn Azrah al-Dhuba'i and Rabi'ah ibn Amr read ba'da amahin, with a fatha on the hamza, the mim lightened and a ha. Ibn Umar, Mujahid and Ikrimah also read it this way, though there was a difference in their reports. Ikrimah and also Mujahid and Shubayl ibn Azrah read ba'da umhin, with the mim sukun, as a verbal noun of amaha without analogy. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Whoever reads it with the mim sukun has erred," end of quote. This is consistent with his habit of attributing error to al-Farra'.

"I will inform you of its interpretation" means I will tell you about it from one who has its knowledge, not from myself. Al-Hasan read anā ātīkum (I will come to you), the present tense of ata from al-ityan. This is also the reading in the Imam (the codex standard). In the codex of Ubayy: "so send me forth" (fa-arsilun), meaning send me to him that I may ask him, and instruct me to seek his interpretation. He asked permission to go to Joseph. Ibn Abbas said: he was in the prison, outside the king's city. It was also said he was in the city. People today mark Joseph's prison at a place on the Nile, eight miles between it and al-Fustat. In the speech there is an omission. The intended meaning is: send him to Joseph, so he went to him and said.

Al-Siddiq is an intensive form like al-sharrib and al-sikkir. He had accompanied Joseph for a time and tested his truthfulness in many matters, such as the interpretation of his dream and his fellow prisoner's dream. His words "that I may return to the people" mean with the interpretation of this dream. He used the word "that perhaps" (la'alli) because he was not certain of returning to them, since it was possible that he would die before reaching them. His words "that perhaps they will know" are like an explanation for his return to them with the interpretation of the dream. It was also said: "that perhaps they will know your merit and your standing in knowledge, so they will seek you and rescue you from your trial." In that case, "that perhaps" is like an explanation for his words "give us an interpretation."

He said: "You will sow" to the end. This speech from Joseph contained three kinds of speech.
The first: interpretation according to meaning, not according to the wording.
The second: presenting an opinion and commanding it, which is his words "leave it in its ears."
The third: informing about the unseen concerning the matter of the eighth year. This was said by Qatadah.

Ibn Atiyyah said: This may not be unseen knowledge, rather the knowledge of interpretation indicated that the fear would end after seven years, and it is known that it would be the most fertile.

The apparent meaning is that his words "you will sow seven years consecutively" are a report. He informed that these years would follow one another for them, and their sowing would not cease during them, through the irrigation that is available. Al-Zamakhshari said: "You will sow" is a report in the sense of a command, like His words: "You believe in Allah and His Messenger and strive" (al-Saff: 11). A command comes out in the form of a report only for emphasis on the necessity of carrying out the commanded act, so it is treated as though it has already occurred, and so he reports it. The evidence that it has the meaning of a command is His words "leave it in its ears." End of quote. However, the command to leave it in its ears does not indicate that "you will sow" means "sow." Rather, "you will sow" is a report of the unseen about what will occur from them, of the continuation of sowing for seven years. As for His words "leave it," it is a command of direction about what they should do.

"Da'aban" means continuously, as is your custom in cultivation. Hafs read da'aban with a fatha on the hamza, while the majority read it with sukun. Both are verbal nouns of da'aba. Its accusative case depends on a verb deleted from the same root, meaning "you will persist with persistence." It is thus a verbal noun in the accusative. According to al-Mubarrad, it is governed by "you sow," with the meaning "you will persist." For him it is like "he sat in the qurfusa posture." It was also said it is a verbal noun in the position of a state: "persevering," or "possessors of persistence," a state of the subject in "you sow."

The "ma" in His words "whatever you harvest" is either conditional or a relative pronoun connected with "leave it in its ears," as a direction in accordance with Nafi's opinion, given the food of Egypt and its wheat, which cannot be kept for two years by any means except by the trick of keeping it in its ears. When it remains in them, it is preserved. The meaning is: leave the crop in its ears except what is necessary for eating, so that the food accumulates and is preserved, and the oldest is eaten first. When the years of drought come, the oldest of that stored food is eaten first.

Al-Sulami read "what they eat" with the yaa, in the third person, meaning "what the people eat." He omitted the specifier in His words "seven hard years," meaning seven hard years, because of the indication in the words "seven years." The verb "they consume" in His words "they consume" is attributed in a figurative sense, since it is consumed in them, as He said: "and the day giving sight" (Yunus: 67). The meaning of "you preserve" is you keep safe and store away. It derives from al-hisn, which means a safeguard and refuge.

Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and the majority said yughath is from al-ghayth (rain). It was also said it is from al-ghawth, which means relief. In the first case it is formed from a triliteral root, and in the second from a quadriliteral. You say: "Allah gave us rain (ghathana)" from al-ghayth, and "Allah gave us relief (aghathana)" from al-ghawth.

Al-Akhawan read ta'sirun with the ta, in the second person address. The remaining seven read it with the ya, in the third person. The majority hold that it derives from pressing plants, such as grapes, sugarcane, olives, sesame, radish and everything that is pressed. Misr is a land of much pressing for many things. Milking is from this, because it is a pressing of the udders. It is narrated that they did not press anything during the period of drought.

Abu Ubaydah and others said it derives from al-usrah, meaning deliverance, and al-asr, meaning the one who saves. From this is the saying of Abu Zubayd about Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him:

"Thirsting, seeking relief but not relieved, and indeed he was the deliverance of the saved one."

So the meaning is: they will be saved by the deliverance.

Ja'far ibn Muhammad, al-A'raj and Isa al-Basrah read yu'sirun with a damma on the ya and a fatha on the sad, in the passive. Also from Isa: tu'sirun with the ta in the address, in the passive. Its meaning is: they will be delivered from his pressing, when he delivers them. This fits with the words "people are given rain."

Ibn al-Mustanir said: its meaning is they will be rained upon. It is from aSra al-sahabah ma'aha (the cloud released its water upon them), so they were made into "pressers" (mu'sirin) figuratively by attributing that to them. It refers to the water by which they are rained upon. Al-Naqqash related that it was read yu'assirun with a damma on the ya, a kasra on the sad, and a shadda, from assara with intensification for multiplicity. Zayd ibn Ali read: "wa fihi ti'ssirun," with a kasra on the ta and the ayn and the sad and the shadda. Its origin is ta'tasirun. He assimilated the ta into the sad, moved its vowel to the ayn, and made the vowel of the ta follow the vowel of the ayn. It may also be from i'tasara al-inab wa nahwahu (he pressed grapes and the like), and from i'tasara meaning he was saved. The poet said:

[Here the text is cut off mid-quotation.]

Had my throat choked on anything other than water,
I would be like one choking on water, my deliverance lying in it.

I.e., my deliverance. Yusuf (peace be upon him) interpreted the fat cows and the green ears of grain as years of abundance, and the lean and dry ones as years of drought. Then, after finishing the interpretation (*ta'wil*) of the dream, he gave them the good news of the coming of a blessed eighth year, fertile, abounding in good and plentiful in blessings. This came by way of revelation (*wahy*). Qatadah said: God gave him knowledge of the year. What came by way of revelation was the specification of the condition of that year: that in it people would be given rain and relief, ﴿and in it they will press [grapes and oil]﴾. Otherwise, it is known that fertility comes after the end of the seven hard years.

The commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 12, verses 50–51:

﴿And the king said, "Bring him to me." But when the messenger came to him, he said, "Return to your lord and ask him what happened with the women who cut their hands. Indeed, my Lord is Knowing of their plot."﴾ ﴿He said, "What was your affair when you sought to seduce Joseph?" They said, "Far be God from it! We know no evil against him." The wife of the chief said, "Now the truth has become evident. It was I who sought to seduce him, and indeed he is of the truthful."﴾

There is an omission in the speech. Its implied meaning is: the messenger memorized what Joseph had interpreted of the dream, went to the king and those who had sent him, informed them of that, and the king said... Ibn 'Atiyyah said: within these verses there are omitted elements that the apparent wording gives and that point to them. The meaning is: the messenger returned to the king and those with the king, and related to them Joseph's statement. The king and those present saw the nobility of the interpretation, the goodness of the opinion, and the inclusion of the unseen in the matter of the eighth year, together with what the messenger described of him regarding truthfulness in the earlier dream. So Joseph grew great in the king's esteem, and he said, "Bring him to me." When the messenger reached Joseph to bring him out and said, "Indeed the king has commanded that you come out to him," Joseph said to him, "Return to your lord," that is, to the king, and say to him, "What is the matter with the women?" The aim of Joseph, peace be upon him, was only that he should say to him: investigate my offence and examine my affair. Was I imprisoned justly or unjustly? This act by Joseph was patience, forbearance, and a desire to establish his innocence. This is because, as it is related, he feared that if he came out and gained a rank with the king, people would remain silent about the matter of his religion, and would always see him in that light and say, "This is the one who sought to seduce his master's wife." So Joseph, peace be upon him, wished to demonstrate his innocence and to establish his standing in chastity and goodness, and then he would come out for honour and status.

Al-Zamakhshari said: He only delayed and deliberated in answering the king, and he placed the question of the women first, so that his innocence might be made clear regarding what he had been accused of and imprisoned for. This was so that the envious would not use it to climb up and disparage his affair in the king's eyes, making it a ladder to lower his standing with him. It was also so that they would not say: he remained in prison for seven years only because of a great matter and a serious crime, deserving imprisonment and torment, and that his secret should be uncovered. In this there is evidence that striving to remove accusations is obligatory, in the manner of keeping away from positions of suspicion. He, peace be upon him, said: "Whoever believes in God and the Last Day, let him not stand in places of suspicion." End of quotation. For this reason, al-Zamakhshari, who had a severed leg, proved before the judges that his leg had not been cut off for betrayal or corruption, and he would display that written testimony in every city he entered, out of fear of the accusation of evil. He said, "Ask the king about the matter of the women," and did not say, "Ask him to investigate them," because a question stirs a person and moves him to search for what he has been asked about. So he wanted to put the question to him so that he would carry out an investigation into the reality of the story, and he related the account so that his innocence would become clear to him, with a manifest explanation in which truth is distinguished from falsehood. It was also from the generosity of Joseph, peace be upon him, that he did not mention the wife of the chief, despite what she had done and caused him of imprisonment and suffering, and he limited himself to mentioning the women who had cut their hands.

Abu Hayyan: Abu Hayyah and Abu Bakr, from 'Asim in one transmission, read (al-nuswah) with a ḍammah on the nūn. A group read (al-lāy) with a yā'. Both are plural forms of (allatī), "the ones who." (Indeed my Lord) means: indeed God (is Knowing of their plot). He intended that their plot is great and that no one knows it except God, because its return is far off. He cited the knowledge of God as evidence that they had plotted against him and that he was innocent of what he had been accused of. Or he intended a warning to them. Or it means that He is Knowing of their plot and will recompense them for it. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: It is possible that by "the Lord" he meant the chief, his master, and in that there is an appeal to him and a rebuke. What Ibn 'Atiyyah mentioned of this possibility is not valid. The pronoun in (bi-kaydihinna) refers to the women mentioned, not to the category in general, because this is a situation of interrogation about a sin.

He said: (What was your affair?) In the speech there is an omission, whose implied meaning is: the messenger returned and informed him of what Joseph had said. So the king gathered the women and the wife of the chief and said to them, "What was your affair?" This was a summons from him for them to inform him of the story. He cleared Joseph's side with his words, "when you sought to seduce Joseph from himself." Their seduction of him was their saying to Joseph, "Obey your mistress." Al-Zamakhshari said: Did you find any inclination from him towards you? They said, "Far be God from it!" in amazement at his chastity, and at his mind being far from any suspicion, and at his purity from it. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: The women answered with a good reply, from which the innocence of themselves is entirely apparent, and they gave Joseph a partial innocence. That is because when the king established that they had sought to seduce him, they replied to that (saying), "Far be God from it!" It is possible that their saying "Far be God from it!" concerns Joseph, peace be upon him. Their saying, "We know no evil against him," is not a complete exoneration. The complete exoneration would be a description of the story as it actually was, so that the error would be established on their part. When the wife of the chief heard their statement and saw them turning away from falling into disgrace, she said, "Now the truth has become evident." (Ḥuṣḥiṣa) is also read in the passive form. She admitted to the seduction on her own part, took upon herself the sin, and fully absolved Joseph.

The apparent meaning is that this is from the speech of the wife of the ruler (al-'Aziz), and it falls under his saying: (She said). The meaning is: "That acknowledgement and confession of the truth [is so] that Yusuf may know that I did not betray him in his absence, defaming him and attributing to him a sin of which he is innocent." Then she offered an excuse for what she had fallen into, of the kind of desires to which humans are prone, with her saying: ﴿And I do not absolve myself﴾. Souls are inclined to desires and are commanding of evil. Al-Zamakhshari said: "﴿And I do not absolve myself﴾ even with that from betrayal, for I did betray him when I slandered him and said: ﴿What is the penalty for one who intended evil to your wife except that he be imprisoned﴾ [Yusuf: 25] and I put him in prison." She intends by this an excuse for what she had done: that every soul is commanding of evil, except a soul upon which Allah has had mercy by preserving it from sin.

﴿Indeed, my Lord is Forgiving and Merciful﴾: she sought forgiveness from her Lord and asked Him for mercy for what she had committed.

As for the one who holds that His saying: (That [was so] that he may know) to the end is from the speech of Yusuf, it requires a forced connection between it and what precedes it, and there is no proof indicating that it is from the speech of Yusuf. Ibn Jurayj said: there is inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir) in the speech, and this speech is connected to Yusuf's saying: ﴿Indeed, my Lord is Knowing of their plotting﴾ [Yusuf: 50]. On this view, the reference in His saying: (That) is to his being cast into prison and his seeking acquittal; that is: "This knowledge, my master, that I did not betray him." Some said: Yusuf only said this statement when the wife of the ruler finished her speech up to her saying: ﴿And indeed he is among the truthful﴾ [Yusuf: 51]; so the reference on this view is to her saying and to what Allah did in it. This view is weak, because it requires his presence with the women before the king, and then how would the king say after that: (Bring him to me)?

Al-Zamakhshari first interpreted the verse as being from the speech of Yusuf, saying: That is, that deliberation and striving for the manifestation of innocence, so that the ruler (al-'Aziz) may know that I did not betray him in his absence regarding his honour. ﴿And that Allah does not guide the plotting of the betrayers﴾: He does not make it succeed or set it right. It seems to be an allusion to his wife in her betrayal of her husband's trust, and to himself in his betrayal of Allah's trust when he assisted her after the signs had appeared (for his imprisonment). End of quotation.

In this there is excessive elaboration and imposing on the wording what is not in it, and it exceeds his usual manner of exposition.

When al-Zamakhshari sensed the difficulty in the view of those who said it is from the speech of Yusuf, he said: "If you say: how is it correct to make it from the speech of Yusuf when there is no proof for that?" I say: the meaning itself is sufficient as an indication leading to it being taken as his speech. A similar example is His saying: ﴿The chiefs of the people of Pharaoh said: Indeed, this is a skilful sorcerer﴾ [al-A'raf: 109] ﴿He wants to drive you out of your land, so what do you advise?﴾ [al-A'raf: 110] ﴿They said﴾ [al-A'raf: 111], and this is from the speech of Pharaoh addressing them and consulting them. End of quotation.

This is not as he mentioned, for in this construction it is not necessarily the case that it is from the speech of Pharaoh. Rather, it is from the speech of the chiefs, Pharaoh having preceded them with this statement, and they then said it to one another. (Bil-ghayb) may be a circumstantial phrase (hal) from the agent: that is, absent from him; or from the object: that is, absent from me; or an adverbial of place (zarf): that is, in a place of absence.

The apparent view is that ﴿except those upon which my Lord has mercy﴾ is a connected exception (istithna' muttasil) from His saying: ﴿commanding of evil﴾, because he intended by (the soul) the genus. The apparent meaning is that this is from the speech of the wife of the ruler (al-'Aziz), and it falls under his saying: (She said). ﴿Indeed, my Lord is Forgiving and Merciful﴾: she sought forgiveness from her Lord and asked Him for mercy for what she had committed.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 12, verse 54–57:

﴿The king said, "Bring him to me; I will take him exclusively for myself." So when he spoke with him, he said, "Indeed, today you are with us established and trusted."﴾ ﴿He said, "Appoint me over the treasuries of the land; indeed, I am a knowing guardian."﴾ ﴿And thus We established Joseph in the land, to settle therein wherever he willed. We bestow Our mercy upon whom We will, and We do not waste the reward of the doers of good.﴾ ﴿And the reward of the Hereafter is better for those who believed and used to fear Allah.﴾

(p-319) It is narrated that the messenger came to him and said: "Answer the king." So he came out of the prison and supplicated for his family: "O Allah, incline toward them the hearts of the righteous, and do not blind them to news, for they are the most knowledgeable of people regarding the reports of events." And he wrote on the gate of the prison: "This is the abode of affliction, the graveyard of the living, the gloating of enemies, and the testing of friends." Then he bathed and cleansed himself of the grime of the prison, and wore new garments. When he entered upon the king, he said: "O Allah, I ask You for Your good through His good, and I seek refuge in Your might and Your power from his evil." Then he greeted him and supplicated for him in Hebrew. He said: "What is this tongue?" He said: "The tongue of my forefathers." The king used to speak seventy tongues, so he spoke to him in them, and he answered him in all of them. He marveled at him and said: "O truthful one, I love to hear my dream from you." He said: "You saw cows, fat ones," and he described their colors and their conditions, and what their emergence was, and he described the ears of grain and what was upon them in the form in which the king had seen them, without omitting a single letter. He also said to him: "Out of your preservation, make the food to be stored in granaries, so that people will come to you from every direction seeking provision from you, and there will be gathered for you from the hoarded stores what has not been gathered for anyone before you." Joseph had first intended, through his steadfastness in prison, to rise to the highest ranks, so the king's summoning him first was because of his knowledge of dream interpretation. Therefore he said: "Bring him to me," only. When Joseph did what he did, his trustworthiness, patience, resolve, excellence of judgment, and his deliberateness in not hastening to answer the first request became apparent, and his station with him became great. So he requested him a second time, and his intention was: to take him exclusively for himself. The meaning of (astakhlisuhu) is: make him sincere to myself and special to me. Allah called the Pharaoh of Egypt "king," since it is a narration of a title whose rule has passed and whose time has ended. Had he been alive, it would have been a ruling for him when said of an unbeliever, "king" or "amir." For this reason the Prophet ﷺ wrote to Heraclius, the great one of the Romans, and did not say "king" or "amir," because that would be a ruling. The reply is "peace be upon the one who follows the guidance, and be submissive." As for his being their great one, that is an attribute that does not leave him whatever turns he takes. In the speech there is an omission; the estimate is: So the king heard the speech of the women and Joseph's innocence of what he had been accused of, so he wished to see him and said: "Bring him to me," and he came to him. "So when he spoke with him": the apparent subject of (kallamahu) is the pronoun of the king, meaning: so when the king spoke with him and saw the goodness of his answer and his discourse. It is also possible that the subject is the pronoun of Joseph, meaning: so when Joseph spoke with the king, and the king saw the goodness of his speech, the report confirmed the report, and "a person is hidden beneath his tongue." He said: "Indeed, today you are with us established" meaning: one of standing and rank. "Trusted" meaning: entrusted with everything. It was said: "trustworthy, most trustworthy." Describing him with trustworthiness is the most eloquent in honoring him, whereas describing him with security would diminish Joseph's honor. When the king described him with being established with him and with trustworthiness, he sought from the offices what suits these two attributes, and he said: "Appoint me over the treasuries of the land," meaning: put me in charge of the treasuries of your land. "Indeed, I am a guardian": I preserve what you entrust to me; "knowing": knowledgeable of the ways of disposal. He described himself with trustworthiness and capability, and these are what kings seek in those they appoint, since they encompass all aspects of management and safekeeping, and nothing is lacking with them for anyone. It was said: "guardian of the reckoning, knowing of languages." It was said: "guardian of what you entrust to me, knowing of the years of hunger." This specification has no basis. Joseph's praise of himself indicates that it is permissible for a person to praise himself in truth when his situation is unknown, and this is not the forbidden self-purification. It also indicates the permissibility of a righteous man working for a merchant man according to what the Sharia and justice require, not according to what he chooses and desires of what the Sharia does not permit. Joseph requested this position only to reach the enforcement of Allah's ruling, the establishment of truth, the spreading of justice, and the empowerment to do that for which the prophets were sent to the servants; and knowing that no one else could stand in his place in that. If the king had accepted Islam, as Mujahid narrated, there is no discussion. If he was a disbeliever, and there is no way to rule by Allah's command and repel injustice except through his empowerment, then the one in charge may rely on him. It was said: the king used to act upon Joseph's opinion and would not object to anything he saw, so he was in the position of a follower. The judges of Islam have continued to assume judgeship on behalf of those who are not righteous; were it not for that, the rulings of the Sharia would be nullified, and they are rewarded for it if they act justly. And (kadhalika), meaning: like that empowerment in the king's own self, We established Joseph in the land of Egypt.

﴿to settle therein wherever he willed﴾ meaning: he takes from it an abode and a dwelling, every place he wishes, so he gained control over all of it, and it came under his authority. It is narrated that the king placed his crown upon him, sealed him with his ring, girded him with his sword, and set for him a throne of gold adorned with pearls and rubies. He sat upon the throne, kings submitted to him, and the king entrusted his affairs to him and dismissed Qitfir. Then he died afterward, and the king married him to his wife. When he entered upon her, he said: "Is this not better than what you asked for?" He found her a virgin, because the Aziz did not have intercourse with her. She bore him two sons: Afraithim and Manasha. He established justice in Egypt, men and women loved him, and the king and many people embraced Islam at his hand. In the years of famine he sold food to the people of Egypt for dinars and dirhams in the first year until none of them had anything of them left; then for jewelry and gems; then for animals; then for estates and property; then for their necks, and then he enslaved them all. They said: "By Allah, we have never seen a king more majestic or greater than him today." He said to the king: "How do you see the handiwork of Allah toward me in what He has granted me; what do you think?" He said: "The opinion is your opinion." He said: "I call Allah and you to witness that I have freed the people of Egypt entirely, and returned their properties to them." He would not sell to any of the buyers more than a camel's load, distributing it among the people. He reached the land of Canaan and the lands of the Levant with what reached Egypt, so Jacob sent his sons to buy grain and kept Benjamin back. Al-Hasan and Ibn Kathir (with variation from them), Abu Ja'far, Shayba, and Nafi' read (haythu nashau) with the nun; the majority read it with the ya'. The apparent reading with the ya' is that the subject of (yashau) is a pronoun referring to Joseph, and his will is bound to the will of Allah, since he is His prophet and messenger. Or the pronoun may refer back to Allah, meaning: wherever Allah wills, and this would be a shift (iltifat).

﴿We bestow Our mercy upon whom We will﴾ meaning: with Our blessing, of kingship, wealth, and other things. ﴿And We do not waste in this world the reward of the one who does good.﴾ Then he mentioned that the reward of the Hereafter is better, because it is lasting and does not perish. Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna said: the believer is rewarded for his good deeds in this world and the Hereafter, while the wicked is hastened good in this world, and has no share in the Hereafter; and he recited this verse. There is in the hadith what agrees with what Sufyan said. In the verse there is an indication that Joseph's state in the Hereafter is better than his great state in this world.

That is: they came from the villages (al-qurayat) in the land of Palestine, in the land of Sham (Greater Syria). It was also said that they came by the mountain passes (al-awlaj), from the direction of the ravine (al-shi'b), into Egypt to obtain provisions (al-mirah) from it. They reached Yusuf to obtain food, and he recognised them, because he had parted from them when they were men and he saw their dress was close to their dress at that time. He also recognised them because his resolve was filled with them and with knowing them, so he kept reflecting and perceiving. It is narrated that when they asked permission to enter, they gave their lineage, and he recognised them and ordered that they be lodged. For this reason al-Hasan said: "He did not recognise them until they made themselves known to him." Their failure to recognise him was, al-Zamakhshari said, due to the long time that had passed and his separation from them at a young age; to their belief that he had perished; to his having slipped from their thoughts because they gave little thought to him; and to the great distance between his present state of kingship and authority and his former state in which they had left him, thrown down in the well and sold for a few counted dirhams. Even if it had occurred to them that he was he, they would have denied it to themselves. Also, kingship changes one's appearance and clothes its possessor with such awe and majesty that what was once familiar becomes unrecognisable. It was also said: they saw him in the attire of Pharaoh, wearing silk garments, seated on a throne, with a gold collar around his neck and a crown on his head, so it did not occur to them that he was he. It was also said: they only saw him from afar, with distance and a screen between them and him, and they only stood where those seeking needs stand.

"When he had furnished them with their provisions": the provisions (al-jihaz) they had were the food they had obtained. There is an ellipsis in the speech, its implied meaning being: he had already learned from them that they had a brother who stayed with their father. It is narrated that when he recognised them, he wished them to tell him all of their affair. So he questioned them, and his interpreter said to them: "I think you are spies." They needed to introduce themselves, so they said: "We are the sons of a truthful man. We were twelve; one of us went missing in the wilderness, and our youngest remained with our father. We came for provisions, and we brought the camel of the one who remained with us." They were ten and had eleven camels. Yusuf said: "Why did one of you stay behind?" They said: "Because of our father's love for him." He said: "Bring me this brother, so that I may know the truth of your words, and see why your father loved him more than you, if you are truthful?" Al-Zamakhshari related this story in words different from these, close in meaning, and at its end he said: "Who will testify for you that you are not spies, and that what you say is true?" They said: "We are in lands where no one knows us, so no one can testify for us." He said: "Leave one of you with me as a pledge, and bring me your brother from your father, who is carrying a message from your father, until I believe you." They drew lots, and the lot fell on Shim'un, who was the best of them in opinion regarding Yusuf, so they left him with him. He had treated them well in lodging and hospitality. It was also said: he did not take anyone as a pledge.

Something other than this is also related about seeking the brother from their father. It was said: Yusuf always veiled his face to conceal his beauty. He would strike the drinking cup (al-sawa') and from its resonance he would understand whether the speech was true or false. They were questioned about their news, and whenever they spoke truthfully he said to them, "You have spoken truly." But when they said, "We had a brother whom the wolf devoured," Yusuf struck the cup and said, "You have lied." Then he changed towards them and said, "I see you are spies," and he obliged them to bring the remaining brother so that their truthfulness would be made clear.

It is recited "bijihazihim" (with a kasra on the jim). The word "akh" (brother) is indefinite and he did not say "bi-akhikum" (with your brother), although he had identified him. The phrase "'arrafahum" (he recognised them) is an intensification, to indicate that he did not wish to make himself known to them, nor that he knew who he was. Do you not see the difference between "marartu bi-ghulamika" (I passed by your boy) and "marartu bi-ghulamin laka" (I passed by a boy belonging to you)? In the definite form you know the boy, while in the indefinite form you are ignorant of him. The definite form implies a known referent between you and the addressee, whereas the indefinite has no such referent at all. It is permissible to report about a person you know using an indefinite noun, so you say: "A man said to us," while you know him, because the indefinite is used with a truthful application to the definite. Then he mentioned what urged them to bring their brother, in his saying: ﴿Do you not see that I give full measure, and that I am the best of hosts?﴾ That is: "the best of those who host." He means, in his region and in his time, he would make them feel at ease and win them over with this. Then he threatened them that if they did not bring him to him, he would deprive them of provisions in the future. The phrase ﴿and do not come near me﴾ may be a prohibition, or it may be an independent negation whose meaning is prohibition, and the nun was omitted while the verb is in the nominative, as it was omitted in ﴿فَبِمَ تُبَشِّرُونَي﴾ [al-Hijr: 54]. It may also be a negation entering into the conditional clause, coordinated with the position of ﴿فَلا كَيْلَ لَكم عِنْدِي﴾ (so there is no measure for you with me), in which case it is jussive. The meaning is: they will not approach him with any goods or obedience.

The apparent meaning of everything Yusuf, peace be upon him, did with them is that it was by revelation. Otherwise, the proper course of righteousness would have been for him to go at once to his father and summon him. But God, exalted, willed to complete the reward and trial of Ya'qub, and so that the first dream might be interpreted.

They said: ﴿We will seek to persuade his father concerning him﴾, meaning: we will deceive him and win him over gently until he lets him come with us to you. Then they confirmed this promise by saying that they would undoubtedly do this; they would not neglect it or be remiss.

Al-Akhawan (the two brothers, Hamza and al-Kisa'i) and Hafs read "li-fityanihi" (to his servants), while the rest of the seven (readers) read "li-fitayatihi" (to his servants, in the singular collective form). The plural reading considers those commanded, and the singular considers those who interpret the order. They were the servants who measured out the grain, and he commanded them to place the money with which they had bought the food into their saddlebags, as an exaggerated means of winning them over.

﴿So that they may recognise it﴾, that is, that they may recognise the right of returning it and the honour of giving the two counterparts, and so they will be eager for us when they return to their families and empty their containers. The phrase ﴿so that they may recognise it﴾ is connected to the act of placing it. The phrase ﴿so that they may return﴾ is connected to the hope that they will recognise the goods in order to return to Yusuf. It was said: their goods were sandals and hides. It was also said: "yarji'una" (they return) is transitive, so the meaning is: so that they may return the goods. It was also said: he feared that his father would not have enough supplies with which they could return. It was also said: he knew that their religion would compel them to return the goods, since they would not consider it lawful to keep them, and so they would come back on their account. It was also said: he made this a prelude to placing the drinking cup in his brother's saddlebag afterwards, so that it would become clear that he had not stolen, for anyone who reflects on the story. Ibn 'Atiyya said: It appears that what Yusuf did, in connecting with them and consoling them in that hardship, was obligatory upon him, since he was a just king and they were people of faith and prophethood.
