Al-Zamakhshari said: it was a sunnah. In the religion of Egypt, the thief was to be beaten and the fine doubled upon him. Therefore they answered according to their own law, and they allowed several possibilities in the parsing of this statement:

The first: that **"its recompense"** is the subject, and **"whoever"** is either a conditional or a relative pronoun, a second subject, and **"then he is its recompense"** is the answer to the condition or the predicate of the relative "mā"; and the clause beginning **"whoever was found"** to the end is the predicate of the first subject. The pronoun in **"They said: its recompense"** refers to the thief. This is the statement of Ibn ʿAṭiyyah, but it is not correct, because the clause that serves as the predicate of **"its recompense"** lacks a connecting pronoun.

The second: that the meaning is "They said: the recompense for his theft," and **"its recompense"** is the subject, and the conditional clause, as it is, is its predicate, by placing the apparent noun in the place of the pronoun. The original would be: "its recompense is whoever is found in his baggage, so he is it." So the position of the recompense is the position of "he is it," as when you say to your companion: "Who is Zayd's brother?" and he replies: "His brother is whoever sits beside him." Then "he is it": the first pronoun refers to "whoever," and the second refers to the brother. Then you say "so he is his brother," making the apparent noun stand in place of the pronoun. This is the statement of al-Zamakhshari. Placing the apparent noun in the position of the pronoun for linking is eloquent only in contexts of exaltation and awe, and it is not eloquent elsewhere, as in "Zayd stood, Zayd." Sibawayh said: if you say "Zayd was going, Zayd," it would not be the opposite of speech, but it would be weak here; and it would not be like your saying "Zayd is not going, he," because you have dispensed with its explicit mention, and you ought rather to use the pronoun.

The third: that **"its recompense"** is the predicate of an elided subject, meaning: "what is asked about is its recompense." Then they gave their ruling by saying: **"whoever is found in his baggage, then he is its recompense,"** as when you say: "Whoever asks for a fatwa about the recompense for hunting in the sacred precinct, [the answer is] the recompense for hunting in the sacred precinct," and then you say: **"And whoever of you kills it intentionally, its recompense is the like of what he killed from the livestock"** [al-Mā'idah 5:95]. This is the statement of al-Zamakhshari, but it is contrived, since the clause in his statement "what is asked about is its recompense," under this assumption, has little benefit. It is already known from **"then what is its recompense?"** that the thing asked about is the recompense for its theft, so what is the point of their saying it? The same applies to the example given of the questioner's statement.

The fourth: that **"its recompense"** is the subject, meaning: the recompense for the theft of the vessel; and the predicate is **"whoever is found in his baggage,"** meaning: whoever in whose baggage it is found is taken [as the recompense]. Their statement **"then he is its recompense"** is an affirmation of a ruling, meaning: the taking of the thief himself is the recompense, and nothing else, like your saying: "Zayd's right is that he be clothed, fed, and shown favor, so that is his recompense," or "so it is his due," to confirm what I have mentioned of his entitlement. This is the statement of al-Zamakhshari. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said the same thing but made the one statement into two, saying: it is also valid for **"whoever"** to be the predicate, in the sense that "the recompense of the thief is whoever is found in his baggage," with a returning pronoun referring to "whoever," and **"then he is its recompense"** serves as an added clarification and emphasis. Then he said: it is also possible that the implied meaning is "its recompense is the enslaving of whoever is found in his baggage," and then it is emphasized by the words **"then he is its recompense."** This statement is the same as the one before it, except that it brings out the omitted genitive in the phrase "the enslaving of whoever is found in his baggage," whereas in the earlier statement the omitted element must be supplied, because the essence cannot be the predicate of a verbal noun. So the implied meaning in the earlier statement is: "its recompense is the taking of whoever is found in his baggage, or the enslaving of this is necessary," according to this parsing. This final option is the best of the possibilities and the furthest from strained construction.

**(Thus)**, i.e., like this recompense, which is enslavement, **"We recompense the wrongdoers,"** i.e., for theft. This is our religion and our custom regarding the people of theft.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 12, verses 69–75 (part 1 of 2):

﴿When they entered upon Joseph, he drew his brother to himself and said: "Indeed, I am your brother, so do not grieve over what they used to do."﴾ ﴿When he had equipped them with their provision, he placed the drinking-cup in his brother's saddlebag. Then a crier called out: "O caravan, you are surely thieves!"﴾ ﴿They turned toward them and said: "What is it that you are missing?"﴾ ﴿They said: "We are missing the king's measuring-cup, and for whoever brings it there is a camel-load, and I guarantee it."﴾ ﴿They said: "By God, you know that we did not come to cause corruption in the land, and we were not thieves."﴾ ﴿They said: "What then is its penalty, if you are liars?"﴾ ﴿They said: "Its penalty is that whoever it is found in his saddlebag, he himself is its penalty. Thus do we requite the wrongdoers."﴾ ﴿So he began with their bags before his brother's bag, then he brought it out from his brother's bag. Thus did We devise for Joseph. He could not have taken his brother under the king's law unless God willed. We raise by degrees whom We will, and above every possessor of knowledge is one who knows.﴾ [Yusuf: 76] ﴿They said: "If he has stolen, then a brother of his had stolen before." But Joseph kept it hidden within himself and did not disclose it to them. He said: "You are worse in position, and God knows best what you describe."﴾ [Yusuf: 77] ﴿They said: "O Chief, he has an aged father, so take one of us in his place. Indeed, we see you are of the good-doers."﴾ [Yusuf: 78] ﴿He said: "God forbid that we should take anyone except him with whom we found our property. Indeed, then we would be wrongdoers."﴾ [Yusuf: 79] ﴿So when they despaired of him, they withdrew apart in private consultation. Their eldest said: "Do you not know that your father has taken a solemn pledge from you before God, and that previously you neglected Joseph? So I will not leave this land until my father permits me or God judges for me, and He is the best of judges."﴾ [Yusuf: 80] ﴿Return to your father and say: "O our father, indeed your son has stolen. We bear witness only to what we knew, and we were not guardians of the unseen."﴾ [Yusuf: 81] ﴿And ask the town in which we were, and the caravan in which we came, and indeed we are truthful.﴾ [Yusuf: 82] ﴿He said: "Rather, your souls have beautified a matter for you. So patience is beautiful. Perhaps God will bring them all to me. Indeed, He is the All-Knowing, the All-Wise."﴾ [Yusuf: 83] ﴿And he turned away from them and said: "Alas for Joseph!" and his eyes turned white from grief, and he was suppressing (his anguish).﴾ [Yusuf: 84] ﴿They said: "By God, you will not cease remembering Joseph until you become wasted away or become among the perishing."﴾ [Yusuf: 85]

Al-'Ir (the caravan): the camels that carry loads. It was so named because they go back and forth (ta'ir), that is, they go and come. It was also said that it is a caravan of donkeys. Then the term became widespread, so that every caravan was called 'ir, as though it were the plural of 'ayr. Its root form is fu'l, like saqf and suqf, and it underwent what happened to bid and 'in (i.e., the vowel of the middle radical was changed in the same manner). 'Ir is feminine. In the plural they said 'iyarat, so they deviated in its plural by using the suffix alif-ta' and in opening its ya'. The poet said:

*I passed by the dwellings of the tribe at al-Bakarat, at Fa'arima and the lightning-flash of the 'iyarat.*

Al-A'lam said: "Here, the places of the 'ayr, which are donkeys." Al-suwa' (the measuring-cup): the sa' (a unit of measure). It has dialects that appear in the Qur'an, and it is both feminine and masculine. Al-wi'a' (the container): the vessel in which a thing is kept, and its waw may be given a damma; it is also permissible to replace its waw with a hamza. Fati'a: one of the sisters of kana (the defective verbs). Aws ibn Hajar said:

*Its dust has not ceased, as though it were a canopy of an owl with winds raising it up.*

He also said:

*Horses have not ceased returning and claiming, and of them there is one who overtakes and one who is cut off.*

It is also said fata' with the pattern of daraba, and afta' with the pattern of akrama. Ibn Malik claimed that it can mean "to be calm" and "to extinguish," so that it would be a complete verb (taamma). We refuted him on that in our commentary on al-Tashil, and we showed that this was a mistake on his part: he misread the tha' as a double ta' with two dots above, and explained it as "calm" and "extinguish." Al-haraḍ: one who is on the verge of destruction. It is said: haraḍa, so he is ḥaraḍ with a kasra on the ra', and ḥarañ (haraḍan) with a fatha on it, which is the verbal noun. For this reason, the masculine and feminine, the singular and plural are equal in it. Al-maraḍ made him ill (aḥraḍahu), so he is muḥraḍ. The poet said:

*I see a man like provisions, becoming in the morning a sickly one, like the sickness of a camel in the dwellings.*

Another said:

*Indeed I am a man whom love has caused to be passionate, and it made me ill until I wasted away, and until illness wore me down.*

He also said: a man is ḥurud, with two dammas, like junub and shulul.

* *

﴿When they entered upon Joseph, he drew his brother to himself and said: "Indeed, I am your brother, so do not grieve over what they used to do."﴾ ﴿When he had equipped them with their provision, he placed the drinking-cup in his brother's saddlebag. Then a crier called out: "O caravan, you are surely thieves!"﴾ ﴿They turned toward them and said: "What is it that you are missing?"﴾ ﴿They said: "We are missing the king's measuring-cup, and for whoever brings it there is a camel-load, and I guarantee it."﴾ ﴿They said: "By God, you know that we did not come to cause corruption in the land, and we were not thieves."﴾ ﴿They said: "What then is its penalty, if you are liars?"﴾ ﴿They said: "Its penalty is that whoever it is found in his saddlebag, he himself is its penalty. Thus do we requite the wrongdoers."﴾

It was narrated that they said to him: "This is our brother; we have brought him to you." He said: "You have done well and rightly; you will find that with me." So he lodged them and honored them, then he gave them a meal, and seated every two of them at a table. Benjamin was left alone, so he wept and said: "If my brother Joseph were alive, he would seat me with him." Joseph said: "Your brother has remained alone," so he seated him with him at his table. He began to eat with them and said: "You are ten; let every two of you go down to a room, and this one has no second, so he will be with me." Joseph spent the night embracing him and smelling his scent until morning. He asked him about his children, and he said: "I have ten sons; I have derived their names from the name of a brother of mine who perished." So he said to him: "Would you like me to be your brother in place of your perished brother?" He said: "Who would find a brother like you? But Ya'qub and Rahil did not bear you." Then Joseph wept, rose to him, embraced him, and said to him: "I am your brother Joseph, so do not grieve over what they used to do to us in the past. God has been good to us and has gathered us upon good; do not inform them of what I have informed you." It was reported from Ibn 'Abbas: he made himself known to him as his brother, and this is the apparent meaning; it is also the view of Ibn Ishaq and others. He informed him that he was truly his brother, and asked him to keep it secret, and said to him: "Do not mind whatever disagreeable thing you see in my scheming to take you from them." Ibn 'Atiyya said: "On this interpretation, it is possible that by his saying 'over what they used to do' he refers to what the servants of Joseph were doing concerning the drinking-cup and the like." End of quote. But this is not admissible, because if the construction had been "over what they used to do" without a pronoun, it would have been possible, though remote, since the speech is with the brothers of Joseph. As for mentioning his servants, it is very remote, for no mention of them has preceded except in His saying: "And he said to his servants" (Yusuf: 62), and the narrative intervened between them.

The speech is coherent with the brothers in a way that does not call for deviating from the pronoun referring to them. That reference is to what they had inflicted upon him in the past of harm, since he was now secure from that through his reunion with his brother Joseph. Wahb said: "He only informed him that he was his brother in affection, in the place of his departed brother, and did not reveal the matter to him. Rather, he left him, and the trick could be carried out upon him as with the rest of his brothers." Apparently, the one who placed the drinking-cup in his brother's saddlebag was Joseph. From his position as king, it appears that he did not carry this out himself, but rather had someone else from his servants, or others, place it. Wahb's statement has already been mentioned: that he did not reveal to him that he was his brother, and that he left him so that the trick could be carried out upon him. It was narrated that he (Benjamin) said to Joseph: "I will not leave you." He said: "You know the grief of my father; if I detain you, his grief will increase, and there is no way to that except that I attribute to you something that cannot be borne." He said: "I do not mind; do as you see fit." He said: "I will place my measuring-cup in your saddlebag, then I will call out against you that you stole it, so that I can have you returned after you are released with them." He said: "Do so." Al-Zamakhshari reported that 'Abdullah read: "He placed the drinking-cup in his brother's saddlebag." He gave them time until they set off, then he called out. In Ibn 'Atiyya's transmission, "and he placed the drinking-cup" has an added waw in "ja'ala," which is not the addition al-Zamakhshari added after His saying "in his brother's saddlebag." So it is possible that the waw is extra according to the school of the Kufans. It is also possible that the answer to "lamma" (when) is omitted, its estimated meaning being: "its guardian lost it," as it was said: "Joseph was only inspired to place the drinking-cup alone; then its guardian lost it, so he called out according to his own opinion as it appeared to him." Al-Tabari preferred this. But the searching of the containers refutes this view. What appears is that the crier's proclamation was by Joseph's command. Al-Suddi said: "This placing was without Benjamin's knowledge," but what has preceded indicates that it was with his knowledge.

The majority, along with Ibn 'Umar, Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Mujahid, al-Dahhak, and Ibn Zayd, said: al-siqaya is a vessel from which the king drinks, and with which food was measured out for the people. It was also said: the king used to be given drink from it, then it was made a measure with which to measure. It was also said: the animals used to be watered with it, and measurement was done with it. Ibn Jubayr said: al-suwa' is like the Persian makkuk, and it was Joseph's vessel from which he drank, and it was for the one with a long height/of great skill (?). He said: "Ibn 'Abbas told me that al-'Abbas had one like it, from which he used to drink in the Jahiliyya." Ibn Jubayr also said: "The suwa' is the Persian makkuk whose two ends meet; the non-Arabs used to drink from it." The siqaya was of silver, or gold, or silver plated with gold, or copper, or musk, or it was adorned with jewels. These are opinions; the first of them belongs to the majority. And because food was scarce in those years, its measuring was restricted to that vessel.

﴿Then a crier called out﴾ meaning: a caller called out. Adhdhana: he informed; and ādhana is more intensive in informing, and the mu'adhdhin (muezzin) is derived from it because of its frequency. The "then" (thumma) requires an interval between placing the drinking-cup and the proclamation. It is narrated that when the caravan had departed with its loads and went out of Egypt, they were overtaken and were told this. It was also said: before they left Egypt they were ordered to be detained, and the crier called out. The apparent and the majority's view is that the caravan (al-'ir) is the camels. Mujahid said: their mounts were donkeys. The calling out to the caravan, while meaning its people, is like His saying: "O horses of God, mount" (the people who are addressed). For this reason the address came: "Indeed, you are surely thieves," so the omitted referent was observed, and the caravan itself was not regarded, as was observed in "mount," and in His saying: "and the caravan in which we came" (Yusuf: 82). It is also permissible to apply "caravan" to the company or the party, in which case it is not a metonymy by omission. What appears is that this deception, the throwing of innocent people with theft, and the bringing of grief upon Ya'qub, was by inspiration from God, since He, exalted is He, knew the benefit in it, and because He willed their trial through it. This is strengthened by His saying: "Thus did We devise for Joseph" (Yusuf: 76). It was also said: since they had sold Joseph, it was permitted to say this to them, and the attribution of theft to all of them is possible even though the measuring-cup was found in the saddlebag of only one of them, just as you say: "The sons of so-and-so killed so-and-so," while the killer is one of them.

(They said) meaning the brothers of Joseph. (And they turned) is a circumstantial clause: that is, "and they had turned toward them," meaning toward those who sought the drinking-cup, or toward the crier if he is meant as a plural, as though he had made criers who call out. It distressed them to be accused of this disgrace. They said: ﴿What is it that you are missing?﴾ so that the search would take place and their innocence would become apparent. They did not resort to denial from the start; rather, they asked for the full charge, hoping that in it there would be something by which it could be refuted, so that there would be no need for dispute. It is possible that (mādhā) is an interrogative in the accusative position governed by (taf-qidūna, "you miss"). It is also possible that "mā" alone is an interrogative subject, and "dhā" is a relative pronoun meaning "that which," the predicate about "mā," and "you miss" is the relative clause of "dhā," and the returning pronoun is omitted; that is, "you miss it." As-Sulami read (tufqidūna) with a damma on the ta', from afqadtuhu, when you find him missing, like aḥmadtuhu when you find him praised. Abu Hatim criticized this reading, and its explanation is what we have mentioned.

The "ṣuwāʿ" of the king is the measuring vessel, and it is the water-vessel (siqāyah). He named it first by one of its two aspects and last by the second.

Most readers recited (ṣuwāʿa) with a ḍammah on the ṣād, then a fatḥah-marked wāw, then a long ʾalif, then the unpointed ʿayn. Abu Ḥayyah, Al-Ḥasan, and Ibn Jubayr, as transmitted by Ibn ʿAṭiyyah, recited it the same way except with a kasrah on the ṣād. Abu Hurayrah and Mujahid recited (ṣāʿa) without a wāw, on the pattern faʿala, so the ʾalif in it replaces the fatḥah-marked wāw. Abu Rajāʾ recited (ṣawʿa) on the pattern qawsun. ʿAbdullah ibn ʿAwn ibn Abi Arṭabān recited (ṣuwaʿa) with a ḍammah on the ṣād. All of these are dialectal forms for the ṣāʿ (measure).

Al-Ḥasan and Ibn Jubayr, as transmitted from them by the author of al-Lawāmiḥ (a grammatical work), recited (ṣuwāgha) with an unpointed ghayn, on the pattern ghurāb. Yaḥyā ibn Yaʿmar recited it the same way, except that he dropped the ʾalif and made the wāw sukūn. Zayd ibn ʿAli recited (ṣawgha), the verbal noun of ṣāgh (to fashion). Ṣuwāgh and ṣawgh are both derived from al-ṣawgh, the verbal noun of ṣāgha yaṣūgh, and they are used in the sense of maṣūgh (the thing fashioned): the king's fashioned vessel.

**(And for him who brings it)**, i.e., for whoever points to its thief and exposes him. This is a juʿl (a stipulated reward), and the caller's words are the speech of the crier: "And I am surety for it (the camel's load)" — I will pay it to whoever brings it. He meant by it a camel-load of food, as a reward for whoever recovers it.

They said: **"By God!"** They swore using the particle tāʾ, one of the particles of oath, because it generally carries a sense of wonder, as if they were astonished at being accused of this matter. It is related that they returned the merchandise they had found in their food-sacks and were scrupulous about eating the food without payment. They were known in Egypt for their righteousness, and they used to place a muzzle on their camels' mouths so that they would not graze on people's crops. So they swore to affirm something they were known for, namely: "You know that our coming was not for corruption." Then they resumed by denying the attribute of theft from themselves, and that it had never occurred from them at all. It is possible that this falls within the scope of the answer to the oath, so that it is coordinated with their statement "You know," and Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: the tāʾ in (tāllāh) is a substitute for a wāw, as it was substituted in turāth, in al-Tawrāh, and in al-tukhmah. The tāʾ does not enter into oaths except with the names of God that are written [in the Qur'an], and other than that: you do not say tārraḥmān nor tārraḥīm. End of quotation.

As for his statement that the tāʾ in (tāllāh) is a substitute for a wāw, this is the view of most grammarians. Al-Suhayli disagreed with them, claiming that it is an original letter in its own right and not a substitute for a wāw, and this is the correct view according to what we have established in grammar. As for his statement "and in al-Tawrāh," this is according to the school of the Basrans, who claimed that its origin is (wawrāh) from (wara) (the fire-starter), as in the saying "wirā al-zand" (the tinder kindled). Some grammarians claimed that the tāʾ is an extra letter, and this is mentioned in grammar. As for his statement "and it does not enter..." and so on, it has been related from the Arabs that it enters before (al-Rabb) (the Lord), before (al-Raḥmān), and before (ḥayātika): they say "tarabb al-kaʿbah" (by the Lord of the Kaʿbah), "tārraḥmān," and "taḥayyātika."

The address in **"You know"** is to those seeking the measuring vessel. The pronoun in **"its recompense"** refers to the thief. So what is the recompense of the thief, if you are lying in your statement: **"We were not thieves"**? This is said by Ibn ʿAṭiyyah. Al-Zamakhshari said: the pronoun in **"its recompense"** refers to the vessel, i.e., what is the recompense for its theft, if you are lying in your denial and your claim of innocence concerning it. End of quotation.

As for his statement that this is the apparent meaning, because the pronouns are unified in his statement **"They said: its recompense is whoever is found in his baggage,"** since the implied meaning then is: "He said: the recompense of the vessel is that whoever in whose baggage the vessel is found..." Their statement **"its recompense is whoever is found in his baggage"** is the speech of someone who did not doubt that they were innocent of what they had been accused of. Because they believed in their innocence, they tied the ruling to finding the vessel, not to its theft. So it is as if they were saying: "It is impossible for us to steal; it is impossible for the vessel to be found in our baggage." In the religion of Jacob, enslaving the thief was the custom. Al-Zamakhshari said: it was a sunnah. In the religion of Egypt, the thief was to be beaten and the fine doubled upon him. Therefore they answered according to their own law, and they allowed several possibilities in the parsing of this statement:

The first: that **"its recompense"** is the subject, and **"whoever"** is either a conditional or a relative pronoun, a second subject, and **"then he is its recompense"** is the answer to the condition or the predicate of the relative "mā"; and the clause beginning **"whoever was found"** to the end is the predicate of the first subject. The pronoun in **"They said: its recompense"** refers to the thief. This is the statement of Ibn ʿAṭiyyah, but it is not correct, because the clause that serves as the predicate of **"its recompense"** lacks a connecting pronoun.

The second: that the meaning is "They said: the recompense for his theft," and **"its recompense"** is the subject, and the conditional clause, as it is, is its predicate, by placing the apparent noun in the place of the pronoun. The original would be: "its recompense is whoever is found in his baggage, so he is it." So the position of the recompense is the position of "he is it," as when you say to your companion: "Who is Zayd's brother?" and he replies: "His brother is whoever sits beside him." Then "he is it": the first pronoun refers to "whoever," and the second refers to the brother. Then you say "so he is his brother," making the apparent noun stand in place of the pronoun. This is the statement of al-Zamakhshari. Placing the apparent noun in the position of the pronoun for linking is eloquent only in contexts of exaltation and awe, and it is not eloquent elsewhere, as in "Zayd stood, Zayd." Sibawayh said: if you say "Zayd was going, Zayd," it would not be the opposite of speech, but it would be weak here; and it would not be like your saying "Zayd is not going, he," because you have dispensed with its explicit mention, and you ought rather to use the pronoun.

The third: that **"its recompense"** is the predicate of an elided subject, meaning: "what is asked about is its recompense." Then they gave their ruling by saying: **"whoever is found in his baggage, then he is its recompense,"** as when you say: "Whoever asks for a fatwa about the recompense for hunting in the sacred precinct, [the answer is] the recompense for hunting in the sacred precinct," and then you say: **"And whoever of you kills it intentionally, its recompense is the like of what he killed from the livestock"** [al-Mā'idah 5:95]. This is the statement of al-Zamakhshari, but it is contrived, since the clause in his statement "what is asked about is its recompense," under this assumption, has little benefit. It is already known from **"then what is its recompense?"** that the thing asked about is the recompense for its theft, so what is the point of their saying it? The same applies to the example given of the questioner's statement.

The fourth: that **"its recompense"** is the subject, meaning: the recompense for the theft of the vessel; and the predicate is **"whoever is found in his baggage,"** meaning: whoever in whose baggage it is found is taken [as the recompense]. Their statement **"then he is its recompense"** is an affirmation of a ruling, meaning: the taking of the thief himself is the recompense, and nothing else, like your saying: "Zayd's right is that he be clothed, fed, and shown favor, so that is his recompense," or "so it is his due," to confirm what I have mentioned of his entitlement. This is the statement of al-Zamakhshari. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said the same thing but made the one statement into two, saying: it is also valid for **"whoever"** to be the predicate, in the sense that "the recompense of the thief is whoever is found in his baggage," with a returning pronoun referring to "whoever," and **"then he is its recompense"** serves as an added clarification and emphasis. Then he said: it is also possible that the implied meaning is "its recompense is the enslaving of whoever is found in his baggage," and then it is emphasized by the words **"then he is its recompense."** This statement is the same as the one before it, except that it brings out the omitted genitive in the phrase "the enslaving of whoever is found in his baggage," whereas in the earlier statement the omitted element must be supplied, because the essence cannot be the predicate of a verbal noun. So the implied meaning in the earlier statement is: "its recompense is the taking of whoever is found in his baggage, or the enslaving of this is necessary," according to this parsing. This final option is the best of the possibilities and the furthest from strained construction.

**(Thus)**, i.e., like this recompense, which is enslavement, **"We recompense the wrongdoers,"** i.e., for theft. This is our religion and our custom regarding the people of theft.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 12, verses 69–75 (part 1 of 2):

﴿When they entered upon Joseph, he drew his brother to himself and said: "Indeed, I am your brother, so do not grieve over what they used to do."﴾ ﴿When he had equipped them with their provision, he placed the drinking-cup in his brother's saddlebag. Then a crier called out: "O caravan, you are surely thieves!"﴾ ﴿They turned toward them and said: "What is it that you are missing?"﴾ ﴿They said: "We are missing the king's measuring-cup, and for whoever brings it there is a camel-load, and I guarantee it."﴾ ﴿They said: "By God, you know that we did not come to cause corruption in the land, and we were not thieves."﴾ ﴿They said: "What then is its penalty, if you are liars?"﴾ ﴿They said: "Its penalty is that whoever it is found in his saddlebag, he himself is its penalty. Thus do we requite the wrongdoers."﴾ ﴿So he began with their bags before his brother's bag, then he brought it out from his brother's bag. Thus did We devise for Joseph. He could not have taken his brother under the king's law unless God willed. We raise by degrees whom We will, and above every possessor of knowledge is one who knows.﴾ [Yusuf: 76] ﴿They said: "If he has stolen, then a brother of his had stolen before." But Joseph kept it hidden within himself and did not disclose it to them. He said: "You are worse in position, and God knows best what you describe."﴾ [Yusuf: 77] ﴿They said: "O Chief, he has an aged father, so take one of us in his place. Indeed, we see you are of the good-doers."﴾ [Yusuf: 78] ﴿He said: "God forbid that we should take anyone except him with whom we found our property. Indeed, then we would be wrongdoers."﴾ [Yusuf: 79] ﴿So when they despaired of him, they withdrew apart in private consultation. Their eldest said: "Do you not know that your father has taken a solemn pledge from you before God, and that previously you neglected Joseph? So I will not leave this land until my father permits me or God judges for me, and He is the best of judges."﴾ [Yusuf: 80] ﴿Return to your father and say: "O our father, indeed your son has stolen. We bear witness only to what we knew, and we were not guardians of the unseen."﴾ [Yusuf: 81] ﴿And ask the town in which we were, and the caravan in which we came, and indeed we are truthful.﴾ [Yusuf: 82] ﴿He said: "Rather, your souls have beautified a matter for you. So patience is beautiful. Perhaps God will bring them all to me. Indeed, He is the All-Knowing, the All-Wise."﴾ [Yusuf: 83] ﴿And he turned away from them and said: "Alas for Joseph!" and his eyes turned white from grief, and he was suppressing (his anguish).﴾ [Yusuf: 84] ﴿They said: "By God, you will not cease remembering Joseph until you become wasted away or become among the perishing."﴾ [Yusuf: 85]

Al-'Ir (the caravan): the camels that carry loads. It was so named because they go back and forth (ta'ir), that is, they go and come. It was also said that it is a caravan of donkeys. Then the term became widespread, so that every caravan was called 'ir, as though it were the plural of 'ayr. Its root form is fu'l, like saqf and suqf, and it underwent what happened to bid and 'in (i.e., the vowel of the middle radical was changed in the same manner). 'Ir is feminine. In the plural they said 'iyarat, so they deviated in its plural by using the suffix alif-ta' and in opening its ya'. The poet said:

*I passed by the dwellings of the tribe at al-Bakarat, at Fa'arima and the lightning-flash of the 'iyarat.*

Al-A'lam said: "Here, the places of the 'ayr, which are donkeys." Al-suwa' (the measuring-cup): the sa' (a unit of measure). It has dialects that appear in the Qur'an, and it is both feminine and masculine. Al-wi'a' (the container): the vessel in which a thing is kept, and its waw may be given a damma; it is also permissible to replace its waw with a hamza. Fati'a: one of the sisters of kana (the defective verbs). Aws ibn Hajar said:

*Its dust has not ceased, as though it were a canopy of an owl with winds raising it up.*

He also said:

*Horses have not ceased returning and claiming, and of them there is one who overtakes and one who is cut off.*

It is also said fata' with the pattern of daraba, and afta' with the pattern of akrama. Ibn Malik claimed that it can mean "to be calm" and "to extinguish," so that it would be a complete verb (taamma). We refuted him on that in our commentary on al-Tashil, and we showed that this was a mistake on his part: he misread the tha' as a double ta' with two dots above, and explained it as "calm" and "extinguish." Al-haraḍ: one who is on the verge of destruction. It is said: haraḍa, so he is ḥaraḍ with a kasra on the ra', and ḥarañ (haraḍan) with a fatha on it, which is the verbal noun. For this reason, the masculine and feminine, the singular and plural are equal in it. Al-maraḍ made him ill (aḥraḍahu), so he is muḥraḍ. The poet said:

*I see a man like provisions, becoming in the morning a sickly one, like the sickness of a camel in the dwellings.*

Another said:

*Indeed I am a man whom love has caused to be passionate, and it made me ill until I wasted away, and until illness wore me down.*

He also said: a man is ḥurud, with two dammas, like junub and shulul.

* *

﴿When they entered upon Joseph, he drew his brother to himself and said: "Indeed, I am your brother, so do not grieve over what they used to do."﴾ ﴿When he had equipped them with their provision, he placed the drinking-cup in his brother's saddlebag. Then a crier called out: "O caravan, you are surely thieves!"﴾ ﴿They turned toward them and said: "What is it that you are missing?"﴾ ﴿They said: "We are missing the king's measuring-cup, and for whoever brings it there is a camel-load, and I guarantee it."﴾ ﴿They said: "By God, you know that we did not come to cause corruption in the land, and we were not thieves."﴾ ﴿They said: "What then is its penalty, if you are liars?"﴾ ﴿They said: "Its penalty is that whoever it is found in his saddlebag, he himself is its penalty. Thus do we requite the wrongdoers."﴾

It was narrated that they said to him: "This is our brother; we have brought him to you." He said: "You have done well and rightly; you will find that with me." So he lodged them and honored them, then he gave them a meal, and seated every two of them at a table. Benjamin was left alone, so he wept and said: "If my brother Joseph were alive, he would seat me with him." Joseph said: "Your brother has remained alone," so he seated him with him at his table. He began to eat with them and said: "You are ten; let every two of you go down to a room, and this one has no second, so he will be with me." Joseph spent the night embracing him and smelling his scent until morning. He asked him about his children, and he said: "I have ten sons; I have derived their names from the name of a brother of mine who perished." So he said to him: "Would you like me to be your brother in place of your perished brother?" He said: "Who would find a brother like you? But Ya'qub and Rahil did not bear you." Then Joseph wept, rose to him, embraced him, and said to him: "I am your brother Joseph, so do not grieve over what they used to do to us in the past. God has been good to us and has gathered us upon good; do not inform them of what I have informed you." It was reported from Ibn 'Abbas: he made himself known to him as his brother, and this is the apparent meaning; it is also the view of Ibn Ishaq and others. He informed him that he was truly his brother, and asked him to keep it secret, and said to him: "Do not mind whatever disagreeable thing you see in my scheming to take you from them." Ibn 'Atiyya said: "On this interpretation, it is possible that by his saying 'over what they used to do' he refers to what the servants of Joseph were doing concerning the drinking-cup and the like." End of quote. But this is not admissible, because if the construction had been "over what they used to do" without a pronoun, it would have been possible, though remote, since the speech is with the brothers of Joseph. As for mentioning his servants, it is very remote, for no mention of them has preceded except in His saying: "And he said to his servants" (Yusuf: 62), and the narrative intervened between them.

The speech is coherent with the brothers in a way that does not call for deviating from the pronoun referring to them. That reference is to what they had inflicted upon him in the past of harm, since he was now secure from that through his reunion with his brother Joseph. Wahb said: "He only informed him that he was his brother in affection, in the place of his departed brother, and did not reveal the matter to him. Rather, he left him, and the trick could be carried out upon him as with the rest of his brothers." Apparently, the one who placed the drinking-cup in his brother's saddlebag was Joseph. From his position as king, it appears that he did not carry this out himself, but rather had someone else from his servants, or others, place it. Wahb's statement has already been mentioned: that he did not reveal to him that he was his brother, and that he left him so that the trick could be carried out upon him. It was narrated that he (Benjamin) said to Joseph: "I will not leave you." He said: "You know the grief of my father; if I detain you, his grief will increase, and there is no way to that except that I attribute to you something that cannot be borne." He said: "I do not mind; do as you see fit." He said: "I will place my measuring-cup in your saddlebag, then I will call out against you that you stole it, so that I can have you returned after you are released with them." He said: "Do so." Al-Zamakhshari reported that 'Abdullah read: "He placed the drinking-cup in his brother's saddlebag." He gave them time until they set off, then he called out. In Ibn 'Atiyya's transmission, "and he placed the drinking-cup" has an added waw in "ja'ala," which is not the addition al-Zamakhshari added after His saying "in his brother's saddlebag." So it is possible that the waw is extra according to the school of the Kufans. It is also possible that the answer to "lamma" (when) is omitted, its estimated meaning being: "its guardian lost it," as it was said: "Joseph was only inspired to place the drinking-cup alone; then its guardian lost it, so he called out according to his own opinion as it appeared to him." Al-Tabari preferred this. But the searching of the containers refutes this view. What appears is that the crier's proclamation was by Joseph's command. Al-Suddi said: "This placing was without Benjamin's knowledge," but what has preceded indicates that it was with his knowledge.

The majority, along with Ibn 'Umar, Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Mujahid, al-Dahhak, and Ibn Zayd, said: al-siqaya is a vessel from which the king drinks, and with which food was measured out for the people. It was also said: the king used to be given drink from it, then it was made a measure with which to measure. It was also said: the animals used to be watered with it, and measurement was done with it. Ibn Jubayr said: al-suwa' is like the Persian makkuk, and it was Joseph's vessel from which he drank, and it was for the one with a long height/of great skill (?). He said: "Ibn 'Abbas told me that al-'Abbas had one like it, from which he used to drink in the Jahiliyya." Ibn Jubayr also said: "The suwa' is the Persian makkuk whose two ends meet; the non-Arabs used to drink from it." The siqaya was of silver, or gold, or silver plated with gold, or copper, or musk, or it was adorned with jewels. These are opinions; the first of them belongs to the majority. And because food was scarce in those years, its measuring was restricted to that vessel.

﴿Then a crier called out﴾ meaning: a caller called out. Adhdhana: he informed; and ādhana is more intensive in informing, and the mu'adhdhin (muezzin) is derived from it because of its frequency. The "then" (thumma) requires an interval between placing the drinking-cup and the proclamation. It is narrated that when the caravan had departed with its loads and went out of Egypt, they were overtaken and were told this. It was also said: before they left Egypt they were ordered to be detained, and the crier called out. The apparent and the majority's view is that the caravan (al-'ir) is the camels. Mujahid said: their mounts were donkeys. The calling out to the caravan, while meaning its people, is like His saying: "O horses of God, mount" (the people who are addressed). For this reason the address came: "Indeed, you are surely thieves," so the omitted referent was observed, and the caravan itself was not regarded, as was observed in "mount," and in His saying: "and the caravan in which we came" (Yusuf: 82). It is also permissible to apply "caravan" to the company or the party, in which case it is not a metonymy by omission. What appears is that this deception, the throwing of innocent people with theft, and the bringing of grief upon Ya'qub, was by inspiration from God, since He, exalted is He, knew the benefit in it, and because He willed their trial through it. This is strengthened by His saying: "Thus did We devise for Joseph" (Yusuf: 76). It was also said: since they had sold Joseph, it was permitted to say this to them, and the attribution of theft to all of them is possible even though the measuring-cup was found in the saddlebag of only one of them, just as you say: "The sons of so-and-so killed so-and-so," while the killer is one of them.

(They said) meaning the brothers of Joseph. (And they turned) is a circumstantial clause: that is, "and they had turned toward them," meaning toward those who sought the drinking-cup, or toward the crier if he is meant as a plural, as though he had made criers who call out. It distressed them to be accused of this disgrace. They said: ﴿What is it that you are missing?﴾ so that the search would take place and their innocence would become apparent. They did not resort to denial from the start; rather, they asked for the full charge, hoping that in it there would be something by which it could be refuted, so that there would be no need for dispute. It is possible that (mādhā) is an interrogative in the accusative position governed by (taf-qidūna, "you miss"). It is also possible that "mā" alone is an interrogative subject, and "dhā" is a relative pronoun meaning "that which," the predicate about "mā," and "you miss" is the relative clause of "dhā," and the returning pronoun is omitted; that is, "you miss it." As-Sulami read (tufqidūna) with a damma on the ta', from afqadtuhu, when you find him missing, like aḥmadtuhu when you find him praised. Abu Hatim criticized this reading, and its explanation is what we have mentioned.

The "ṣuwāʿ" of the king is the measuring vessel, and it is the water-vessel (siqāyah). He named it first by one of its two aspects and last by the second.

Most readers recited (ṣuwāʿa) with a ḍammah on the ṣād, then a fatḥah-marked wāw, then a long ʾalif, then the unpointed ʿayn. Abu Ḥayyah, Al-Ḥasan, and Ibn Jubayr, as transmitted by Ibn ʿAṭiyyah, recited it the same way except with a kasrah on the ṣād. Abu Hurayrah and Mujahid recited (ṣāʿa) without a wāw, on the pattern faʿala, so the ʾalif in it replaces the fatḥah-marked wāw. Abu Rajāʾ recited (ṣawʿa) on the pattern qawsun. ʿAbdullah ibn ʿAwn ibn Abi Arṭabān recited (ṣuwaʿa) with a ḍammah on the ṣād. All of these are dialectal forms for the ṣāʿ (measure).

Al-Ḥasan and Ibn Jubayr, as transmitted from them by the author of al-Lawāmiḥ (a grammatical work), recited (ṣuwāgha) with an unpointed ghayn, on the pattern ghurāb. Yaḥyā ibn Yaʿmar recited it the same way, except that he dropped the ʾalif and made the wāw sukūn. Zayd ibn ʿAli recited (ṣawgha), the verbal noun of ṣāgh (to fashion). Ṣuwāgh and ṣawgh are both derived from al-ṣawgh, the verbal noun of ṣāgha yaṣūgh, and they are used in the sense of maṣūgh (the thing fashioned): the king's fashioned vessel.

**(And for him who brings it)**, i.e., for whoever points to its thief and exposes him. This is a juʿl (a stipulated reward), and the caller's words are the speech of the crier: "And I am surety for it (the camel's load)" — I will pay it to whoever brings it. He meant by it a camel-load of food, as a reward for whoever recovers it.

They said: **"By God!"** They swore using the particle tāʾ, one of the particles of oath, because it generally carries a sense of wonder, as if they were astonished at being accused of this matter. It is related that they returned the merchandise they had found in their food-sacks and were scrupulous about eating the food without payment. They were known in Egypt for their righteousness, and they used to place a muzzle on their camels' mouths so that they would not graze on people's crops. So they swore to affirm something they were known for, namely: "You know that our coming was not for corruption." Then they resumed by denying the attribute of theft from themselves, and that it had never occurred from them at all. It is possible that this falls within the scope of the answer to the oath, so that it is coordinated with their statement "You know," and Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: the tāʾ in (tāllāh) is a substitute for a wāw, as it was substituted in turāth, in al-Tawrāh, and in al-tukhmah. The tāʾ does not enter into oaths except with the names of God that are written [in the Qur'an], and other than that: you do not say tārraḥmān nor tārraḥīm. End of quotation.

As for his statement that the tāʾ in (tāllāh) is a substitute for a wāw, this is the view of most grammarians. Al-Suhayli disagreed with them, claiming that it is an original letter in its own right and not a substitute for a wāw, and this is the correct view according to what we have established in grammar. As for his statement "and in al-Tawrāh," this is according to the school of the Basrans, who claimed that its origin is (wawrāh) from (wara) (the fire-starter), as in the saying "wirā al-zand" (the tinder kindled). Some grammarians claimed that the tāʾ is an extra letter, and this is mentioned in grammar. As for his statement "and it does not enter..." and so on, it has been related from the Arabs that it enters before (al-Rabb) (the Lord), before (al-Raḥmān), and before (ḥayātika): they say "tarabb al-kaʿbah" (by the Lord of the Kaʿbah), "tārraḥmān," and "taḥayyātika."

The address in **"You know"** is to those seeking the measuring vessel. The pronoun in **"its recompense"** refers to the thief. So what is the recompense of the thief, if you are lying in your statement: **"We were not thieves"**? This is said by Ibn ʿAṭiyyah. Al-Zamakhshari said: the pronoun in **"its recompense"** refers to the vessel, i.e., what is the recompense for its theft, if you are lying in your denial and your claim of innocence concerning it. End of quotation.

As for his statement that this is the apparent meaning, because the pronouns are unified in his statement **"They said: its recompense is whoever is found in his baggage,"** since the implied meaning then is: "He said: the recompense of the vessel is that whoever in whose baggage the vessel is found..." Their statement **"its recompense is whoever is found in his baggage"** is the speech of someone who did not doubt that they were innocent of what they had been accused of. Because they believed in their innocence, they tied the ruling to finding the vessel, not to its theft. So it is as if they were saying: "It is impossible for us to steal; it is impossible for the vessel to be found in our baggage." In the religion of Jacob, enslaving the thief was the custom. Al-Zamakhshari said: it was a sunnah. In the religion of Egypt, the thief was to be beaten and the fine doubled upon him. Therefore they answered according to their own law, and they allowed several possibilities in the parsing of this statement:

The first: that **"its recompense"** is the subject, and **"whoever"** is either a conditional or a relative pronoun, a second subject, and **"then he is its recompense"** is the answer to the condition or the predicate of the relative "mā"; and the clause beginning **"whoever was found"** to the end is the predicate of the first subject. The pronoun in **"They said: its recompense"** refers to the thief. This is the statement of Ibn ʿAṭiyyah, but it is not correct, because the clause that serves as the predicate of **"its recompense"** lacks a connecting pronoun.

The second: that the meaning is "They said: the recompense for his theft," and **"its recompense"** is the subject, and the conditional clause, as it is, is its predicate, by placing the apparent noun in the place of the pronoun. The original would be: "its recompense is whoever is found in his baggage, so he is it." So the position of the recompense is the position of "he is it," as when you say to your companion: "Who is Zayd's brother?" and he replies: "His brother is whoever sits beside him." Then "he is it": the first pronoun refers to "whoever," and the second refers to the brother. Then you say "so he is his brother," making the apparent noun stand in place of the pronoun. This is the statement of al-Zamakhshari. Placing the apparent noun in the position of the pronoun for linking is eloquent only in contexts of exaltation and awe, and it is not eloquent elsewhere, as in "Zayd stood, Zayd." Sibawayh said: if you say "Zayd was going, Zayd," it would not be the opposite of speech, but it would be weak here; and it would not be like your saying "Zayd is not going, he," because you have dispensed with its explicit mention, and you ought rather to use the pronoun.

The third: that **"its recompense"** is the predicate of an elided subject, meaning: "what is asked about is its recompense." Then they gave their ruling by saying: **"whoever is found in his baggage, then he is its recompense,"** as when you say: "Whoever asks for a fatwa about the recompense for hunting in the sacred precinct, [the answer is] the recompense for hunting in the sacred precinct," and then you say: **"And whoever of you kills it intentionally, its recompense is the like of what he killed from the livestock"** [al-Mā'idah 5:95]. This is the statement of al-Zamakhshari, but it is contrived, since the clause in his statement "what is asked about is its recompense," under this assumption, has little benefit. It is already known from **"then what is its recompense?"** that the thing asked about is the recompense for its theft, so what is the point of their saying it? The same applies to the example given of the questioner's statement.

The fourth: that **"its recompense"** is the subject, meaning: the recompense for the theft of the vessel; and the predicate is **"whoever is found in his baggage,"** meaning: whoever in whose baggage it is found is taken [as the recompense]. Their statement **"then he is its recompense"** is an affirmation of a ruling, meaning: the taking of the thief himself is the recompense, and nothing else, like your saying: "Zayd's right is that he be clothed, fed, and shown favor, so that is his recompense," or "so it is his due," to confirm what I have mentioned of his entitlement. This is the statement of al-Zamakhshari. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said the same thing but made the one statement into two, saying: it is also valid for **"whoever"** to be the predicate, in the sense that "the recompense of the thief is whoever is found in his baggage," with a returning pronoun referring to "whoever," and **"then he is its recompense"** serves as an added clarification and emphasis. Then he said: it is also possible that the implied meaning is "its recompense is the enslaving of whoever is found in his baggage," and then it is emphasized by the words **"then he is its recompense."** This statement is the same as the one before it, except that it brings out the omitted genitive in the phrase "the enslaving of whoever is found in his baggage," whereas in the earlier statement the omitted element must be supplied, because the essence cannot be the predicate of a verbal noun. So the implied meaning in the earlier statement is: "its recompense is the taking of whoever is found in his baggage, or the enslaving of this is necessary," according to this parsing. This final option is the best of the possibilities and the furthest from strained construction.

**(Thus)**, i.e., like this recompense, which is enslavement, **"We recompense the wrongdoers,"** i.e., for theft. This is our religion and our custom regarding the people of theft.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 12, verses 76–77:**

﴿So he began with their bags before the bag of his brother, then he brought it out from his brother's bag. Thus did We plan for Joseph. He could not have taken his brother under the king's law, unless God willed it. We raise in degrees whom We will, and above every possessor of knowledge is One who is All-Knowing.﴾ ﴿They said: "If he steals, a brother of his has stolen before." But Joseph kept it hidden within himself and did not reveal it to them. He said: "You are worse in position, and God knows best what you describe."﴾

[p. 332] It is said: the one appointed over them said to them: "There must be a search of your bags." So he took them to Joseph, and he began searching their bags before the bag of Benjamin, to remove suspicion and to establish the stratagem, and to let it remain hidden until he reached his bag. He said: "I do not think this one took anything." They said: "By God, you will not leave him until you look in his baggage, for that is better for your soul and ours." So they brought it out from it.

Al-Hasan recited: (min wu'ā'i) with a *ḍamma* on the *wāw*, and this is also transmitted from Nafi'. Ibn Jubayr recited: (min i'ā'i), replacing the kasra-marked *wāw* with a *hamza*, as they said: *ishāḥ* and *isāda* for *wishāḥ* and *wisāda*. This is regular in the dialect of Hudhayl, who replace an initial kasra-marked *wāw* with a *hamza*. The feminine pronoun in His words (thumma istakhrajahā, "then he brought it out") is in view of the *siqāya* (the drinking vessel), or because the *ṣuwā'* (the cup) may be masculine or feminine. Abu 'Ubayd said: the *ṣuwā'* is feminine insofar as it is called *siqāya*, and masculine insofar as it is a *ṣā'*. It seems that Abu 'Ubayd did not memorize the feminine form of *ṣuwā'*. It is also said that the pronoun in His words (thumma istakhrajahā) refers to the theft. (Kadhālika), that is: like that great scheme, (kidnā li-Yūsuf), meaning: We taught it to him and inspired it in him. Al-Daḥḥāk and al-Suddī said: (kidnā) means "We devised." Ibn 'Aṭiyya said: God attributed the scheme to Himself when He brought out the portion that He permitted Joseph to take his brother by, a manner that is, in people's custom, a scheme. Ibn 'Abbās explained (fī dīn al-malik) as "in his authority," and Qatada explained it as "by judgment and ruling." End.

Al-Zamakhshari said: (mā kāna li-ya'khudha akhāhu fī dīn al-malik) is an explanation of the scheme and a clarification of it, because it was under the law of the king of Egypt, and what he would judge concerning a thief was that he pay double what he took, unless he be held and enslaved. (illā an yasha'a Allāh) except by His will and permission. Ibn 'Aṭiyya said: the exception is a narrative of the state of the estimation: "except that God wills what occurred of this stratagem." End. What appears is that it is a *istithnā' munqaṭi'* (disjunctive exception), meaning: "But by the will of God he took him under a law other than the king's," which is the law of the family of Jacob, namely that enslavement is the penalty for the thief.

The Kufans and Ibn Muḥaysin recited (narfa'u) with a *nūn* and (darajātin) with tanwin, and (man nashā'u) with a *nūn*. The rest of the Seven did likewise, except that they gave (darajāt) an annexed form. Ya'qub recited with *yā'* in (yarfa'u and yashā'u), meaning: God raises in degrees whom He wills, raising their degrees. He said: "The One who put the merchandise in your baggage."

Al-Zamakhshari said, in substance: they were accused of theft by way of allusion to what had happened, which had the character of theft, namely their action toward Joseph. (wa-in kuntum kādhibīn) is a supposition for the negation of their innocence, and supposing a lie is not itself a lie. God knew in this stratagem that He taught Joseph great benefits, and He made it a means and a path to them, so it became good and beautiful. End.

Al-Zamakhshari said: he means the saying or the speech. End.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 12, verses 76–77:**

﴿So he began with their bags before the bag of his brother, then he brought it out from his brother's bag. Thus did We plan for Joseph. He could not have taken his brother under the king's law, unless God willed it. We raise in degrees whom We will, and above every possessor of knowledge is One who is All-Knowing.﴾ ﴿They said: "If he steals, a brother of his has stolen before." But Joseph kept it hidden within himself and did not reveal it to them. He said: "You are worse in position, and God knows best what you describe."﴾

[p. 332] It is said: the one appointed over them said to them: "There must be a search of your bags." So he took them to Joseph, and he began searching their bags before the bag of Benjamin, to remove suspicion and to establish the stratagem, and to let it remain hidden until he reached his bag. He said: "I do not think this one took anything." They said: "By God, you will not leave him until you look in his baggage, for that is better for your soul and ours." So they brought it out from it.

Al-Hasan recited: (min wu'ā'i) with a *ḍamma* on the *wāw*, and this is also transmitted from Nafi'. This is regular in the dialect of Hudhayl, who replace an initial kasra-marked *wāw* with a *hamza*. The feminine pronoun in His words (thumma istakhrajahā, "then he brought it out") is in view of the *siqāya* (the drinking vessel), or because the *ṣuwā'* (the cup) may be masculine or feminine. Abu 'Ubayd said: the *ṣuwā'* is feminine insofar as it is called *siqāya*, and masculine insofar as it is a *ṣā'*. It seems that Abu 'Ubayd did not memorize the feminine form of *ṣuwā'*. It is also said that the pronoun in His words (thumma istakhrajahā) refers to the theft. (Kadhālika), that is: like that great scheme, (kidnā li-Yūsuf), meaning: We taught it to him and inspired it in him. Al-Daḥḥāk and al-Suddī said: (kidnā) means "We devised." He said, "God forbid that we should take anyone except him with whom we found our property. Indeed, we would then be wrongdoers."

They sought Joseph's compassion (istim'attafa), since the covenant had been taken from them (ukhidha 'alayhimu al-mithaq). The meaning of "kabiran" (great/elderly) is in age or in rank (al-qadr). It is also possible that their statement is literal, but it is far-fetched that they, being prophets, would want to enslave a free man. (p. 335) *Istaf'ala* (اسْتَفْعَلَ) here carries the meaning of the basic form (*mujarrad*), so *yaisa* (يَئِسَ) and *istay'asa* (اسْتَيْأسَ) have the same meaning, as in *sakhira* and *istaskhara*, or *'ajiba* and *ista'jaba*. Al-Zamakhshari claimed that the addition of the *sin* and the *ta'* serves to intensify the meaning, as he said of *ista'sama* (اسْتَعْصَمَ) earlier. End of quote.

Ibn Kathir read *istay'asu* (اسْتَيْأسُوا) as *istaf'alu*, from *ayisa* (أيِسَ) by metathesis (*maqlub*) of *yaisa* (يَئِسَ). The evidence for metathesis is that the *ya'* of *ayisa* has not become an *alif*, although it is vowelled and preceded by an open letter. The meaning of *khalasu najiyyan* (خَلَصُوا نَجِيًّا) is that they withdrew from others, so that they consulted one another privately. *Najiyy* is a *fa'il* form in the sense of *mufa'il*, like *khalit* and *'ashir*. The verbal noun *al-tanajji* (التَّناجِي) is expressed by *al-najwa* (النَّجْوى), a word used to describe one person or a group, singular or plural, masculine or feminine; it is like *'adl*. Its plural is *anjiya* (أنْجِيَةٍ). Labid said:

*And I attended the nijya of al-Afaqa, my ankle held high, and the retinues of kings were witnesses.*

Another poet said:

*Indeed, when the people are a nijya...*

People also say *qawmun najiyyun* (قَوْمٌ نَجِيٌّ) and *hum najwa* (هم نَجْوى), treating the verbal noun as an adjective. It is also permissible for *hum najiyy* to follow the pattern of *hum sadiq*, since it has the form of verbal nouns and is restricted to consultation. They looked at what they should say to their father concerning their brother, because of the calamity that had befallen them in this matter, so they needed to consult.

*Kabiruhum* (كَبِيرُهم) means greatest in opinion, planning and knowledge. It is said that this was Shim'un, according to Mujahid; or that he was the eldest in age, Ruben, according to Qatadah; or that it refers to intellect and judgment, and this was Yahudha. He reminded them of the covenant in Ya'qub's words: *You shall surely bring him back to me unless you are surrounded* (Yusuf 66). The *ma* (ما) in *ma farratum* is superfluous, meaning: (p. 336) *and before this you neglected Yusuf*. The phrase *min qablu* (مِن قَبْلُ) is connected to *farratum* (فَرَّطْتُمْ). They permitted several readings of its i'rab (grammatical analysis):

First: *ma* is a verbal-noun particle (*masdariyya*), meaning *and before, your neglect*. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya also permitted *ma* to be verbal (*masdariyya*), with the verbal noun in the accusative position. Al-Dahhak read *sariq* as an active participle.

On the reading *suriqa* and *sariq*, the interpretation of *illa bima 'alimna* differs. Al-Zamakhshari said: *what we know of his theft, which we are certain of, because the cup was taken out of its container, and nothing is clearer than this.* Ibn 'Atiyya said: our statement to you that your son stole is only a testimony before you of what we have known from the apparent course of events; knowledge of the unseen belongs to God, and it is not within our keeping. This is the view of Ibn Ishaq. Ibn Zayd said: they meant, *and we only testified to what we knew, that the thief is enslaved in your law*, and *we did not guard the unseen, that theft would come out of the baggage of one of us; rather we thought that this could never happen. So when he asked us we testified by our knowledge.* It is also possible that *wa ma kunna lil-ghaybi hafizin* means: at the time we made a covenant with you, we intended only that nothing from us should come to him that he would dislike, and we did not know the unseen, that he would come with what makes him enslaved. Al-Zamakhshari said: *we did not know the unseen*, that he would be enslaved when we gave you the covenant, or perhaps we knew that you would be afflicted as you were afflicted with Yusuf. It is a strange interpretation that *lil-ghayb* means *lil-layl* (for the night), since *al-ghayb* in the language of Himyar means night. As if they said: *we testified only to what we knew of the apparent situation, and we did not guard by night what happened of his theft, or the deception practised upon him.* In the speech there is an elision, its estimate being: *they returned to their father and he was told the story.* And the words of one who said: *return*, then they called upon the people of the town in which they were, which was Egypt, said by Ibn 'Abbas, meaning: *send to the town and ask about the essence of the story*. The *'ir* (caravan) were a people from Kan'an, from the neighbourhood of Ya'qub; it is said they were from San'a. The apparent view is that this is an elision of *ahl* (people), as if it were said: *and ask the people of the town and the people of the caravan*, unless by *'ir* is meant the company itself, in which case there is no elision in *wal-'ir*. They referred the clarification of the story to people present at the scene, who would testify to what they heard, and to absent people who would be sent to and asked. Another group said that they referred him to asking the inanimate things and animals literally, since he was a prophet, and it is not unlikely that they would tell him the truth. The elision of the modifier is the view of the majority. Ibn 'Atiyya said: *this is metaphor (majaz)*. Abu al-Ma'ali related from some theologians that he said: *this is elision, not metaphor.* He said: *metaphor is a word borrowed for something other than what it is for, and the elision of the modifier is the very essence of metaphor.* He considered this the view of Sibawayh and others, and related that it is the view of the majority or something close to it. End of quote.

Al-Zamakhshari claimed that the addition of the *sin* and the *ta'* serves to intensify the meaning, as he said of *ista'sama* (اسْتَعْصَمَ) earlier. End of quote.

The evidence for metathesis is that the *ya'* of *ayisa* has not become an *alif*, although it is vowelled and preceded by an open letter. The verbal noun *al-tanajji* (التَّناجِي) is expressed by *al-najwa* (النَّجْوى), a word used to describe one person or a group, singular or plural, masculine or feminine; it is like *'adl*. Its plural is *anjiya* (أنْجِيَةٍ). Labid said:

*And I attended the nijya of al-Afaqa, my ankle held high, and the retinues of kings were witnesses.*

Another poet said:

*Indeed, when the people are a nijya...*

People also say *qawmun najiyyun* (قَوْمٌ نَجِيٌّ) and *hum najwa* (هم نَجْوى), treating the verbal noun as an adjective. They looked at what they should say to their father concerning their brother, because of the calamity that had befallen them in this matter, so they needed to consult.

And he turned away from them and said, "Alas for Joseph!" and his eyes turned white from grief, for he was suppressing it. ﴿And he turned away from them and said, "Alas for Joseph!" and his eyes turned white from the sorrow, and he was filled with suppressed grief.﴾

[Verse 84 is quoted above as it stands in the Qur'an.]

﴿They said, "By God, you will not cease remembering Joseph until you become afflicted or become among the perished."﴾

﴿He said, "I only complain of my anguish and my grief to God, and I know from God what you do not know."﴾

﴿"O my sons, go and search for Joseph and his brother, and do not despair of the mercy of God. Indeed, none despairs of the mercy of God except the disbelieving people."﴾

And "he turned away from them" means he turned away from them out of dislike for what they had brought, and his opinion of them became bad, and he did not believe their words. He began to lament and grieve. Al-Hasan said: "This Ummah was singled out for the istirja' (the saying "Indeed we belong to God and to Him we return"). Do you not see the saying of Ya'qub: ﴿Alas for Joseph!﴾?" He called out to grief (asaf) figuratively, meaning: "This is your time, so be present." Apparently it is attached to the first-person pronoun ya' (my), which was converted into an alif, as they say: "Ya ghulami" becomes "ya ghulaman." It was also said that it is an invocation of lament (nudba), and the ha' of pause (ha' al-sakt) was omitted.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "The paronomasia (tajnis) between the two words 'asafa' and 'Yusufa' is of the kind that occurs naturally and is not contrived, so it is elegant and original. Similar to it is: ﴿Did you cling heavily to the earth? Are you pleased with the life of this world?﴾ [al-Tawba: 38], ﴿They forbid it and keep away from it﴾ [al-An'am: 26], and ﴿They think they are doing good work﴾ [al-Kahf: 104], and (from Saba' with a news [nabaʾ]) the end." This is called tajnis al-tasrif (morphological paronomasia), which is that each of the two words is distinguished from the other by one letter.

Ya'qub mentioned what had befallen him regarding Binyamin and the one who said ﴿I will not leave this land﴾ [Yusuf: 80], and the loss of Joseph. He grieved over him alone and did not grieve over the two of them, because he was the one about whom he did not know whether he was alive or dead, unlike his brothers. Also because he was the origin of the calamities for him, since they were consequences of him, and he was the dearest of his sons to him, and he always remembered him and did not forget him. The whitening of his eyes resulted from the continual flow of tears, so the blackness of the eye turns into a dull whiteness. Apparently he had gone blind, due to the saying: ﴿So his sight returned﴾ [Yusuf: 96], and His saying: ﴿The blind and the seeing are not equal﴾ [Fatir: 19], where He set the seeing against the blind. It was also said that he perceived with weak perception. He attributed the whitening to grief, but it actually came from the continuous weeping, which is the fruit of grief, so he attributed it to the root from which the weeping arose, which is grief.

Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid read (min al-hazan) with a fatha on the ha' and the za', Qatada read it with a damma, and the majority read it with a damma on the ha' and sukun on the za'. The word kazim is either intensive, and this is the apparent meaning which suits Ya'qub's condition, meaning one who greatly suppresses, as He said: ﴿Those who restrain anger﴾ [Al 'Imran: 134]. Ya'qub did not complain to anyone; rather he kept it hidden within himself and held his concern in his chest, so he suppressed it (yakzimuhu), that is, he returned it to his heart and did not release it in complaint, anger, or distress. Or it may be fa'il in the sense of maf'ul (passive), though this is not a regular pattern, and some people said this, as He said regarding Yunus: ﴿when he called out while he was suppressed﴾ [al-Qalam: 48]. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "It only fits if one assumes he was filled with his grief, so it is as if he suppressed his grief in his chest." Some interpreted kazim as "distressed" and "smoldering." It is narrated that his eyes did not dry from separation from Joseph until reunion with him, eighty years, and that his grief over him was the grief of seventy bereaved mothers, and his reward was the reward of one hundred martyrs. Fī al-kalām ḥadhf (there is an ellipsis in the speech); its implied sense: they went from Syria to Egypt and entered it, ﴿فَلَمَّا دَخَلُوا عَلَيْهِ﴾. The pronoun in ﴿عَلَيْهِ﴾ refers to Yusuf. The most emphatic thing they told him was their complaint about the distress that had befallen them, before he had instructed them to search for news of Yusuf and his brother. *Al-ḍurr* (hardship) means emaciation resulting from severe hardship and hunger. The merchandise was counterfeit coins, according to Ibn ʿAbbas. Al-Ḥasan said it was scanty. Ibn Jubayr said it was deficient. It was also said it was goods (ʿurūḍ). It was said it was wool and butter. It was said it was terebinth (ṣanawbar), the seed of the ḥabbat al-khaḍrāʾ, which is the pistachio, as reported by Abu Salih and Zayd ibn Aslam. It was said it was sawīq (parched flour) of the doum palm and aqiṭ (dried curd). It was said it was dried game meat. It was said it was ropes, pack saddles, and sacks. Then they asked him to fulfil the measure. This verse has been cited as evidence that the duty of measuring falls upon the seller, but there is no proof in it.

﴿وَتَصَدَّقْ عَلَيْنَا﴾ means: by overlooking and disregarding the poor quality of the merchandise, or give us more than our due. They called what is surplus and extra, which is not obligatory, "charity." It was said: this is because charities are forbidden to the prophets, peace be upon them. It was said: it was permissible for other than our Prophet. Ibn ʿUyayna was asked about this and said: Did you not hear ﴿وَتَصَدَّقْ عَلَيْنَا﴾? He meant that it was lawful for them.

Al-Zamakhshari said: The apparent meaning is that they humbled themselves before him and asked him to be charitable to them, and hence he was moved and mercy overcame him, so he could not restrain himself from making himself known to them. His saying ﴿إِنَّ اللَّهَ يَجْزِي الْمُتَصَدِّقِينَ﴾ is evidence of this, for it mentions God and His reward. End of quotation.

It was also said: charity was forbidden, but they said it figuratively, seeking his sympathy in the transaction, just as you say to one with whom you are bargaining over a commodity: "Give me a discount of such-and-such from its price." You do not intend that he should give it to you outright; rather, the words are used so that he may return from his offer to your bargain. Ibn Jurayj said: They specified in their saying ﴿وَتَصَدَّقْ عَلَيْنَا﴾ the matter of their brother Binyamin; that is, "Give us full measure in the transaction, and be charitable to us by returning our brother to his father."

Al-Naqqash said regarding His saying ﴿إِنَّ اللَّهَ يَجْزِي الْمُتَصَدِّقِينَ﴾: it is one of the allusions (maʿārīḍ), which are a substitute for lying. They believed him to be a king who was a disbeliever, not of their religion. Had they said, "God will reward you for your charity in the Hereafter," they would have been disbelieved. So they spoke to him in words that suggest they meant what he might think, while they could justify excluding it by interpretation. It is related that when they said to him ﴿مَسَّنَا وَأَهْلَنَا الضُّرُّ﴾ and implored his pity, he was moved and had mercy on them. Ibn Ishaq said: His tears flowed as he wept, and he began to reveal his identity to them. It is reported that he uncovered his face and said to them: ﴿هَلْ عَلِمْتُمْ مَا فَعَلْتُمْ بِيُوسُفَ وَأَخِيهِ﴾, that is, of separating the two of them in childhood, and of harming Binyamin after Yusuf's disappearance; and they used to humiliate him and revile him.

Ibn ʿAtiyya said: He attributed to them either the ignorance of disobedience, or the ignorance of evil deeds and lack of prudence.

Al-Zamakhshari said: He approached them from the standpoint of religion. He was forbearing and divinely guided, so he addressed them in the form of a question seeking knowledge of the aspect of ugliness that a repentant person must take into account. He said: Do you know the ugliness of what you did to Yusuf and his brother when you were ignorant, not knowing its ugliness, and therefore you proceeded to it? That is, do you know its ugliness so that you repent to God for it? For knowledge of ugliness calls for disapproval, and disapproval leads to repentance. His speech was therefore an expression of compassion for them and sincere counsel to them in religion, and a preference for God's right over his own right in that situation, in which the distressed person finds relief, the aggrieved vents his anguish, the enraged one is satisfied, and the one who has been wronged obtains his vengeance. How noble are the morals of the prophets, how generous and tolerant they are, and how firm and weighty are their minds. End of quotation.

It was also said: He did not intend to deny them knowledge, for they were learned men. But when they did what knowledge does not permit, and what only an ignorant person would proceed to, he called them ignorant. In al-Taḥrīr, what is summarized is as follows: the statement of the majority, "Do you know?", is a question whose meaning is rebuke and reproach, and whose purpose is to magnify the event; that is, how great is what you committed against Yusuf, just as one says, "Do you know whom you have disobeyed?" It was also said: "Hal" here means "qad" (indeed), because they were aware. And ﴿فَعَلْتُمْ بِيُوسُفَ﴾ refers to their separating him from his father, their claim that a wolf had eaten him, their casting him into the well, and selling him for a paltry price, if they were the ones who sold him; and their saying ﴿إِنْ يَسْرِقْ فَقَدْ سَرَقَ أَخٌ لَهُ مِنْ قَبْلُ﴾ ["If he steals, a brother of his stole before"]. As for what they did to his brother, it was their harm to him and their harshness toward him, accusing him of stealing the cup and declaring that he had stolen. He did not mention what they had done when he confronted their father, out of respect for their father's rank and in glorification of his station, by not mentioning it together with himself and his brother.

Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Ḥasan said: ﴿جَاهِلُونَ﴾ means children. Muqatil said: sinners. It was said: ignorant of what is required of dutiful treatment of a father, maintaining family ties, and abandoning desire. It was said: ignorant of what the matter of Yusuf would come to. It was said: ignorant of reflection on the outcome and of not considering the public interest.

The exegetes said: Yusuf's purpose was to rebuke his brothers and reprove them for what they had done against their father and against their two brothers. He said: The correct view is that he said this to put their hearts at ease and to offer an excuse, as if he were saying: "I only put you forward to that ugly act out of the ignorance of youth or deception." It is as if he were teaching them the argument, as in His saying ﴿مَا غَرَّكَ بِرَبِّكَ الْكَرِيمِ﴾ ["What has deceived you concerning your Generous Lord?"] [al-Infitar: 6].

As for what Ibn al-Haytham related in a story, that he crucified them, and what al-Tha'labi related, that he became angry with them and ordered their execution, whereupon they wept and lamented, and he felt pity for them and said ﴿هَلْ عَلِمْتُمْ﴾, the verse—none of this is sound at all. Yusuf was among the most tender of God's creatures and the most compassionate of them toward strangers; how then with his brothers? When they acknowledged their error, he said: ﴿لَا تَثْرِيبَ عَلَيْكُمُ﴾ ["No reproach upon you today"] [Yusuf: 92], and so on.
