Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 12, verse 90–93:

﴿They said, "Are you indeed Joseph?" He said, "I am Joseph, and this is my brother. Allah has certainly shown favor to us. Indeed, whoever fears Allah and is patient – then indeed, Allah does not allow the reward of the doers of good to be lost."﴾ ﴿They said, "By Allah, Allah has certainly preferred you over us, and we were indeed sinners."﴾ ﴿He said, "No reproach will there be upon you today. May Allah forgive you, and He is the Most Merciful of the merciful."﴾ ﴿Take this shirt of mine and cast it over the face of my father; he will regain his sight. And bring me your family, all of them.﴾

(p-342) When he addressed them with his saying: ﴿Do you know...?﴾ [Yusuf: 89], they realized that he was not a king who would ask such a question, one who had not grown up among them and had not followed their affairs, and there was none among them, as is apparent, who did not have knowledge of his circumstances. It is said that he was speaking to them from behind a screen. He then raised the veil, placed the crown down, and smiled, and the light of his smile illuminated what was around him. Or they saw a white gleam like a mole (shamah) on his forehead (faraq) when he set down the crown, and such a mark was on his father, his grandfather, and Sarah. So they surmised that he was Yusuf, and they questioned him with the question of inquiry (istikhbar). It is also said that it was the interrogative of confirmation (taqrir), because they had recognized him by those signs previously mentioned.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, "How did they recognize him?" I answer: they saw in his complexion and his features, when he spoke to them in that manner, something that made them feel that he was he, together with their knowledge that what he addressed them with could only come from an upright Muslim (hanif muslim) of the lineage of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, and not from some of the notables of Egypt. The majority of readers recited (ā’innaka) as an interrogative. The difference concerning the realization of the two hamzas, or the softening of the second and the insertion of an alif in softening or realization, is mentioned in the seven readings. Qatada, Ibn Muhaysin and Ibn Kathir recited (innaka) without the interrogative hamza, and the apparent meaning is that the interrogative is intended. To take it as a plain statement is unlikely, though some have said so, because of the conflict between interrogative and declarative if the speakers are one in the utterance, which is the apparent case. If it is assumed that some asked and some stated, and in each of the two readings the saying of some is attributed to the whole group, it is possible, but it is still distant. Ubayy recited (ā’innaka) or (anta Yusuf). Ibn Jinni took it as an ellipsis of the predicate of "inna" and estimated it as: ﴿ā’innaka la-anta Yusuf﴾, or "anta Yusuf." Al-Zamakhshari estimated it as: "ā’innaka Yusuf," or "anta Yusuf," deleting the first because the second indicates it, and he said: this is a wondering, astonished speech at what is heard, so he repeats the seeking of confirmation, end of quote. Abu 'Amr al-Dani reported in the reading of Ubayy ibn Ka'b: "qalu: (a-wa anta Yusuf)?" In the reading of the majority, ﴿ā’innaka la-anta﴾, it is permissible that the lam entered upon "anta" and it is a separator (fasl), and the predicate of "inna" is "Yusuf," as you say: "in kana Zayd la-huwa al-fadil." It is also permissible that it entered upon "anta," which is a subject (mubtada'), with "Yusuf" as its predicate, and the clause stands in the position of the predicate of "inna," and "anta" cannot be a corroborative (tawkid) of the pronoun which is the subject of "inna," because the lam intervenes between them.

When they questioned him, he answered them: ﴿I am Joseph﴾, revealing his matter to them, and he added in his answer his saying: ﴿and this is my brother﴾, because his saying ﴿Do you know what you did to Joseph and his brother?﴾ [Yusuf: 89] had preceded, and mention of his brother was an explanation of what they asked about, even though it was known to them, and a preparation for what is mentioned after (man), namely piety and patience. The best view is that piety is not restricted to one state, nor patience.

Mujahid said: "whoever is pious" in abstaining from disobedience, and "is patient" in prison.

Al-Nakha'i said: "whoever is pious" regarding fornication, and "is patient" in celibacy. It is also said: whoever fears Allah and is patient through calamities.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿man yattaqi﴾ means whoever fears Allah and His punishment and is patient in refraining from sins and in obeying Him. It is also said: whoever guards against Allah's disobediences and is patient under the harm of people. All these are particularizations according to the state of Joseph and his circumstances.

Qunbul read (man yattaqi). It is said that it is jussive by deleting the yā’ which is the final radical, and this yā’ is a prolongation (ishba'). It is also said that he made it jussive by deleting the vowel, according to the dialect of those who say "lam yarmi Zayd," and they have reported this as a dialect. It is also said that it is nominative, and "man" is a relative pronoun in the sense of "alladhi," and the jussive "wa yasbir" is conjoined to it, by way of mental association (tawahhum), as if he imagined that "man" was conditional and "yattaqi" jussive. It is also said that "wa yasbir" is nominative, conjoined to a nominative, and the ra' was made quiescent not for jussiveness but to avoid successive vowels, even though that is across two words, as it was made quiescent in "ya'murkum wa yush'irkum wa bu'ulatuhunna"; or it is quiescent for pausal reasons, and the connection is treated as pause. The best of these views is that "yattaqi" is jussive according to a dialect, though it is rare, and it does not revert to the saying of Abu 'Ali, who said: "this is of what should not be applied to, because it only occurs in poetry and not in speech," because other leading grammarians have transmitted that it is a dialect.

"Al-muhsinin" is general, encompassing those previously mentioned, or it was placed in the position of the pronoun because it includes the pious and the patient, as if it were said: "He does not waste their reward."

"Ather-aka" means He preferred you with kingship, or with patience and knowledge, as said by Ibn 'Abbas; or with forbearance and pardon, mentioned by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi; or with beauty of form, character, knowledge, forbearance, goodness, kingship and authority, and your patience with our harm, as said by the author of al-Ghuniyan; or with piety, patience and the conduct of the good-doers, as said by al-Zamakhshari, and it is suitable to His saying: ﴿Indeed, whoever fears Allah...﴾ the verse. Their addressing him with this is a solicitation of his goodness and an acknowledgment of what proceeded from them toward him. "Khati'in" is from "khati'a" when one does it intentionally; as for "akhta'a," it is aiming at the right but not being guided to it. "La tathrib" means no reproach and no punishment. "Tathrib" is the subject of "la," "alaykum" is the predicate, and "al-yawm" is in the accusative governed by the element operating in the predicate; that is: no reproach is established upon you today. Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, "To what is 'al-yawm' connected?" I answer: to "tathrib," or to what is implied in "alaykum" of the sense of establishment, or to "yaghfiru." The meaning is: I do not blame you today, and this is the day that is the place of blame, so what do you think about other days? Then he began: ﴿Allah forgives you﴾, having given them confidence in the forgiveness of what had passed from them. It is said "Ghafara Allahu laka" and "yaghfiru Allahu laka" in both past and present forms, and from it is the saying of one who blesses a sneezer: "may Allah guide you and set right your affairs." Or "al-yawm yaghfiru Allahu lakum" is glad tidings of prompt forgiveness, because of their repentance and regret over their wrongdoing that renewed that day, end of quote.

As for his saying that "al-yawm" is connected to "tathrib," this is not permissible, because "tathrib" is a verbal noun, and its complement has been separated from it by "alaykum," which is either the predicate or an adjective of "tathrib," and separating them is not permitted, since the complement of a verbal noun is part of it. Also, if "al-yawm" were connected to "tathrib," it would not be permissible for it to be indeclinable; it would be of the type of the nominal resembling the genitive construction, which is called the lengthened (mutawwal) or stretched (mamtul), and would be declinable and nunated.

As for his second estimation, it is a good estimation, and for that reason most readers stopped at his saying "al-yawm," and began with "Allah forgives you" as a supplication; this is the interpretation of Ibn Ishaq and al-Tabari.

As for his third estimation, that "al-yawm" is connected to "yaghfiru," it is acceptable, and some readers stopped at "alaykum" and began "al-yawm yaghfiru Allahu lakum." Ibn 'Atiyya said: stopping at "al-yawm" is preferable in meaning, because the other reading contains a judgment about Allah's forgiveness, unless that is by revelation. As for his saying "it is glad tidings," etc., this follows the way of the Mu'tazila, for forgiveness occurs only for one who repents. Ibn al-Anbari said: he pointed to that day only because it is the first of the times of pardon, and the way of one who pardons in such a case is not to revert to punishment. Or they saw a white gleam like a mole (shamah) on his forehead (faraq) when he set down the crown, and such a mark was on his father, his grandfather, and Sarah. So they surmised that he was Yusuf, and they questioned him with the question of inquiry (istikhbar). It is also said that it was the interrogative of confirmation (taqrir), because they had recognized him by those signs previously mentioned.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, "How did they recognize him?" When they questioned him, he answered them: ﴿I am Joseph﴾, revealing his matter to them, and he added in his answer his saying: ﴿and this is my brother﴾, because his saying ﴿Do you know what you did to Joseph and his brother?﴾ [Yusuf: 89] had preceded, and mention of his brother was an explanation of what they asked about, even though it was known to them, and a preparation for what is mentioned after (man), namely piety and patience. The best view is that piety is not restricted to one state, nor patience.

Mujahid said: "whoever is pious" in abstaining from disobedience, and "is patient" in prison.

Al-Nakha'i said: "whoever is pious" regarding fornication, and "is patient" in celibacy. It is also said: whoever fears Allah and is patient through calamities.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿man yattaqi﴾ means whoever fears Allah and His punishment and is patient in refraining from sins and in obeying Him. It is also said: whoever guards against Allah's disobediences and is patient under the harm of people. All these are particularizations according to the state of Joseph and his circumstances.

It is also said that he made it jussive by deleting the vowel, according to the dialect of those who say "lam yarmi Zayd," and they have reported this as a dialect. It is also said that it is nominative, and "man" is a relative pronoun in the sense of "alladhi," and the jussive "wa yasbir" is conjoined to it, by way of mental association (tawahhum), as if he imagined that "man" was conditional and "yattaqi" jussive. "Al-muhsinin" is general, encompassing those previously mentioned, or it was placed in the position of the pronoun because it includes the pious and the patient, as if it were said: "He does not waste their reward."

"Ather-aka" means He preferred you with kingship, or with patience and knowledge, as said by Ibn 'Abbas; or with forbearance and pardon, mentioned by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi; or with beauty of form, character, knowledge, forbearance, goodness, kingship and authority, and your patience with our harm, as said by the author of al-Ghuniyan; or with piety, patience and the conduct of the good-doers, as said by al-Zamakhshari, and it is suitable to His saying: ﴿Indeed, whoever fears Allah...﴾ the verse. (p-342) When he addressed them with his saying: ﴿Do you know...?﴾ [Yusuf: 89], they realized that he was not a king who would ask such a question, one who had not grown up among them and had not followed their affairs, and there was none among them, as is apparent, who did not have knowledge of his circumstances. It is said that he was speaking to them from behind a screen. He then raised the veil, placed the crown down, and smiled, and the light of his smile illuminated what was around him. Or they saw a white gleam like a mole (shamah) on his forehead (faraq) when he set down the crown, and such a mark was on his father, his grandfather, and Sarah. So they surmised that he was Yusuf, and they questioned him with the question of inquiry (istikhbar). It is also said that it was the interrogative of confirmation (taqrir), because they had recognized him by those signs previously mentioned.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, "How did they recognize him?" I answer: they saw in his complexion and his features, when he spoke to them in that manner, something that made them feel that he was he, together with their knowledge that what he addressed them with could only come from an upright Muslim (hanif muslim) of the lineage of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, and not from some of the notables of Egypt. The majority of readers recited (ā’innaka) as an interrogative. The difference concerning the realization of the two hamzas, or the softening of the second and the insertion of an alif in softening or realization, is mentioned in the seven readings. Qatada, Ibn Muhaysin and Ibn Kathir recited (innaka) without the interrogative hamza, and the apparent meaning is that the interrogative is intended. To take it as a plain statement is unlikely, though some have said so, because of the conflict between interrogative and declarative if the speakers are one in the utterance, which is the apparent case. If it is assumed that some asked and some stated, and in each of the two readings the saying of some is attributed to the whole group, it is possible, but it is still distant. Ubayy recited (ā’innaka) or (anta Yusuf). Ibn Jinni took it as an ellipsis of the predicate of "inna" and estimated it as: ﴿ā’innaka la-anta Yusuf﴾, or "anta Yusuf." Al-Zamakhshari estimated it as: "ā’innaka Yusuf," or "anta Yusuf," deleting the first because the second indicates it, and he said: this is a wondering, astonished speech at what is heard, so he repeats the seeking of confirmation, end of quote. Abu 'Amr al-Dani reported in the reading of Ubayy ibn Ka'b: "qalu: (a-wa anta Yusuf)?" In the reading of the majority, ﴿ā’innaka la-anta﴾, it is permissible that the lam entered upon "anta" and it is a separator (fasl), and the predicate of "inna" is "Yusuf," as you say: "in kana Zayd la-huwa al-fadil." It is also permissible that it entered upon "anta," which is a subject (mubtada'), with "Yusuf" as its predicate, and the clause stands in the position of the predicate of "inna," and "anta" cannot be a corroborative (tawkid) of the pronoun which is the subject of "inna," because the lam intervenes between them.

When they questioned him, he answered them: ﴿I am Joseph﴾, revealing his matter to them, and he added in his answer his saying: ﴿and this is my brother﴾, because his saying ﴿Do you know what you did to Joseph and his brother?﴾ [Yusuf: 89] had preceded, and mention of his brother was an explanation of what they asked about, even though it was known to them, and a preparation for what is mentioned after (man), namely piety and patience. The best view is that piety is not restricted to one state, nor patience.

Mujahid said: "whoever is pious" in abstaining from disobedience, and "is patient" in prison.

Al-Nakha'i said: "whoever is pious" regarding fornication, and "is patient" in celibacy. It is also said: whoever fears Allah and is patient through calamities.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿man yattaqi﴾ means whoever fears Allah and His punishment and is patient in refraining from sins and in obeying Him. It is also said: whoever guards against Allah's disobediences and is patient under the harm of people. All these are particularizations according to the state of Joseph and his circumstances.

Qunbul read (man yattaqi). It is said that it is jussive by deleting the yā’ which is the final radical, and this yā’ is a prolongation (ishba'). It is also said that he made it jussive by deleting the vowel, according to the dialect of those who say "lam yarmi Zayd," and they have reported this as a dialect. It is also said that it is nominative, and "man" is a relative pronoun in the sense of "alladhi," and the jussive "wa yasbir" is conjoined to it, by way of mental association (tawahhum), as if he imagined that "man" was conditional and "yattaqi" jussive. It is also said that "wa yasbir" is nominative, conjoined to a nominative, and the ra' was made quiescent not for jussiveness but to avoid successive vowels, even though that is across two words, as it was made quiescent in "ya'murkum wa yush'irkum wa bu'ulatuhunna"; or it is quiescent for pausal reasons, and the connection is treated as pause. The best of these views is that "yattaqi" is jussive according to a dialect, though it is rare, and it does not revert to the saying of Abu 'Ali, who said: "this is of what should not be applied to, because it only occurs in poetry and not in speech," because other leading grammarians have transmitted that it is a dialect.

"Al-muhsinin" is general, encompassing those previously mentioned, or it was placed in the position of the pronoun because it includes the pious and the patient, as if it were said: "He does not waste their reward."

"Ather-aka" means He preferred you with kingship, or with patience and knowledge, as said by Ibn 'Abbas; or with forbearance and pardon, mentioned by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi; or with beauty of form, character, knowledge, forbearance, goodness, kingship and authority, and your patience with our harm, as said by the author of al-Ghuniyan; or with piety, patience and the conduct of the good-doers, as said by al-Zamakhshari, and it is suitable to His saying: ﴿Indeed, whoever fears Allah...﴾ the verse. Their addressing him with this is a solicitation of his goodness and an acknowledgment of what proceeded from them toward him. "Khati'in" is from "khati'a" when one does it intentionally; as for "akhta'a," it is aiming at the right but not being guided to it. "La tathrib" means no reproach and no punishment. "Tathrib" is the subject of "la," "alaykum" is the predicate, and "al-yawm" is in the accusative governed by the element operating in the predicate; that is: no reproach is established upon you today. Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, "To what is 'al-yawm' connected?" I answer: to "tathrib," or to what is implied in "alaykum" of the sense of establishment, or to "yaghfiru." The meaning is: I do not blame you today, and this is the day that is the place of blame, so what do you think about other days? Then he began: ﴿Allah forgives you﴾, having given them confidence in the forgiveness of what had passed from them. It is said "Ghafara Allahu laka" and "yaghfiru Allahu laka" in both past and present forms, and from it is the saying of one who blesses a sneezer: "may Allah guide you and set right your affairs." Or "al-yawm yaghfiru Allahu lakum" is glad tidings of prompt forgiveness, because of their repentance and regret over their wrongdoing that renewed that day, end of quote.

As for his saying that "al-yawm" is connected to "tathrib," this is not permissible, because "tathrib" is a verbal noun, and its complement has been separated from it by "alaykum," which is either the predicate or an adjective of "tathrib," and separating them is not permitted, since the complement of a verbal noun is part of it. Also, if "al-yawm" were connected to "tathrib," it would not be permissible for it to be indeclinable; it would be of the type of the nominal resembling the genitive construction, which is called the lengthened (mutawwal) or stretched (mamtul), and would be declinable and nunated.

As for his second estimation, it is a good estimation, and for that reason most readers stopped at his saying "al-yawm," and began with "Allah forgives you" as a supplication; this is the interpretation of Ibn Ishaq and al-Tabari.

As for his third estimation, that "al-yawm" is connected to "yaghfiru," it is acceptable, and some readers stopped at "alaykum" and began "al-yawm yaghfiru Allahu lakum." Ibn 'Atiyya said: stopping at "al-yawm" is preferable in meaning, because the other reading contains a judgment about Allah's forgiveness, unless that is by revelation. As for his saying "it is glad tidings," etc., this follows the way of the Mu'tazila, for forgiveness occurs only for one who repents. Ibn al-Anbari said: he pointed to that day only because it is the first of the times of pardon, and the way of one who pardons in such a case is not to revert to punishment. Al-Hawfi permitted that "alaykum" be in the position of an adjective to "tathrib" and that the predicate be "al-yawm," which is a good view. It is also said that "alaykum" is an explanation, like "laka" in their saying "suqyan laka," and so it is connected to an elided element. They stated explicitly that "alaykum" may not be connected to "tathrib," because then it would be declined and nunated, becoming of the type of the nominal resembling the genitive. If it were said that the predicate is elided and "alaykum" is connected to an elided element indicated by "tathrib," and that elided element is what governs "al-yawm," with the estimation: "la tathrib alaykum al-yawm," as they estimated in "la 'asima al-yawm min amr Allah" [Hud: 43], meaning "ya'simu al-yawm," it would be a strong view, because when the predicate of "la" is known it is frequently elided among the people of the Hijaz, while the Banu Tamim do not pronounce it. When he prayed for them for forgiveness, he informed about Allah with the attribute that is the cause of forgiveness, namely that He, exalted is He, is the most merciful of the merciful, so he hopes from Him acceptance of his prayer for them for forgiveness.

The "ba'" in "bi-qamisi" is apparently for accompaniment (hal); that is, accompanied by it or attached to it. It is also said that it is for transitivity; that is, take my shirt, i.e., carry my shirt. It is said that it is the shirt which Joseph inherited and which was on his neck, and that it was from Paradise, which Gabriel, peace be upon him, commanded him to send to him, for in it is the scent of Paradise; it does not fall upon one afflicted or sick without his being healed. It is also said that it belonged to Ibrahim, which Allah clothed him with from Paradise when he came out of the fire, then to Ishaq, then to Ya'qub, then to Yusuf. It is also said that it is the shirt torn from behind, which he sent so that Ya'qub would know that he had been protected from indecency.

It is apparent that it is a shirt from the clothing of Yusuf, like the shirt of any one person, as Ibn 'Atiyya said. Thus the strangeness appears in that Ya'qub found its scent afterward; if it had been from the shirts of Paradise there would have been no strangeness in that, and everyone would have found it. His saying ﴿cast it over the face of my father; he will come seeing﴾ indicates that he knew his father had gone blind from grief, either by their informing him or by revelation. His saying ﴿he will come seeing﴾ appears to be by revelation. The number of his family whom he was commanded to bring was said to be seventy, or eighty, or ninety-three, or ninety-six; the first of these sayings is from al-Kalbi and the third is from Masruq. In one of these numbers they settled in Egypt and multiplied, until from their descendants there came out with Musa, peace be upon him, six hundred thousand. The meaning of "ya'ti" is "ya'tini" (he will come to me), and "basiran" is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (hal).

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 12, verses 94–98:**

﴿When the caravan departed, their father said: "Indeed, I sense the scent of Joseph, were it not that you think me senile."﴾ ﴿They said: "By Allah, you are surely in your old error."﴾ ﴿Then when the bearer of good news arrived, he cast it over his face, and his sight returned. He said: "Did I not tell you that I know from Allah what you do not know?"﴾ ﴿They said: "O our father, ask forgiveness for us for our sins. Indeed, we have been sinners."﴾ ﴿He said: "I will ask my Lord to forgive you. Indeed, He is the Oft-Forgiving, the Most Merciful."﴾

*fasala* (to depart) from the land is used as *yafsilu fusulan*, meaning he departed from it and went beyond its walls, and it is intransitive. *Fasala al-shay'* (he separated the thing) means he divided it, and it is transitive. The meaning of ﴿fasalat al-'ir﴾ is that the caravan departed from the district of Egypt heading for the place of Ya'qub, which was near Bayt al-Maqdis. It was said: it was in the Peninsula (al-Jazirah). Bayt al-Maqdis is the correct view, because their traces and graves are there until now. Ibn 'Abbas recited: (wa-lamma infasala al-'ir). Ibn 'Abbas said: he (Ya'qub) smelled his scent from a distance of eight days; a wind blew and carried his fragrance. Al-Hasan and Ibn Jurayj said: from eighty farsakh (a distance measure). The period of his separation from him was seventy-seven years. Also from al-Hasan: he smelled it from a distance of thirty days; and from him: a distance of ten nights. From Abu Ayyub al-Mahrawi: the wind asked permission to convey Joseph's fragrance to Ya'qub, and it was permitted to do so. Mujahid said: the wind fluttered the shirt, and the scents of Paradise spread in this world, and reached Ya'qub, so he smelled the scent of Paradise. He knew that there is no scent of Paradise in this world except what came from that shirt. The meaning of (la-ajidu) is la-ashummu (I smell); it is the existence of the sense of smell. The poet said:

*"And indeed I seek healing with every cloud that blows toward me with it from the direction of your land, a wind."*

The meaning of ﴿tufannidun﴾: Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatadah said: you deem me foolish (tusaffihun). Also from Ibn 'Abbas: you deem me ignorant (tujahhilun). Also from him: you deem me weak (tudh'ifun). 'Ata' and Ibn Jubayr said: you deem me a liar (tukadhdhibun). Al-Hasan said: you deem me senile (tuhrimun). Ibn Zayd, al-Dahhak and Mujahid also said: you say, "Your mind has gone and you have become senile (kharif)." Abu 'Amr said: you find me repugnant (tuqabbihun). Al-Kisa'i said: you deem me incapable (tu'ajjizun). Abu 'Ubaydah said: you deem me misguided (tudallilun). It was also said: you deem me mistaken (tukhati'un). All of these are close in meaning, and they return to the belief that the opinion of the one being deemed is corrupt, either due to his ignorance, or due to a dominant passion within him, or due to his lying, or due to his weakness and incapacity from the loss of his mind through old age. Mundhir ibn Sa'id al-Ballluti said: one says "a senile old man (shaykh mufannad)," meaning his opinion has become corrupted; one does not say "an old woman (ajuzah mufannadah)," because a woman never had a mature opinion, so tafnid cannot apply to her. Al-Zamakhshari said the same, and said: tafnid means attributing to someone *al-fanad*, which is fear and the denial of reason, due to old age. One says "a senile old man (shaykh mufannad)," and one does not say "an old woman (ajuzah mufannadah)," because she was never possessed of an opinion in her youth to be deemed senile in her old age. Here (lawla) is a particle of prohibition due to existence (harf imtina' li-wujud), and its response is omitted. Al-Zamakhshari said: the meaning is, "Were it not for your deeming me senile, you would have believed me." It has been said: its estimated meaning is, "Were it not that you deem me senile, I would have told you that he is alive and has not died, because my finding his scent indicates his life." The addressee of His saying ﴿tufannidun﴾ — the apparent meaning from the coherence of the pronouns is that it refers to those of his sons who remained with him, other than those who went off to buy grain, since his sons were a group. It was said: the addressee is his grandson and those of his relatives who were in his presence.

The misguidance (al-dalal) here is not intended as the opposite of guidance and rectitude. Ibn 'Abbas said: the meaning is "you are in your error." Ya'qub's grief had been renewed by the story of Binyamin, and for this reason he is called "the one of two griefs (dhu al-huznayn)." Muqatil said: misery and hardship. Ibn Jubayr said: madness; and he means, Allah knows best, the overwhelming of love. It was said: ruin and loss, from their saying: "water got lost in milk," meaning it went into it. It was said: love, and misguidance is applied to love. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: that is from the harshness that they should not have confronted him with, and some people interpreted it this way. For this reason Qatadah said: they said to their father a harsh word which they should not have said to their father, nor to the Prophet of Allah (ﷺ). Al-Zamakhshari said: "in your loss of the right course, going to extremes in your excessive love for Joseph, your constant mention of him, and your hope of meeting him, while they believed he had died." It was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that the bearer of good news was Yahudha, because he had brought the bloodied shirt. Abu al-Fadl al-Jawhari said: Yahudha said to his brothers, "You know that I went to him with the shirt of wounds, so let me go to him with the shirt of joy." They left him, and al-Suddi said this meaning.

(*An*) is regularly elided after (*lamma*), and the hidden pronoun in ﴿alqahu﴾ refers to ﴿al-bashir﴾ (the bearer of good news), which is the apparent reading; it refers to his saying ﴿fa-alqawhu﴾ ["cast it"] [Yusuf: 93]. It was said: it refers to Ya'qub. The apparent view is that the whole face was intended, as it is the custom that when a person finds something to which he attributes blessing, he wipes his face with it. It was said: he expressed "face" to mean the two eyes, because they are in it. It was said: he expressed the whole for a part. As for (irtadda), some of them counted it among the sisters of (kana) (the verbs that take a predicate in the accusative), but the correct view is that it is not among its sisters, so (basiran) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (*hal*). The meaning is: he returned to his original condition of soundness of sight. Thus, the statement suggests that his sight returned stronger than it had been and better, because *fa'il* (*fa'il* being the pattern) is among the intensive forms (*sigha al-mubalaghah*), and what is shifted from *mufil* to *fa'il* is only for this meaning, as he said. But this is not so, because *fa'il* here is not intensive; the *fa'il* that is intensive is a derived form deviating from *fa'il* for this meaning. As for (basiran) here, it is an active participle (*ism fa'il*) from *basura bi-al-shay'*, so it follows the pattern of *fa'ula*, like *zarufa*, so he is *zarif*. Even if it were, as he claimed, in the sense of *mubsir*, it would not be intensive either, because *fa'il* in the sense of a non-intensive form, like *alim* (painful) and *sami'* (hearing), meaning *mu'lim* (causing pain) and *musmi'* (causing to hear). It is narrated that Ya'qub asked the bearer of good news, "How is Yusuf?" He said, "He is king of Egypt." He said, "What do I do with kingship?" He said, "On what religion did you leave him?" He said, "On Islam." He said, "Now the blessing is complete." Al-Hasan said: the bearer of good news did not find anything with Ya'qub to give him to eat, and he said, "We have not baked anything for seven nights, but Allah has made the agonies of death easy for you." Al-Dahhak said: his sight returned to him after blindness, strength after weakness, youth after old age, and joy after distress.

The apparent view is that His saying ﴿inni a'lamu﴾ is quoted speech, and he intends by it ﴿innama ashku baththi wa-huzni ila Allah wa-a'lamu min Allah ma la ta'lamun﴾ [Yusuf: 86]. It was said: "what you do not know" refers to the life of Yusuf, and that Allah will bring us and him together. It was said: it refers to the truth of Yusuf's dream, peace be upon him. It was said: it refers to the trial of prophets with grief and the coming of relief. It was said: it refers to information from the Angel of Death to me, for he had told him that he had not taken his soul. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: ﴿ma la ta'lamun﴾ [Yusuf: 86] is his waiting for the interpretation of the dream, and it may refer only to his good opinion of Allah. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Did I not tell you," meaning his saying ﴿inni la-ajidu rih Yusuf﴾ ["I surely smell the scent of Yusuf"], or his saying ﴿wa-la tay'asu min rawh Allah﴾ ["do not despair of Allah's mercy"] [Yusuf: 87]. And his saying ﴿inni a'lamu﴾ is an independent statement not governed by the verb "said," and this is contrary to the apparent meaning we have mentioned earlier.

When his sight returned to him, his eye was consoled by going out to his son Yusuf, and he confirmed to them his saying ﴿alam aqul lakum﴾ ["Did I not tell you"], they asked him to ask Allah to forgive them for their sins, and they acknowledged their earlier mistake. His saying ﴿sawfa astaghfiru lakum﴾ ["I will ask forgiveness for you"] is a promise to them to seek forgiveness, using *sawfa*, which is stronger in deferment than *sin*. It is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that he delayed seeking forgiveness for them until the pre-dawn hour (al-sahar). From Ibn 'Abbas: until Friday night, and from him: until its pre-dawn. Al-Suddi, Muqatil and al-Zajjaj said: he delayed it to await the answer to supplication, not out of stinginess toward them in seeking forgiveness. A group said: *sawfa* means until the night prayer (qiyam al-layl). Ibn Jubayr and a group said: until the bright nights (al-layali al-bidh), for supplication is answered in them. Al-Sha'bi said: he delayed it until he asked Yusuf; if he pardoned them, he would seek forgiveness for them. It was said: he delayed them in order to know their state regarding the sincerity and purity of their repentance. It was said: he intended continuity in seeking forgiveness for them. When he promised them to seek forgiveness, he gave them hope of attaining forgiveness by his saying ﴿innahu huwa al-Ghafur al-Rahim﴾ ["Indeed, He is the Oft-Forgiving, the Most Merciful"].

He said: "Did I not tell you that I know from Allah what you do not know?"﴾ ﴿They said: "O our father, ask forgiveness for us for our sins. Indeed, we have been sinners."﴾ ﴿He said: "I will ask my Lord to forgive you. Indeed, He is the Oft-Forgiving, the Most Merciful."﴾

*fasala* (to depart) from the land is used as *yafsilu fusulan*, meaning he departed from it and went beyond its walls, and it is intransitive. *Fasala al-shay'* (he separated the thing) means he divided it, and it is transitive. The meaning of ﴿fasalat al-'ir﴾ is that the caravan departed from the district of Egypt heading for the place of Ya'qub, which was near Bayt al-Maqdis. It was said: it was in the Peninsula (al-Jazirah). Bayt al-Maqdis is the correct view, because their traces and graves are there until now. Ibn 'Abbas recited: (wa-lamma infasala al-'ir). Ibn 'Abbas said: he (Ya'qub) smelled his scent from a distance of eight days; a wind blew and carried his fragrance. Al-Hasan and Ibn Jurayj said: from eighty farsakh (a distance measure). The period of his separation from him was seventy-seven years. Also from al-Hasan: he smelled it from a distance of thirty days; and from him: a distance of ten nights. From Abu Ayyub al-Mahrawi: the wind asked permission to convey Joseph's fragrance to Ya'qub, and it was permitted to do so. Mujahid said: the wind fluttered the shirt, and the scents of Paradise spread in this world, and reached Ya'qub, so he smelled the scent of Paradise. He knew that there is no scent of Paradise in this world except what came from that shirt. The meaning of (la-ajidu) is la-ashummu (I smell); it is the existence of the sense of smell. The poet said:

*"And indeed I seek healing with every cloud that blows toward me with it from the direction of your land, a wind."*

The meaning of ﴿tufannidun﴾: Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatadah said: you deem me foolish (tusaffihun). Also from Ibn 'Abbas: you deem me ignorant (tujahhilun). Also from him: you deem me weak (tudh'ifun). 'Ata' and Ibn Jubayr said: you deem me a liar (tukadhdhibun). Al-Hasan said: you deem me senile (tuhrimun). Ibn Zayd, al-Dahhak and Mujahid also said: you say, "Your mind has gone and you have become senile (kharif)." Abu 'Amr said: you find me repugnant (tuqabbihun). Al-Kisa'i said: you deem me incapable (tu'ajjizun). Abu 'Ubaydah said: you deem me misguided (tudallilun). It was also said: you deem me mistaken (tukhati'un). All of these are close in meaning, and they return to the belief that the opinion of the one being deemed is corrupt, either due to his ignorance, or due to a dominant passion within him, or due to his lying, or due to his weakness and incapacity from the loss of his mind through old age. Mundhir ibn Sa'id al-Ballluti said: one says "a senile old man (shaykh mufannad)," meaning his opinion has become corrupted; one does not say "an old woman (ajuzah mufannadah)," because a woman never had a mature opinion, so tafnid cannot apply to her. Al-Zamakhshari said the same, and said: tafnid means attributing to someone *al-fanad*, which is fear and the denial of reason, due to old age. One says "a senile old man (shaykh mufannad)," and one does not say "an old woman (ajuzah mufannadah)," because she was never possessed of an opinion in her youth to be deemed senile in her old age. Here (lawla) is a particle of prohibition due to existence (harf imtina' li-wujud), and its response is omitted. Al-Zamakhshari said: the meaning is, "Were it not for your deeming me senile, you would have believed me." It has been said: its estimated meaning is, "Were it not that you deem me senile, I would have told you that he is alive and has not died, because my finding his scent indicates his life." The addressee of His saying ﴿tufannidun﴾ — the apparent meaning from the coherence of the pronouns is that it refers to those of his sons who remained with him, other than those who went off to buy grain, since his sons were a group. It was said: the addressee is his grandson and those of his relatives who were in his presence.

The misguidance (al-dalal) here is not intended as the opposite of guidance and rectitude. Ibn 'Abbas said: the meaning is "you are in your error." Ya'qub's grief had been renewed by the story of Binyamin, and for this reason he is called "the one of two griefs (dhu al-huznayn)." Muqatil said: misery and hardship. Ibn Jubayr said: madness; and he means, Allah knows best, the overwhelming of love. It was said: ruin and loss, from their saying: "water got lost in milk," meaning it went into it. It was said: love, and misguidance is applied to love. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: that is from the harshness that they should not have confronted him with, and some people interpreted it this way. For this reason Qatadah said: they said to their father a harsh word which they should not have said to their father, nor to the Prophet of Allah (ﷺ). Al-Zamakhshari said: "in your loss of the right course, going to extremes in your excessive love for Joseph, your constant mention of him, and your hope of meeting him, while they believed he had died." It was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that the bearer of good news was Yahudha, because he had brought the bloodied shirt. Abu al-Fadl al-Jawhari said: Yahudha said to his brothers, "You know that I went to him with the shirt of wounds, so let me go to him with the shirt of joy." They left him, and al-Suddi said this meaning.

(*An*) is regularly elided after (*lamma*), and the hidden pronoun in ﴿alqahu﴾ refers to ﴿al-bashir﴾ (the bearer of good news), which is the apparent reading; it refers to his saying ﴿fa-alqawhu﴾ ["cast it"] [Yusuf: 93]. It was said: it refers to Ya'qub. The apparent view is that the whole face was intended, as it is the custom that when a person finds something to which he attributes blessing, he wipes his face with it. It was said: he expressed "face" to mean the two eyes, because they are in it. It was said: he expressed the whole for a part. As for (irtadda), some of them counted it among the sisters of (kana) (the verbs that take a predicate in the accusative), but the correct view is that it is not among its sisters, so (basiran) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (*hal*). The meaning is: he returned to his original condition of soundness of sight. Thus, the statement suggests that his sight returned stronger than it had been and better, because *fa'il* (*fa'il* being the pattern) is among the intensive forms (*sigha al-mubalaghah*), and what is shifted from *mufil* to *fa'il* is only for this meaning, as he said. But this is not so, because *fa'il* here is not intensive; the *fa'il* that is intensive is a derived form deviating from *fa'il* for this meaning. As for (basiran) here, it is an active participle (*ism fa'il*) from *basura bi-al-shay'*, so it follows the pattern of *fa'ula*, like *zarufa*, so he is *zarif*. Even if it were, as he claimed, in the sense of *mubsir*, it would not be intensive either, because *fa'il* in the sense of a non-intensive form, like *alim* (painful) and *sami'* (hearing), meaning *mu'lim* (causing pain) and *musmi'* (causing to hear). It is narrated that Ya'qub asked the bearer of good news, "How is Yusuf?" He said, "He is king of Egypt." He said, "What do I do with kingship?" He said, "On what religion did you leave him?" He said, "On Islam." He said, "Now the blessing is complete." Al-Hasan said: the bearer of good news did not find anything with Ya'qub to give him to eat, and he said, "We have not baked anything for seven nights, but Allah has made the agonies of death easy for you." Al-Dahhak said: his sight returned to him after blindness, strength after weakness, youth after old age, and joy after distress.

The apparent view is that His saying ﴿inni a'lamu﴾ is quoted speech, and he intends by it ﴿innama ashku baththi wa-huzni ila Allah wa-a'lamu min Allah ma la ta'lamun﴾ [Yusuf: 86]. It was said: "what you do not know" refers to the life of Yusuf, and that Allah will bring us and him together. It was said: it refers to the truth of Yusuf's dream, peace be upon him. It was said: it refers to the trial of prophets with grief and the coming of relief. It was said: it refers to information from the Angel of Death to me, for he had told him that he had not taken his soul. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: ﴿ma la ta'lamun﴾ [Yusuf: 86] is his waiting for the interpretation of the dream, and it may refer only to his good opinion of Allah. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Did I not tell you," meaning his saying ﴿inni la-ajidu rih Yusuf﴾ ["I surely smell the scent of Yusuf"], or his saying ﴿wa-la tay'asu min rawh Allah﴾ ["do not despair of Allah's mercy"] [Yusuf: 87]. And his saying ﴿inni a'lamu﴾ is an independent statement not governed by the verb "said," and this is contrary to the apparent meaning we have mentioned earlier.

When his sight returned to him, his eye was consoled by going out to his son Yusuf, and he confirmed to them his saying ﴿alam aqul lakum﴾ ["Did I not tell you"], they asked him to ask Allah to forgive them for their sins, and they acknowledged their earlier mistake. His saying ﴿sawfa astaghfiru lakum﴾ ["I will ask forgiveness for you"] is a promise to them to seek forgiveness, using *sawfa*, which is stronger in deferment than *sin*. It is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that he delayed seeking forgiveness for them until the pre-dawn hour (al-sahar). From Ibn 'Abbas: until Friday night, and from him: until its pre-dawn. Al-Suddi, Muqatil and al-Zajjaj said: he delayed it to await the answer to supplication, not out of stinginess toward them in seeking forgiveness. A group said: *sawfa* means until the night prayer (qiyam al-layl). Ibn Jubayr and a group said: until the bright nights (al-layali al-bidh), for supplication is answered in them. Al-Sha'bi said: he delayed it until he asked Yusuf; if he pardoned them, he would seek forgiveness for them. It was said: he delayed them in order to know their state regarding the sincerity and purity of their repentance. It was said: he intended continuity in seeking forgiveness for them. When he promised them to seek forgiveness, he gave them hope of attaining forgiveness by his saying ﴿innahu huwa al-Ghafur al-Rahim﴾ ["Indeed, He is the Oft-Forgiving, the Most Merciful"].

(p. 347) There is an omission in the speech, its implied sense being: So Ya'qub set out with his whole family, and they travelled until they met Yusuf. It was said: Yusuf prepared for his father a provision and two hundred riding animals so that he and those with him could be equipped to come to him. Yusuf went out, and it was said that the king went out with four thousand troops, the notables, and all the people of Egypt. They met Ya'qub, peace be upon him, as he walked leaning on Yahudha. He looked at the horses and the people and said: "O Yahudha, is this the Pharaoh of Egypt?" He said: "No, this is your son." When he met him, Ya'qub, peace be upon him, said: "Peace be upon you, O remover of sorrows." It was also said that when they met, Yusuf said to him: "O father, you wept for me until your sight was lost. Did you not know that the Resurrection will gather us?" He said: "Yes, but I feared that your religion would be taken from you, and that I would be kept from you."

"Āwā ilayhi abawayh" means he embraced them and took them to himself. The apparent meaning is that the two were his father and his mother, Rahil. Al-Hasan and Ibn Ishaq said: his mother was alive. It was also said that she had died from childbirth (nifas) of Binyamin, and that Allah brought her back to life for him, so that his dream would come true in His words: ﴿And the sun and the moon and eleven stars, I saw them prostrating to me﴾ [Yusuf: 4]. This was also related from al-Hasan and Ibn Ishaq. It was also said that the two were his father and his maternal aunt, for Ya'qub had married her after the death of Rahil, and the maternal aunt is called "mother." This was related from Ibn 'Abbas, and she had raised Yusuf, and the one who raises a child is called "mother." Some said: his father and his grandmother, the mother of his mother; this was related by al-Zahrawi. In the codex of 'Abdullah it reads: "He took his two parents and his brothers to himself." The apparent meaning of His words "Enter Egypt" is that he commanded them to enter Egypt in the future. Al-Suddi said: he said this to them while they were on the road, when he met them. End of quote. Then His words "When they entered upon Yusuf" remain, as if a tent or a house had been set up for him on the road at the time of the meeting, and they entered upon him there. It was also said: they entered upon him in Egypt. The meaning of "Enter Egypt" is: settle in it and remain there.

The apparent meaning is that the entering is connected to the will of Allah. When He commanded them to enter, He made that conditional upon the will of Allah, because all beings come into existence only by the will of Allah, and what He does not will does not occur. Al-Zamakhshari said: the sense is "Enter Egypt, if Allah wills, secure"; "if Allah wills, you will enter secure." Then the answer (the apodosis) was omitted because the speech indicates it. Then the answering clause was inserted between the circumstantial phrase and the one it describes. Among the strange interpretations is that His words "if Allah wills" are placed out of order, and that their proper position is after His words "I will ask my Lord to forgive you" [Yusuf: 98] in the speech of Ya'qub. End of quote.

(p. 348) This strange interpretation was related from Ibn Jurayj, and it is extremely remote, indeed extremely impossible.

"Al-'Arsh" means the throne of kingship. When Yusuf entered Egypt, sat in his seat upon his throne, and they gathered around him, he honoured his parents and raised them with him onto the throne. It is possible that the raising and the prostration happened before they entered Egypt, after His words "Enter Egypt." He would then have been in a tent of the kings' tents that are carried on mules or camels. So when they came in to him, he took his parents to himself and said: "Enter Egypt," and "He raised his parents," and "they fell down before him." The pronoun in "they fell down" refers to his parents and his brothers. It was also said that the pronoun in "they fell down" refers to his brothers and all others who would enter upon him because of his awe, and that his parents were not included in the pronoun; rather he raised them on his royal throne to honour them. The apparent meaning of His words "they fell down before him in prostration" is that it was the well-known prostration, and that the pronoun in "before him" refers to Yusuf, in agreement with the dream in His words: "Indeed, I saw eleven stars" [Yusuf: 4], and so on. Prostration at that time was permitted as a form of honour, by handshake, kissing the hand, and standing, which was known among people as a form of reverence and respect. Qatada said: it was the greeting of kings among them, and Allah gave this nation the greeting of the people of Paradise, which is peace. It was also said that this prostration was only a nod of the head. It was also said that it was like a deep bow without placing the forehead on the ground. But the word "they fell down" rejects these two explanations. Al-Hasan said: the pronoun in "before him" refers to Allah, meaning they fell down before Allah in prostration, thanking Him for the blessing He had granted them. His words "I saw them prostrating to me" [Yusuf: 4] have been interpreted as meaning "I saw them prostrating for my sake." If the pronoun refers to Yusuf, the commentators said the prostration was a greeting, not worship. Abu 'Abdullah al-Darani said: prostration is only for Allah, not for Yusuf, and it is far from his intellect and religion that his father would consent to prostrate to him, given his prior station: his preservation of his children, his old age, his knowledge, his religion, and the perfection of his prophethood. It was also said: even if the pronoun refers to Yusuf, the prostration was for Allah the Exalted, and they made Yusuf a qibla, as you say "I prayed toward the Ka'ba" and "I prayed to the Ka'ba." Hassan said:

"I did not know that time would turn away from Hashim, then from her, from Abu Hasan.
Was he not the first to pray toward your qibla, and the one most knowledgeable of things and the sunan?"

It was also said: prostration here means humility, and "they fell down" means "they passed by," not falling to the ground, in accordance with His words: "And those who, when reminded of the signs of their Lord, do not fall down before them deaf and blind" [al-Furqan: 73], meaning they do not pass by them. Thabit said: His words "This is the interpretation of my dream from before" mean: your prostration now is the interpretation, that is, the outcome of my dream, that those stars, the sun and the moon, I saw them prostrating to me.

"Min qabl" [Yusuf: 80] is connected to "my dream." What is omitted in "min qabl" is, in its estimate: from before these events and occurrences which took place after my dream. Whoever interprets that his parents did not prostrate to him claims that the interpretation of a dream need not match the dream in every respect. The prostration of the stars, the sun and the moon is interpreted as the reverence of the great among people. There is no doubt that Ya'qub, peace be upon him, going with his children from Canaan to Egypt on account of Yusuf is the utmost in honouring him, and so this degree is enough for the dream to be true. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that when he saw the prostration of his parents and brothers, it overwhelmed him and his skin shivered, and he said to Ya'qub: "This is the interpretation of my dream from before." Then Yusuf, peace be upon him, began to enumerate the blessings of Allah upon him, saying: "My Lord has made it true" meaning: truthful. What I saw in my sleep came to pass in waking, with no falsehood or vanity in it. In the period between his dream and their prostration there is a contradictory disagreement: it was said eighty years, and it was said eighteen years, and other numbers have been said. Likewise there is contradictory disagreement about the period Ya'qub stayed in Egypt with his son Yusuf.

"Ahsana" originally takes "ila" (to), as in His words: "And do good as Allah has done good to you" [al-Qasas: 77]. It may also take "bi" (with), as the Exalted said: "And to the two parents, good" [al-Baqara: 83], just as one says "asa'a ilayhi" (he wronged him). The poet said this:

"Be bad to us, or be good, there is no blame on you with us, nor are you hated, if you turn away."

It may be that "ahsana" implies the meaning of "lataf" (to be kind), so it takes "bi." He mentioned his release from prison and passed over his release from the well, avoiding mention of what was connected to his brothers' words, and ignoring what they had done when he said: "No blame upon you today; may Allah forgive you" [Yusuf: 92]; and as a reminder of the purity of his soul and its freedom from what was attributed to him of solicitation. Also as a reminder of the leadership he reached in this world after leaving prison, unlike what he reached by leaving the well, when he was sold with the slaves. "And brought you from the desert", that is from the badiya (the desert). Ya'qub, peace be upon him, used to stay on the outskirts of Syria in the desert of Palestine, and he was the owner of camels, sheep, and desert life. Al-Zamakhshari said: they were people of tents and owners of livestock, moving from water to pasture. It was said: he had moved to the desert and settled there, for Allah never sent a prophet from among desert people. It was also said: he had gone out to Bada, which is a place, and Jamil meant it when he said:

"You are the one who made the people of Bada beloved to me, while my homelands are other lands."

For Ya'qub, peace be upon him, there is a mosque at this place under a mountain. It is said: "the people went out to Bada (badwan)" when they came to Bada, just as one says "they went down to the lowland (ghawran)" when they came to the lowland. The meaning is: "and brought you from a place called Bada." This was mentioned by al-Qushayri, and al-Mawardi related it from al-Dahhak and from Ibn 'Abbas. Yusuf, peace be upon him, set the blessing of his release from prison against their coming from the desert, and the reference by this to the reunion with his father and brothers and the removal of his father's sorrow. So in the hadith: "Whoever Allah wills good for, He transfers him from the desert to the settled town." "After Shaytan had stirred up" means: after he had corrupted. The stirring was mentioned earlier, and the stirring was attributed to Shaytan because he is the whisperer, as He said: "Then Shaytan caused them to slip from it" [al-Baqara: 36]. He mentioned this much of the matter of his brothers because a blessing that comes after hardship and trial has a more beautiful effect. "Indeed my Lord is Latif", meaning: gentle in arranging what He wills of affairs, kind. The "min" in His words "of the kingship" and "of the interpretation" is partitive, because He did not give him except part of the kingdom of this world, and did not teach him except part of the interpretation. The view of those who treat "min" as superfluous, or as explaining the kind, is remote.

The apparent meaning here is that the kingship is the kingship of Egypt. It was also said: the kingship of his own self, in carrying out his desires. 'Ata' said: the kingship over his envious ones through obedience, and attaining wishes from kingship. 'Abdullah and 'Amr ibn Dharr read: "ataytani" and "'allamtani" with the ya' removed from both, relying on the kasra instead, though both are written in the script. Ibn 'Atiyya related from Ibn Dharana that he read "Rabbi ataytani" without "qad." "Fatir" is in the accusative as an attribute or as a vocative. "You are my protector" meaning: You take care of me with blessing in both abodes, and You join the perishing kingdom to the enduring kingdom.

Many commentators mentioned that when he counted Allah's blessings upon him, he longed to meet his Lord and to join the righteous among his predecessors, and he saw that the whole world is perishing, so he wished for death. Ibn 'Abbas said: no living person wished for death except Yusuf. What appears is that the verse does not contain a wish for death; rather he enumerated his blessings, then prayed that He complete His blessings upon him for the rest of his affairs, that is: "Cause me to die when my term comes upon Islam, and make my joining the righteous." He wished for death upon Islam, not death itself. "The righteous" are the people of Paradise, or the prophets, or his forefathers Ibrahim, Ishaq and Ya'qub.

Historians claim that Yusuf, peace be upon him, lived one hundred and seven years. His children were Ifrathim, Manasha, and Rahma, wife of Ayyub, peace be upon him. Al-Dhahabi said: Ifrathim had a son Nun, and Nun had a son Yusha', who was the young companion of Musa, peace be upon him. Manasha had a son Musa, who was before Musa ibn 'Imran, peace be upon him. The People of the Torah claim that he is the companion of al-Khadir, and Ibn 'Abbas denied that. It is established in the Sahih that the companion of al-Khadir is Musa ibn 'Imran. The Pharaohs inherited the kingship of Egypt, and the Children of Israel remained under their hands upon remnants of the religion of Yusuf, peace be upon him, until Musa, peace be upon him, was sent.

It was also said: even if the pronoun refers to Yusuf, the prostration was for Allah the Exalted, and they made Yusuf a qibla, as you say "I prayed toward the Ka'ba" and "I prayed to the Ka'ba." Hassan said:

"I did not know that time would turn away from Hashim, then from her, from Abu Hasan.
Was he not the first to pray toward your qibla, and the one most knowledgeable of things and the sunan?"

It was also said: prostration here means humility, and "they fell down" means "they passed by," not falling to the ground, in accordance with His words: "And those who, when reminded of the signs of their Lord, do not fall down before them deaf and blind" [al-Furqan: 73], meaning they do not pass by them. Thabit said: His words "This is the interpretation of my dream from before" mean: your prostration now is the interpretation, that is, the outcome of my dream, that those stars, the sun and the moon, I saw them prostrating to me.

"Min qabl" [Yusuf: 80] is connected to "my dream." What is omitted in "min qabl" is, in its estimate: from before these events and occurrences which took place after my dream. Whoever interprets that his parents did not prostrate to him claims that the interpretation of a dream need not match the dream in every respect. The prostration of the stars, the sun and the moon is interpreted as the reverence of the great among people. There is no doubt that Ya'qub, peace be upon him, going with his children from Canaan to Egypt on account of Yusuf is the utmost in honouring him, and so this degree is enough for the dream to be true. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that when he saw the prostration of his parents and brothers, it overwhelmed him and his skin shivered, and he said to Ya'qub: "This is the interpretation of my dream from before." Then Yusuf, peace be upon him, began to enumerate the blessings of Allah upon him, saying: "My Lord has made it true" meaning: truthful. What I saw in my sleep came to pass in waking, with no falsehood or vanity in it. In the period between his dream and their prostration there is a contradictory disagreement: it was said eighty years, and it was said eighteen years, and other numbers have been said. Likewise there is contradictory disagreement about the period Ya'qub stayed in Egypt with his son Yusuf.

"Ahsana" originally takes "ila" (to), as in His words: "And do good as Allah has done good to you" [al-Qasas: 77]. It may also take "bi" (with), as the Exalted said: "And to the two parents, good" [al-Baqara: 83], just as one says "asa'a ilayhi" (he wronged him). The poet said this:

"Be bad to us, or be good, there is no blame on you with us, nor are you hated, if you turn away."

It may be that "ahsana" implies the meaning of "lataf" (to be kind), so it takes "bi." He mentioned his release from prison and passed over his release from the well, avoiding mention of what was connected to his brothers' words, and ignoring what they had done when he said: "No blame upon you today; may Allah forgive you" [Yusuf: 92]; and as a reminder of the purity of his soul and its freedom from what was attributed to him of solicitation. Also as a reminder of the leadership he reached in this world after leaving prison, unlike what he reached by leaving the well, when he was sold with the slaves. "And brought you from the desert", that is from the badiya (the desert). Ya'qub, peace be upon him, used to stay on the outskirts of Syria in the desert of Palestine, and he was the owner of camels, sheep, and desert life. Al-Zamakhshari said: they were people of tents and owners of livestock, moving from water to pasture. It was said: he had moved to the desert and settled there, for Allah never sent a prophet from among desert people. It was also said: he had gone out to Bada, which is a place, and Jamil meant it when he said:

"You are the one who made the people of Bada beloved to me, while my homelands are other lands."

For Ya'qub, peace be upon him, there is a mosque at this place under a mountain. It is said: "the people went out to Bada (badwan)" when they came to Bada, just as one says "they went down to the lowland (ghawran)" when they came to the lowland. The meaning is: "and brought you from a place called Bada." This was mentioned by al-Qushayri, and al-Mawardi related it from al-Dahhak and from Ibn 'Abbas. Yusuf, peace be upon him, set the blessing of his release from prison against their coming from the desert, and the reference by this to the reunion with his father and brothers and the removal of his father's sorrow. So in the hadith: "Whoever Allah wills good for, He transfers him from the desert to the settled town." "After Shaytan had stirred up" means: after he had corrupted. The stirring was mentioned earlier, and the stirring was attributed to Shaytan because he is the whisperer, as He said: "Then Shaytan caused them to slip from it" [al-Baqara: 36]. He mentioned this much of the matter of his brothers because a blessing that comes after hardship and trial has a more beautiful effect. "Indeed my Lord is Latif", meaning: gentle in arranging what He wills of affairs, kind. The "min" in His words "of the kingship" and "of the interpretation" is partitive, because He did not give him except part of the kingdom of this world, and did not teach him except part of the interpretation. The view of those who treat "min" as superfluous, or as explaining the kind, is remote.

The apparent meaning here is that the kingship is the kingship of Egypt. It was also said: the kingship of his own self, in carrying out his desires. 'Ata' said: the kingship over his envious ones through obedience, and attaining wishes from kingship. 'Abdullah and 'Amr ibn Dharr read: "ataytani" and "'allamtani" with the ya' removed from both, relying on the kasra instead, though both are written in the script. Ibn 'Atiyya related from Ibn Dharana that he read "Rabbi ataytani" without "qad." "Fatir" is in the accusative as an attribute or as a vocative. "You are my protector" meaning: You take care of me with blessing in both abodes, and You join the perishing kingdom to the enduring kingdom.

Many commentators mentioned that when he counted Allah's blessings upon him, he longed to meet his Lord and to join the righteous among his predecessors, and he saw that the whole world is perishing, so he wished for death. Ibn 'Abbas said: no living person wished for death except Yusuf. What appears is that the verse does not contain a wish for death; rather he enumerated his blessings, then prayed that He complete His blessings upon him for the rest of his affairs, that is: "Cause me to die when my term comes upon Islam, and make my joining the righteous." He wished for death upon Islam, not death itself. "The righteous" are the people of Paradise, or the prophets, or his forefathers Ibrahim, Ishaq and Ya'qub.

Historians claim that Yusuf, peace be upon him, lived one hundred and seven years. His children were Ifrathim, Manasha, and Rahma, wife of Ayyub, peace be upon him. Al-Dhahabi said: Ifrathim had a son Nun, and Nun had a son Yusha', who was the young companion of Musa, peace be upon him. Manasha had a son Musa, who was before Musa ibn 'Imran, peace be upon him. The People of the Torah claim that he is the companion of al-Khadir, and Ibn 'Abbas denied that. It is established in the Sahih that the companion of al-Khadir is Musa ibn 'Imran. The Pharaohs inherited the kingship of Egypt, and the Children of Israel remained under their hands upon remnants of the religion of Yusuf, peace be upon him, until Musa, peace be upon him, was sent.

(p. 347) There is an omission in the speech, its implied sense being: So Ya'qub set out with his whole family, and they travelled until they met Yusuf. It was said: Yusuf prepared for his father a provision and two hundred riding animals so that he and those with him could be equipped to come to him. Yusuf went out, and it was said that the king went out with four thousand troops, the notables, and all the people of Egypt. They met Ya'qub, peace be upon him, as he walked leaning on Yahudha. He looked at the horses and the people and said: "O Yahudha, is this the Pharaoh of Egypt?" He said: "No, this is your son." When he met him, Ya'qub, peace be upon him, said: "Peace be upon you, O remover of sorrows." It was also said that when they met, Yusuf said to him: "O father, you wept for me until your sight was lost. Did you not know that the Resurrection will gather us?" He said: "Yes, but I feared that your religion would be taken from you, and that I would be kept from you."

"Āwā ilayhi abawayh" means he embraced them and took them to himself. The apparent meaning is that the two were his father and his mother, Rahil. Al-Hasan and Ibn Ishaq said: his mother was alive. It was also said that she had died from childbirth (nifas) of Binyamin, and that Allah brought her back to life for him, so that his dream would come true in His words: ﴿And the sun and the moon and eleven stars, I saw them prostrating to me﴾ [Yusuf: 4]. This was also related from al-Hasan and Ibn Ishaq. It was also said that the two were his father and his maternal aunt, for Ya'qub had married her after the death of Rahil, and the maternal aunt is called "mother." This was related from Ibn 'Abbas, and she had raised Yusuf, and the one who raises a child is called "mother." Some said: his father and his grandmother, the mother of his mother; this was related by al-Zahrawi. In the codex of 'Abdullah it reads: "He took his two parents and his brothers to himself." The apparent meaning of His words "Enter Egypt" is that he commanded them to enter Egypt in the future. Al-Suddi said: he said this to them while they were on the road, when he met them. End of quote. Then His words "When they entered upon Yusuf" remain, as if a tent or a house had been set up for him on the road at the time of the meeting, and they entered upon him there. It was also said: they entered upon him in Egypt. The meaning of "Enter Egypt" is: settle in it and remain there.

The apparent meaning is that the entering is connected to the will of Allah. When He commanded them to enter, He made that conditional upon the will of Allah, because all beings come into existence only by the will of Allah, and what He does not will does not occur. Al-Zamakhshari said: the sense is "Enter Egypt, if Allah wills, secure"; "if Allah wills, you will enter secure." Then the answer (the apodosis) was omitted because the speech indicates it. Then the answering clause was inserted between the circumstantial phrase and the one it describes. Among the strange interpretations is that His words "if Allah wills" are placed out of order, and that their proper position is after His words "I will ask my Lord to forgive you" [Yusuf: 98] in the speech of Ya'qub. End of quote.

(p. 348) This strange interpretation was related from Ibn Jurayj, and it is extremely remote, indeed extremely impossible.

"Al-'Arsh" means the throne of kingship. When Yusuf entered Egypt, sat in his seat upon his throne, and they gathered around him, he honoured his parents and raised them with him onto the throne. It is possible that the raising and the prostration happened before they entered Egypt, after His words "Enter Egypt." He would then have been in a tent of the kings' tents that are carried on mules or camels. So when they came in to him, he took his parents to himself and said: "Enter Egypt," and "He raised his parents," and "they fell down before him." The pronoun in "they fell down" refers to his parents and his brothers. It was also said that the pronoun in "they fell down" refers to his brothers and all others who would enter upon him because of his awe, and that his parents were not included in the pronoun; rather he raised them on his royal throne to honour them. The apparent meaning of His words "they fell down before him in prostration" is that it was the well-known prostration, and that the pronoun in "before him" refers to Yusuf, in agreement with the dream in His words: "Indeed, I saw eleven stars" [Yusuf: 4], and so on. Prostration at that time was permitted as a form of honour, by handshake, kissing the hand, and standing, which was known among people as a form of reverence and respect. Qatada said: it was the greeting of kings among them, and Allah gave this nation the greeting of the people of Paradise, which is peace. It was also said that this prostration was only a nod of the head. It was also said that it was like a deep bow without placing the forehead on the ground. But the word "they fell down" rejects these two explanations. Al-Hasan said: the pronoun in "before him" refers to Allah, meaning they fell down before Allah in prostration, thanking Him for the blessing He had granted them. His words "I saw them prostrating to me" [Yusuf: 4] have been interpreted as meaning "I saw them prostrating for my sake." Was he not the first to pray toward your qibla, and the one most knowledgeable of things and the sunan?"
