(p-350) ﴿That is among the tidings of the unseen which We reveal to you. You were not with them when they resolved on their affair while they were scheming.﴾ ﴿Yet most people, however eager you are, will not be believers.﴾ ﴿And you do not ask them any reward for it. It is only a reminder to the worlds.﴾ ﴿And how many a sign there is in the heavens and the earth, which they pass by while turning away from it.﴾ ﴿And most of them do not believe in God without associating others with Him.﴾ ﴿Do they then feel secure that an overwhelming punishment from God will not come upon them, or that the Hour will not come upon them suddenly while they are unaware?﴾

Ibn al-Anbari said: Quraysh and the Jews asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) about the story of Joseph, so it was revealed in full detail, and he hoped that this would be a cause of their conversion to Islam. But they went against his expectation, so God consoled him with His words: ﴿Yet most people, however eager you are, will not be believers.﴾ and the verses that follow. It is also said that it concerns the hypocrites. It is said that it concerns the Dualists (al-Thanawiyya). It is said that it concerns the Christians. Ibn ʿAbbas said that it concerns the talbiya (the call of the pilgrim) of the polytheists. It is also said that it concerns the People of the Book, who believed in some things and disbelieved in others, thus combining belief with polytheism.

The reference in "that" is to what God related of the story of Joseph and his brothers. ﴿You were not with them﴾ meaning: you were not with the sons of Jacob when they resolved on their affair, to put him in the well, nor when they threw him into it, nor when the caravan picked him up, nor when he was sold. ﴿While they were scheming﴾ meaning: they were seeking ways to harm Joseph and consulting one another about what to do to him. Or it means they were scheming against Jacob when they brought the shirt stained with blood. In this there is a declaration to Quraysh of the truthfulness of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). This type of the science of eloquence (ʿilm al-bayan) is called theoretical argumentation (al-ihtijaj al-nazari), and some call it the kalami method (al-madhhab al-kalami). It consists of binding the opponent to what is necessarily entailed by this argument. A similar case has been mentioned in Al ʿImran and in Hud. This is a rebuke to Quraysh and to those who denied him, because it is not hidden from anyone that he was not among the bearers of this narrative or its like, nor did he meet anyone who had knowledge of it or hear it from anyone, nor was it part of the knowledge of his people. So when he informs of it and relates this account which defeated its bearers and transmitters, no doubt remains that it is not from him, but rather it comes from the earlier generations. A similar verse is: ﴿You were not on the western side when We decreed the command to Moses﴾ (Al-Qasas: 44). So His words ﴿You were not﴾ here are a mockery of them, because everyone knows that Muhammad (ﷺ) was not with them. (And they resolved on their affair) meaning: they determined to throw Joseph into the well. (p-351) ﴿While they were scheming﴾ is a circumstantial clause (jumla haliyya). Al-makr (scheming) means to plot against a person in a way that harms and injures him. The word "people" (al-nas) is apparently general, based on His words: ﴿But most people do not believe﴾ (Hud: 17). It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas that they are the people of Mecca. ﴿However eager you are﴾ meaning: even if you strive hard to seek their belief, they will not believe, because of their intense obstinacy and their determination in disbelief. The answer to (law, "even if") is omitted, meaning: even if you were eager, they would not believe. Only the one whom God wills will be granted belief. The pronoun in (ʿalayhi, "for it") refers to the religion of God, meaning: you do not seek a reward for it, for the religion of God. It is also said that it refers to the Qur'an, and it is said that it refers to the conveying of the message, and it is said that it refers to the tidings in the sense of speech. In this there is a rebuke to the disbelievers and an establishment of proof against them. Or it means: you do not ask them for anything in return for what you narrate to them and remind them of, that they should bestow upon you some benefit or reward, as is given for the transmission of stories and reports. It is only an exhortation and a reminder from God to the worlds in general, and an urging to seek salvation through the tongue of the Messenger of God (ﷺ).

Bishr ibn ʿUbayd read (wa-ma nasʾaluhum, "and We do not ask them") with the letter nun. Then God informed that, because of the intensity of their disbelief, they pass by the signs which would be a cause of belief, yet these do not affect them. Those signs are both in the higher world and in the lower world. The reading of Ibn Kathir (wa-kaʾayyin, "and how many") was mentioned earlier. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: it is an active participle from "to be" (kana), so it is kaʾin, and its meaning is the meaning of "kam" (how many) in expressing multitude, end quote. This is something reported from Yunus (ibn Habib), but it is a weak opinion in grammar. The well-known view among them is that it is composed of the particle of comparison (kaf al-tashbih) and "ayy", and the Arabs played with it, so various dialects came from it. Sahib al-Lawami' (Ibn Khalawayh/the author of al-Lawami') mentioned that al-Hasan read (wa-kay, "and kay") with a kasra-vowelled ya, without "hum", without alif, and without shadda. This is also reported from Ibn Muhaysin, so it is a dialect, end quote.

(min aya, "a sign") means an indication of the oneness of God and His attributes, and of the truth of what has been brought from Him. ʿIkrima and ʿAmr ibn Fa'id read (wa-l-ardu, "and the earth") with a damma, as a nominative beginning, and what follows is its predicate. The meaning of ﴿they pass by it﴾ is that they observe what is in it of signs. Al-Suddi read (wa-l-arda, "and the earth") with a fatha, and this is of the grammatical construction called al-ishtighal (the verb occupied with a pronoun), meaning: and they traverse the earth, passing by it, observing its signs and what He has deposited in it of indications. The pronoun in (ʿalayha, "by it") and (ʿanha, "from it") in these two readings refers to the earth. In the reading of the majority, where "al-ard" is in the genitive, the pronoun refers to (aya, "sign"), meaning: they pass by those signs and observe those indications, yet they do not take heed. ʿAbdullah (ibn Masʿud) read (wa-l-ardu) with a damma on the dad. The place of (yamurruna, "they pass") is (yamshuna, "they walk"), and what is meant is what they see of the traces of the destroyed nations and other lessons.

﴿And they are polytheists﴾ is a circumstantial clause, meaning: their belief is mixed with polytheism. Ibn ʿAbbas said: they are the People of the Book, who associated others with God by disbelieving in His Prophet, or by what they said about ʿUzayr and the Messiah. ʿIkrima, Mujahid, Qatada and Ibn Zayd said: they are the disbelieving Arabs, who acknowledged the Creator, the Provider, the Giver of life and death, but disbelieved by worshipping idols and images. Ibn ʿAbbas also said: they are those who liken God to His creation. It is said: they are the people of Mecca, who said: God is our Lord, He has no partner, and the angels are His daughters; so they associated others with Him and did not affirm His oneness. It is also reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, ʿIkrima, al-Shaʿbi and Qatada that it refers to their talbiya, saying: "Here I am, O God, You have no partner, except a partner who belongs to You, You possess him and what he possesses." In a hadith, when the Prophet (ﷺ) heard one of them saying: "Here I am, You have no partner," he said to him: "Qatt qatt" (enough, enough), meaning: stop here and do not add except "a partner who belongs to You." It is said: they are the Dualists, who believe in light and darkness. ʿAta' said: this is about supplication, when the disbelievers forget their Lord in ease, but when affliction befalls them, they devote themselves sincerely in supplication. It is said: they are the hypocrites, who openly professed belief and concealed disbelief. It is said: it refers to some Jews who worshipped ʿUzayr, and to Christians who worshipped the stars. It is said: when the smoke overtook Quraysh in the years of drought, they said: "We are believers," then they returned to polytheism after it was lifted. It is said: all creation, both believers in the Messenger and disbelievers, are meant; the disbelievers have their polytheism evident, while among the believers there is hidden polytheism, and the closest of them to disbelief are the Mushabbiha (anthropomorphists). (p-350) ﴿That is among the tidings of the unseen which We reveal to you. You were not with them when they resolved on their affair while they were scheming.﴾ ﴿Yet most people, however eager you are, will not be believers.﴾ ﴿And you do not ask them any reward for it. It is only a reminder to the worlds.﴾ ﴿And how many a sign there is in the heavens and the earth, which they pass by while turning away from it.﴾ ﴿And most of them do not believe in God without associating others with Him.﴾ ﴿Do they then feel secure that an overwhelming punishment from God will not come upon them, or that the Hour will not come upon them suddenly while they are unaware?﴾

Ibn al-Anbari said: Quraysh and the Jews asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) about the story of Joseph, so it was revealed in full detail, and he hoped that this would be a cause of their conversion to Islam. But they went against his expectation, so God consoled him with His words: ﴿Yet most people, however eager you are, will not be believers.﴾ and the verses that follow. It is also said that it concerns the hypocrites. It is said that it concerns the Dualists (al-Thanawiyya). It is said that it concerns the Christians. Ibn ʿAbbas said that it concerns the talbiya (the call of the pilgrim) of the polytheists. It is also said that it concerns the People of the Book, who believed in some things and disbelieved in others, thus combining belief with polytheism.

The reference in "that" is to what God related of the story of Joseph and his brothers. ﴿You were not with them﴾ meaning: you were not with the sons of Jacob when they resolved on their affair, to put him in the well, nor when they threw him into it, nor when the caravan picked him up, nor when he was sold. ﴿While they were scheming﴾ meaning: they were seeking ways to harm Joseph and consulting one another about what to do to him. Or it means they were scheming against Jacob when they brought the shirt stained with blood. In this there is a declaration to Quraysh of the truthfulness of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). This type of the science of eloquence (ʿilm al-bayan) is called theoretical argumentation (al-ihtijaj al-nazari), and some call it the kalami method (al-madhhab al-kalami). It consists of binding the opponent to what is necessarily entailed by this argument. A similar case has been mentioned in Al ʿImran and in Hud. This is a rebuke to Quraysh and to those who denied him, because it is not hidden from anyone that he was not among the bearers of this narrative or its like, nor did he meet anyone who had knowledge of it or hear it from anyone, nor was it part of the knowledge of his people. So when he informs of it and relates this account which defeated its bearers and transmitters, no doubt remains that it is not from him, but rather it comes from the earlier generations. A similar verse is: ﴿You were not on the western side when We decreed the command to Moses﴾ (Al-Qasas: 44). So His words ﴿You were not﴾ here are a mockery of them, because everyone knows that Muhammad (ﷺ) was not with them. (And they resolved on their affair) meaning: they determined to throw Joseph into the well. (p-351) ﴿While they were scheming﴾ is a circumstantial clause (jumla haliyya). Al-makr (scheming) means to plot against a person in a way that harms and injures him. The word "people" (al-nas) is apparently general, based on His words: ﴿But most people do not believe﴾ (Hud: 17). It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas that they are the people of Mecca. ﴿However eager you are﴾ meaning: even if you strive hard to seek their belief, they will not believe, because of their intense obstinacy and their determination in disbelief. The answer to (law, "even if") is omitted, meaning: even if you were eager, they would not believe. Only the one whom God wills will be granted belief. The pronoun in (ʿalayhi, "for it") refers to the religion of God, meaning: you do not seek a reward for it, for the religion of God. It is also said that it refers to the Qur'an, and it is said that it refers to the conveying of the message, and it is said that it refers to the tidings in the sense of speech. In this there is a rebuke to the disbelievers and an establishment of proof against them. Or it means: you do not ask them for anything in return for what you narrate to them and remind them of, that they should bestow upon you some benefit or reward, as is given for the transmission of stories and reports. It is only an exhortation and a reminder from God to the worlds in general, and an urging to seek salvation through the tongue of the Messenger of God (ﷺ).

Bishr ibn ʿUbayd read (wa-ma nasʾaluhum, "and We do not ask them") with the letter nun. Then God informed that, because of the intensity of their disbelief, they pass by the signs which would be a cause of belief, yet these do not affect them. Those signs are both in the higher world and in the lower world. The reading of Ibn Kathir (wa-kaʾayyin, "and how many") was mentioned earlier. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: it is an active participle from "to be" (kana), so it is kaʾin, and its meaning is the meaning of "kam" (how many) in expressing multitude, end quote. This is something reported from Yunus (ibn Habib), but it is a weak opinion in grammar. The well-known view among them is that it is composed of the particle of comparison (kaf al-tashbih) and "ayy", and the Arabs played with it, so various dialects came from it. Sahib al-Lawami' (Ibn Khalawayh/the author of al-Lawami') mentioned that al-Hasan read (wa-kay, "and kay") with a kasra-vowelled ya, without "hum", without alif, and without shadda. This is also reported from Ibn Muhaysin, so it is a dialect, end quote.

(min aya, "a sign") means an indication of the oneness of God and His attributes, and of the truth of what has been brought from Him. ʿIkrima and ʿAmr ibn Fa'id read (wa-l-ardu, "and the earth") with a damma, as a nominative beginning, and what follows is its predicate. Al-Suddi read (wa-l-arda, "and the earth") with a fatha, and this is of the grammatical construction called al-ishtighal (the verb occupied with a pronoun), meaning: and they traverse the earth, passing by it, observing its signs and what He has deposited in it of indications. The pronoun in (ʿalayha, "by it") and (ʿanha, "from it") in these two readings refers to the earth. In the reading of the majority, where "al-ard" is in the genitive, the pronoun refers to (aya, "sign"), meaning: they pass by those signs and observe those indications, yet they do not take heed. ʿAbdullah (ibn Masʿud) read (wa-l-ardu) with a damma on the dad. ﴿Say: This is my way. I call to God with insight, I and whoever follows me. Glory be to God, and I am not of the polytheists.﴾ ﴿We sent before you only men, to whom We revealed, from the people of the towns. Have they not travelled in the land and seen how was the end of those before them? And the abode of the Hereafter is better for those who are God-fearing. Will you not reason?﴾ ﴿Until, when the messengers despaired and thought they had been denied, Our help came to them, and whom We willed was delivered. And Our punishment is not turned back from the criminal people.﴾

(p-353) When Yusuf, peace be upon him, had said: ﴿Take my soul as a Muslim﴾ [Yusuf: 101], and God's words ﴿And most people, even if you should strive, will not be believers﴾ [Yusuf: 103] indicated that he was eager for their faith, striving for that, calling to it and persevering in it, He mentioned ﴿You ask them no wage for it﴾ [Yusuf: 104], pointing to what was in them of that, namely the law of Islam, faith, and the oneness of God. So He said: Say, O Muhammad, this method and this call is my path, which I have followed and upon which I am. Then He explained that path, saying: ﴿I call to God﴾, meaning: not to anyone else, whether an angel, a human, a star or an idol. My call is only to God alone. Ibn Abbas said: "my path" means "my call". Ikrimah said: my prayer. Ibn Zayd said: my sunnah. Muqatil and the majority said: my religion.

Abdullah [Ibn Mas'ud] read: "Say, this is my path", in the masculine form. The word sabil (path) is both masculine and feminine. The object of "I call" is omitted, its estimate being: I call people. The apparent sense is that ﴿upon insight﴾ is attached to "I call", and "I" (anā) is an emphatic pronoun for the concealed pronoun in "I call". "Whoever" (man) is conjoined to that pronoun, and the meaning is: I call to it, I, and whoever follows me. It is permissible that ﴿upon insight﴾ be a fronted predicate, with "I" as the subject and "whoever" conjoined to it. It is also permissible that ﴿upon insight﴾ be a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "I call", so it is attached to a deleted element, and "I" is the agent of the prepositional phrase that stands in place of that deleted element; ﴿whoever follows me﴾ is conjoined to "I". Abu al-Baqa' permitted that ﴿whoever follows me﴾ be a subject whose predicate is deleted, its estimate being likewise: one who calls to God upon insight. The meaning of "insight" (basirah) is clear proof and certain evidence, from His saying: ﴿There has come to you insights from your Lord﴾ [al-An'am: 104].

﴿Glory be to God﴾ falls under the word "say", i.e. say: Glory be to God, and the declaration of God's freedom from partners, i.e. God's being free of having any partner. When He commanded him to inform about himself that he, and whoever followed him, calls to God, and commanded him to say that he exalts God above partners, He commanded him to say that he personally is free of polytheism, and that he is not among those who associate partners. This is a general negation across times: none of them was, nor at any time, except men. He restricted the messengers to being callers to God, so he would not be an angel. This is a rebuttal of those who said: ﴿If our Lord had willed, He would have sent down angels﴾ [Fussilat: 14]; and likewise He said: ﴿And had We made him an angel, We would have made him a man﴾ [al-An'am: 9]. Ibn Abbas said: He means men, not women, so a messenger cannot be a woman. Was there any prophetess among women? There is disagreement on this. The prophet (nabi) is more general than the messenger (rasul), because it applies to one to whom revelation comes, whether he is sent or not sent. The poet said about Sajah the false prophetess:

"Our prophet has become a female, around whom they circle, though the prophets of God have always been males.
So may the curse of God and of all the peoples be upon Sajah and upon whoever deluded us with falsehood,
I mean Musaylimah the liar; may his echoes never be watered with rain-cloud wherever he may be."

Abu Abd al-Rahman, Talhah and Hafs read: "We reveal (nuhi)" with the nun and kasrah on the ha', agreeing with His saying: ﴿We sent﴾. The majority read with the ya' and fathah on the ha', in the passive. Al-Qura means towns. Ibn Zayd said: the people of the towns are more knowledgeable and more forbearing than the people of the desert, for their nobility is little, and God never raised from them a messenger. al-Hasan said: God did not send a messenger from the people of the desert, nor from women, nor from the jinn. Nomadism (tabaddi) is disliked except in times of trials; in a hadith: "Whoever goes out to the desert becomes coarse." Then He asked a question of reproach and rebuke. The pronoun in "they travel" refers to those who denied that messengers should be sent from among humans, and whoever opposed the messenger and denied his mission disbelieved. That is: Will they not travel in the land, and by widespread report learn the news of earlier messengers, and see the places where the denying nations fell, and thereby take warning? ﴿And the abode of the Hereafter is better﴾: this is an exhortation to work for the Hereafter, to prepare for it, and to guard against destructive things. In this construction there are two analyses: one, that it is an attribution of a noun to its adjective, its original form being "and the abode of the Hereafter"; and the second, that the qualified noun is deleted and its adjective stands in its place, the original being: "and the abode of the final period" or "the final creation". The first is the Kufan analysis, the second the Basran analysis.

The majority read ﴿Will you not reason?﴾ [Ya-Sin: 68] with the ya', in deference to His saying: ﴿Have they not travelled﴾. al-Hasan, Alqamah, al-A'raj, Asim, Ibn Amir and Nafi' read with the ta' (you), addressing this community, as a warning to them from what those fell into, so that what befell them would befall these. al-Kirmani said: "Will you not reason that it is better, so that you may draw near to it by faith?" End of quote.

Despair (istiya's) of help, or of their people's faith, are two opinions. ("Until", hatta) indicates a limit to what precedes it, but there is nothing in the wording that has a limit, so a supplied element is needed. az-Zamakhshari supplied: "We did not send before you except men," so their help was delayed until the messengers despaired of help. Ibn Atiyyah said: His saying ﴿Have they not travelled﴾ implies what came before, that the messengers whom God sent from the people of the towns called their peoples, but they did not believe in them until the calamities struck them, and they came to be among those who take warning from their end. Because of this implied sense, it is good that "until" enters into His saying: ﴿until, when the messengers despaired﴾. End of quote. Nothing from his words yielded for us anything that could be the limit of what follows "until", because he tied the limit to what he claimed to understand from His saying ﴿Have they not travelled﴾ and so on. Abu al-Faraj Ibn al-Jawzi said: the meaning is connected to the first verse; its estimate is: "We sent before you only men who called their peoples, and they denied them, and they endured, and their calling and their people's denial went on long, until, when the messengers despaired." al-Qurtubi said in his commentary: the meaning is: "We sent before you, O Muhammad, only men, then We did not punish their nations with punishment, until, when the messengers despaired."

Ubayy, Ali, Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Talhah, al-A'mash and the Kufans read ﴿they had been denied﴾ (kudhibu) with the dhal lightened. The rest of the seven, al-Hasan, Qatadah, Muhammad ibn Ka'b, Abu Raja', Ibn Mulaykah, al-A'raj, and A'ishah in one report, read it with the dhal doubled, and both are passive. On the doubled reading, all the pronouns refer to the messengers, and the meaning is that the messengers were certain that their polytheist people had denied them. Ibn Atiyyah said: It is possible that "thought" (zann) is in its original sense, namely the preponderance of one of two possibilities. He said: the pronoun refers to the messengers, and "the deniers" are believers whom they had been sent to; that is: when the promises were prolonged, the messengers supposed that the believers at first had denied them, and they doubted because of their words. On the lightened reading, the pronoun in "they thought" refers to those to whom they were sent, because they were mentioned earlier in His saying ﴿how was the end of those before them﴾, and because messengers require those to whom they are sent; and in ﴿that they﴾ and in ﴿they had been denied﴾ the reference is to the messengers. The meaning: those to whom they were sent thought that the messengers had been denied by those who claimed that he had come to them with revelation from God and with help for them, since they did not believe in him. It is also permissible in this reading that all three pronouns refer to those to whom they were sent: that is, the one sent (to them) thought that the messengers had denied them in what they claimed of prophethood, and in what they threatened against whoever did not believe in them of punishment. This is the well-known opinion of Ibn Abbas, and the interpretation of Abdullah, Ibn Jubayr and Mujahid. It is not permissible in this reading that the pronouns refer to "the messengers", because they are protected from error, so none of them could think that he had been denied by one who came to him with revelation from God. az-Zamakhshari said about this reading: ("until, when they despaired of help and thought they had been denied") meaning: their own selves denied them when they told them that they would be helped, or their hope deceived them, like His saying: "a true hope and a false hope." The meaning: the period of denial and enmity from the disbelievers, and the waiting for help from God and hoping for it, had stretched out over them and lengthened, until they sensed despair and imagined that there would be no help for them in this world; then Our help came to them suddenly, without their expecting it. End of quote. He made all the pronouns refer to the messengers, and made the subject that was turned from "they had been denied" either their selves or their hope. In his words there is a removal of "thought" from the meaning of preponderance and from the meaning of certainty to the meaning of imagining, so that he may run all the pronouns in both readings in one manner.

It is reported from Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Abbas and Ibn Jubayr that the pronoun in "they thought" and in "they had been denied" refers to the messengers, and the meaning is: those who informed them about God denied them, and "thought" is in its original sense. They said: the messengers are human, so they grew weak, and their opinion worsened. A'ishah and a group of the people of knowledge rejected this interpretation and considered it grave that the messengers should be described this way.

az-Zamakhshari said: If this is authentically from Ibn Abbas, then he meant by "thought" what occurs to the mind and comes to the heart of the whisperings of doubt and inner speech, as humans are disposed to; but "thought" as the preponderance of one side over the other is impermissible for any Muslim man, so what of the messengers of God, who know their Lord best, and that He is exalted above breaking His promise, and free of every ugliness. End of quote, and its end is the doctrine of the Mu'tazilah. Abu Ali [al-Farisi] said: If someone holds that the meaning is: the messengers thought that what God had promised their peoples through them had been falsely attributed to Him, then he has said something grave, which may not be attributed to the prophets or to the righteous servants of God. He said: And likewise whoever claims that Ibn Abbas meant that the messengers had grown weak and thought they had been let down, because God does not break His promise, and none can change His words.

Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and al-Dahhak read ﴿they had lied (kadhabu)﴾ with the dhal lightened and in the active voice, meaning: the one to whom they were sent thought that the messengers had lied to them about what they said from God concerning the punishment; and "thought" is in its original sense. The answer of "when" (idha) is ﴿Our help came to them﴾.

The apparent reading is that the pronoun in (جاءهم, "came to them") refers to "the messengers." It has also been said that it refers to them and to those who believed in them. Ꜥ Ꜥāṣim and Ibn ʿĀmir read (فَنُجِّيَ, fa-nujjiya, "then there was saved") with a single nūn, a shaddah on the jīm, and a fatḥah on the yāʾ, in the passive voice. Mujāhid, al-Ḥasan, al-Jaḥdarī and Ṭalḥa ibn Hurmuz read it likewise, except that they pronounced the yāʾ with sukūn. Its better explanation is that it is a past-tense form, and the yāʾ in it was given sukūn in the dialect of those who find the vowel burdensome as a connecting element on the yāʾ, like the reading of one who read (ما تُطْعِمُونَ أهالِيكم, "what you feed your families") with a sukūn on the yāʾ. This reading is reported from al-Kisāʾī and Nāfiʿ, and both of them read it so in the well-known transmission. The rest of the seven read (فَنُنْجِي, fa-nunjī, "so We save") with two nūns, a present-tense form of anjā. A group read it likewise, except that they gave the yāʾ a fatḥah. Abū ʿAmr al-Dānī said: "I read for Ibn Muḥaysin (فَنَجّى, fa-najjā) with a shaddah on the jīm, as a past-tense verb, meaning 'then He saved the victory.'" Al-Dānī mentioned that the codices agree on writing it with a single nūn. Abū Ḥaywah read (مَن يَشاءُ, man yashāʾ, "whom He wills") with the yāʾ, meaning: "then whom God wills is saved." The (مَن يَشاءُ, "whom He wills") are the believers, because of His saying: ﴿ولا يُرَدُّ بَأْسُنا عَنِ القَوْمِ المُجْرِمِينَ﴾ ["and Our punishment is not turned back from the criminal people"]. The "ba's" (بَأْس) here means destruction. Al-Ḥasan read ﴿بَأْسُهُ﴾ [Al-An'am: 147] with the pronoun of the absent third person, meaning: "the punishment of God." This sentence contains a warning and a threat to the contemporaries of the Messenger (ﷺ).

﴿Say: This is my way. I call to God with insight, I and whoever follows me. Glory be to God, and I am not of the polytheists.﴾ ﴿We sent before you only men, to whom We revealed, from the people of the towns. Have they not travelled in the land and seen how was the end of those before them? And the abode of the Hereafter is better for those who are God-fearing. Will you not reason?﴾ ﴿Until, when the messengers despaired and thought they had been denied, Our help came to them, and whom We willed was delivered. And Our punishment is not turned back from the criminal people.﴾

So He said: Say, O Muhammad, this method and this call is my path, which I have followed and upon which I am. Then He explained that path, saying: ﴿I call to God﴾, meaning: not to anyone else, whether an angel, a human, a star or an idol. My call is only to God alone. Ibn Abbas said: "my path" means "my call". Ikrimah said: my prayer. Ibn Zayd said: my sunnah. Muqatil and the majority said: my religion.

Abdullah [Ibn Mas'ud] read: "Say, this is my path", in the masculine form. The word sabil (path) is both masculine and feminine. The object of "I call" is omitted, its estimate being: I call people. The apparent sense is that ﴿upon insight﴾ is attached to "I call", and "I" (anā) is an emphatic pronoun for the concealed pronoun in "I call". "Whoever" (man) is conjoined to that pronoun, and the meaning is: I call to it, I, and whoever follows me. It is permissible that ﴿upon insight﴾ be a fronted predicate, with "I" as the subject and "whoever" conjoined to it. It is also permissible that ﴿upon insight﴾ be a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "I call", so it is attached to a deleted element, and "I" is the agent of the prepositional phrase that stands in place of that deleted element; ﴿whoever follows me﴾ is conjoined to "I". Abu al-Baqa' permitted that ﴿whoever follows me﴾ be a subject whose predicate is deleted, its estimate being likewise: one who calls to God upon insight. The meaning of "insight" (basirah) is clear proof and certain evidence, from His saying: ﴿There has come to you insights from your Lord﴾ [al-An'am: 104].

﴿Glory be to God﴾ falls under the word "say", i.e. say: Glory be to God, and the declaration of God's freedom from partners, i.e. God's being free of having any partner. When He commanded him to inform about himself that he, and whoever followed him, calls to God, and commanded him to say that he exalts God above partners, He commanded him to say that he personally is free of polytheism, and that he is not among those who associate partners. This is a general negation across times: none of them was, nor at any time, except men. He restricted the messengers to being callers to God, so he would not be an angel. This is a rebuttal of those who said: ﴿If our Lord had willed, He would have sent down angels﴾ [Fussilat: 14]; and likewise He said: ﴿And had We made him an angel, We would have made him a man﴾ [al-An'am: 9]. Ibn Abbas said: He means men, not women, so a messenger cannot be a woman. Was there any prophetess among women? There is disagreement on this. The prophet (nabi) is more general than the messenger (rasul), because it applies to one to whom revelation comes, whether he is sent or not sent. The poet said about Sajah the false prophetess:

"Our prophet has become a female, around whom they circle, though the prophets of God have always been males.
So may the curse of God and of all the peoples be upon Sajah and upon whoever deluded us with falsehood,
I mean Musaylimah the liar; may his echoes never be watered with rain-cloud wherever he may be."

Abu Abd al-Rahman, Talhah and Hafs read: "We reveal (nuhi)" with the nun and kasrah on the ha', agreeing with His saying: ﴿We sent﴾. So He said: Say, O Muhammad, this method and this call is my path, which I have followed and upon which I am. Then He explained that path, saying: ﴿I call to God﴾, meaning: not to anyone else, whether an angel, a human, a star or an idol. My call is only to God alone. Ibn Abbas said: "my path" means "my call". Ikrimah said: my prayer. Ibn Zayd said: my sunnah. Muqatil and the majority said: my religion.

Abdullah [Ibn Mas'ud] read: "Say, this is my path", in the masculine form. The word sabil (path) is both masculine and feminine. The object of "I call" is omitted, its estimate being: I call people. The apparent sense is that ﴿upon insight﴾ is attached to "I call", and "I" (anā) is an emphatic pronoun for the concealed pronoun in "I call". "Whoever" (man) is conjoined to that pronoun, and the meaning is: I call to it, I, and whoever follows me. It is permissible that ﴿upon insight﴾ be a fronted predicate, with "I" as the subject and "whoever" conjoined to it. It is also permissible that ﴿upon insight﴾ be a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "I call", so it is attached to a deleted element, and "I" is the agent of the prepositional phrase that stands in place of that deleted element; ﴿whoever follows me﴾ is conjoined to "I". Abu al-Baqa' permitted that ﴿whoever follows me﴾ be a subject whose predicate is deleted, its estimate being likewise: one who calls to God upon insight. The meaning of "insight" (basirah) is clear proof and certain evidence, from His saying: ﴿There has come to you insights from your Lord﴾ [al-An'am: 104].

﴿Glory be to God﴾ falls under the word "say", i.e. say: Glory be to God, and the declaration of God's freedom from partners, i.e. God's being free of having any partner. When He commanded him to inform about himself that he, and whoever followed him, calls to God, and commanded him to say that he exalts God above partners, He commanded him to say that he personally is free of polytheism, and that he is not among those who associate partners. This is a general negation across times: none of them was, nor at any time, except men. He restricted the messengers to being callers to God, so he would not be an angel. This is a rebuttal of those who said: ﴿If our Lord had willed, He would have sent down angels﴾ [Fussilat: 14]; and likewise He said: ﴿And had We made him an angel, We would have made him a man﴾ [al-An'am: 9]. Ibn Abbas said: He means men, not women, so a messenger cannot be a woman. Was there any prophetess among women? There is disagreement on this. The prophet (nabi) is more general than the messenger (rasul), because it applies to one to whom revelation comes, whether he is sent or not sent. The poet said about Sajah the false prophetess:

"Our prophet has become a female, around whom they circle, though the prophets of God have always been males.
So may the curse of God and of all the peoples be upon Sajah and upon whoever deluded us with falsehood,
I mean Musaylimah the liar; may his echoes never be watered with rain-cloud wherever he may be."

Abu Abd al-Rahman, Talhah and Hafs read: "We reveal (nuhi)" with the nun and kasrah on the ha', agreeing with His saying: ﴿We sent﴾. The majority read with the ya' and fathah on the ha', in the passive. Al-Qura means towns. Ibn Zayd said: the people of the towns are more knowledgeable and more forbearing than the people of the desert, for their nobility is little, and God never raised from them a messenger. al-Hasan said: God did not send a messenger from the people of the desert, nor from women, nor from the jinn. Nomadism (tabaddi) is disliked except in times of trials; in a hadith: "Whoever goes out to the desert becomes coarse." Then He asked a question of reproach and rebuke. The pronoun in "they travel" refers to those who denied that messengers should be sent from among humans, and whoever opposed the messenger and denied his mission disbelieved. That is: Will they not travel in the land, and by widespread report learn the news of earlier messengers, and see the places where the denying nations fell, and thereby take warning? ﴿And the abode of the Hereafter is better﴾: this is an exhortation to work for the Hereafter, to prepare for it, and to guard against destructive things. In this construction there are two analyses: one, that it is an attribution of a noun to its adjective, its original form being "and the abode of the Hereafter"; and the second, that the qualified noun is deleted and its adjective stands in its place, the original being: "and the abode of the final period" or "the final creation". The first is the Kufan analysis, the second the Basran analysis.

The majority read ﴿Will you not reason?﴾ [Ya-Sin: 68] with the ya', in deference to His saying: ﴿Have they not travelled﴾. al-Hasan, Alqamah, al-A'raj, Asim, Ibn Amir and Nafi' read with the ta' (you), addressing this community, as a warning to them from what those fell into, so that what befell them would befall these. al-Kirmani said: "Will you not reason that it is better, so that you may draw near to it by faith?" End of quote.

Despair (istiya's) of help, or of their people's faith, are two opinions. ("Until", hatta) indicates a limit to what precedes it, but there is nothing in the wording that has a limit, so a supplied element is needed. az-Zamakhshari supplied: "We did not send before you except men," so their help was delayed until the messengers despaired of help. Ibn Atiyyah said: His saying ﴿Have they not travelled﴾ implies what came before, that the messengers whom God sent from the people of the towns called their peoples, but they did not believe in them until the calamities struck them, and they came to be among those who take warning from their end. Because of this implied sense, it is good that "until" enters into His saying: ﴿until, when the messengers despaired﴾. End of quote. Nothing from his words yielded for us anything that could be the limit of what follows "until", because he tied the limit to what he claimed to understand from His saying ﴿Have they not travelled﴾ and so on. Abu al-Faraj Ibn al-Jawzi said: the meaning is connected to the first verse; its estimate is: "We sent before you only men who called their peoples, and they denied them, and they endured, and their calling and their people's denial went on long, until, when the messengers despaired." al-Qurtubi said in his commentary: the meaning is: "We sent before you, O Muhammad, only men, then We did not punish their nations with punishment, until, when the messengers despaired."

Ubayy, Ali, Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Talhah, al-A'mash and the Kufans read ﴿they had been denied﴾ (kudhibu) with the dhal lightened. The rest of the seven, al-Hasan, Qatadah, Muhammad ibn Ka'b, Abu Raja', Ibn Mulaykah, al-A'raj, and A'ishah in one report, read it with the dhal doubled, and both are passive. On the doubled reading, all the pronouns refer to the messengers, and the meaning is that the messengers were certain that their polytheist people had denied them. Ibn Atiyyah said: It is possible that "thought" (zann) is in its original sense, namely the preponderance of one of two possibilities. He said: the pronoun refers to the messengers, and "the deniers" are believers whom they had been sent to; that is: when the promises were prolonged, the messengers supposed that the believers at first had denied them, and they doubted because of their words. On the lightened reading, the pronoun in "they thought" refers to those to whom they were sent, because they were mentioned earlier in His saying ﴿how was the end of those before them﴾, and because messengers require those to whom they are sent; and in ﴿that they﴾ and in ﴿they had been denied﴾ the reference is to the messengers. The meaning: those to whom they were sent thought that the messengers had been denied by those who claimed that he had come to them with revelation from God and with help for them, since they did not believe in him. It is also permissible in this reading that all three pronouns refer to those to whom they were sent: that is, the one sent (to them) thought that the messengers had denied them in what they claimed of prophethood, and in what they threatened against whoever did not believe in them of punishment. This is the well-known opinion of Ibn Abbas, and the interpretation of Abdullah, Ibn Jubayr and Mujahid. It is not permissible in this reading that the pronouns refer to "the messengers", because they are protected from error, so none of them could think that he had been denied by one who came to him with revelation from God. az-Zamakhshari said about this reading: ("until, when they despaired of help and thought they had been denied") meaning: their own selves denied them when they told them that they would be helped, or their hope deceived them, like His saying: "a true hope and a false hope." The meaning: the period of denial and enmity from the disbelievers, and the waiting for help from God and hoping for it, had stretched out over them and lengthened, until they sensed despair and imagined that there would be no help for them in this world; then Our help came to them suddenly, without their expecting it. End of quote. He made all the pronouns refer to the messengers, and made the subject that was turned from "they had been denied" either their selves or their hope. In his words there is a removal of "thought" from the meaning of preponderance and from the meaning of certainty to the meaning of imagining, so that he may run all the pronouns in both readings in one manner.

It is reported from Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Abbas and Ibn Jubayr that the pronoun in "they thought" and in "they had been denied" refers to the messengers, and the meaning is: those who informed them about God denied them, and "thought" is in its original sense. They said: the messengers are human, so they grew weak, and their opinion worsened. A'ishah and a group of the people of knowledge rejected this interpretation and considered it grave that the messengers should be described this way.

az-Zamakhshari said: If this is authentically from Ibn Abbas, then he meant by "thought" what occurs to the mind and comes to the heart of the whisperings of doubt and inner speech, as humans are disposed to; but "thought" as the preponderance of one side over the other is impermissible for any Muslim man, so what of the messengers of God, who know their Lord best, and that He is exalted above breaking His promise, and free of every ugliness. End of quote, and its end is the doctrine of the Mu'tazilah. Abu Ali [al-Farisi] said: If someone holds that the meaning is: the messengers thought that what God had promised their peoples through them had been falsely attributed to Him, then he has said something grave, which may not be attributed to the prophets or to the righteous servants of God. He said: And likewise whoever claims that Ibn Abbas meant that the messengers had grown weak and thought they had been let down, because God does not break His promise, and none can change His words.

Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and al-Dahhak read ﴿they had lied (kadhabu)﴾ with the dhal lightened and in the active voice, meaning: the one to whom they were sent thought that the messengers had lied to them about what they said from God concerning the punishment; and "thought" is in its original sense. The answer of "when" (idha) is ﴿Our help came to them﴾.

The apparent reading is that the pronoun in (جاءهم, "came to them") refers to "the messengers." It has also been said that it refers to them and to those who believed in them. Ꜥ Ꜥāṣim and Ibn ʿĀmir read (فَنُجِّيَ, fa-nujjiya, "then there was saved") with a single nūn, a shaddah on the jīm, and a fatḥah on the yāʾ, in the passive voice. Mujāhid, al-Ḥasan, al-Jaḥdarī and Ṭalḥa ibn Hurmuz read it likewise, except that they pronounced the yāʾ with sukūn. This reading was explained as a present-tense form in which the nūn was assimilated into the jīm, but this is nothing (ليس بشيء), because the nūn is not assimilated into the jīm. Its better explanation is that it is a past-tense form, and the yāʾ in it was given sukūn in the dialect of those who find the vowel burdensome as a connecting element on the yāʾ, like the reading of one who read (ما تُطْعِمُونَ أهالِيكم, "what you feed your families") with a sukūn on the yāʾ. This reading is reported from al-Kisāʾī and Nāfiʿ, and both of them read it so in the well-known transmission. The rest of the seven read (فَنُنْجِي, fa-nunjī, "so We save") with two nūns, a present-tense form of anjā. A group read it likewise, except that they gave the yāʾ a fatḥah. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: "Hubayrah reported it from Ḥafṣ from ʿĀṣim, and it is an error on Hubayrah's part," end of quote. It is not an error, and it has a basis in Arabic, namely that after the conditional particle and its response, the present tense may come in the subjunctive by the implied (أنْ, an, "that") after the fāʾ, like the reading of one who read: ﴿وإنْ تُبْدُوا ما في أنْفُسِكم أوْ تُخْفُوهُ يُحاسِبْكم بِهِ اللَّهُ فَيَغْفِرُ﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 284] with (يَغْفِرَ, yaghfira) in the subjunctive by the implied "an" after the fāʾ. There is no difference in this between the conditional particle being jussive or non-jussive. Naṣr ibn ʿĀṣim, al-Ḥasan, Abū Ḥaywah, Ibn al-Samayqaʿ, Mujāhid, ʿĪsā and Ibn Muḥaysin read (فَنَجى, fa-naja, "then he saved") as a past-tense verb with a light jīm. Abū ʿAmr al-Dānī said: "I read for Ibn Muḥaysin (فَنَجّى, fa-najjā) with a shaddah on the jīm, as a past-tense verb, meaning 'then He saved the victory.'" Al-Dānī mentioned that the codices agree on writing it with a single nūn. In al-Taḥbīr it is stated that al-Ḥasan read (فَنُنَجِّي, fa-nunajjī) with two nūns, the second with a fatḥah, the jīm with a shaddah, and the yāʾ with sukūn. Abū Ḥaywah read (مَن يَشاءُ, man yashāʾ, "whom He wills") with the yāʾ, meaning: "then whom God wills is saved." The (مَن يَشاءُ, "whom He wills") are the believers, because of His saying: ﴿ولا يُرَدُّ بَأْسُنا عَنِ القَوْمِ المُجْرِمِينَ﴾ ["and Our punishment is not turned back from the criminal people"]. The "ba's" (بَأْس) here means destruction. Al-Ḥasan read ﴿بَأْسُهُ﴾ [Al-An'am: 147] with the pronoun of the absent third person, meaning: "the punishment of God." This sentence contains a warning and a threat to the contemporaries of the Messenger (ﷺ).

(p-356) The pronoun in "qaṣaṣihim" (their narratives) refers either to the Messengers, or to Yusuf and his parents and brothers, or to them (the Messengers). On the reference to the Messengers there are three opinions. The first is the one chosen by al-Zamakhshari, who said: "What supports it is the reading of the one who reads (qiṣaṣahum) with a kasra on the qaf," end of quote. But it is not supported by this, since the narrative of Yusuf and his father and brothers comprises many stories and various accounts. The one who read with a kasra on the qaf was Ahmad ibn Jubayr al-Antaki, from al-Kisa'i and al-Qasabi, from 'Abd al-Warith, from Abu 'Amr, and it is the plural of qissah (story). Ibn 'Atiyyah chose the third opinion, indeed no one else mentioned it. And 'ibrah (lesson) is the indication by which one is led to knowledge. If the pronoun refers to Yusuf, peace be upon him, and his parents and brothers, then the lesson drawn from their narratives lies in aspects such as: the exaltation of Yusuf, peace be upon him, after being thrown into the well; his elevation after his imprisonment; his gaining possession of Egypt after being enslaved; his reunion with his parents and brothers in what he loved after long separation; and the reporting of this story as news of the unseen, and the informing, by God the Exalted, of knowledge, power and control over things beyond what occurs to the mind or passes through thought. The people of understanding (ulu al-albab) are singled out because they are the ones who benefit from lessons, and whoever has intellect and examines well, and sees in them trial, gentleness and kindness, knows that it is a matter from God the Exalted and from His own presence.

The apparent reading is that the subject of "kana" (was) is a pronoun referring back to the narrative: that is, the narrative was not a fabricated discourse, but rather a truthful discourse, speaking the truth, brought by one who had not read books, nor studied under anyone, nor mixed with scholars; so it is impossible that he could invent this story in such a way that it matches what is in the Torah without any discrepancy. It has also been said that it refers to the Qur'an, meaning: the Qur'an, which contained the story of Yusuf, peace be upon him, and other things, was not a discourse invented, but it was a confirmation of the earlier divine books, and a detailed explanation of every matter concerning Yusuf with his parents and brothers. This is if the pronoun refers to the story of Yusuf, or to everything that requires detailing in the Law if it refers to the Qur'an.

Ḥumran ibn A'yan and 'Isa al-Kufi, as mentioned by the author of al-Lawami', and 'Isa al-Thaqafi, as mentioned by Ibn 'Atiyyah, read "taṣdīqun wa tafṣīlun wa hudan wa raḥmatun" with the four nouns in the nominative; that is: "but it is a confirmation". The majority read them in the accusative, by supposing "kana" (was) elided, meaning: "but [it was] a confirmation" — that is, the discourse was a confirmation of what lies before it. And he cites the verse of Dhu al-Rummah:

"Nor was my wealth from dust inherited, nor a blood-money that was, nor gain of a sinful deed,
But it was the gift of God from every journey, to every concealed hiding-place of thieves, a wanderer."

With the nominative in "'aṭā'" and with the accusative, meaning: "but it is the gift of God," or "but it was the gift of God." Similar is the saying of Lut ibn 'Ubayd al-'A'i, the thief:

"And I, by the praise of God, took no wealth of a Muslim, nor of one who gives oaths, a sworn one.
But it was the gift of God from the wealth of a wicked one, far in his place, exposed to the one who commits sin."

"Hudan" means: a cause of guidance in this world. "Raḥmatan" means: a cause for obtaining mercy in the Hereafter. The believers are singled out for this because they are the ones who benefit from it, as God the Exalted said: ﴿a guidance for the God-fearing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 2]. And earlier, at the beginning of the surah, God the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, We have sent it down as an Arabic Qur'an﴾ [Yusuf: 2], and His saying: ﴿We relate to you the best of narratives﴾ [Yusuf: 3]; and at its end: ﴿it was not a discourse invented﴾ to the end of it. Therefore it is possible that the pronoun refers to the Qur'an, and that it refers to the narrative. And God knows best.
